chapters.title: Preface to A Wonder Book
paragraphs: For a long time the author has believed that many of the old classical myths could be turned into very fine reading for children. In this little book he offers to the public six of them, retold with that purpose. His plan required a great deal of freedom in handling the stories. But anyone who tries to melt these legends down and reshape them in the furnace of his own mind will notice how wonderfully independent they are of any particular time or circumstance. After changes that would destroy the identity of almost anything else, they remain essentially the same.

So he does not admit to any sacrilege in having sometimes reshaped, as his imagination suggested, forms that have been held sacred for two or three thousand years. No age can claim a copyright on these undying tales. They seem never to have been made at all, and as long as people exist they can certainly never die. But because they cannot be destroyed, every age has a rightful claim to dress them in its own manners and feelings and to fill them with its own morals. In this version they may have lost much of their classical look (or, at any rate, the author has not been careful to keep it), and they may have taken on a Gothic or romantic costume.

In doing this pleasant work—and it really was work, the kind that suits hot weather, and one of the most enjoyable literary jobs he has ever taken on—the author did not always feel he had to write down to a child’s understanding. Whenever a theme tended to soar, and he felt light enough to follow it without effort, he usually let it soar. Children are far more sensitive than people realize to anything deep or lofty in imagination or feeling, as long as it is also simple. Only what is artificial and complicated confuses them.
LENOX, _July 15, 1851_.

chapters.title: The Gorgon’s Head
paragraphs: One fine autumn morning, a cheerful crowd of little children had gathered under the porch of a country house called Tanglewood, with a tall young man in the middle of them. They had planned a trip to gather nuts. Now they waited impatiently for the mists to lift from the hillsides, and for the sun to spread the warmth of Indian summer over the fields and pastures and into the corners of the many-colored woods. It promised to be as lovely a day as ever brightened this beautiful, comfortable world. For the moment, though, the morning mist filled the whole valley from end to end. The house stood above it, on a gently sloping rise of ground.

This bank of white vapor reached to within a hundred yards of the house. It hid everything beyond that distance, except a few red or yellow treetops that poked up here and there and glowed in the early sunshine, just as the wide surface of the mist did. Four or five miles to the south, the top of Monument Mountain seemed to float on a cloud. About fifteen miles farther in the same direction, the taller Dome of Taconic looked blue and hazy, hardly more solid than the misty sea that almost rolled over it. The nearer hills along the valley were half sunk in the mist, and flecked with little wisps of cloud all the way to their summits. Altogether there was so much cloud and so little solid ground that the scene looked like a dream.

The children I have mentioned were as full of life as they could possibly be, and they kept spilling out of the porch at Tanglewood, scampering along the gravel path or racing across the dewy grass of the lawn. I can hardly say how many of them there were. There were at least nine or ten and no more than a dozen, of every sort, size and age, girls and boys alike. They were brothers, sisters and cousins, together with a few young friends whom Mr and Mrs Pringle had invited to spend some of this lovely weather with their own children at Tanglewood. I am afraid to tell you their real names, or even to give them any names that other children have ever had. I know for certain that authors sometimes get into serious trouble by accidentally giving the names of real people to characters in their books. So I will call them Primrose, Periwinkle, Sweet Fern, Dandelion, Blue Eye, Clover, Huckleberry, Cowslip, Squash-Blossom, Milkweed, Plantain and Buttercup, though these names would suit a band of fairies better than a group of ordinary earthly children.

Of course, the careful fathers and mothers, uncles, aunts and grandparents of these little people would never have let them wander off into the woods and fields without some particularly grave and elderly person to look after them. Oh no, indeed! In the first sentence of my book, you may remember, I mentioned a tall young man standing among the children. I will tell you his real name, because he thinks it a great honor to have told the stories that are about to be printed. His name was Eustace Bright. He was a student at Williams College, and at this time he had reached, I believe, the venerable age of eighteen. He felt almost like a grandfather toward Periwinkle, Dandelion, Huckleberry, Squash-Blossom, Milkweed and the rest, who were only half or a third as venerable as he was. He had trouble with his eyes (the kind of trouble many students think they need these days to show how hard they work at their books), and it had kept him away from college for a week or two after the term began. But for my part, I have rarely met a pair of eyes that looked as though they could see farther or better than Eustace Bright’s.

This learned student was slim and rather pale, as all Yankee students are, but he still looked healthy, and he was as light and quick on his feet as if his shoes had wings. Incidentally, since he loved wading through streams and across meadows, he had put on cowhide boots for the outing. He wore a linen smock, a cloth cap and a pair of green spectacles, which he had probably put on less to protect his eyes than to give his face an air of dignity. Either way, he might as well have left them at home. Huckleberry, a mischievous little elf, crept up behind Eustace as he sat on the porch steps, snatched the spectacles off his nose and clapped them onto her own. The student forgot to take them back, so they fell off into the grass and lay there until the next spring.

Now, you must understand that Eustace Bright had won great fame among the children as a teller of wonderful stories. He sometimes pretended to be annoyed when they teased him for more, and more, and always more, but I truly doubt that he liked anything as much as telling them. So you could have seen his eyes twinkle when Clover, Sweet Fern, Cowslip, Buttercup and most of their playmates begged him to tell one of his stories while they waited for the mist to clear.

“Yes, Cousin Eustace,” said Primrose, a bright girl of twelve with laughing eyes and a slightly upturned nose, “morning is certainly the best time for the stories that you so often use to wear out our patience. We’ll be less likely to hurt your feelings by falling asleep at the most exciting parts—the way little Cowslip and I did last night!”

“Naughty Primrose,” cried Cowslip, who was only six. “I wasn’t asleep! I just closed my eyes so I could picture what Cousin Eustace was telling us. His stories are good at night, because we can dream about them in our sleep. They’re good in the morning too, because then we can dream about them wide awake. So I hope he’ll start one right this minute.”

“Thank you, my little Cowslip,” said Eustace. “You shall certainly have the best story I can think of, if only because you defended me so well against that naughty Primrose. But children, I’ve already told you so many fairy tales that I doubt there’s a single one you haven’t heard at least twice. I’m afraid you’ll really fall asleep if I tell any of them again.”
“No, no, no!” cried Blue Eye, Periwinkle, Plantain and half a dozen more. “A story is even nicer when we’ve already heard it two or three times.”

And it is true of children that a story often sinks deeper into their interest, not just after two or three tellings, but after countless repetitions. But Eustace Bright, with his overflowing supply of tales, scorned to take advantage of something that an older storyteller would gladly have seized.

“It would be a great shame,” he said, “if a man of my learning (not to mention my original imagination) could not come up with a new story every day, year in and year out, for children like you. I will tell you one of the nursery tales that were made to amuse our great old grandmother, the Earth, when she was a little girl in a frock and pinafore. There are a hundred of them, and I wonder that they haven’t long since been put into picture books for little girls and boys. Instead, old gray-bearded grandfathers pore over them in musty volumes of Greek, and puzzle over when and how and why they were ever made.”
“Well, well, well, well, Cousin Eustace!” cried all the children at once. “Stop talking about your stories and begin!”

“Sit down, then, every one of you,” said Eustace Bright, “and keep as quiet as so many mice. At the slightest interruption, whether it comes from big, naughty Primrose, little Dandelion or anyone else, I will bite the story off short between my teeth and swallow the part I haven’t told. But first of all, does anyone know what a Gorgon is?”
“I do,” said Primrose.
“Then hold your tongue!” Eustace shot back, wishing she had known nothing about it. “Hold all your tongues, and I will tell you a sweet, pretty story about a Gorgon’s head.”

And so he did, as you can start reading on the next page. He used his schoolboy learning with a good deal of skill and owed a great debt to Professor Anthon, but whenever the wandering boldness of his imagination pushed him to it, he ignored all the classical authorities.

Perseus was the son of Danae, who was a king’s daughter. When Perseus was a very little boy, some wicked people shut him and his mother in a chest and set it afloat on the sea. The wind blew hard and drove the chest away from the shore, and the restless waves tossed it up and down. Danae held her child tightly to her chest, afraid that some huge wave would break its foaming crest over them both. But the chest sailed on without sinking or tipping over. At last, as night was falling, it floated so close to an island that it got tangled in a fisherman’s nets and was dragged out onto the sand, high and dry. The island was called Seriphus, and its ruler was King Polydectes, who happened to be the fisherman’s brother.

This fisherman, I am glad to say, was a very kind and honest man. He treated Danae and her little boy with great kindness, and he kept on helping them until Perseus had grown into a handsome young man, very strong and quick and skilled with weapons. Long before that, King Polydectes had noticed the two strangers, the mother and her child, who had come to his lands in a floating chest. Unlike his brother the fisherman, he was not good and kind but thoroughly wicked. He decided to send Perseus on a dangerous mission in which he would probably be killed, and then to do some terrible harm to Danae herself. So this bad-hearted king spent a long time thinking about the most dangerous thing a young man could possibly try to do. At last he hit on a mission that seemed likely to end as fatally as he wished, and he sent for the young Perseus.
The young man went to the palace, where he found the king seated on his throne.

“Perseus,” said King Polydectes, giving him a sly smile, “you have grown into a fine young man. You and your good mother have received great kindness from me, as well as from my worthy brother the fisherman, and I imagine you would be glad to repay some of it.”
“Your Majesty,” answered Perseus, “I would gladly risk my life to do so.”

“Well, then,” the king went on, still with a cunning smile on his lips, “I have a small adventure to suggest to you. You are a brave and enterprising young man, so you will surely think it great good luck to have such a rare chance to make a name for yourself. You see, my good Perseus, I am thinking of marrying the beautiful Princess Hippodamia. On these occasions it is the custom to give the bride some elegant curiosity from far away. I must honestly confess I have been a little puzzled about where to find anything that would please a princess of her exquisite taste. But this morning, I flatter myself, I have thought of exactly the right thing.”
“And can I help Your Majesty get it?” cried Perseus eagerly.

“You can, if you are as brave a young man as I believe you are,” answered King Polydectes, in the most gracious manner. “The wedding gift I have set my heart on giving the beautiful Hippodamia is the head of the Gorgon Medusa with the snaky hair, and I am counting on you, my dear Perseus, to bring it to me. I am eager to settle matters with the princess, so the sooner you go off to find the Gorgon, the happier I shall be.”
“I will set out tomorrow morning,” answered Perseus.

“Please do, my gallant young man,” replied the king. “And Perseus, when you cut off the Gorgon’s head, be careful to make a clean stroke, so you don’t spoil its looks. You must bring it home in perfect condition, to suit the exquisite taste of the beautiful Princess Hippodamia.”

Perseus left the palace, but he was hardly out of earshot before Polydectes burst out laughing. The wicked king was delighted to see how easily the young man had walked into his trap. News quickly spread that Perseus had promised to cut off the head of Medusa with the snaky hair. Everyone was overjoyed, because most of the people on the island were as wicked as the king and would have liked nothing better than to see some terrible harm come to Danae and her son. The fisherman seems to have been the only good man on this unfortunate island of Seriphus. So as Perseus walked along, people pointed after him, made faces, winked at one another and mocked him as loudly as they dared.
“Ho, ho!” they cried. “Medusa’s snakes will sting him good!”

At that time there were three Gorgons in the world, and they were the strangest, most terrible monsters ever seen since the world began, or that anyone will see in all the ages to come. I hardly know what to call them, whether creatures or hobgoblins. There were three sisters, and they looked a little like women, but they were really a frightful, spiteful kind of dragon. It is hard even to picture how hideous they were. Believe it or not, instead of hair, each of them had a hundred huge snakes growing from her head, all of them alive, twisting and wriggling and coiling, and flicking out their poisonous tongues with stingers at the tips! The Gorgons’ teeth were enormously long tusks, their hands were made of brass, and their bodies were covered in scales, which, if not iron, were something just as hard and impossible to pierce. They had wings, too, and splendid ones, I promise you, for every feather was pure, bright, glittering, polished gold. No doubt they looked dazzling when the Gorgons flew about in the sunshine.

But when people happened to glimpse that glittering brightness high in the air, they rarely stayed to stare. They ran and hid as fast as they could. You may think they were afraid of being stung by the serpents that served the Gorgons for hair, or of having their heads bitten off by the ugly tusks, or of being torn to pieces by the brazen claws. Well, those were certainly some of the dangers, but not the greatest, and not the hardest to avoid. The worst thing about these abominable Gorgons was this: if a poor mortal once looked straight into the face of one of them, he was sure to be changed, that very instant, from warm flesh and blood into cold, lifeless stone!

So you can easily see what a dangerous adventure wicked King Polydectes had cooked up for this innocent young man. When Perseus thought it over, even he could see that he had very little chance of coming through it safely, and that he was far more likely to become a stone statue than to bring back the head of Medusa with the snaky locks. Setting other difficulties aside, there was one that would have stumped a much older man than Perseus. He had to fight and kill this golden-winged, iron-scaled, long-tusked, brazen-clawed, snaky-haired monster, and he had to do it with his eyes shut, or at least without so much as a glance at the enemy he was fighting. Otherwise, with his arm raised to strike, he would stiffen into stone and stand there with that arm in the air for centuries, until time, wind, and weather crumbled him away. That would be a very sad fate for a young man who hoped to do many brave deeds and enjoy a great deal of happiness in this bright and beautiful world.

These thoughts made him so gloomy that Perseus could not bear to tell his mother what he had promised to do. Instead, he picked up his shield, buckled on his sword, and crossed from the island to the mainland. There he sat down in a lonely spot and could hardly keep from crying.
But as he sat there in such a sorrowful mood, he heard a voice right beside him.
“Perseus,” said the voice, “why are you sad?”

He raised his head from the hands in which he had hidden it, and look! Perseus had thought himself quite alone, but there was a stranger in that lonely place. He was a lively, clever, very sharp-looking young man, with a cloak over his shoulders, an odd sort of cap on his head, a strangely twisted staff in his hand, and a short, very crooked sword hanging at his side. He was slim and quick-moving, like someone used to athletics, who could leap and run with ease. Above all, the stranger looked so cheerful, knowing, and helpful (though also a little mischievous) that Perseus felt his spirits rise as he gazed at him. Besides, Perseus was truly a brave young man, and he was very ashamed that anyone should find him with tears in his eyes like a timid little schoolboy, when there might be no reason for despair after all. So he wiped his eyes and answered the stranger quite briskly, putting on as brave a face as he could.
“I’m not really so sad,” he said. “I’m only thinking hard about an adventure I’ve taken on.”

“Aha!” the stranger answered. “Well, tell me all about it, and perhaps I can help. I’ve helped plenty of young men through adventures that looked hard enough at the start. Maybe you’ve heard of me. I have more than one name, but Quicksilver suits me as well as any. Tell me what the trouble is, and we’ll talk it over and see what can be done.”

The stranger’s words and manner put Perseus in a very different mood from before. He decided to tell Quicksilver all his troubles, since he could hardly be worse off than he was, and his new friend might well give him advice that would turn out well in the end. So he told the stranger, in a few words, exactly how matters stood: King Polydectes wanted the head of Medusa with the snaky locks as a wedding gift for the beautiful Princess Hippodamia, Perseus had promised to get it for him, and now he was afraid of being turned into stone.

“That would be a great shame,” said Quicksilver, with his mischievous smile. “You’d make a very handsome marble statue, I grant you, and it would take many centuries to wear you away. Still, on the whole, I’d rather be a young man for a few years than a block of stone for ages upon ages.”
“Oh, far rather!” exclaimed Perseus, with tears standing in his eyes again. “And besides, what would my dear mother do if her beloved son were turned to stone?”

“Well, well, let’s hope it won’t turn out so badly,” replied Quicksilver, in an encouraging tone. “I’m just the person to help you, if anyone is. My sister and I will do all we can to bring you safely through, ugly as it looks right now.”
“Your sister?” Perseus repeated.

“Yes, my sister,” said the stranger. “She is very wise, I promise you, and as for me, I usually keep my wits about me, such as they are. If you are bold and careful, and follow our advice, you needn’t fear becoming a stone image for a good while yet. But first, you must polish your shield until you can see your face in it as clearly as in a mirror.”

This seemed to Perseus a strange way to begin the adventure. He thought it far more important that the shield be strong enough to protect him from the Gorgon’s brazen claws than that it be bright enough to show his reflection. Still, he decided that Quicksilver knew better than he did, and he set to work at once. He scrubbed the shield so hard and so willingly that it soon shone like the harvest moon. Quicksilver looked at it with a smile and nodded his approval. Then he took off his own short, crooked sword and buckled it around Perseus in place of the one he had been wearing.

“No sword but mine will do for what you have to do,” he said. “The blade has excellent temper, and it will cut through iron and brass as easily as through the thinnest twig. Now let’s set out. The next thing is to find the Three Gray Women, who will tell us where to find the Nymphs.”
“The Three Gray Women!” cried Perseus, to whom this seemed only one more obstacle on the road to his adventure. “Please, who are the Three Gray Women? I’ve never heard of them.”

“They’re three very strange old ladies,” said Quicksilver, laughing. “They have only one eye between them, and only one tooth. What’s more, you have to look for them by starlight or in the dusk of evening, because they never show themselves in the light of either the sun or the moon.”
“But why should I waste my time on these Three Gray Women?” said Perseus. “Wouldn’t it be better to go straight off in search of the terrible Gorgons?”

“No, no,” answered his friend. “There are other things to do before you can find your way to the Gorgons. We have no choice but to hunt up these old ladies, and once we find them, you can be sure the Gorgons are not far off. Come, let’s get moving!”

By this time Perseus trusted his companion’s good sense so much that he raised no more objections and said he was ready to begin the adventure right away. So they set off at a fairly quick pace, so quick that Perseus found it hard to keep up with his nimble friend. To tell the truth, he had a strange notion that Quicksilver was wearing winged shoes, which of course helped him along wonderfully. And when Perseus looked at him sideways, out of the corner of his eye, he seemed to see wings on the sides of his head, though when he looked straight at him there was nothing there but an odd sort of cap. In any case, the twisted staff was plainly a great help to Quicksilver and let him go so fast that Perseus, though a very active young man, began to run out of breath.

“Here!” cried Quicksilver at last (for he knew perfectly well, the rogue, how hard Perseus found it to keep up with him), “you take the staff, since you need it much more than I do. Are there no better walkers than you on the island of Seriphus?”
“I’d manage fine,” said Perseus, with a sly glance at his companion’s feet, “if I only had winged shoes like yours.”
“We’ll have to see about getting you a pair,” answered Quicksilver.

But the staff helped Perseus along so bravely that he no longer felt the least bit tired. In fact, the stick seemed to be alive in his hand and to lend some of its life to Perseus. He and Quicksilver now walked on at their ease, chatting together like old friends. Quicksilver told so many entertaining stories about his earlier adventures, and how well his wits had served him on different occasions, that Perseus began to think him a truly remarkable person. He plainly knew the world, and nobody is so charming to a young man as a friend with that kind of knowledge. Perseus listened all the more eagerly, hoping to sharpen his own wits with what he heard.
Finally he remembered that Quicksilver had spoken of a sister, who was supposed to lend a hand in the adventure they were now bound for.
“Where is she?” he asked. “Won’t we meet her soon?”

“All in good time,” said his companion. “But you must understand that this sister of mine is a very different sort of person from me. She is serious and sensible, seldom smiles, never laughs, and has a rule against saying a word unless she has something especially deep to say. She won’t listen to anything but the wisest conversation, either.”
“Goodness!” said Perseus. “I’ll be afraid to say a single word.”

“She is a very accomplished person, I assure you,” Quicksilver went on, “and she has all the arts and sciences at her fingertips. In short, she is so enormously wise that many people call her wisdom itself. But to tell you the truth, she isn’t lively enough for my taste, and I think you would hardly find her as pleasant a traveling companion as me. Still, she has her good points, and you will benefit from them in your meeting with the Gorgons.”

By now it had grown quite dark. They had come to a very wild, empty place, overgrown with shaggy bushes and so silent and lonely that nobody seemed ever to have lived or traveled there. Everything was barren and desolate in the gray twilight, which grew dimmer every moment. Perseus looked around rather gloomily and asked Quicksilver whether they had much farther to go.

“Shh! Shh!” whispered his companion. “Don’t make a sound! This is exactly the right time and place to meet the Three Gray Women. Be careful that they don’t see you before you see them. They have only one eye among the three, but it is as sharp as half a dozen ordinary eyes.”
“But what should I do,” asked Perseus, “when we meet them?”

Quicksilver explained to Perseus how the Three Gray Women managed with their one eye. It seems they were in the habit of passing it from one to another, as if it were a pair of spectacles, or (which would have suited them better) a monocle. When one of the three had kept the eye for a certain time, she took it out of its socket and handed it to whichever sister’s turn it was, and that sister promptly popped it into her own head and enjoyed a peek at the visible world. So you can easily see that only one of the Three Gray Women could see at a time, while the other two were in total darkness. And at the moment when the eye was passing from hand to hand, none of the poor old ladies could see a thing. I have heard of a great many strange things in my day, and seen quite a few, but none, it seems to me, that can match the oddity of these Three Gray Women, all peeping through a single eye.
Perseus thought so too, and he was so amazed that he half suspected his companion of joking, and that there were no such old women in the world at all.
“You’ll soon find out whether I’m telling the truth,” said Quicksilver. “Listen! Hush! Shh! Here they come now!”

Perseus peered hard through the dusk, and sure enough, not far off, he made out the Three Gray Women. The light was so dim that he couldn’t tell what sort of figures they were. He could see only that they had long gray hair, and as they came nearer, he saw that two of them had nothing but an empty eye socket in the middle of the forehead. But in the middle of the third sister’s forehead was a very large, bright, piercing eye, which sparkled like a great diamond in a ring. It looked so penetrating that Perseus couldn’t help thinking it must see as perfectly in the darkest midnight as at noon. The sight of three people’s eyes seemed to have been melted down and gathered into that one.

So the three old dames got along about as comfortably as if they could all see at once. The one who happened to have the eye in her forehead led the other two by the hands, peering sharply about all the while. Perseus was afraid she would see right through the thick clump of bushes where he and Quicksilver were hiding. Goodness me! It was truly terrifying to be within reach of such a sharp eye!
Just before they got to the bushes, though, one of the Three Gray Women began to speak.
“Sister! Sister Scarecrow!” she cried. “You’ve had the eye long enough. It’s my turn now!”
“Let me hold it a little longer, Sister Nightmare,” Scarecrow answered. “I thought I caught a glimpse of something behind that thick bush.”

“So what if you did?” Nightmare snapped crossly. “Can’t I see into a thick bush as well as you can? The eye belongs to me as much as to you, and I know how to use it every bit as well, maybe even a little better. I insist on taking a look right now!”

At this the third sister, whose name was Shakejoint, began to complain. It was her turn to have the eye, she said, and Scarecrow and Nightmare wanted to hog it for themselves. To settle the argument, old Dame Scarecrow pulled the eye out of her forehead and held it out in her hand.
“One of you take it,” she cried, “and stop this silly squabbling. As for me, I’ll be glad of a little deep darkness. But be quick about it, or I’ll have to pop it back into my own head!”

So Nightmare and Shakejoint both stretched out their hands, feeling about eagerly to grab the eye from Scarecrow’s palm. But since both were blind, they had trouble finding where Scarecrow’s hand was. And Scarecrow, who was now as much in the dark as the other two, could not manage to touch either of their hands to put the eye into it. So, as you can see with half an eye, my wise little listeners, these good old ladies had landed themselves in a strange fix. The eye shone and sparkled like a star as Scarecrow held it out, yet the Gray Women could not catch the faintest gleam of it. All three stood in complete darkness, simply because they were too impatient to see.
Quicksilver was so amused to watch Shakejoint and Nightmare fumbling for the eye, each blaming Scarecrow and one another, that he could hardly keep from laughing out loud.
“Now’s your chance!” he whispered to Perseus. “Quick, quick, before they can pop the eye into either of their heads! Dash out at the old ladies and snatch it from Scarecrow’s hand!”

In a flash, while the Three Gray Women were still scolding one another, Perseus sprang out from behind the clump of bushes and seized the prize. As he held it in his hand, the marvelous eye shone very brightly. It seemed to gaze up into his face with a knowing look, as if it would have winked if only it had eyelids. But the Gray Women had no idea what had happened. Each of them thought one of her sisters had the eye, and they started their quarrel all over again. In the end, Perseus did not want to cause these respectable ladies any more trouble than he had to, so he decided it was right to explain.
“My good ladies,” he said, “please don’t be angry with one another. If anyone is to blame, it is me, for I have the honor of holding your very brilliant and excellent eye in my own hand!”

“You! You’ve got our eye! Who are you?” the Three Gray Women shrieked together. Of course they were terribly frightened to hear a stranger’s voice and to learn that their eyesight was in the hands of someone they could not even guess at. “Oh, sisters, what are we going to do? We’re all in the dark! Hand over our eye! Hand over our one precious eye, the only one we have! You’ve got two of your own! Give us our eye!”
“Tell them,” Quicksilver whispered to Perseus, “that they can have the eye back once they point you to the Nymphs who keep the flying slippers, the magic wallet, and the helmet of darkness.”

“My dear, good, admirable old ladies,” said Perseus, speaking to the Gray Women, “there is no need to be so frightened. I am not a bad young man at all. You will get your eye back, safe and sound and as bright as ever, the moment you tell me where to find the Nymphs.”

“The Nymphs! Goodness me! Sisters, which Nymphs does he mean?” Scarecrow shrieked. “People say there are a great many Nymphs: some who go hunting in the woods, some who live inside trees, and some who have a comfortable home in fountains of water. We know nothing at all about them. We are three unlucky old souls who wander around in the twilight, and we only ever had one eye among us, and you have stolen that one away. Oh, give it back, kind stranger! Whoever you are, give it back!”
All this time the Three Gray Women were groping with their arms stretched out, doing their best to get hold of Perseus. But he took good care to stay out of their reach.

“My respectable ladies,” he said, for his mother had taught him always to be perfectly polite, “I have your eye tight in my hand, and I will keep it safe for you until you are kind enough to tell me where to find these Nymphs. I mean the Nymphs who keep the enchanted wallet, the flying slippers, and the—what is it called?—the helmet of invisibility.”

“Mercy on us, sisters! What is the young man talking about?” Scarecrow, Nightmare, and Shakejoint exclaimed to one another, looking very astonished. “A pair of flying slippers, he says! His heels would soon fly higher than his head if he were foolish enough to put them on. And a helmet of invisibility! How could a helmet make him invisible, unless it were big enough for him to hide underneath? And an enchanted wallet! What kind of gadget is that, I wonder? No, no, good stranger! We can tell you nothing about these marvelous things. You have two eyes of your own, and we have only one between the three of us. You can find out about such wonders far better than three blind old creatures like us.”

Listening to them talk like this, Perseus began to believe that the Gray Women really knew nothing about the matter. It upset him to have caused them so much trouble, and he was just about to give back their eye and apologize for his rudeness in snatching it. But Quicksilver caught his hand.

“Don’t let them trick you!” he said. “These Three Gray Women are the only ones in the world who can tell you where the Nymphs live. Without that knowledge, you will never manage to cut off the head of Medusa with the snaky locks. Keep a firm grip on the eye, and everything will turn out well.”

As it turned out, Quicksilver was right. Few things are as precious to people as their eyesight, and the Gray Women prized their single eye as highly as if it were half a dozen, which is the number they should have had. Finding no other way to get it back, they finally told Perseus what he wanted to know. The moment they had done so, he politely and respectfully pushed the eye into the empty socket in one of their foreheads, thanked them for their kindness, and said goodbye. Before the young man was even out of earshot, they had started a new argument, because he happened to have given the eye to Scarecrow, who had already had her turn with it when their trouble with Perseus began.

I am afraid the Three Gray Women were in the habit of spoiling their peace with this sort of bickering. That was a great pity, since they could hardly get along without one another and were plainly meant to be inseparable companions. As a general rule, I would advise everyone who has only one eye between them, whether sisters or brothers, old or young, to practice patience and not all insist on looking through it at once.

Meanwhile, Quicksilver and Perseus hurried off to find the Nymphs. The old ladies had given such exact directions that it did not take them long. The Nymphs turned out to be very different people from Nightmare, Shakejoint, and Scarecrow. Instead of being old, they were young and beautiful, and instead of sharing one eye among the sisterhood, each Nymph had two very bright eyes of her own, and she looked kindly at Perseus with them. They seemed to know Quicksilver, and when he told them about the adventure Perseus had taken on, they had no objection to handing over the valuable things in their keeping. First they brought out what looked like a small purse, made of deer skin and curiously embroidered, and told him to be sure to keep it safe. This was the magic wallet. Next the Nymphs produced a pair of shoes, or slippers, or sandals, each with a neat little pair of wings at the heel.
“Put them on, Perseus,” said Quicksilver. “You will find yourself as light on your feet as you could wish for the rest of our journey.”

So Perseus put one of the slippers on, while he set the other on the ground beside him. But all at once this other slipper spread its wings, fluttered up off the ground, and would probably have flown away if Quicksilver had not leaped up and luckily caught it in the air.
“Be more careful,” he said, handing it back to Perseus. “It would scare the birds up there if they saw a flying slipper among them.”

Once Perseus had both of these wonderful slippers on, he was far too light to walk on the earth. He took a step or two, and what do you know! Up he popped into the air, high above the heads of Quicksilver and the Nymphs, and he found it very hard to get back down. Winged slippers and other high-flying gadgets like them are seldom easy to manage until you get a little used to them. Quicksilver laughed at his companion’s accidental acrobatics and told him not to be in such a desperate hurry, but to wait for the invisible helmet.

The good-natured Nymphs had the helmet, with its dark tuft of waving plumes, all ready to put on his head. And now something happened that was about as wonderful as anything I have told you so far. The instant before the helmet went on, there stood Perseus, a handsome young man with golden curls and rosy cheeks, the curved sword at his side and the brightly polished shield on his arm—a figure that seemed made entirely of courage, liveliness, and glorious light. But when the helmet came down over his white brow, there was no Perseus to be seen anymore! Nothing but empty air! Even the helmet that covered him with invisibility had vanished!
“Where are you, Perseus?” asked Quicksilver.
“Why, right here, of course!” Perseus answered very calmly, though his voice seemed to come out of the clear air. “Just where I was a moment ago. Can’t you see me?”
“No, indeed!” said his friend. “You are hidden under the helmet. But if I can’t see you, neither can the Gorgons. So follow me, and we will test how well you can handle the winged slippers.”

As he said this, Quicksilver’s cap spread its wings, as though his head meant to fly right off his shoulders. But his whole body rose lightly into the air, and Perseus followed him up. When they had climbed a few hundred feet, the young man began to realize how delightful it was to leave the dull earth far below and flit around like a bird.

It was now deep night. Perseus looked up and saw the round, bright, silvery moon, and he thought he would want nothing better than to soar up there and spend his life on it. Then he looked down again and saw the earth, with its seas and lakes, the silver ribbons of its rivers, its snowy mountain peaks, the wide spread of its fields, the dark clusters of its woods, and its cities of white marble. With the moonshine sleeping over the whole scene, it was as beautiful as the moon or any star could be. Among other things, he spotted the island of Seriphus, where his dear mother was. Now and then he and Quicksilver came near a cloud that looked from a distance as if it were made of fleecy silver, though when they plunged into it, they found themselves chilled and damp with gray mist. They flew so fast, however, that in an instant they burst out of the cloud into the moonlight again. Once a high-soaring eagle flew smack into the invisible Perseus. The most splendid sights were the meteors, which flashed out suddenly as if a bonfire had been lit in the sky, and made the moonshine look pale for as much as a hundred miles around.

As the two companions flew on, Perseus thought he could hear the rustle of a garment close beside him. It was on the side opposite from where he saw Quicksilver, yet Quicksilver was the only one he could see.
“Whose garment is this,” Perseus asked, “that keeps rustling right beside me in the breeze?”

“Oh, that is my sister’s!” Quicksilver answered. “She is coming along with us, as I told you she would. We could do nothing without my sister’s help. You have no idea how wise she is. And what eyes she has! Why, she can see you at this very moment as clearly as if you were not invisible, and I’ll wager she will be the first to spot the Gorgons.”

By now, in their swift journey through the air, they had come within sight of the great ocean and were soon flying over it. Far below them the waves tossed wildly in mid-sea, or rolled a white line of surf onto the long beaches, or foamed against the rocky cliffs. Down in the lower world the roar was thunderous, though by the time it reached Perseus’s ears it had softened to a gentle murmur, like the voice of a baby half asleep. Just then a voice spoke in the air close by him. It seemed to be a woman’s voice. It was melodious, though not exactly what you would call sweet, but grave and mild.
“Perseus,” said the voice, “there are the Gorgons.”
“Where?” exclaimed Perseus. “I can’t see them.”
“On the shore of that island below you,” the voice replied. “A pebble dropped from your hand would land right in the middle of them.”
“What did I tell you? She was bound to see them first,” Quicksilver said to Perseus. “And there they are!”

Straight down, two or three thousand feet below him, Perseus saw a small island, with the sea breaking in white foam all around its rocky shore, except on one side where there was a beach of snowy sand. He flew down toward it, and as he looked intently at a cluster or heap of brightness at the foot of a cliff of black rocks, behold, there were the terrible Gorgons! They lay fast asleep, lulled by the thunder of the sea, for it took a racket that would have deafened anyone else to put such fierce creatures to sleep. The moonlight glistened on their steely scales and on their golden wings, which drooped lazily over the sand. Their brazen claws, horrible to look at, were stretched out and clutching the wave-beaten chunks of rock, while the sleeping Gorgons dreamed of tearing some poor mortal to pieces. The snakes that served them as hair seemed to be asleep too, though now and then one would writhe and lift its head and flick out its forked tongue with a drowsy hiss, and then sink back among its sister snakes.

The Gorgons looked most like some awful, gigantic kind of insect—enormous golden-winged beetles, or dragonflies, or something of the sort—both ugly and beautiful at once, except that they were a thousand or a million times bigger. And yet, for all that, there was something a little human about them too. Luckily for Perseus, the way they lay kept their faces turned completely away from him. If he had looked at them for even one instant, he would have dropped out of the air like a stone, turned into a senseless statue.
“Now,” Quicksilver whispered, hovering at Perseus’s side, “now is your chance to do it! Be quick, because if one of the Gorgons wakes up, you will be too late!”
“Which one should I strike?” asked Perseus, drawing his sword and dropping a little lower. “All three look the same. All three have snakes for hair. Which of them is Medusa?”

You should know that Medusa was the only one of these dragon-monsters whose head Perseus could possibly cut off. The other two could not be hurt at all. Even with the sharpest sword ever forged, he could have hacked at them for hours on end without doing them the slightest harm.

“Be careful,” said the calm voice that had spoken to him before. “One of the Gorgons is stirring in her sleep and is just about to roll over. That one is Medusa. Do not look at her! The sight of her would turn you to stone! Watch her face and body in the reflection, in the bright mirror of your shield.”

Now Perseus understood why Quicksilver had urged him so earnestly to polish his shield. On its surface he could look at the Gorgon’s face in safety. And there it was—that terrible face—reflected in the shining metal, with the moonlight falling over it and showing all its horror. The snakes, whose poisonous nature never fully slept, kept writhing across her forehead. It was the fiercest, most horrible face ever seen or imagined, and yet it had a strange, fearful, savage sort of beauty. Her eyes were shut and she was sound asleep, but an uneasy look troubled her features, as if the monster were having a bad dream. She ground her white tusks together and dug her brass claws into the sand.

The snakes seemed to feel Medusa’s dream too, and it made them more restless. They twisted themselves into wild knots, thrashed about fiercely, and lifted a hundred hissing heads, though they never opened their eyes.
“Hurry, hurry!” Quicksilver whispered, growing impatient. “Swoop down on the monster!”
“But stay calm,” said the grave, musical voice beside the young man. “Keep your eyes on your shield as you fly down, and make sure you do not miss with your first stroke.”

Perseus flew carefully downward, never taking his eyes off Medusa’s face in the reflection on his shield. The closer he came, the more terrible the snaky face and metallic body of the monster looked. At last he was hovering over her, within arm’s reach. He raised his sword, and at that very moment every single snake on the Gorgon’s head stretched upward in a threat, and Medusa opened her eyes. But she woke too late. The sword was sharp, the blow fell like a flash of lightning, and the head of the wicked Medusa tumbled from her body!
“Well done!” cried Quicksilver. “Hurry up and pop the head into your magic wallet.”

To Perseus’s amazement, the little embroidered wallet that he had hung around his neck, which until now had been no bigger than a purse, suddenly grew large enough to hold Medusa’s head. Quick as a thought, he snatched up the head, with the snakes still squirming on it, and pushed it inside.
“Your task is done,” said the calm voice. “Now fly, because the other Gorgons will do everything they can to avenge Medusa’s death.”

Flying away was certainly necessary. Perseus had not done the deed quietly enough: the clang of his sword, the hissing of the snakes, and the thump of Medusa’s head landing on the sea-beaten sand had woken the other two monsters. They sat there for a moment, sleepily rubbing their eyes with their brass fingers, while the snakes on their heads reared up in surprise and in poisonous spite, though they did not know at what. But when the Gorgons saw Medusa’s scaly body lying headless, her golden wings ruffled and half spread on the sand, it was truly awful to hear the yells and screeches they let out. And then the snakes! They sent up a hundredfold hiss all together, and Medusa’s snakes answered them from inside the magic wallet.

As soon as the Gorgons were fully awake, they shot up into the air, waving their brass talons, grinding their horrible tusks, and flapping their huge wings so wildly that some of the golden feathers were shaken loose and floated down onto the shore. Perhaps those very feathers are still lying there today. The Gorgons rose up, as I tell you, glaring around horribly in the hope of turning somebody to stone. If Perseus had looked them in the face, or fallen into their clutches, his poor mother would never have kissed her boy again! But he took good care to look the other way, and since he was wearing the helmet of invisibility, the Gorgons had no idea which direction to chase him. He also made good use of the winged slippers, rocketing straight up about a mile. At that height, when the screams of those hateful creatures sounded faint below him, he set a straight course for the island of Seriphus, to deliver Medusa’s head to King Polydectes.

I don’t have time to tell you about the several marvelous things that happened to Perseus on his way home. One was how he killed a hideous sea monster just as it was about to devour a beautiful maiden. Another was how he turned an enormous giant into a mountain of stone, simply by showing him the Gorgon’s head. If you doubt that second story, you can sail to Africa one of these days and see the very mountain, which is still called by the old giant’s name.

At last our brave Perseus reached the island, where he expected to see his dear mother. But while he was away, the wicked king had treated Danae so cruelly that she had been forced to run away. She had taken refuge in a temple, where some good old priests were very kind to her. These admirable priests, and the kind-hearted fisherman who had first welcomed Danae and little Perseus when he found them floating in the chest, seem to have been the only people on the island who cared about doing right. Everyone else, King Polydectes included, behaved remarkably badly, and deserved no better fate than the one that was about to come to them.

Since his mother was not at home, Perseus went straight to the palace and was shown at once into the king’s presence. Polydectes was not at all glad to see him. In his own evil mind he had felt almost sure that the Gorgons would tear the poor young man to pieces and eat him up, so he would be out of the way. But seeing him back safe and sound, he made the best of it and asked Perseus how he had done.

“Did you keep your promise?” he demanded. “Is the head of Medusa, the one with the snakes for hair, in your hands? If not, young man, you will pay dearly. I need a wedding gift for the lovely Princess Hippodamia, and nothing else would please her half as much.”
“Yes, if it please Your Majesty,” answered Perseus quietly, as if it were no great feat for a young man like him. “I have brought you the Gorgon’s head, snaky hair and all!”
“Really! Please let me see it,” said King Polydectes. “It must be a most curious sight, if everything travelers say about it is true!”

“Your Majesty is right,” replied Perseus. “It is an object that is certain to hold the gaze of everyone who looks at it. And if Your Majesty agrees, I would suggest declaring a holiday and summoning all your subjects to see this wonderful curiosity. I imagine few of them have ever seen a Gorgon’s head before, and perhaps they never will again!”

The king knew very well that his subjects were a lazy bunch of scoundrels, and as fond of sightseeing as lazy people usually are. So he took the young man’s advice and sent heralds and messengers in every direction to blow trumpets at the street corners, in the marketplaces, and wherever two roads met, calling everybody to court. A great crowd of good-for-nothing vagabonds came running, every one of whom, out of sheer love of mischief, would have been glad to hear that Perseus had come to grief in his fight with the Gorgons. If there were any better people on the island (and I truly hope there were, though the story says nothing of them), they stayed quietly at home, minding their own business and looking after their little children. Most of the islanders, at any rate, raced to the palace as fast as they could, shoving and pushing and elbowing one another to get close to a balcony where Perseus stood, holding the embroidered wallet in his hand.

On a platform in full view of the balcony sat the mighty King Polydectes, surrounded by his evil counselors, with his flattering courtiers in a half circle around him. King, counselors, courtiers and common people all stared eagerly at Perseus.

“Show us the head! Show us the head!” shouted the people. There was such fierceness in their cry that they seemed ready to tear Perseus to pieces unless he gave them what he had promised to show. “Show us the head of Medusa with the snaky hair!”
The young Perseus was filled with sorrow and pity.
“O King Polydectes,” he cried, “and all you people, I am very unwilling to show you the Gorgon’s head!”

“What a scoundrel and a coward!” the people yelled, louder than ever. “He is making fun of us! There is no Gorgon’s head! Let us see it if you have one, or we will kick your head around like a football!”

The evil counselors whispered bad advice into the king’s ear. The courtiers murmured, all together, that Perseus had shown disrespect to their royal lord and master. And the great King Polydectes himself waved his hand and ordered Perseus, in the stern, deep voice of authority, on pain of death, to produce the head.
“Show me the Gorgon’s head, or I will cut off your own!”
And Perseus sighed.
“This instant,” Polydectes repeated, “or you die!”
“Then look at it!” cried Perseus, in a voice like a trumpet blast.

He suddenly held up the head, and before anyone had time to blink, the wicked King Polydectes, his evil counselors and all his fierce subjects were nothing but statues of a king and his people. They were all fixed forever in the look and pose of that moment! At the first glimpse of Medusa’s terrible head, they turned white as marble! Perseus pushed the head back into his wallet and went to tell his dear mother that she no longer had to be afraid of the wicked King Polydectes.
“Wasn’t that a very fine story?” asked Eustace.
“Oh yes, yes!” cried Cowslip, clapping her hands.
“And those funny old women who shared a single eye! I have never heard of anything so odd.”
“That one tooth they passed back and forth,” said Primrose, “was not so remarkable. I suppose it was a false tooth. But making Mercury into Quicksilver, and giving him a sister! You are absurd!”
“Well, wasn’t she his sister?” Eustace Bright replied. “If I had thought of it earlier, I would have made her a spinster with a pet owl!”
“Well, anyway,” said Primrose, “your story seems to have chased away the mist.”

And it was true: while the tale went on, the vapors had cleared completely from the landscape. A view lay open now that the listeners might almost have thought had been created since they last looked in that direction. About half a mile away, in the hollow of the valley, a beautiful lake had appeared, reflecting a perfect picture of its wooded banks and of the tops of the more distant hills. It gleamed in glassy stillness, without a ripple from any breeze on its surface. Beyond the far shore lay Monument Mountain, stretched out across almost the whole valley. Eustace Bright compared it to a huge headless sphinx wrapped in a Persian shawl, and the autumn leaves on its woods were so rich and varied in color that the shawl was by no means too bright a comparison for the real thing. On the lower ground between Tanglewood and the lake, the clumps of trees and the edges of the woods were mostly golden or dusky brown, because the frost had hit them harder than the trees on the hillsides.

A warm, friendly sunshine lay over the whole scene, mixed with a slight haze that made it unspeakably soft and tender. Oh, what a day of Indian summer it was going to be! The children grabbed their baskets and set off, hopping, skipping and jumping and frisking about in every way. Cousin Eustace proved he was fit to lead the party by outdoing all their antics, and he performed several new capers that none of them could ever hope to copy. Behind them came a good old dog named Ben. He was one of the most respectable and kind-hearted of four-footed creatures, and he probably felt it was his duty not to trust the children away from their parents without a better guardian than that feather-brained Eustace Bright.

chapters.title: The Golden Touch
paragraphs: At noon our young party gathered in a dell with a little brook running through its depths. The dell was narrow, and its steep sides, from the edge of the stream upward, were thick with trees, mostly walnuts and chestnuts, with a few oaks and maples among them. In summer, the shade of so many crowded branches, meeting and mingling across the brook, was deep enough to make a twilight at noon. That is how it got the name Shadow Brook. But ever since autumn had crept into this hidden place, all the dark green had turned to gold, so that the trees lit up the dell instead of shading it. The bright yellow leaves would have seemed to hold the sunlight among them even on a cloudy day, and enough of them had fallen to spread sunlight over the bed and banks of the brook as well. So the shady nook where summer had once cooled herself was now the sunniest spot to be found anywhere.

The little brook ran along its path of gold, here stopping to form a pool where minnows darted to and fro, and then hurrying on faster, as if in a rush to reach the lake. Forgetting to look where it was going, it tumbled over a tree root that stretched right across its current. You would have laughed to hear how noisily it babbled about this mishap. Even after it had run on, the brook kept talking to itself, as if it were lost in a maze. I suppose it was struck with wonder at finding its dark dell so lit up, and at hearing the chatter and merriment of so many children. So it slipped away as quickly as it could and hid itself in the lake.

Down in the hollow of Shadow Brook, Eustace Bright and his young friends had finished their dinner. They had carried plenty of good food from Tanglewood in their baskets, set it out on tree stumps and mossy logs, and enjoyed a cheerful, hearty meal. When it was over, nobody felt like moving.
“We’ll take a rest right here,” several of the children said, “and Cousin Eustace can tell us one more of his pretty tales.”

Cousin Eustace had every right to be as tired as the children, because he had done amazing things that morning. Dandelion, Clover, Cowslip, and Buttercup had nearly decided that he wore winged slippers like the ones the Nymphs gave Perseus, since the student kept turning up at the very top of a nut tree when a moment earlier he had been standing on the ground. And what showers of walnuts he had sent rattling down on their heads, for their eager little hands to collect in the baskets! In short, he had been as lively as a squirrel or a monkey, and now he threw himself down on the yellow leaves and looked ready for a little rest.
But children show no pity and no thought for anyone’s tiredness. If you had only one breath left, they would ask you to use it on telling them a story.
“Cousin Eustace,” said Cowslip, “the story about the Gorgon’s Head was really good. Do you think you could tell us another one just as good?”
“Yes, child,” said Eustace, tugging the brim of his cap down over his eyes as if getting ready for a nap. “If I felt like it, I could tell you a dozen, just as good or better.”
“Oh, Primrose and Periwinkle, did you hear what he said?” cried Cowslip, dancing with joy. “Cousin Eustace is going to tell us a dozen stories better than the one about the Gorgon’s Head!”

“I didn’t promise you even one, you silly little Cowslip!” said Eustace, a bit crossly. “Still, I suppose you have to get one. That’s what comes of earning a reputation! I wish I were much duller than I am, or that I had never shown off half the talents nature gave me. Then I could finish my nap in peace and comfort!”

But Cousin Eustace, as I think I have hinted before, enjoyed telling his stories just as much as the children enjoyed hearing them. His mind was free and cheerful, took pleasure in its own activity, and hardly needed any push from outside to get going.

How different this natural play of the mind is from the trained diligence of later years! By then work may have grown easy through long habit, and the day’s labor may have become necessary to the day’s comfort, even though the point of it has all bubbled away. This remark, however, is not meant for the children to hear.

Without any more urging, Eustace Bright began telling the following truly splendid story. It had come to him as he lay gazing up into the depths of a tree and watching how the touch of autumn had turned every green leaf into something like the purest gold. This change, which all of us have seen, is as wonderful as anything Eustace described in his story of Midas.

Once upon a time there lived a very rich man, who was also a king, named Midas. He had a little daughter, whom nobody but me has ever heard of, and whose name I either never knew or have completely forgotten. Since I love unusual names for little girls, I have decided to call her Marygold.

King Midas loved gold more than anything else in the world. He prized his royal crown mainly because it was made of that precious metal. If he loved anything more, or even half as much, it was the one little girl who played so happily around her father’s footstool. But the more Midas loved his daughter, the more he wanted and chased after wealth. The foolish man thought the best thing he could do for his dear child was to leave her the biggest pile of shining yellow coins ever heaped up since the world began. So he gave all his thoughts and all his time to this one goal. If he happened to glance for a moment at the golden clouds at sunset, he wished they were real gold that he could safely pack into his strongbox. When little Marygold ran to meet him with a bunch of buttercups and dandelions, he would say, “Poh, poh, child! If these flowers were as golden as they look, they would be worth picking!”

And yet in his earlier days, before this mad hunger for riches had taken complete hold of him, King Midas had loved flowers. He had planted a garden where the biggest, loveliest, sweetest-smelling roses that any mortal ever saw or smelled were growing. These roses still bloomed in the garden, as large, as beautiful, and as fragrant as when Midas used to spend whole hours looking at them and breathing in their scent. But now, if he looked at them at all, it was only to work out how much the garden would be worth if every one of its countless rose petals were a thin sheet of gold. He had also once loved music (in spite of a silly story about his ears, which were said to look like a donkey’s). Now, though, the only music poor Midas cared for was the clink of one coin against another.

In the end, because people keep getting more foolish unless they take care to grow wiser, Midas became so unreasonable that he could hardly stand to look at or touch anything that wasn’t gold. So he made a habit of spending a large part of every day in a dark, gloomy room underground, in the basement of his palace. This was where he kept his wealth. Whenever he wanted to be especially happy, Midas went to this miserable hole, which was little better than a dungeon. There he would carefully lock the door, then take a bag of gold coins, or a gold cup as big as a washbowl, or a heavy gold bar, or a peck-measure of gold dust, and carry them out of the dim corners of the room into the one bright, narrow sunbeam that fell through the dungeon-like window. He valued that sunbeam only because his treasure would not shine without its help. Then he would count the coins in the bag, toss the bar into the air and catch it on the way down, sift the gold dust through his fingers, look at the funny picture of his own face reflected in the polished curve of the cup, and whisper to himself, “Oh, Midas, rich King Midas, what a happy man you are!” But it was funny to see how the face in the cup kept grinning back at him from the shiny surface. It seemed to know how foolish he was being, and to have a naughty urge to make fun of him.

Midas called himself a happy man, but he felt he was not yet as happy as he could be. He would never reach the very peak of enjoyment, he thought, until the whole world became his treasure room, filled with yellow metal that belonged to him alone.

Now, I hardly need to remind clever little people like you that in the old, old days when King Midas lived, many things happened that we would find amazing if they happened in our own time and country. On the other hand, plenty of things happen nowadays that seem amazing to us and that would have made people in those old times stare in disbelief. All in all, I think our own age is the stranger of the two. But however that may be, I must get on with my story.

One day Midas was enjoying himself in his treasure room as usual, when he noticed a shadow fall across the heaps of gold. He looked up suddenly, and what should he see but a stranger standing in the bright, narrow sunbeam! It was a young man with a cheerful, rosy face. Maybe King Midas’s imagination cast a yellow tint over everything, or maybe there was some other reason, but he could not help thinking that the stranger’s smile as he looked at him had a kind of golden glow in it. One thing was certain: although the stranger’s body blocked the sunlight, a brighter gleam now lay over all the piled-up treasure than before. Even the farthest corners got their share of it, and whenever the stranger smiled they lit up, as if with flame tips and sparks of fire.

Midas knew he had turned the key carefully in the lock and that no human strength could break into his treasure room. So naturally he decided that his visitor must be more than human. It doesn’t matter who he was. In those days, when the earth was still fairly new, people believed it was often visited by beings with supernatural power, who took an interest in the joys and sorrows of men, women, and children, partly in play and partly in earnest. Midas had met such beings before and was not unhappy to meet one again. The stranger looked so good-humored and kind, even generous, that it would have been unreasonable to suspect him of any mischief. It was far more likely that he had come to do Midas a favor. And what could that favor be, if not to add to his heaps of treasure?
The stranger looked around the room. When his shining smile had glittered over every golden object there, he turned back to Midas.
“You are a wealthy man, friend Midas!” he said. “I doubt that any other four walls on earth hold as much gold as you have managed to pile up in this room.”

“I’ve done fairly well—fairly well,” answered Midas, in a discontented voice. “But after all, it’s only a trifle, when you think that it has taken my whole life to gather it. If a man could live a thousand years, he might have time to get rich!”
“What!” cried the stranger. “So you are not satisfied?”
Midas shook his head.
“And what, may I ask, would satisfy you?” said the stranger. “I would simply like to know, out of curiosity.”

Midas paused and thought. He had a feeling that this stranger, with such a golden shine in his good-humored smile, had come with both the power and the purpose to grant his greatest wishes. So now was the lucky moment, when all he had to do was speak and he would get whatever he could think of asking for, possible or seemingly impossible. So he thought and thought and thought, piling one golden mountain on top of another in his imagination, and still could not picture them big enough. At last a bright idea came to King Midas. It seemed truly as bright as the shining metal he loved so much.
He raised his head and looked the shining stranger in the face.
“So, Midas,” said his visitor, “you have at last found something that will content you, I can see. What is your wish?”

“It is only this,” replied Midas. “I am tired of collecting my treasures with so much trouble and then seeing the pile so small, after I have done my very best. I wish that everything I touch would turn to gold!”

The stranger’s smile grew so broad that it seemed to fill the room like the sun bursting into a shady hollow where yellow autumn leaves lie scattered in the glow—for that is how the lumps and specks of gold looked.
“The Golden Touch!” he exclaimed. “You certainly deserve credit, friend Midas, for coming up with such a brilliant idea. But are you quite sure this will satisfy you?”
“How could it not?” said Midas.
“And you will never regret having it?”
“What could make me?” asked Midas. “I ask for nothing else to make me perfectly happy.”
“Then let it be as you wish,” replied the stranger, waving his hand in farewell. “Tomorrow at sunrise you will find yourself given the Golden Touch.”

Then the stranger’s figure grew extremely bright, and Midas shut his eyes without meaning to. When he opened them again, he saw only a single yellow sunbeam in the room, and all around him the gleam of the precious metal he had spent his life hoarding.

Whether Midas slept as usual that night, the story does not say. Asleep or awake, his mind was probably like a child’s who has been promised a beautiful new toy in the morning. At any rate, daylight had barely peeped over the hills when King Midas was wide awake. He stretched his arms out of bed and began touching whatever was within reach. He was eager to find out whether the Golden Touch had really come, as the stranger had promised. So he put his finger on a chair beside the bed, and on various other things, but was bitterly disappointed to see that they stayed exactly the same as before. In fact, he became very afraid that he had only dreamed of the shining stranger, or else that the stranger had been making fun of him. And what a miserable thing it would be if, after all his hopes, Midas had to make do with whatever little gold he could scrape together by ordinary means, instead of creating it with a touch!

All this time it was only the gray of early morning, with just a streak of brightness along the edge of the sky, out of Midas’s sight. He lay there gloomily, regretting the collapse of his hopes and growing sadder and sadder, until the first sunbeam came through the window and lit the ceiling above his head with gold. It seemed to Midas that this bright yellow sunbeam was reflected in a rather odd way on the white bed covering. He looked closer, and what was his astonishment and delight to find that the linen had been changed into what seemed a woven fabric of the purest, brightest gold! The Golden Touch had come to him with the first sunbeam!

Midas jumped up in a kind of joyful frenzy and ran around the room, grabbing at everything in his way. He seized one of the bedposts, and it instantly became a fluted golden pillar. He pulled aside a window curtain to get a clear view of the wonders he was working, and the tassel grew heavy in his hand—a lump of gold. He picked up a book from the table. At his first touch it took on the look of one of those splendidly bound, gilt-edged volumes you often see nowadays; but when he ran his fingers through the pages, behold! it was a bundle of thin golden plates, and all the wisdom in the book had become unreadable. He hurriedly put on his clothes and was thrilled to see himself in a magnificent suit of gold cloth, which stayed flexible and soft though its weight burdened him a little. He pulled out his handkerchief, which little Marygold had hemmed for him. That was gold too, with the dear child’s neat and pretty stitches running all along the border in gold thread!
Somehow, this last change did not quite please King Midas. He would rather have had his little daughter’s handiwork stay just as it was when she climbed on his knee and put it into his hand.

But it wasn’t worth fretting over such a small thing. Midas took his spectacles out of his pocket and put them on, so he could see more clearly what he was doing. In those days ordinary people had no spectacles, though kings already wore them; otherwise, how could Midas have owned a pair? To his great bewilderment, however, fine as the lenses were, he found he couldn’t see through them at all. That was only natural, since when he took them off, the clear crystals had turned into plates of yellow metal. They were useless as spectacles, of course, though valuable as gold. It struck Midas as rather inconvenient that, with all his wealth, he could never again be rich enough to own a pair of spectacles that actually worked.

“Still, it’s no great matter,” he told himself, very calmly. “We can’t expect any great good without a little inconvenience attached. The Golden Touch is worth the loss of a pair of spectacles, and even of my eyesight, if it came to that. My own eyes will do for everyday purposes, and little Marygold will soon be old enough to read to me.”

Wise King Midas was so lifted up by his good fortune that the palace didn’t seem big enough to hold him. So he went downstairs, and smiled to see the banister turn into a bar of polished gold as his hand slid along it. He lifted the door latch (it had been plain brass a moment before, but it was gold the instant his fingers let go) and walked out into the garden. There, as it happened, he found a great many beautiful roses in full bloom, and others at every stage from tender bud to blossom. Their fragrance was delicious in the morning breeze. Their delicate blush was one of the loveliest sights in the world, for these roses looked so gentle, so modest, and so full of sweet calm.

But Midas knew a way to make them far more precious, as he saw it, than roses had ever been. So he went to a great deal of trouble, moving from bush to bush and using his magic touch tirelessly, until every single flower and bud, even the worms inside the hearts of some of them, had turned to gold. By the time this good work was done, King Midas was called to breakfast. The morning air had given him a fine appetite, so he hurried back to the palace.

What a king usually ate for breakfast in the days of Midas, I really don’t know, and I can’t stop now to find out. As best I can tell, though, on this particular morning the breakfast was hot cakes, some nice little brook trout, roasted potatoes, fresh boiled eggs, and coffee for King Midas himself, and a bowl of bread and milk for his daughter Marygold. In any case, that is a breakfast fit to set before a king; and whether he had it or not, King Midas could not have had a better one.

Little Marygold hadn’t come in yet. Her father ordered someone to call her, then sat down at the table and waited for the child before starting his own breakfast. To be fair to Midas, he really did love his daughter, and he loved her all the more this morning because of the good fortune that had come to him. Before long he heard her coming along the passage, crying bitterly. This surprised him, because Marygold was one of the cheeriest little people you could meet on a summer’s day, and she hardly shed a thimbleful of tears in a whole year. When Midas heard her sobs, he decided to lift her spirits with a pleasant surprise. So he leaned across the table and touched his daughter’s bowl (a china one, with pretty figures painted all around it), and turned it into gleaming gold.
Meanwhile Marygold opened the door slowly and sadly and came in, with her apron held over her eyes, still sobbing as if her heart would break.
“Well, my little lady!” cried Midas. “What on earth is the matter with you on this bright morning?”
Without taking the apron from her eyes, Marygold held out her hand. In it was one of the roses Midas had just turned to gold.
“Beautiful!” exclaimed her father. “What could there be in this splendid golden rose to make you cry?”

“Oh, dear father!” answered the child, as well as her sobs would let her. “It isn’t beautiful. It’s the ugliest flower that ever grew! As soon as I was dressed, I ran into the garden to pick some roses for you, because I know you like them, and like them even better when your little daughter picks them. But oh dear, dear me! What do you think has happened? Such a misfortune! All the beautiful roses, that smelled so sweet and had such lovely blushes, are withered and spoiled! They’ve turned quite yellow, like this one, and they don’t smell at all! What can have happened to them?”

“Pooh, my dear little girl—please don’t cry about it!” said Midas. He was ashamed to admit that he himself had made the change that upset her so much. “Sit down and eat your bread and milk! It will be easy enough to trade a golden rose like that (which will last hundreds of years) for an ordinary one that would wither in a day.”
“I don’t want roses like this one!” cried Marygold, tossing it scornfully away. “It has no smell, and the hard petals prick my nose!”

The child sat down at the table, but she was so taken up with grief over the ruined roses that she didn’t even notice what had happened to her china bowl. Perhaps that was just as well. Marygold always enjoyed looking at the odd figures, strange trees, and houses painted around the rim of the bowl, and now all those decorations were lost in the yellow of the metal.

Meanwhile Midas had poured himself a cup of coffee. Naturally, the coffee pot, whatever metal it had been when he picked it up, was gold when he set it down. He thought to himself that it was rather extravagant splendor for a king of his simple habits to eat breakfast off a gold service, and he began to worry about how to keep his treasures safe. The cupboard and the kitchen would no longer be secure places to store things as valuable as golden bowls and coffee pots.

While thinking this over, he raised a spoonful of coffee to his lips and sipped it. To his astonishment, the instant his lips touched the liquid it turned into molten gold, and a moment later it hardened into a lump!
“Ha!” exclaimed Midas, rather shocked.
“What’s wrong, father?” little Marygold asked, gazing up at him while tears still stood in her eyes.
“Nothing, child, nothing!” said Midas. “Finish your milk before it goes cold.”

He took one of the nice little trout on his plate and, as an experiment, touched its tail with his finger. To his horror, it instantly turned from a perfectly fried brook trout into a goldfish. It wasn’t the sort of goldfish people often keep in glass bowls as parlor ornaments, either. No, it was really a metal fish, and it looked as if the finest goldsmith in the world had made it with great skill. Its little bones were now golden wires, and its fins and tail were thin plates of gold. The marks of the fork were in it, and so was all the delicate, frothy look of a nicely fried fish, copied exactly in metal. It was a very pretty piece of work, as you can imagine; only King Midas, at that moment, would much rather have had a real trout on his plate than this elaborate and valuable imitation.
“I don’t quite see,” he thought to himself, “how I’m going to get any breakfast!”

He took one of the steaming hot cakes and had barely broken it open when, to his bitter disappointment, it turned the yellow of cornmeal, though a moment before it had been of the whitest wheat. To tell the truth, if it had really been a hot corn cake, Midas would have valued it much more than he did now, when its hardness and extra weight made him painfully aware that it was gold. Almost in despair, he helped himself to a boiled egg, which went through the same change as the trout and the cake. The egg might well have been mistaken for one of those that the famous goose in the storybook used to lay; but King Midas was the only goose who had anything to do with this matter.

“Well, this is a fine fix!” he thought, leaning back in his chair and looking almost jealously at little Marygold, who was eating her bread and milk with great enjoyment. “Such an expensive breakfast in front of me, and nothing I can eat!”

King Midas hoped that by moving very fast he could avoid what he now saw was a serious inconvenience. He snatched a hot potato and tried to cram it into his mouth and swallow it in a hurry. But the Golden Touch was too quick for him. His mouth was full, not of mealy potato, but of solid metal, which burned his tongue so badly that he roared out loud. He jumped up from the table and began to dance and stamp around the room, in pain and terror both.
“Father, dear father!” cried little Marygold, who was a very loving child. “What is the matter? Have you burned your mouth?”
“Ah, dear child,” groaned Midas sadly, “I don’t know what will become of your poor father!”

And honestly, my dear little folks, have you ever heard of such a pitiful case in all your lives? Here was literally the richest breakfast ever set before a king, and its very richness made it good for nothing at all. The poorest laborer, sitting down to his crust of bread and cup of water, was far better off than King Midas, whose dainty food was truly worth its weight in gold. And what could be done? Already, at breakfast, Midas was dreadfully hungry. Would he be any less hungry by dinnertime? And think how ravenous he would be by supper, which would surely be made up of the same indigestible dishes now in front of him! How many days, do you suppose, he could survive on such rich fare?
