These thoughts troubled wise King Midas so much that he began to wonder whether riches are, after all, the one thing worth wanting in the world, or even the thing most worth wanting. But this was only a passing thought. Midas was so taken with the glitter of the yellow metal that he would still have refused to give up the Golden Touch for such a small price as a breakfast. Just imagine what a price for one meal’s food! It would have been like paying millions and millions of money (and as many millions more as it would take forever to count) for some fried trout, an egg, a potato, a hot cake, and a cup of coffee!
“That would be far too expensive,” thought Midas.

Even so, his hunger was so great, and his situation so baffling, that he groaned aloud again, and very painfully. Our dear Marygold could stand it no longer. She sat for a moment looking at her father, trying with all the strength of her little wits to find out what was wrong with him. Then, with a sweet and sorrowful wish to comfort him, she jumped down from her chair, ran to Midas, and threw her arms lovingly around his knees. He bent down and kissed her. He felt that his little daughter’s love was worth a thousand times more than everything he had gained from the Golden Touch.
“My precious, precious Marygold!” he cried.
But Marygold did not answer.

Alas, what had he done? How deadly was the gift the stranger had given him! The moment the lips of Midas touched Marygold’s forehead, a change came over her. Her sweet, rosy face, so full of love a moment before, took on a glittering yellow color, with yellow teardrops hardening on her cheeks. Her beautiful brown curls turned the same shade. Her soft, tender little body grew hard and stiff in her father’s arms. Oh, terrible misfortune! A victim of her father’s endless greed for wealth, little Marygold was no longer a human child, but a golden statue!

Yes, there she was, with the questioning look of love, grief, and pity frozen into her face. It was the prettiest and the saddest sight any mortal ever saw. All Marygold’s features and her little ways were there; even the dear little dimple remained in her golden chin. But the more perfect the likeness was, the greater was her father’s agony at seeing this golden image, which was all that was left him of a daughter. Whenever Midas felt especially fond of the child, he had always liked to say that she was worth her weight in gold. Now the saying had come literally true. And now, at last, when it was too late, he felt how infinitely more a warm and tender heart that loved him was worth than all the wealth that could be piled up between the earth and the sky!

It would be too sad a story if I told you how Midas, with all his desires fulfilled, began to wring his hands and lament, and how he could neither bear to look at Marygold nor bear to look away from her. Unless his eyes were fixed on the image, he couldn’t believe she had turned to gold. But whenever he stole another glance, there was the precious little figure, with a yellow teardrop on its yellow cheek, and a look so pitiful and tender that it seemed this very expression must soften the gold and make it flesh again. This, however, could not be. So Midas could only wring his hands and wish that he were the poorest man in the wide world, if losing all his wealth might bring the faintest rose color back to his dear child’s face.

While he was in this storm of despair, he suddenly saw a stranger standing near the door. Midas bowed his head and said nothing, because he recognized the same figure who had appeared to him the day before in the treasure room and had given him this disastrous power, the Golden Touch. The stranger’s face still wore a smile, which seemed to spread a yellow glow all around the room. It shone on little Marygold’s image, and on the other things that the touch of Midas had changed.
“Well, friend Midas,” said the stranger, “how are you getting along with the Golden Touch?”
Midas shook his head.
“I am very miserable,” he said.
“Very miserable, indeed!” exclaimed the stranger. “And how did that happen? Haven’t I faithfully kept my promise to you? Don’t you have everything your heart desired?”
“Gold isn’t everything,” Midas replied. “And I have lost everything my heart truly cared for.”

“Ah! So you have learned something since yesterday?” remarked the stranger. “Then let us see. Which of these two do you think is truly worth more: the gift of the Golden Touch, or a single cup of clear, cold water?”
“Oh, blessed water!” cried Midas. “It will never cool my parched throat again!”
“The Golden Touch,” the stranger went on, “or a crust of bread?”
“One slice of bread,” Midas replied, “is worth all the gold in the world!”
“Which is worth more,” the stranger asked, “the Golden Touch, or your own little Marygold, as warm, soft, and loving as she was an hour ago?”
“Oh, my child, my dear, dear child!” cried poor Midas, wringing his hands. “I wouldn’t trade that one tiny dimple in her chin for the power to turn this entire big earth into one solid lump of gold!”

“You’ve grown wiser, King Midas!” said the stranger, studying him gravely. “I can see that your own heart hasn’t been turned from flesh to gold. If it had, you would truly be beyond help. But you still seem able to understand that the most ordinary things, the ones anyone can reach, are worth more than the riches so many people sigh and struggle for. Tell me, then: do you honestly want to be rid of this Golden Touch?”
“I hate it!” Midas answered.
A fly landed on his nose, but it dropped to the floor at once, because it had turned to gold as well. Midas shuddered.

“Then go,” said the stranger. “Dive into the river that flows past the bottom of your garden. Take a jug of that same water with you, and sprinkle it on anything you want changed back from gold into what it was before. If you do this earnestly and sincerely, it may perhaps undo the harm your greed has caused.”
King Midas bowed low, and when he raised his head again, the shining stranger was gone.

You can easily believe that Midas lost no time. He grabbed a big clay pitcher (though, alas, it was no longer clay once he touched it) and hurried to the riverside. As he scampered along and pushed through the bushes, it was truly amazing to watch the leaves turn yellow behind him, as though autumn had arrived in that spot and nowhere else. When he reached the edge of the river, he dived straight in, without even stopping to pull off his shoes.

“Pooh! Pooh! Pooh!” snorted King Midas as his head came up out of the water. “Well, this is a truly refreshing bath, and I think it must have washed the Golden Touch right off. Now to fill my pitcher!”

As he dipped the pitcher into the water, his heart leaped to see it turn from gold back into the same plain, honest clay vessel it had been before he touched it. He also felt a change inside himself. A cold, hard, heavy weight seemed to have lifted from his chest. No doubt his heart had been slowly losing its human nature and turning into lifeless metal, and now it had softened back into flesh. He noticed a violet growing on the riverbank and touched it with his finger. He was overjoyed to see that the delicate flower kept its purple color instead of withering to yellow. The curse of the Golden Touch had really been lifted from him.

King Midas hurried back to the palace. I suppose the servants had no idea what to think when they saw their royal master carrying a clay pitcher of water home so carefully. But that water, which was going to undo all the harm his foolishness had done, was worth more to Midas than an ocean of molten gold. The first thing he did, as you hardly need to be told, was to sprinkle it by the handful over the golden statue of little Marygold.

You would have laughed to see how quickly the rosy color came back to the dear child’s cheeks, the moment the water touched her! And how she began to sneeze and sputter! And how astonished she was to find herself dripping wet, with her father still pouring more water over her!
“Please stop, dear father!” she cried. “Look how you’ve soaked my nice frock, which I only put on this morning!”
For Marygold didn’t know she had been a little golden statue. She couldn’t remember anything that had happened since the moment she ran to comfort poor King Midas with her arms stretched out.

Her father didn’t think it necessary to tell his beloved child how foolish he had been. He was content to show her how much wiser he had become. So he led little Marygold into the garden and sprinkled all the rest of the water over the rosebushes, with such good effect that more than five thousand roses bloomed again in all their beauty. Still, two things reminded King Midas of the Golden Touch for as long as he lived. One was that the sand of the river sparkled like gold. The other was that little Marygold’s hair now had a golden tinge, which he had never noticed in it before his kiss turned her to gold. This change of color was really an improvement, and her hair was richer than it had been when she was a baby.

When King Midas was quite an old man and bounced Marygold’s children on his knee, he loved to tell them this marvelous story, much as I have just told it to you. Then he would stroke their glossy curls and tell them that their hair had a rich shade of gold too, which they had inherited from their mother.
“And to tell you the truth, my precious little ones,” said King Midas, bouncing the children busily all the while, “from that morning on, I have hated the very sight of any other gold except this!”
“Well, children,” asked Eustace, who liked to get a clear opinion out of his listeners, “did you ever in all your lives hear a better story than this one, ‘The Golden Touch’?”

“Well, as for the story of King Midas,” said saucy Primrose, “it was famous thousands of years before Mr Eustace Bright was born, and it will stay famous long after he’s gone. But some people have what we might call ‘The Leaden Touch,’ and they make everything they handle dull and heavy.”

“You’re a clever child, Primrose, for someone not yet in her teens,” said Eustace, a little taken aback by the sting of her criticism. “But in your naughty little heart you know very well that I’ve polished the old gold of Midas all over again and made it shine as it never has before. And what about that figure of Marygold? Don’t you see some fine workmanship in that? And how well I’ve brought out the moral and made it deeper! What do you say, Sweet Fern, Dandelion, Clover, Periwinkle? After hearing this story, would any of you be foolish enough to wish for the power to turn things to gold?”

“I would like,” said Periwinkle, a girl of ten, “to have the power to turn everything to gold with my right forefinger. But with my left forefinger, I’d want the power to change it back again, in case I didn’t like the first change. And I know just what I would do this very afternoon!”
“Please tell me,” said Eustace.

“Why,” answered Periwinkle, “I’d touch every one of these golden leaves on the trees with my left forefinger and make them all green again. Then we could have summer back right away, with no ugly winter in between.”

“Oh, Periwinkle!” cried Eustace Bright. “You’re wrong there, and you would do a great deal of harm. If I were Midas, I would make nothing but golden days just like these, over and over, all year long. My best thoughts always come a little too late. Why didn’t I tell you how old King Midas came to America and changed the dusky autumn of other countries into the glowing beauty it wears here? He gilded the leaves of the great book of Nature.”

“Cousin Eustace,” said Sweet Fern, a good little boy who was always asking for exact details about how tall giants were and how small fairies were, “how big was Marygold, and how much did she weigh after she turned to gold?”

“She was about as tall as you are,” replied Eustace, “and since gold is very heavy, she weighed at least two thousand pounds, and could have been made into thirty or forty thousand gold dollars. I wish Primrose were worth half as much. Come on, little people, let’s climb out of this hollow and look around.”

They did. The sun was now an hour or two past noon, and it filled the great hollow of the valley with its western light, so that the valley seemed to brim over with mellow glow and spill it onto the surrounding hillsides, like golden wine from a bowl. It was the kind of day when you can’t help saying, “There never was a day like this before!” even though yesterday was just like it, and tomorrow will be too. But ah, there are very few such days in a whole year! One remarkable thing about these October days is that each of them seems to take up a great deal of space, even though the sun rises rather late at that time of year and goes to bed, as little children should, at a sensible six o’clock or even earlier. So we can’t call the days long. Somehow, though, they make up for being short by being broad, and when the cool night comes, we feel we have enjoyed a big armful of life since morning.
“Come on, children, come on!” cried Eustace Bright. “More nuts, more nuts, more nuts! Fill all your baskets, and at Christmas time I’ll crack them for you and tell you beautiful stories!”

Off they went, all in excellent spirits, except little Dandelion. I’m sorry to say he had been sitting on a chestnut burr and was stuck full of prickles like a pincushion. Dear me, how uncomfortable he must have felt!

chapters.title: The Paradise of Children
paragraphs: The golden days of October passed, as so many Octobers have, and so did brown November and most of chilly December. At last came merry Christmas, and Eustace Bright came with it, making it all the merrier by being there. The day after he arrived home from college, a mighty snowstorm struck. Until then the winter had held back and given us many mild days, like smiles on its wrinkled face. The grass had stayed green in sheltered places, such as the nooks of south-facing hillsides and the sheltered side of the stone fences. It was only a week or two earlier, well into the month, that the children had found a dandelion in bloom on the bank of Shadow Brook, where it flows out of the dell.

But there was no more green grass or dandelions now. This was some snowstorm! You might have seen twenty miles of it at once, from the windows of Tanglewood to the dome of Taconic, if it had been possible to see so far through the swirling drifts that turned the whole air white. It seemed as if the hills were giants, flinging enormous handfuls of snow at each other in their huge game. The snowflakes fluttered so thickly that most of the time they hid even the trees halfway down the valley. Now and then, it’s true, the little prisoners of Tanglewood could make out the dim outline of Monument Mountain, the smooth white of the frozen lake at its foot, and the black or gray stretches of woodland nearby. But these were only peeks through the storm.

Even so, the children were delighted with the snowstorm. They had already gotten to know it by tumbling head over heels into its deepest drifts and throwing snow at each other, just as we imagined the Berkshire mountains doing. Now they had come back to their roomy playroom, which was as big as the great drawing room and cluttered with every kind of plaything, large and small. The biggest was a rocking horse that looked like a real pony. There was a whole family of dolls made of wood, wax, plaster, and china, besides rag babies, and enough blocks to build the Bunker Hill Monument, and ninepins, and balls, and humming tops, and battledores, and grace-sticks, and skipping ropes, and more such valuable property than I could list on a printed page. But the children liked the snowstorm better than all of it. It promised so many lively pleasures for tomorrow and the rest of the winter: the sleigh ride, the slides down the hill into the valley, the snow figures to be shaped, the snow forts to be built, and the snowballing to be carried on!

The little folks gave the storm their blessing. They cheered as the flakes fell thicker and thicker, and they kept hopeful watch on the long drift building along the avenue, which already stood taller than any of them.
“Why, we’ll be snowed in until spring!” they cried, hugely delighted. “What a pity the house is too tall to be completely covered! The little red house down there will be buried up to its eaves.”

“You silly children, what do you want more snow for?” asked Eustace, who had grown tired of some novel he was skimming and had wandered into the playroom. “It’s already done enough harm by spoiling the only skating I could hope for all winter. We won’t see the lake again until April, and today was going to be my first day on it! Don’t you feel sorry for me, Primrose?”

“Oh, of course!” answered Primrose, laughing. “But to comfort you, we’ll listen to another of your old stories, like the ones you told us under the porch and down in the hollow by Shadow Brook. Maybe I’ll like them better now, when there’s nothing to do, than when there were nuts to gather and beautiful weather to enjoy.”

At this, Periwinkle, Clover, Sweet Fern, and as many others of the little band of brothers, sisters, and cousins as were still at Tanglewood gathered around Eustace and eagerly begged him for a story. The student yawned and stretched. Then, to the great admiration of the small people, he hopped back and forth over the top of a chair three times, which he explained was to set his wits in motion.

“Well, well, children,” he said after these preliminaries, “since you insist, and Primrose has set her heart on it, I’ll see what I can do for you. And so that you can see what happy days there were before snowstorms came into fashion, I’ll tell you a story from the oldest of all old times, when the world was as new as Sweet Fern’s brand-new humming top. In those days there was only one season of the year, the delightful summer, and only one age for mortals, which was childhood.”
“I never heard that before,” said Primrose.

“Of course you didn’t,” answered Eustace. “It will be a story about something nobody but me has ever dreamed of: a Paradise of children, and how it all came to nothing because of the naughtiness of a little imp just like Primrose here.”

So Eustace Bright sat down in the chair he had just been jumping over, took Cowslip on his knee, ordered silence throughout his audience, and began a story about a very naughty child named Pandora and her playmate Epimetheus. You can read it, word for word, on the pages that follow.

Long, long ago, when this old world was in its tender infancy, there was a child named Epimetheus who had neither father nor mother. So that he wouldn’t be lonely, another child, fatherless and motherless like him, was sent from a faraway country to live with him and be his playmate and helper. Her name was Pandora.
The first thing Pandora saw when she entered the cottage where Epimetheus lived was a large box. And almost the first question she asked him, after stepping over the threshold, was this:
“Epimetheus, what do you have in that box?”
“Dear little Pandora,” Epimetheus answered, “that is a secret. Please be kind and don’t ask me about it. Someone left the box here to be looked after, and even I don’t know what’s inside.”
“Who gave it to you, though?” Pandora asked. “Where did it come from?”
“That’s a secret too,” replied Epimetheus.
“How annoying!” exclaimed Pandora, pouting. “I wish that big ugly box were out of the way!”
“Oh, come on, stop thinking about it,” cried Epimetheus. “Let’s run outside and have a good game with the other children.”

Epimetheus and Pandora lived thousands of years ago, and the world today is very different from the one they knew. In those days everybody was a child. Children needed no fathers and mothers to look after them, because there was no danger and no trouble of any kind, no clothes to mend, and always plenty to eat and drink. When a child wanted dinner, he simply found it growing on a tree. If he looked at the tree in the morning, he could watch the blossom opening that would become that night’s supper, and in the evening he could see the tender bud of tomorrow’s breakfast. It was a very pleasant life indeed. There was no work to do and no lessons to learn. There was nothing but games and dances and the sweet voices of children chatting, or singing like birds, or bursting into merry laughter, all day long.

Best of all, the children never quarreled with one another, and they never had crying fits. Not once since time began had a single one of these little mortals gone off into a corner to sulk. Oh, what a wonderful time that was to be alive! The truth is that those ugly little winged monsters called Troubles, which are now nearly as common as mosquitoes, had never yet been seen on earth. Probably the greatest unease any child had ever felt was Pandora’s annoyance at not being able to find out the secret of the mysterious box.
At first this was only the faint shadow of a Trouble. But it grew more solid every day, until before long the cottage of Epimetheus and Pandora was less sunny than the cottages of the other children.
“Where can the box have come from?” Pandora kept saying, to herself and to Epimetheus. “And what on earth can be inside it?”

“You’re always talking about this box!” said Epimetheus at last, for he had grown very tired of the subject. “Dear Pandora, I wish you would talk about something else. Come on, let’s go and pick some ripe figs and eat them under the trees for supper. And I know a vine that has the sweetest, juiciest grapes you ever tasted.”
“You’re always talking about grapes and figs!” cried Pandora crossly.
“All right, then,” said Epimetheus, who was an easygoing child, like so many children in those days. “Let’s run outside and have a wonderful time with our friends.”

“I’m tired of happy times, and I wouldn’t care if I never had another!” answered our cross little Pandora. “Besides, I never do have any. I can’t stop thinking about this ugly box. I insist that you tell me what is inside it.”
“I’ve told you fifty times already that I don’t know!” replied Epimetheus, growing a little annoyed. “So how can I tell you what’s inside?”
“You could open it,” said Pandora, giving Epimetheus a sideways look, “and then we would see for ourselves.”
“Pandora, what are you thinking?” exclaimed Epimetheus.

His face showed such horror at the idea of looking inside a box that had been entrusted to him on the condition that he never open it, that Pandora decided not to suggest it again. Still, she could not stop thinking and talking about the box.
“At least,” she said, “you can tell me how it got here.”

“A person left it at the door,” replied Epimetheus, “just before you came. He looked very cheerful and clever, and he could hardly keep from laughing as he set it down. He wore an odd sort of cloak and a cap that seemed to be made partly of feathers, so that it looked almost as if it had wings.”
“What kind of staff did he carry?” asked Pandora.
“Oh, the strangest staff you ever saw!” cried Epimetheus. “It looked like two snakes twisting around a stick, and they were carved so lifelike that at first I thought they were alive.”

“I know him,” said Pandora thoughtfully. “Nobody else has a staff like that. It was Quicksilver, and he brought me here as well as the box. He must have meant it for me. It probably holds pretty dresses for me to wear, or toys for you and me to play with, or something delicious for us both to eat!”
“Could be,” answered Epimetheus, turning away. “But until Quicksilver returns and says so, neither one of us is allowed to raise the lid.”
“How dull he is!” Pandora grumbled as Epimetheus walked out of the cottage. “If only he had a bit more daring!”

For the first time since she had arrived, Epimetheus had gone out without asking Pandora to come along. He went to pick figs and grapes by himself, or to look for some amusement in company other than his little playmate’s. He was sick to death of hearing about the box, and he wished with all his heart that Quicksilver, or whatever the messenger’s name was, had left it at some other child’s door, where Pandora would never have laid eyes on it. She chattered so stubbornly about this one thing! The box, the box, and nothing but the box! It seemed as if the box were bewitched, and as if the cottage were too small to hold it, because Pandora kept tripping over it and making Epimetheus trip over it too, until they had bruised all four of their shins.

It really was hard on poor Epimetheus to have a box ringing in his ears from morning till night. The little people of the earth were so unused to annoyances in those happy days that they had no idea how to handle them. So a small annoyance caused as much upset then as a far bigger one would in our own time.

After Epimetheus had gone, Pandora stood staring at the box. She had called it ugly more than a hundred times. But in spite of everything she had said against it, it was in fact a very handsome piece of furniture, and it would have been an ornament in any room. It was made of a lovely wood with dark, rich veins running over its surface, and it was polished so brightly that little Pandora could see her face in it. Since the child had no other mirror, it is odd that she did not value the box for that reason alone.

The edges and corners of the box were carved with wonderful skill. All around the border were graceful men and women and the prettiest children ever seen, resting or playing among a wealth of flowers and leaves. These figures were so beautifully made, and so harmoniously worked together, that the flowers, leaves and people seemed to join in one wreath of mingled beauty. But here and there, peeping out from behind the carved leaves, Pandora once or twice thought she saw a face that was not so lovely, or something unpleasant that stole the beauty from all the rest. Yet when she looked more closely and touched the spot with her finger, she could find nothing of the kind. Some perfectly beautiful face had only looked ugly because she had caught it out of the corner of her eye.

The most beautiful face of all was carved in high relief in the center of the lid. Nothing else was there except the dark, smooth richness of the polished wood and this one face, with a garland of flowers about its brow. Pandora had looked at this face many times, and she imagined that its mouth could smile if it liked, or turn serious when it chose, just like a living mouth. In fact, the whole face had a lively and rather mischievous look, as if it were about to burst out of the carved lips and speak.
If the mouth had spoken, it would probably have said something like this:

“Have no fear, Pandora! Where is the harm in opening the box? Pay no attention to poor, simple Epimetheus! You are cleverer than he is, and ten times bolder. Lift the lid and see whether something lovely isn’t waiting inside!”

I almost forgot to mention that the box was fastened, not with a lock or any such device, but with a very intricate knot of gold cord. The knot seemed to have no end and no beginning. Never was a knot so cleverly twisted, with so many loops and turns that slyly defied even the most skillful fingers to untangle them. And yet the very difficulty of it made Pandora want all the more to examine the knot and see how it was made. Two or three times already she had bent over the box and taken the knot between her thumb and finger, though without really trying to undo it.

“I honestly think I’m beginning to see how it was done,” she said to herself. “Maybe I could even tie it up again after undoing it. There could be no harm in that. Even Epimetheus wouldn’t blame me for that. I wouldn’t have to open the box, and of course I wouldn’t, without that silly boy’s permission, even if the knot were untied.”

It might have been better for Pandora if she had had some work to do, or anything at all to occupy her mind, so that she would not think so constantly about this one subject. But life was so easy for children before any Troubles came into the world that they had far too much free time. They could not play hide-and-seek among the flowering shrubs forever, or blind-man’s-buff with garlands over their eyes, or whatever other games had been invented while Mother Earth was still a baby. When life is all play, work becomes the real fun. There was simply nothing to do. A little sweeping and dusting around the cottage, I suppose, and picking fresh flowers (which grew far too thickly everywhere) and arranging them in vases, and poor little Pandora’s day’s work was done. And then, for the rest of the day, there was the box!

After all, I am not quite sure that the box wasn’t a blessing to her in its way. It gave her so many ideas to think about, and so much to talk about whenever she had anyone to listen! When she was in a good mood, she could admire the bright polish of its sides and the rich border of lovely faces and leaves running all around it. Or if she happened to be in a bad temper, she could shove it, or kick it with her naughty little foot. And many a kick the box got (though it was a mischievous box, as we shall see, and deserved every one of them). But it is certain that without the box, our busy-minded little Pandora would not have known half so well how to spend her time as she did now.

For it was truly endless work to guess what was inside. What could it be? Just imagine, my little listeners, how busy your minds would be if there were a big box in the house that you had reason to think held something new and pretty for your Christmas or New Year’s presents. Do you think you would be less curious than Pandora? If you were left alone with the box, might you not feel a little tempted to lift the lid? But of course you wouldn’t do it. Oh, shame! No, no! Only, if you thought there were toys in it, it would be very hard to pass up the chance of taking just one peek! I don’t know whether Pandora expected toys, because none had probably been made yet in those days, when the world itself was one great plaything for the children who lived on it. But Pandora was convinced that something beautiful and valuable was in the box, and so she was just as eager to peek as any of the little girls here around me would be. Perhaps even a little more eager, though I am not so sure of that.

But on this particular day, the one we have been talking about for so long, her curiosity grew much stronger than usual, and at last she walked up to the box. She was more than half decided to open it if she could. Ah, naughty Pandora!

First, though, she tried to lift it. It was heavy, much too heavy for the slender strength of a child like Pandora. She raised one end a few inches off the floor and let it drop again with a loud thump. A moment later she almost thought she heard something stir inside the box. She pressed her ear as close as she could and listened. There really did seem to be a sort of muffled murmur inside! Or was it only a ringing in Pandora’s ears? Or could it be the beating of her own heart? The child could not tell for certain whether she had heard anything or not. But in any case her curiosity was stronger than ever.
As she pulled her head back, her eyes fell on the knot of gold cord.
“Whoever tied this knot must have been very clever,” Pandora said to herself. “But I still think I could untie it. At least I’m determined to find the two ends of the cord.”

So she took the golden knot in her fingers and searched its twists and turns as keenly as she could. Almost without meaning to, or quite knowing what she was doing, she was soon hard at work trying to undo it. Meanwhile the bright sunshine came in through the open window, and so did the merry voices of the children playing in the distance, perhaps with the voice of Epimetheus among them. Pandora stopped to listen. What a beautiful day it was! Wouldn’t it be wiser to leave the troublesome knot alone, stop thinking about the box, and run to join her little playmates and be happy?

All this time, though, her fingers were half unconsciously busy with the knot. When she happened to glance at the flower-wreathed face on the lid of the enchanted box, she thought she saw it grinning slyly at her.
“That face looks very mischievous,” thought Pandora. “I wonder whether it’s smiling because I’m doing something wrong! I have a very good mind to run away!”
But just then, purely by accident, she gave the knot a sort of twist, with an astonishing result. The gold cord untwined itself as if by magic and left the box with no fastening.
“This is the strangest thing I ever knew!” said Pandora. “What will Epimetheus say? And how can I possibly tie it back together?”

She made one or two attempts to put the knot back, but soon found it far beyond her skill. It had come apart so suddenly that she could not remember how the strands had been folded into one another, and when she tried to recall the shape of the knot, it seemed to have vanished completely from her mind. There was nothing to do but leave the box as it was until Epimetheus came in.
“But,” said Pandora, “when he sees that the knot is untied, he will know I did it. How can I make him believe I haven’t looked inside the box?”

Then a thought slipped into her naughty little heart: since she would be suspected of having looked into the box anyway, she might just as well do so at once. Oh, very naughty and very foolish Pandora! You should have thought only about doing right and leaving wrong undone, not about what your playmate Epimetheus would say or believe. And so perhaps she would have, if the enchanted face on the lid had not seemed to look at her so bewitchingly, and if she had not seemed to hear, more clearly than ever, a murmur of tiny voices inside. Whether it was her imagination she could not tell, but she heard quite a little tumult of whispers in her ear—or perhaps it was only her curiosity doing the whispering—
“Let us out, dear Pandora—please let us out! We will be such lovely playmates for you! Just let us out!”

“What could it be?” thought Pandora. “Is something alive in the box? Well! Yes! I have made up my mind to take just one peek! Only one, and then I will shut the lid down as tightly as ever! There can’t possibly be any harm in one little peek!”
But now it is time to find out what Epimetheus was doing.

This was the first time since his little playmate had come to live with him that he had tried to enjoy himself in a way that left her out. But nothing went well, and he was not nearly as happy as on other days. He could not find a sweet grape or a ripe fig (if Epimetheus had a fault, it was being a little too fond of figs), and any he did find were overripe and so sweet they were sickening. There was no cheerfulness in his heart, the kind that usually made his voice burst out on its own and add to his friends’ merriment. In short, he grew so restless and unhappy that the other children could not imagine what was wrong with him. He did not know what ailed him either. For you must remember that in the time we are speaking of, it was everyone’s nature and constant habit to be happy. The world had not yet learned to be otherwise. Not one person, since these children were first sent to enjoy themselves on the beautiful earth, had ever been sick or out of sorts.

At last he realized that, somehow, he had put an end to all the games, and he decided it was best to go back to Pandora, who was in a mood closer to his own. But hoping to please her, he gathered some flowers and wove them into a wreath to put on her head. The flowers were lovely—roses, lilies, orange blossoms, and many more, which left a trail of fragrance behind as Epimetheus carried them along—and the wreath was made with as much skill as anyone could reasonably expect from a boy. It has always seemed to me that little girls have the best fingers for twining flower wreaths, but in those days boys could do it somewhat better than they can now.

And here I should mention that a great black cloud had been gathering in the sky for some time, though it had not yet covered the sun. But just as Epimetheus reached the cottage door, the cloud began to block the sunshine and suddenly made everything dim and sad.

He went in quietly, since he meant to sneak up behind Pandora if he could and toss the wreath over her head before she knew he was there. As it happened, there was no need to tread so lightly. He could have stomped as heavily as he liked—as heavily as a grown man—as heavily, I was about to say, as an elephant—and Pandora would hardly have heard him. She was too busy with her plan. At the moment he came into the cottage, the naughty child had put her hand on the lid and was just about to open the mysterious box. Epimetheus saw her. If he had cried out, Pandora would probably have taken her hand away, and the terrible secret of the box might never have been known.

But Epimetheus himself, though he said very little about it, was just as curious to know what was inside. Seeing that Pandora was determined to find out the secret, he decided that she should not be the only wise one in the cottage. And if there was anything pretty or valuable in the box, he intended to take half of it for himself. So, after all his sensible speeches to Pandora about holding back her curiosity, Epimetheus turned out to be every bit as foolish as she was, and almost as much to blame. Whenever we blame Pandora for what happened, then, we must not forget to shake our heads at Epimetheus too.

As Pandora raised the lid, the cottage turned dark and gloomy, because the black cloud had now swept completely over the sun and seemed to have buried it alive. For a little while there had been a low growling and muttering, and now it suddenly broke into a loud crash of thunder. But Pandora paid no attention to any of this. She lifted the lid almost straight up and looked inside. A sudden swarm of winged creatures seemed to brush past her and fly out of the box, and at the same moment she heard Epimetheus cry out in a miserable voice, as if he were in pain.
“Oh, I’m stung!” he cried. “I’m stung! Naughty Pandora! Why did you open this wicked box?”

Pandora dropped the lid and jumped up to look around and see what had happened to Epimetheus. The thundercloud had made the room so dark that she could not see clearly what was in it. But she heard an unpleasant buzzing, as if a great many huge flies, or giant mosquitoes, or those insects we call dor-bugs and pinching-dogs, were darting about. As her eyes got used to the dim light, she saw a crowd of ugly little shapes with bats’ wings. They looked horribly spiteful, and each had a terribly long stinger in its tail. One of them had stung Epimetheus. It was not long before Pandora herself began to scream, in just as much pain and fright as her playmate and making far more fuss about it. A hateful little monster had landed on her forehead, and I don’t know how deeply it would have stung her if Epimetheus had not run over and brushed it away.

Now, if you want to know what these ugly things were that had escaped from the box, I must tell you that they were the whole family of earthly Troubles. There were evil Passions. There were many kinds of Cares. There were more than a hundred and fifty Sorrows. There were Diseases, in a huge number of miserable and painful forms. There were more kinds of Naughtiness than it would do any good to talk about. In short, everything that has since afflicted the minds and bodies of human beings had been shut up in the mysterious box and given to Epimetheus and Pandora to keep safe, so that the happy children of the world would never be harmed by them. If they had been faithful to that trust, all would have gone well. No grown person would ever have been sad, and no child would have had any reason to shed a single tear, from that hour until this moment.

But—and you can see from this how one mortal’s wrong act brings disaster on the whole world—because Pandora lifted the lid of that wretched box, and because Epimetheus was also at fault for not stopping her, these Troubles have gained a foothold among us, and they do not seem likely to be driven away anytime soon. As you can easily guess, it was impossible for the two children to keep the ugly swarm inside their little cottage. On the contrary, the first thing they did was fling open the doors and windows, hoping to get rid of the creatures. Sure enough, the winged Troubles flew far and wide and pestered and tormented the small people everywhere, so much that none of them smiled for many days afterward. And, most strangely, all the flowers and dewy blossoms on earth, not one of which had ever faded before, began to droop and shed their leaves after a day or two. The children, too, who until then had seemed to stay children forever, now grew older day by day. Soon they were young men and women, and before long grown men and women, and then old people, before they ever dreamed such a thing could happen.

Meanwhile, naughty Pandora and hardly less naughty Epimetheus stayed in their cottage. Both had been badly stung and were in a good deal of pain. It seemed all the harder to bear because it was the very first pain felt since the world began. Naturally they were completely unused to it and had no idea what it meant. On top of that, they were in a dreadful mood, both with themselves and with each other. To give in to that mood as fully as possible, Epimetheus sat down sulkily in a corner with his back to Pandora, while Pandora threw herself on the floor and rested her head on the fatal, hateful box. She was crying bitterly and sobbing as if her heart would break.
All at once there came a gentle little tap on the inside of the lid.
“What could that be?” cried Pandora, lifting her head.
But either Epimetheus had not heard the tap, or he was too sulky to pay attention. Either way, he did not answer.
“How unkind you are,” said Pandora, sobbing again, “to say nothing to me!”
There it was again! It sounded like a fairy’s tiny knuckles, rapping lightly and playfully from inside the box.
“Who is there?” asked Pandora, a little of her old curiosity returning. “Who are you, shut up in this naughty box?”
A sweet little voice answered from inside—
“Just lift the lid, and you will see.”

“No, no,” answered Pandora, starting to sob again, “I have had enough of lifting the lid! You are inside the box, you naughty creature, and inside you will stay! There are plenty of your ugly brothers and sisters flying around the world already. Don’t think for a moment that I will be foolish enough to let you out!”
As she spoke she looked toward Epimetheus, perhaps expecting him to praise her good sense. But the sulky boy only muttered that she had become wise a little too late.

“Ah,” said the sweet little voice once more, “it would be far better to let me out. I am nothing like those naughty creatures with stingers in their tails. They are no relatives of mine, and you would know it at once if you could only get a peek at me. Come now, my pretty Pandora! I am sure you will let me out!”

And there truly was a kind of cheerful magic in the tone, which made it almost impossible to refuse anything this little voice asked. With every word from inside the box, Pandora’s heart had grown lighter without her noticing. Epimetheus, still in his corner, had turned half around and seemed to be in somewhat better spirits than before.
“My dear Epimetheus,” cried Pandora, “did you hear that little voice?”
“Yes, of course I did,” he answered, though not yet in a very good mood. “So what?”
“Shall I lift the lid again?” asked Pandora.

“Do as you like,” said Epimetheus. “You have done so much mischief already that you may as well do a little more. One more Trouble, among the whole swarm you have set loose on the world, can’t make much difference.”
“You might be a little nicer about it!” murmured Pandora, wiping her eyes.

“Ah, naughty boy!” cried the little voice inside the box, in a playful, laughing tone. “He knows he is longing to see me. Come, my dear Pandora, lift the lid. I am in a great hurry to comfort you. Just give me some fresh air, and you will soon see that things are not nearly as gloomy as you think!”
“Epimetheus,” exclaimed Pandora, “whatever happens, I have made up my mind to open the box!”
“The lid looks heavy,” cried Epimetheus, hurrying across the room, “so I will help you!”

So, in complete agreement, the two children lifted the lid again. Out flew a sunny, smiling little figure, who hovered around the room and lit up every place she went. Have you ever made sunshine dance into dark corners by reflecting it from a piece of mirror? That is how the winged cheerfulness of this fairy-like stranger looked in the gloom of the cottage. She flew to Epimetheus and touched the swollen spot where the Trouble had stung him with the very lightest touch of her finger, and at once the pain was gone. Then she kissed Pandora on the forehead, and her hurt was healed too.

After these kind deeds, the bright stranger fluttered playfully over the children’s heads and looked at them so sweetly that they both began to think it was not so terrible to have opened the box after all, since otherwise their cheerful guest would have stayed a prisoner among those naughty imps with stingers in their tails.
“Please, who are you, beautiful creature?” asked Pandora.

“My name is Hope!” answered the sunshiny figure. “And because I am such a cheerful little person, I was packed into the box to make up to humankind for that swarm of ugly Troubles that was meant to be let loose among them. Don’t be afraid! We will do quite well in spite of them all.”
“Your wings are the colors of a rainbow!” exclaimed Pandora. “They’re so lovely!”
“They are,” said Hope, “because glad as I am by nature, I am made partly of tears as well as smiles.”
“Will you stay with us,” Epimetheus asked, “for always?”

“For as long as you need me,” said Hope, smiling her pleasant smile—“and that means as long as you live in the world—I promise I will never abandon you. Now and then there may be seasons when you think I have disappeared for good. But again, and again, and again, just when you least expect it, you will see my wings glimmering on the ceiling of your cottage. Yes, my dear children, and I know of something very good and beautiful that you will be given one day!”
“Oh, tell us,” they exclaimed—“tell us what it is!”
“You mustn’t ask,” replied Hope, laying a finger on her rosy lips. “But do not lose heart, even if it never comes about while you live on this earth. Believe my promise, because it is true.”
“We do believe you!” cried Epimetheus and Pandora together, in a single breath.

And they did. Not only they, but everyone alive since then has trusted Hope. And to tell you the truth, I cannot help being glad—though it was certainly a very naughty thing for her to do—that our foolish Pandora peeked into the box. No doubt, no doubt, the Troubles are still flying around the world. They have grown in number rather than shrunk, and they are a very ugly bunch of imps with most poisonous stingers in their tails. I have felt them already, and I expect to feel them more as I grow older. But then there is that lovely, bright little figure of Hope! What in the world could we do without her? Hope gives the earth a spirit. Hope makes it always new. And even when the earth looks its best and brightest, Hope shows it to be only the shadow of an infinite happiness to come!
“Primrose,” said Eustace, pinching her ear, “what do you think of my little Pandora? Isn’t she just like you? Though you would not have waited nearly so long before opening the box.”

“Then I’d have been well punished for being naughty,” Primrose shot back cleverly, “because the first thing to jump out when I lifted the lid would have been Mr Eustace Bright, in the form of a Trouble.”
“Cousin Eustace,” said Sweet Fern, “was all the trouble that has ever come into the world really inside that box?”
“Every last bit of it!” Eustace answered. “This very snowstorm, which has ruined my skating, was packed away in there.”
“And how big was the box?” Sweet Fern asked.
“Oh, about three feet long,” said Eustace, “by two feet wide, and two and a half feet tall.”

“Oh,” said the child, “you’re teasing me, Cousin Eustace! I know there isn’t enough trouble in the whole world to fill a big box like that. And the snowstorm isn’t trouble at all. It’s fun. So it can’t have been in the box.”
“Listen to the child!” cried Primrose, putting on a superior air. “He knows so little about the troubles of this world! Poor fellow! He’ll be wiser once he has seen as much of life as I have.”
With that, she began skipping rope.

Meanwhile the day was coming to an end. Outside, the view certainly looked dreary. A gray swirl of snow filled the air far and wide in the gathering twilight, the ground was as trackless as the sky, and the snowbank piled over the porch steps showed that no one had come in or gone out for many hours. If there had been only one child at the window of Tanglewood, looking out at this wintry scene, it might have made him sad. But half a dozen children together, though they can’t quite turn the world into a paradise, can dare old Winter and all his storms to dampen their spirits. Eustace Bright, besides, made up several new kinds of games on the spot, and these kept them all roaring with laughter until bedtime, and lasted them through the next stormy day as well.

chapters.title: The Three Golden Apples
paragraphs: The snowstorm lasted one more day, though where it went afterward I really can’t imagine. At any rate, it cleared away completely during the night, and when the sun rose the next morning, it shone down on as bleak a stretch of hill country, here in Berkshire, as you could find anywhere in the world. Frost had covered the window panes so thickly that it was almost impossible to see the scenery outside. But while they waited for breakfast, the small population of Tanglewood scratched peepholes with their fingernails, and saw with great delight that, except for a bare patch or two on a steep hillside, and the gray look of the snow mixed in with the black pine forest, all of nature was as white as a sheet. How very pleasant! And to make it better still, it was cold enough to nip your nose clean off! If a person has enough life in him to stand it, nothing lifts the spirits like a bright, hard frost, or sets the blood rippling and dancing like a brook running down a hillside.

As soon as breakfast was over, the whole party, bundled up in furs and woolens, went stumbling out into the snow. What a day of frosty fun it was! They slid down the hill into the valley a hundred times, nobody knows how far, and to make it merrier they tipped over their sleds and tumbled head over heels almost as often as they reached the bottom safely. Once Eustace Bright took Periwinkle, Sweet Fern and Squash-Blossom on the sled with him, to make sure of a safe ride, and down they flew at top speed. But halfway down, the sled struck a hidden stump and threw all four passengers into a heap. When they picked themselves up, there was no little Squash-Blossom to be found! What could have become of the child? While they wondered and stared around, Squash-Blossom popped up out of a snowbank with the reddest face you ever saw, looking as though a big scarlet flower had suddenly sprouted in the middle of winter. Then everyone laughed and laughed.

When they were tired of sliding, Eustace set the children to digging a cave in the biggest snowdrift they could find. Unluckily, just as it was finished and they had all squeezed into the hollow, the roof fell in on their heads and buried every one of them alive! A moment later all their little heads popped up out of the wreckage, with the tall student’s head in the middle, looking white and venerable from the snow dust that had settled in his brown curls. Then, to punish Cousin Eustace for telling them to dig such a tumbledown cave, the children attacked him all together and pelted him with so many snowballs that he was glad to run for it.

So he ran off into the woods, and from there to the edge of Shadow Brook, where he could hear the little stream grumbling along under huge overhanging banks of snow and ice that hardly let it see daylight. Icicles as hard as diamond glittered around all its little waterfalls. From there he wandered to the shore of the lake and saw a white, untouched plain stretching from his own feet to the foot of Monument Mountain. It was nearly sunset, and Eustace thought he had never seen anything so fresh and beautiful. He was glad the children were not with him, because their lively spirits and tumbling about would have driven away his deeper, more serious mood. He would only have been merry, as he had been all day long, and would never have felt the loveliness of a winter sunset among the hills.

Once the sun had fully set, our friend Eustace headed home for supper. Afterward he retired to the study, intending, I rather suspect, to compose an ode, or a couple of sonnets, or some sort of verses praising the purple and golden clouds he had watched around the sinking sun. But he had not yet hammered out a single rhyme when the door swung open and in came Primrose and Periwinkle.
“Run along, children! I have no time for you right now!” the student cried, glancing back over his shoulder, pen still in hand. “What could you possibly want in here? I thought you were all in bed!”

“Listen to him, Periwinkle, trying to sound like a grown man!” said Primrose. “He seems to forget that I’m thirteen now and can stay up almost as late as I like. But, Cousin Eustace, you must drop your airs and come with us to the drawing room. The children have talked so much about your stories that my father wants to hear one, to judge whether they’re likely to do any harm.”

“Oh, come now, Primrose!” said the student, rather annoyed. “I don’t think I can tell one of my stories in front of grown-ups. Besides, your father is a classical scholar. Not that I’m very afraid of his scholarship, since I’m sure it’s as rusty as an old kitchen knife by now. But he’ll be bound to quarrel with the wonderful nonsense I put into these stories out of my own head, which is what makes them so charming for children like you. No man of fifty who read the classical myths in his youth could possibly appreciate my merit in reinventing and improving them.”

“All that may be perfectly true,” said Primrose, “but you must come anyway! My father won’t open his book, and Mamma won’t open the piano, until you’ve given us some of your nonsense, as you quite rightly call it. So be a good boy and come along.”

Whatever he pretended, on second thought the student was more glad than not to seize the chance to show Mr Pringle what a talent he had for modernizing the myths of ancient times. Until about twenty, a young man may well be shy about showing his poetry and prose, but all the same he is pretty likely to think these very works would put him at the top of literature if only people could see them. So, without much more resistance, Eustace let Primrose and Periwinkle drag him into the drawing room.

It was a large, handsome room with a half-round window at one end, and in the alcove of that window stood a marble copy of Greenough’s Angel and Child. On one side of the fireplace were many shelves of books, serious but richly bound. The white light of the astral lamp and the red glow of the bright coal fire made the room brilliant and cheerful. In front of the fire, in a deep armchair, sat Mr Pringle, looking exactly right for such a chair in such a room. He was a tall, rather handsome gentleman with a bald forehead, and he was always so neatly dressed that even Eustace Bright never liked to go into his presence without at least stopping at the door to straighten his shirt collar. But now, with Primrose holding one of his hands and Periwinkle the other, he had to make his entrance looking rough and rumpled, as if he had been rolling in a snowbank all day. And so he had.
Mr Pringle turned toward the student kindly enough, but in a way that made him feel how uncombed and unbrushed he was, and how uncombed and unbrushed his mind and thoughts were too.

“Eustace,” said Mr Pringle with a smile, “I hear you’re causing quite a stir among the little public of Tanglewood with your gift for storytelling. Primrose here, as the little ones like to call her, and the other children have praised your stories so loudly that Mrs Pringle and I are curious to hear a sample. It would please me all the more because the stories seem to be an attempt to put the fables of classical antiquity into the language of modern imagination and feeling. At least that’s what I gather from a few details that have reached me secondhand.”
“You’re not quite the listener I would have chosen, sir,” the student remarked, “for fantasies of this kind.”
“Perhaps not,” replied Mr Pringle. “But I suspect that a young author’s most useful critic is exactly the one he would be least likely to choose. So please oblige me.”

“I should think sympathy ought to have some small place among a critic’s qualifications,” Eustace Bright murmured. “However, sir, if you will bring the patience, I will bring the stories. But please remember that I’m speaking to the imagination and sympathies of the children, not to yours.”
And so the student grabbed the first subject that came to hand. It was suggested by a plate of apples he happened to notice on the mantelpiece.

Have you ever heard of the golden apples that grew in the garden of the Hesperides? Ah, those were apples that would fetch a great price by the bushel, if any could be found growing in orchards today! But I don’t suppose there is a single graft of that wonderful fruit on any tree in the wide world. Not even a seed of those apples exists anymore.

Even in the old, old, half-forgotten times, before the garden of the Hesperides was overgrown with weeds, many people doubted that there could be real trees with apples of solid gold on their branches. Everyone had heard of them, but nobody could remember seeing any. Still, children used to listen open-mouthed to stories of the golden apple tree, and made up their minds to find it when they were big enough. Adventurous young men who wanted to do something braver than their friends set out in search of this fruit. Many of them never came back, and none of them brought back the apples. No wonder they couldn’t pick them! They say there was a dragon under the tree with a hundred terrible heads, fifty of which were always awake and watching while the other fifty slept.

Personally, I think a solid golden apple was hardly worth running so much danger for. If the apples had been sweet, mellow and juicy, that would be another matter. Then it might have made sense to try to get at them, even with a hundred-headed dragon standing in the way.

But, as I’ve already told you, it was quite common for young people who were tired of too much peace and quiet to go looking for the garden of the Hesperides. And once the adventure was taken up by a hero who had known very little peace or quiet since the day he was born. At the time I’m speaking of, he was wandering through the pleasant land of Italy with a mighty club in his hand and a bow and quiver slung across his shoulders. He was wrapped in the skin of the biggest and fiercest lion that anyone had ever seen, which he had killed himself. Though he was, on the whole, kind and generous and noble, there was a good deal of the lion’s fierceness in his heart. As he went along, he kept asking whether this was the right road to the famous garden. But none of the country people knew anything about it, and many of them looked as if they would have laughed at the question if the stranger hadn’t been carrying such a very big club.
So he traveled on and on, still asking the same question, until at last he came to the bank of a river where some beautiful young women sat weaving wreaths of flowers.
“Pretty maidens,” the stranger asked, “could you tell me if I’m on the right road to the garden of the Hesperides?”

The young women had been having a lovely time together, weaving flowers into wreaths and crowning one another’s heads. There seemed to be a kind of magic in the touch of their fingers, because the flowers looked fresher and dewier, with brighter colors and sweeter scent, while the women played with them than they had when they were growing on their own stems. But when they heard the stranger’s question, they dropped all their flowers on the grass and stared at him in astonishment.
“The garden of the Hesperides!” cried one. “We thought mortals had grown tired of looking for it after so many disappointments. And tell us, adventurous traveler, what do you want there?”
“A certain king, who is my cousin,” he replied, “has ordered me to fetch him three of the golden apples.”

“Most of the young men who go looking for these apples,” another of the maidens remarked, “want them for themselves, or to give to some fair girl they love. Do you love this king, your cousin, so very much?”
“Maybe not,” the stranger replied with a sigh. “He has often been harsh and cruel to me. But it is my destiny to obey him.”
“And do you know,” asked the maiden who had spoken first, “that a terrible dragon with a hundred heads keeps watch under the golden apple tree?”
“I know it well,” the stranger answered calmly. “But since I was in my cradle, dealing with serpents and dragons has been my business, and almost my pastime.”

The young women looked at his huge club and the shaggy lion’s skin he wore, and at his powerful arms and legs and his tall frame. They whispered to one another that this stranger looked like someone who could fairly expect to do deeds far beyond what other men could manage. But then, the dragon with a hundred heads! What mortal, even with a hundred lives to spare, could hope to escape the fangs of such a monster? The maidens were so kind-hearted that they could not stand to watch this brave, handsome traveler try something so dangerous, and most likely end up as a meal for the dragon’s hundred hungry mouths.

“Go back,” they all cried, “go back to your own home! Your mother will weep for joy to see you safe and sound, and what more could she ask, however great a victory you won? Never mind the golden apples! Never mind the king, your cruel cousin! We don’t want the dragon with the hundred heads to eat you up!”

The stranger seemed to lose patience with these protests. He casually raised his mighty club and let it drop on a rock lying half buried in the ground nearby. That one careless blow smashed the great rock to pieces. It took him no more effort to show this giant’s strength than it would take one of the young maidens to brush her sister’s rosy cheek with a flower.
“Don’t you think,” he asked, smiling at the young women, “that a blow like that would have crushed one of the dragon’s hundred heads?”

Then he sat down on the grass and told them the story of his life, or as much of it as he could remember, starting from the day he was first rocked in a warrior’s bronze shield. As he lay there, two enormous serpents had come gliding across the floor and opened their horrible jaws to swallow him. And he, a baby only a few months old, had seized one of the savage snakes in each little fist and choked them both to death. When he was hardly more than a boy, he had killed a huge lion, almost as big as the one whose vast shaggy hide he now wore over his shoulders. The next thing he had done was to fight a battle with an ugly monster called a hydra, which had no fewer than nine heads, each with extremely sharp teeth.
“Remember, though,” one of the young women pointed out, “the dragon that guards the Hesperides has a hundred heads!”

“Even so,” the stranger answered, “I would rather fight two such dragons than one hydra. For every time I cut off a head, two more grew in its place. On top of that, one of the heads could not be killed at all, and it went on biting as fiercely as ever long after it had been cut off. So I had to bury it under a stone, where it is surely still alive today. But the hydra’s body and its other eight heads will never cause any more trouble.”

The young women could tell that the story was going to last a good while. So they had been getting ready a meal of bread and grapes, so that the stranger could refresh himself between parts of his tale. They enjoyed serving him this plain food. Now and then one of them would pop a sweet grape between her rosy lips, so that he wouldn’t feel shy about eating alone.

The traveler went on to tell how he had chased a very swift stag for a whole year without ever stopping to catch his breath, and had finally caught it by the antlers and carried it home alive. He had also fought a very strange race of people, half horse and half man, and had put every one of them to death out of a sense of duty, so that their ugly shapes would never be seen again. Besides all this, he gave himself great credit for having cleaned out a stable.
“And you call that wonderful?” one of the young women asked, smiling. “Any farmhand around here has done the same!”

“If it had been an ordinary stable,” the stranger replied, “I wouldn’t have mentioned it. But the job was so huge that it would have taken me my whole life, if I hadn’t had the luck to think of turning a river through the stable door. That got it done in no time!”

He saw how eagerly his lovely listeners were hanging on his words, so he went on to tell them how he had shot some monstrous birds, caught a wild bull alive and let it go again, tamed a number of very wild horses, and defeated Hippolyta, the warrior queen of the Amazons. He also mentioned that he had taken Hippolyta’s enchanted girdle and given it to the daughter of his cousin, the king.
“Was it the girdle of Venus,” asked the prettiest of the young women, “the one that makes women beautiful?”
“No,” the stranger answered. “It used to be the sword-belt of Mars, and all it can do is make the wearer brave and bold.”
“An old sword-belt!” cried the young woman, tossing her head. “Then I wouldn’t want it!”
“You’re quite right,” said the stranger.

Continuing his wonderful tale, he told the maidens that one of the strangest adventures of all was his fight with Geryon, the six-legged man. This was a very odd and frightful creature, as you can well imagine. Anyone who looked at his tracks in the sand or snow would think three friendly companions had been walking along together. Hearing his footsteps from a little way off, anyone would reasonably conclude that several people were coming. But it was only the strange man Geryon, clattering along on his six legs!
Six legs and one gigantic body! He must have been a very peculiar monster to look at, and, my stars, what a waste of shoe leather!
Having finished the tale of his adventures, he glanced around at the rapt faces of the young women.
“You may have heard of me already,” he said, with modesty. “I am Hercules!”

“We had already guessed,” the young women replied, “because your wonderful deeds are known all over the world. It no longer seems strange to us that you should set out in search of the golden apples of the Hesperides. Come, sisters, let’s crown the hero with flowers!”

Then they threw beautiful wreaths over his noble head and mighty shoulders, until the lion’s skin was almost covered with roses. They took hold of his heavy club and wound the brightest, softest, sweetest-smelling blossoms around it so thickly that not a finger’s width of the oak could be seen. It looked like one huge bunch of flowers. Last of all, they joined hands and danced around him, singing words that turned into poetry all by themselves and grew into a chorus in praise of the famous Hercules.

And Hercules was delighted, as any other hero would have been, to learn that these lovely young girls had heard of the brave deeds that had cost him so much hard work and danger. But still he was not satisfied. He could not believe that what he had already done deserved so much honor, while any bold or difficult adventure remained to be taken on.
“Dear maidens,” he said, when they stopped to catch their breath, “now that you know my name, won’t you tell me how to reach the garden of the Hesperides?”
“Oh! Must you leave so soon?” they exclaimed. “You, who have done so many wonders and lived such a hard life, can’t you be content to rest a little while beside this peaceful river?”
Hercules shook his head.
“I must leave now,” he said.
“Then we will give you the best directions we can,” the young women answered. “You must go to the seashore, find the Old One, and force him to tell you where the golden apples are to be found.”
“The Old One!” Hercules repeated, laughing at the odd name. “And who, may I ask, is the Old One?”

“Why, the Old Man of the Sea, of course!” one of the young women answered. “He has fifty daughters, whom some people call very beautiful, but we don’t think it proper to know them, because they have sea-green hair and taper off like fishes. You must talk to this Old Man of the Sea. He is a seafaring fellow and knows all about the garden of the Hesperides, because it lies on an island that he often visits.”

Hercules then asked where the Old One was most likely to be found. When the young women had told him, he thanked them for all their kindness: for the bread and grapes they had fed him, for the lovely flowers they had crowned him with, and for the songs and dances with which they had honored him. Most of all he thanked them for telling him the right way. Then he set off on his journey at once.
But before he was out of earshot, one of the young women called after him.

“Hold on tight to the Old One when you catch him!” she cried, smiling and raising her finger to make the warning more serious. “Don’t be astonished at anything that happens. Just hold him fast, and he will tell you what you want to know.”
Hercules thanked her again and went on his way, while the young women went back to their pleasant work of making flower wreaths. They talked about the hero long after he was gone.
“When he returns here with the three golden apples, having killed the dragon with a hundred heads,” they said, “we will crown him with the loveliest garlands we have.”

Meanwhile Hercules traveled steadily onward, over hills and valleys and through lonely woods. Sometimes he swung his club high and splintered a mighty oak with one sweeping blow. His mind was so full of the giants and monsters he fought for a living that perhaps he mistook the great tree for a giant or a monster. And Hercules was so eager to finish what he had set out to do that he almost regretted spending so much time with the young women, wasting his breath on the story of his adventures. But that is always how it is with people who are meant to do great things. What they have already done seems worth less than nothing. What they have taken on seems worth any hardship, any danger, and life itself.

Anyone passing through the forest must have been terrified to see him strike the trees with his great club. With a single blow the trunk would split as if struck by lightning, and the broad branches would come rustling and crashing down.

Hurrying forward, never stopping or looking back, he soon heard the sea roaring in the distance. At the sound he went faster, and before long he came to a beach where the great surf waves tumbled onto the hard sand in a long line of snowy foam. At one end of the beach, though, there was a pleasant spot where green shrubs climbed a cliff and made its rocky face look soft and lovely. A carpet of green grass, mixed thickly with sweet-smelling clover, covered the narrow space between the foot of the cliff and the sea. And what should Hercules spot there but an old man, fast asleep!

But was it really and truly an old man? At first glance it certainly looked like one. On a closer look, though, it seemed more like some kind of creature that lived in the sea. On his legs and arms there were scales, like those of a fish. He was web-footed and web-fingered, like a duck. And his long beard, which was tinged with green, looked more like a clump of seaweed than an ordinary beard. Have you ever seen a log that has been tossed about by the waves for a long time, all overgrown with barnacles, and that finally drifts ashore looking as if it had been thrown up from the very deepest part of the sea? Well, the old man would have reminded you of just such a wave-battered spar! But the instant Hercules laid eyes on this strange figure, he was sure it could be no one but the Old One, who was to show him the way.

Yes, it was the very same Old Man of the Sea that the hospitable young women had told him about. Thanking his lucky stars that he had found the old fellow asleep, Hercules crept toward him on tiptoe and seized him by an arm and a leg.
“Tell me,” he cried, before the Old One was properly awake, “which way is it to the garden of the Hesperides?”

As you can easily imagine, the Old Man of the Sea woke up in a fright. But his astonishment could hardly have been greater than that of Hercules a moment later. For suddenly the Old One seemed to vanish from his grasp, and he found himself holding a stag by a front leg and a hind leg! Still, he kept his grip. Then the stag vanished, and in its place was a sea bird, fluttering and screaming, while Hercules clutched it by wing and claw! But the bird could not get away. Right after that came an ugly three-headed dog, which growled and barked at Hercules and snapped fiercely at the hands that held it! But Hercules would not let go. A minute later, in place of the three-headed dog, who should appear but Geryon, the six-legged man-monster, kicking at Hercules with five of his legs to get the last one free! But Hercules held on. Soon there was no Geryon, but a huge snake, like the ones Hercules had strangled as a baby, only a hundred times bigger. It twisted and coiled around the hero’s neck and body, flung its tail high in the air, and opened its deadly jaws as if to swallow him whole. It was really a terrifying sight! But Hercules was not discouraged in the least, and he squeezed the great snake so tightly that before long it began to hiss with pain.

You must understand that the Old Man of the Sea, though he usually looked like the wave-beaten figurehead of a ship, could take on any shape he liked. When Hercules grabbed him so roughly, he had hoped that these magical changes would shock and terrify the hero so much that he would be glad to let him go. If Hercules had loosened his grip, the Old One would surely have dived down to the very bottom of the sea, and he would not have bothered to come up again soon to answer any rude questions. I suppose ninety-nine people out of a hundred would have been scared out of their wits by the very first of his ugly shapes and would have run away at once. For one of the hardest things in this world is to tell real dangers from imaginary ones.

But Hercules held on so stubbornly, and squeezed the Old One all the tighter at every change of shape, and caused him no small pain, that at last the Old One thought it best to appear in his own form again. So there he was once more, a fishy, scaly, web-footed sort of person, with something like a tuft of seaweed on his chin.

“What on earth do you want with me?” cried the Old One, as soon as he could catch his breath, for it is quite tiring to go through so many false shapes. “Why are you squeezing me so hard? Let me go this minute, or I will start to think you very rude indeed!”
“I am Hercules!” roared the mighty stranger. “You will not break out of my grip until you tell me the nearest way to the garden of the Hesperides!”

When the old fellow learned who had caught him, he saw at a glance that he would have to tell Hercules everything he wanted to know. The Old One lived in the sea, remember, and traveled everywhere, as seafaring people do. Naturally he had often heard of the fame of Hercules, of the marvelous deeds he was always performing in different parts of the world, and of how firmly he carried through anything he set out to do. So the Old Man gave up trying to escape. He explained to the hero how to find the garden of the Hesperides, and he also warned him of many hardships he would have to overcome before he got there.

“You must go on in such and such a direction,” said the Old Man of the Sea, after working out the compass points, “until you come in sight of a very tall giant who carries the sky on his shoulders. If he is in a talkative mood, he can tell you exactly where the garden of the Hesperides is.”
“And if he is not in a talkative mood,” said Hercules, balancing his club on one fingertip, “maybe I can think of a way to talk him into it!”

Hercules thanked the Old Man of the Sea, apologized for squeezing him so roughly, and set off on his journey again. He had a great many strange adventures along the way, which would be well worth hearing if I had time to tell them as fully as they deserve.

On this journey, if I remember rightly, he met an enormous giant who had been made by nature in such a remarkable way that every time he touched the earth he became ten times stronger than before. His name was Antaeus. You can easily see what a difficult business it was to fight such a fellow. Every time he was knocked down, up he jumped again, stronger, fiercer, and more skillful with his weapons than if his enemy had left him alone. So the harder Hercules pounded the giant with his club, the farther he seemed from winning. I have sometimes argued with people like that, but I have never fought one. The only way Hercules could end the battle was to lift Antaeus off his feet into the air and squeeze, and squeeze, and squeeze him, until all the strength had been squeezed out of that huge body.

After that was over, Hercules traveled on to the land of Egypt, where he was taken prisoner. He would have been put to death if he had not killed the king of the country and escaped. He crossed the deserts of Africa, hurrying as fast as he could, and at last reached the shore of the great ocean. Here it seemed that his journey must end, unless he could walk across the tops of the waves.

Nothing lay before him but the foaming, crashing, endless ocean. But suddenly, as he looked toward the horizon, he noticed something far away that had not been there a moment before. It shone very brightly, much like the round golden disk of the sun when it rises or sets at the edge of the world. It was plainly coming closer, because every moment this strange object grew larger and brighter. At last it came near enough for Hercules to see that it was an enormous cup or bowl, made either of gold or of polished brass. How it had come to be floating on the sea, I cannot tell you. There it was, anyway, rolling on the stormy waves, which tossed it up and down and heaved their foaming tops against its sides, but never splashed a drop over the rim.
“In my day I have met plenty of giants,” thought Hercules, “but none who needed a cup like this to hold his wine!”

And what a cup it was! It was as big as—as big as—well, I am afraid to say how enormously big it was. To stay within bounds, it was ten times larger than a great mill-wheel, and yet, solid metal as it was, it floated over the heaving waves more lightly than an acorn-cup down a brook. The waves rolled it along until it scraped against the shore, not far from where Hercules was standing.

The moment this happened, he knew what to do. He had been through too many remarkable adventures not to know how to act when something happened that was a little out of the ordinary.
