It was as clear as daylight that some unseen power had set this marvelous cup adrift and steered it to this spot to carry Hercules across the sea on his way to the garden of the Hesperides. So, without a moment’s delay, he climbed over the rim and slid down inside, where he spread out his lion’s skin and settled down for a little rest. He had hardly rested at all since saying farewell to the young women on the riverbank. The waves struck the sides of the hollow cup with a pleasant, ringing sound, and it rocked gently to and fro. The motion was so soothing that it soon rocked Hercules into a comfortable sleep.

His nap had probably lasted a good while when the cup happened to scrape against a rock. At once it rang and echoed through its golden or brazen body, a hundred times louder than any church bell you ever heard. The noise woke Hercules, who jumped up and looked around, wondering where he was. He soon found that the cup had floated across a large part of the sea and was nearing the shore of what looked like an island. And what do you think he saw on that island?

No, you will never guess, not if you tried fifty thousand times! It seems to me that this was the most marvelous sight Hercules had ever seen in all his wonderful travels and adventures. It was a greater wonder than the hydra with nine heads, which grew back twice as fast as they were cut off. It was greater than the six-legged monster in the shape of a man, and greater than Antaeus. It was greater than anything anyone ever saw, before or since the days of Hercules, or anything that travelers will ever see in all the ages to come. It was a giant!

But such an unbelievably big giant! He was as tall as a mountain. He was so vast that clouds rested around his middle like a belt, hung from his chin like a white beard, and drifted in front of his huge eyes, so that he could see neither Hercules nor the golden cup he was sailing in. And the most wonderful thing of all was that the giant held up his great hands and seemed to be holding up the sky, which, as far as Hercules could make out through the clouds, rested on his head! It really does seem almost too much to believe.

Meanwhile the shining cup floated on until it touched the beach. Just then a breeze blew the clouds away from the giant’s face, and Hercules saw all its enormous features: eyes each as big as a lake, a nose a mile long, and a mouth just as wide. It was a terrible face because of its size, but it looked sad and weary, like the faces of many people nowadays who are forced to carry burdens too heavy for them. What the sky was to the giant, the cares of the world are to people who let themselves be weighed down by them. And whenever people take on more than they can properly handle, they meet exactly the sort of fate that had fallen on this poor giant.

Poor fellow! He had clearly been standing there a long time. An ancient forest had been growing and dying around his feet, and oak trees six or seven hundred years old had sprouted from acorns and pushed their way between his toes.
The giant now looked down from the great height of his eyes, and when he noticed Hercules, he roared in a voice like thunder, coming out of the cloud that had just drifted away from his face.
“Who are you, down there at my feet? And where do you come from, in that little cup?”
“I am Hercules!” the hero thundered back, in a voice almost as loud as the giant’s own. “And I am looking for the garden of the Hesperides!”
“Ho! ho! ho!” roared the giant, with a burst of enormous laughter. “That is a wise adventure, indeed!”
“What is wrong with that?” cried Hercules, growing a bit angry at the giant’s laughter. “Do you think the dragon with a hundred heads scares me?”

Just then, while they were talking, some black clouds gathered around the giant’s middle and burst into a tremendous storm of thunder and lightning. It made such an uproar that Hercules could not make out a single word. All he could see were the giant’s immense legs, standing up into the darkness of the storm, and now and then a brief glimpse of his whole figure, wrapped in a heavy mist. He seemed to be speaking most of the time, but his big, deep, rough voice blended with the crashes of thunder and rolled away over the hills just like them. So, by talking at the wrong time, the foolish giant used up an enormous amount of breath for nothing, because the thunder was just as easy to understand as he was.

At last the storm passed, as suddenly as it had come. There again was the clear sky, and the weary giant holding it up, and the pleasant sunshine glowing over his vast height and lighting him against the background of sullen thunderclouds. His head had been so far above the shower that not one hair of it was wet from the raindrops!
When the giant saw that Hercules was still standing on the shore, he roared at him again.
“My name is Atlas, and I am the mightiest giant on earth! It is my head that holds up the sky!”
“I can see that,” Hercules answered. “Now, can you point out the way to the garden of the Hesperides?”
“What do you want there?” asked the giant.
“Three of the golden apples,” Hercules shouted back. “They are for my cousin the king.”

“Nobody but me,” said the giant, “can go to the garden of the Hesperides and pick the golden apples. If it were not for this little job of holding up the sky, I would take half a dozen steps across the sea and get them for you.”
“That is very kind of you,” replied Hercules. “And can’t you rest the sky on a mountain?”

“None of them is quite high enough,” said Atlas, shaking his head. “But if you stood on the top of that nearest one, your head would be almost level with mine. You look like a fellow with some strength. What if you took my load on your shoulders while I do your errand for you?”

Hercules, as you must be sure to remember, was a remarkably strong man. Holding up the sky takes a great deal of muscle, but if any mortal could be expected to manage it, he was the one. Still, it seemed such a difficult task that for the first time in his life he hesitated.
“Is the sky very heavy?” he asked.
“Oh, not especially, at the start,” answered the giant with a shrug. “But after a thousand years it begins to feel like a bit of a load!”
“And how much time,” the hero asked, “will you need to fetch the golden apples?”
“Oh, only a few moments,” cried Atlas. “With strides of ten or fifteen miles, I will be at the garden and back before your shoulders start to hurt.”
“Well, then,” answered Hercules, “I will climb the mountain behind you and take the weight off you.”

The truth is that Hercules had a kind heart, and he thought he would be doing the giant a favor by giving him this chance for a stroll. Besides, he thought it would bring him even more glory to boast that he had held up the sky than merely to do something as ordinary as defeating a dragon with a hundred heads. So, without more words, the sky was moved from the shoulders of Atlas onto those of Hercules.

Once this was safely done, the first thing the giant did was to stretch, and you can imagine what an amazing sight he was then. Next he slowly lifted one foot out of the forest that had grown up around it, and then the other. Then, all at once, he began to prance and leap and dance for joy at being free, flinging himself no one knows how high into the air and crashing down again with a jolt that made the earth shake. Then he laughed—Ho! ho! ho!—with a thundering roar that the mountains echoed far and near, as if they and the giant were brothers celebrating together. When his joy had calmed a little, he stepped into the sea: ten miles with the first stride, which brought him in up to mid-leg; ten miles with the second, when the water came just above his knees; and ten miles more with the third, which sank him almost to his waist. This was the deepest part of the sea.

Hercules watched the giant as he kept going, for it was truly a wonderful sight: this immense human shape, more than thirty miles away, half hidden in the ocean, while his upper half stood as tall, misty, and blue as a distant mountain. At last the gigantic figure faded completely from view. Now Hercules began to wonder what he would do if Atlas should drown in the sea, or if the dragon with the hundred heads, which guarded the golden apples of the Hesperides, should sting him to death. If any such misfortune happened, how would he ever get rid of the sky? And, by the way, its weight was already beginning to feel a little tiresome on his head and shoulders.
“I truly feel sorry for the poor giant,” thought Hercules. “If ten minutes wear me out this much, how worn out he must have been after a thousand years!”

Oh, my sweet little people, you have no idea what a weight there was in that same blue sky, which looks so soft and airy above our heads! And there was the blustering wind, and the cold, damp clouds, and the blazing sun, all taking their turns to make Hercules uncomfortable! He began to be afraid that the giant would never come back. He looked longingly at the world below him and admitted to himself that it was a far happier life to be a shepherd at the foot of a mountain than to stand on its dizzy top and hold up the heavens with all his might. For, as you will easily understand, Hercules had a huge responsibility on his mind as well as a weight on his head and shoulders. Why, if he did not stand perfectly still and keep the sky from moving, the sun might be knocked ajar! Or, after nightfall, a great many of the stars might be shaken loose and shower down like fiery rain on people’s heads! And how ashamed the hero would be if, because he wobbled under its weight, the sky should crack and show a great split right across it!

I don’t know how long it was before, to his unspeakable joy, he saw the huge figure of the giant, like a cloud, on the far-off edge of the sea. As Atlas came closer, he held up one hand, and Hercules could make out three magnificent golden apples in it, each as big as a pumpkin, all hanging from a single branch.
“I’m glad to see you back!” Hercules shouted as soon as the giant was close enough to hear. “So you have the golden apples?”

“Certainly, certainly,” Atlas answered. “And very fine apples they are. I picked the best ones on the whole tree, I promise you. Ah, what a lovely spot that garden of the Hesperides is! And the dragon with a hundred heads is a sight any man would be glad to see. Still, you might as well have gone for the apples yourself.”

“Never mind that,” Hercules replied. “You’ve had a pleasant stroll, and you’ve done the job as well as I could have done it. I thank you heartily for your trouble. Now, I have a long way to go and I’m rather in a hurry—and the king, my cousin, is eager to have the golden apples—so would you be kind enough to take the sky off my shoulders again?”

“Well, as to that,” said the giant, tossing the golden apples twenty miles into the air or thereabouts and catching them as they fell, “as to that, my good friend, I think you’re being a little unreasonable. Couldn’t I carry the apples to your cousin the king much faster than you could? If his majesty is in such a rush to get them, I promise to take my longest strides. Besides, I have no wish to burden myself with the sky just now.”

At this Hercules lost his patience and gave a great shrug of his shoulders. It was twilight by then, and if you had been watching, you might have seen two or three stars tumble out of their places. Everyone on earth looked up in alarm, afraid the sky might be about to fall next.

“Oh, that will never do!” cried Giant Atlas, roaring with laughter. “I haven’t let so many stars fall in the last five hundred years. Once you’ve stood there as long as I did, you’ll start to learn some patience!”
“What!” shouted Hercules in a rage. “Do you mean to make me carry this load forever?”

“We’ll see about that one of these days,” the giant answered. “In any case, you shouldn’t complain if you have to carry it for the next hundred years, or maybe the next thousand. I carried it much longer than that, and with a sore back, too. Well, then, after a thousand years, if I happen to feel like it, we may possibly trade places again. You’re certainly a very strong man, and you’ll never have a better chance to prove it. Future ages will talk about you, I guarantee it!”

“Bah! A fig for what they say!” cried Hercules, hitching his shoulders once more. “Just take the sky on your head for a moment, will you? I want to fold up my lion’s skin into a cushion for it to rest on. It really chafes me, and it will be needlessly uncomfortable over all the centuries I’m going to stand here.”

“That’s only fair, and I’ll do it!” said the giant. He felt no ill will toward Hercules; he was simply thinking too much of his own comfort. “Just for five minutes, then, I’ll take the sky back. Only five minutes, remember! I have no intention of spending another thousand years the way I spent the last. Variety is the spice of life, I always say.”

Ah, the thick-witted old rascal of a giant! He threw down the golden apples and took the sky back from the head and shoulders of Hercules onto his own, where it belonged. Hercules picked up the three golden apples, each as big as a pumpkin or bigger, and set off for home at once. He paid no attention at all to the giant’s thundering voice, bellowing after him to come back. Another forest sprang up around his feet and grew old there, and once again you could see oak trees six or seven centuries old that had grown to that age between his enormous toes.

And there the giant stands to this day. Or at least there stands a mountain as tall as he was, which carries his name; and when thunder rumbles around its summit, we may imagine it is the voice of Giant Atlas, bellowing after Hercules!
“Cousin Eustace,” Sweet Fern asked, gazing up from the storyteller’s feet with his mouth hanging open, “just how tall was this giant?”

“Oh, Sweet Fern, Sweet Fern!” cried the student. “Do you think I was there with a yardstick to measure him? Well, if you must know to a hair’s breadth, I suppose he might have been anywhere from three to fifteen miles straight up, and he might have sat down on Taconic and used Monument Mountain as a footstool.”
“My goodness!” said the good little boy, with a satisfied sort of grunt. “That really was a giant! And how long was his little finger?”
“As long as the distance from Tanglewood to the lake,” said Eustace.
“That really was a giant!” Sweet Fern said again, thrilled by how exact these measurements were. “And how wide, I wonder, were the shoulders of Hercules?”

“That’s something I’ve never been able to find out,” the student answered. “But I think they must have been a great deal broader than mine, or your father’s, or almost any shoulders you see nowadays.”
“Could you tell me,” Sweet Fern whispered, leaning right up to the student’s ear, “how big the oak trees were that grew between the giant’s toes?”
“Bigger,” said Eustace, “than the great chestnut tree standing past Captain Smith’s house.”

“Eustace,” Mr. Pringle said after some thought, “I find it impossible to give an opinion of this story that would please your pride as an author in the slightest. Let me advise you never to meddle with a classical myth again. Your imagination is thoroughly Gothic, and it will Gothicize everything it touches. The effect is like smearing paint over a marble statue. Take this giant, for instance! How could you dare to shove his huge, ill-proportioned bulk in among the graceful outlines of Greek legend, whose whole tendency is to keep even the extravagant within bounds by its all-pervading elegance?”

“I described the giant the way he appeared to me,” the student replied, rather stung. “And, sir, if you would only bring your mind to these fables in the way you must in order to reshape them, you would see at once that an old Greek had no more exclusive right to them than a modern Yankee has. They belong to the whole world, and to all time. The ancient poets reshaped them as they pleased and held them like soft clay in their hands. Why shouldn’t they be soft clay in my hands too?”
Mr Pringle could not help smiling.

“And besides,” Eustace went on, “the moment you put any warmth of heart into a classic mold, any passion or affection, any human or divine moral, you make it something quite different from what it was before. My own opinion is that the Greeks took possession of these legends, which had been the ancient birthright of all humankind, and gave them shapes of indestructible beauty, certainly, but cold and heartless ones. In doing so they did every later age a harm that cannot be measured.”

“And you, no doubt, were born to repair it,” said Mr Pringle, laughing out loud. “Well, well, go on. But take my advice and never put any of your travesties on paper. And for your next effort, what if you tried your hand at one of the legends of Apollo?”

“Ah, sir, you’re suggesting something impossible,” the student said after a moment’s thought. “And of course, at first glance, the idea of a Gothic Apollo does sound rather ridiculous. But I’ll turn your suggestion over in my mind, and I don’t entirely despair of success.”

While all this was being discussed, the children, who understood not a word of it, had grown very sleepy and were sent off to bed. Their drowsy chatter could be heard going up the staircase, while a northwest wind roared among the treetops of Tanglewood and played a hymn around the house. Eustace Bright went back to the study and tried again to hammer out some verses, but he fell asleep between two of the rhymes.

chapters.title: The Miraculous Pitcher
paragraphs: And when and where do you think we find the children next? No longer in winter, but in the merry month of May. No longer in the Tanglewood playroom or by the Tanglewood fireside, but more than halfway up a monstrous hill, or a mountain, as it would probably prefer to be called. They had left home with the mighty goal of climbing this high hill all the way to the very top of its bald head. True, it was not nearly as high as Chimborazo or Mont Blanc, and it was even a good deal lower than old Graylock. But it was certainly higher than a thousand anthills or a million molehills, and measured by the short strides of little children, it could fairly be counted a very respectable mountain.

And was Cousin Eustace with the party? You can be sure of it, or how could the book go any further? He was now in the middle of his spring vacation, and he looked much as we saw him four or five months ago, except that if you looked closely at his upper lip, you could make out the funniest little bit of a mustache. Leaving aside this sign of full manhood, you might have taken Cousin Eustace for just as much of a boy as when you first met him. He was as merry, as playful, as good-humored, as light of foot and spirit, and as much a favorite with the little folks as he had ever been. The whole expedition up the mountain was his idea. All the way up the steep slope he had encouraged the older children with his cheerful voice, and when Dandelion, Cowslip, and Squash-Blossom grew tired, he had carried them on his back, one after another. That was how they had made their way through the orchards and pastures on the lower part of the hill and reached the woods that stretch from there toward the bare summit.

So far, the month of May had been kinder than it often is, and this was as sweet and mild a day as any man or child could wish for. On their way up the hill, the little ones had found plenty of violets, blue and white, and some as golden as if Midas had touched them. The friendly little Houstonia, the most sociable of flowers, was everywhere. It is a flower that never lives alone. It loves its own kind and likes to live with a great many friends and relatives around it. Sometimes you see a family of them covering a patch no bigger than the palm of your hand, and sometimes a large community turning a whole stretch of pasture white, all keeping one another cheerful and alive.

Just inside the edge of the woods there were columbines, looking more pale than red because they were so modest and had thought it proper to hide away too carefully from the sun. There were wild geraniums too, and a thousand white strawberry blossoms. The trailing arbutus had not quite finished blooming, but it hid its precious flowers under last year’s withered forest leaves as carefully as a mother bird hides her little ones. It knew, I suppose, how beautiful and sweet-smelling they were. They were so cleverly hidden that the children sometimes caught the delicate richness of their perfume before they knew where it came from.

Amid so much new life, it was strange and truly sad to see, here and there in the fields and pastures, the gray old wigs of dandelions that had already gone to seed. They had finished with summer before summer had come. Inside those little globes of winged seeds, it was autumn already!

But we mustn’t waste our valuable pages on any more talk about springtime and wildflowers. We hope there is something more interesting to talk about. If you look at the group of children, you will see them all gathered around Eustace Bright, who is sitting on a tree stump and seems to be just about to begin a story. The truth is that the younger ones in the troop have discovered that it takes far too many of their short strides to cover the long climb up the hill. So Cousin Eustace has decided to leave Sweet Fern, Cowslip, Squash-Blossom, and Dandelion right here, halfway up, until the rest of the party comes back from the top. And because they grumble a little and don’t much like being left behind, he gives them some apples from his pocket and offers to tell them a very pretty story. At that they perk up and turn their sad faces into the broadest smiles.
I heard that story myself, crouched out of sight behind a bush, and in the next pages I will retell it to you.

One evening, long ago, old Philemon and his old wife Baucis were sitting at their cottage door, enjoying the calm and beautiful sunset. They had already eaten their simple supper and meant to spend a quiet hour or two before bedtime. So they talked about their garden, their cow, their bees, and their grapevine, which climbed over the cottage wall and whose grapes were just beginning to turn purple. But the rough shouts of children and the fierce barking of dogs in the nearby village grew louder and louder, until at last Baucis and Philemon could hardly hear each other speak.

“Ah, wife,” cried Philemon, “I’m afraid some poor traveler is asking our neighbors over there for hospitality, and instead of giving him food and a bed, they have set their dogs on him, as they always do!”

“Alas!” answered old Baucis. “I do wish our neighbors had a little more kindness for their fellow creatures. And just think of raising their children in such a wicked way, and patting them on the head when they throw stones at strangers!”

“Those children will never come to any good,” said Philemon, shaking his white head. “To tell you the truth, wife, I wouldn’t be surprised if something terrible happened to everyone in that village unless they change their ways. But as for you and me, as long as Providence gives us a crust of bread, let us be ready to share half of it with any poor, homeless stranger who comes along and needs it.”
“That’s right, husband!” said Baucis. “So we will!”

These old folks, you should know, were quite poor and had to work quite hard for a living. Old Philemon labored faithfully in his garden, while Baucis was always busy with her distaff, or making a little butter and cheese from their cow’s milk, or doing one thing or another around the cottage. Their food was seldom anything but bread, milk, and vegetables, with sometimes a bit of honey from their beehive and now and then a bunch of grapes ripened against the cottage wall. But they were two of the kindest old people in the world. They would gladly have gone without their dinners any day rather than refuse a slice of their brown loaf, a cup of fresh milk, and a spoonful of honey to a weary traveler who stopped at their door. They felt that such guests were somehow holy, and that they ought to treat them better and more generously than they treated themselves.

Their cottage stood on a rise of ground, a short way from a village. The village lay down in a hollow valley about half a mile wide. In ages past, when the world was young, this valley had probably been the bed of a lake. Fish had once glided back and forth in its depths, water plants had grown along its edges, and the trees and hills had looked down at their own reflections in its broad, calm surface. But the water had slowly drained away. People had begun to farm the land and build houses on it, until it became rich, fertile ground with no sign of the old lake left, except one very small brook that wound through the middle of the village and gave the people their water. The valley had been dry land for so long that oaks had sprouted, grown tall and mighty, and died of old age, and then other oaks, just as tall and stately, had taken their places. There was never a prettier or more fruitful valley. The very sight of so much plenty around them should have made the villagers kind and gentle, and eager to show their thanks to Providence by doing good to their fellow human beings.

But we are sorry to say that the people of this lovely village did not deserve to live in a place that Heaven had smiled on so generously. They were selfish and hard-hearted, with no pity for the poor and no sympathy for those without a home. They would only have laughed if anyone had told them that human beings owe a debt of love to one another, because that is the only way to repay the debt of love and care that all of us owe to Providence. You will hardly believe what I am about to tell you. These wicked people taught their children to be no better than themselves. They would even clap their hands to encourage the little boys and girls when they chased some poor stranger, shouting at his heels and pelting him with stones. They kept large, fierce dogs, and whenever a traveler dared to show himself in the village street, this pack of nasty curs would race out to meet him, barking, snarling, and baring their teeth. Then they would grab him by the leg or by his clothes, whichever they happened to catch. If he had been ragged when he arrived, he was usually a pitiful sight before he could run away. As you can imagine, this was a terrible thing for poor travelers, especially if they happened to be sick, weak, lame, or old. Anyone who found out how badly these unkind people, their unkind children, and their unkind dogs behaved would walk miles and miles out of the way rather than try to pass through that village again.

What made things seem even worse was this: when rich people came through in their carriages, or riding fine horses with servants in splendid uniforms following behind, nobody could have been more polite and fawning than the villagers. They would take off their hats and make the lowest bows you ever saw. If the children were rude, they were pretty sure to get their ears boxed. And if a single dog in the pack dared to yelp, its master beat it at once with a club and tied it up without any supper. All this would have been well enough, except that it showed the villagers cared a great deal about the money in a stranger’s pocket and nothing at all about the human soul, which lives just the same in the beggar and in the prince.

So now you can understand why old Philemon spoke so sadly when he heard the children shouting and the dogs barking at the far end of the village street. A confused uproar went on for a good while and seemed to sweep right across the whole width of the valley.
“I’ve never heard the dogs so loud!” remarked the kind old man.
“And I’ve never heard the children so rude!” answered his good old wife.

They sat shaking their heads at each other while the noise came closer and closer. At last they saw two travelers on foot, coming up to the bottom of the little hill where their cottage stood. The fierce dogs followed right behind them, snarling at their heels. A little farther back ran a crowd of children, who screamed shrilly and threw stones at the two strangers with all their strength. Once or twice the younger of the two men, a slender and very quick figure, turned around and drove the dogs back with a staff he carried in his hand. His companion, a very tall man, walked calmly on, as if he were too proud to notice either the wicked children or the pack of dogs whose manners the children seemed to copy.

Both travelers were dressed very plainly, and they looked as though they might not have enough money in their pockets to pay for a night’s lodging. I am afraid that was exactly why the villagers had let their children and dogs treat them so rudely.
“Come, wife,” said Philemon to Baucis, “let’s go and meet these poor people. I’m sure they feel almost too weighed down to climb the hill.”
“You go and meet them,” answered Baucis, “while I hurry inside and see whether we can find them something for supper. A nice bowl of bread and milk would do wonders to lift their spirits.”
So she hurried into the cottage. Philemon went forward and held out his hand, looking so welcoming that there was no need for words. But he spoke anyway, in the heartiest voice you can imagine—
“Welcome, strangers! Welcome!”

“Thank you!” replied the younger one, in a lively way, in spite of his weariness and trouble. “This is a very different greeting from the one we got down in the village. Tell me, why do you live in such a bad neighborhood?”
“Ah!” said old Philemon, with a quiet, gentle smile. “I hope Providence put me here, among other reasons, so that I could make up to you, as best I can, for my neighbors’ unkindness.”

“Well said, old father!” cried the traveler, laughing. “And to tell the truth, my companion and I could use some making up to. Those children, the little rascals, have splattered us nicely with mud balls. One of the dogs tore my cloak, which was ragged enough already. But I smacked him across the nose with my staff, and I think you may have heard him yelp, even from this far away.”

Philemon was glad to see him in such good spirits. Indeed, from the traveler’s look and manner you would never have guessed that he was worn out from a long day’s walk and discouraged by rough treatment at the end of it. He was dressed in a rather odd way, with a kind of cap on his head whose brim stuck out over both ears. Although it was a summer evening, he wore a cloak, which he kept wrapped tightly around him, perhaps because the clothes underneath were shabby. Philemon noticed, too, that he wore a strange pair of shoes. But it was getting dark, and the old man’s eyesight was none too sharp, so he could not tell exactly what was strange about them. One thing, at least, seemed peculiar. The traveler was so wonderfully light and quick that his feet seemed to rise off the ground by themselves from time to time, or could only be kept down with an effort.
“I used to be light on my feet when I was young,” Philemon said to the traveler. “But I always found my feet got heavier toward nightfall.”
“Nothing beats a good staff for helping a man along,” answered the stranger, “and I happen to have an excellent one, as you see.”

In fact, this was the oddest-looking staff Philemon had ever seen. It was made of olive wood, and near the top it had something like a little pair of wings. Two snakes were carved into the wood, twisting around the staff, and they were done so skillfully that old Philemon, whose eyes, as you know, were growing dim, almost thought they were alive and could see them wriggling and writhing.
“A curious piece of work, sure enough!” he said. “A staff with wings! It would make a fine stick for a little boy to ride on!”
Meanwhile, Philemon and his two guests had arrived at the door of the cottage.

“Friends,” said the old man, “please sit on this bench and rest. Baucis, my good wife, has gone to see what supper she can scrape together. We are poor people, but whatever is in our cupboard is yours.”

The younger stranger flopped carelessly down on the bench and let his staff fall as he did so. Then something rather marvelous happened, though it was small enough, too. The staff seemed to get up off the ground by itself. Spreading its little wings, it half hopped and half flew over and leaned itself against the cottage wall. There it stood perfectly still, except that the snakes kept on wriggling. But in my own private opinion, old Philemon’s eyes had been playing tricks on him again.
Before he could ask any questions, the older stranger spoke to him and drew his attention away from the wonderful staff.
“Wasn’t there,” the stranger asked, in a remarkably deep voice, “a lake in very ancient times, covering the spot where that village now stands?”

“Not in my day, friend,” answered Philemon, “and yet I am an old man, as you see. There were always the fields and meadows, just as they are now, and the old trees, and the little stream murmuring through the middle of the valley. My father never saw it any other way, as far as I know, and neither did his father before him. And I’m sure it will still be the same when old Philemon is gone and forgotten!”

“That is more than anyone can safely predict,” said the stranger, and there was something very stern in his deep voice. He shook his head, so that his dark, heavy curls swung with the movement. “Since the people of that village have forgotten the love and sympathy that belong to human nature, it would be better if the lake were rippling over their houses again!”

The traveler looked so stern that Philemon was almost frightened. What made it worse was that, when the stranger frowned, the twilight seemed suddenly to grow darker, and when he shook his head, something like a roll of thunder sounded in the air.

But a moment later the stranger’s face became so kind and gentle that the old man forgot his fear. Still, he could not help feeling that this older traveler must be no ordinary person, even though he happened to be dressed so humbly and to be traveling on foot. Philemon did not imagine him to be a prince in disguise or anything of that sort. He thought of him rather as some extremely wise man who wandered the world in this poor clothing, scorning wealth and all worldly things, and looking everywhere to add a little to his wisdom. This idea seemed all the more likely because, when Philemon looked up into the stranger’s face, he seemed to see more thought there in a single glance than he could have worked out in a lifetime.

While Baucis was getting supper ready, both travelers started chatting in a friendly way with Philemon. The younger one in particular was very talkative, and he made such sharp, witty remarks that the good old man kept bursting into laughter. He declared that this was the merriest fellow he had met in many a day.
“Tell me, my young friend,” he said, as they grew comfortable together, “what may I call you?”
“Why, I’m very quick, as you see,” answered the traveler. “So if you call me Quicksilver, the name will suit me fairly well.”

“Quicksilver? Quicksilver?” repeated Philemon, looking into the traveler’s face to see whether he was making fun of him. “That’s a very odd name! And what about your companion there? Does he have a name just as strange?”
“You’ll have to ask the thunder to tell you that!” replied Quicksilver, putting on a mysterious look. “No other voice is loud enough.”

Whether this remark was serious or a joke, it might have filled Philemon with great awe of the older stranger, if he had not seen so much kindness in the man’s face when he dared to look at it. Still, there was no doubt that here was the grandest figure that ever sat so humbly beside a cottage door. When the stranger talked, he spoke with dignity, and in such a way that Philemon felt an irresistible urge to tell him everything that was closest to his heart. People always feel this way when they meet someone wise enough to understand all of their good and bad sides and to look down on not one bit of it.

But Philemon was a simple, kind-hearted old man, and he did not have many secrets to share. Still, he chatted away happily about the events of his past life, in all of which he had never been twenty miles from this very spot. He and his wife Baucis had lived in the cottage since they were young, earning their bread by honest work, always poor but still content. He told how excellent Baucis’s butter and cheese were, and how fine the vegetables were that he grew in his garden. He also said that they loved each other so much that they both wished death would not separate them, but that they would die just as they had lived, together.
The stranger listened, and a smile lit up his face, making it as gentle as it was majestic.
“You are a good old man,” he told Philemon, “and you have a good old wife to stand beside you. Your wish deserves to be granted.”
And just then it seemed to Philemon that the sunset clouds shot up a bright flash from the west and set the sky suddenly aglow.
Baucis now had supper ready. Coming to the door, she began to apologize for the poor fare she had to put before her guests.

“If we had known you were coming,” she said, “my husband and I would have gone without a bite ourselves, so that you could have a better supper. But I used most of today’s milk to make cheese, and our last loaf is already half eaten. Oh dear! I never feel the sorrow of being poor except when a poor traveler knocks at our door.”

“All will be well, so don’t trouble yourself, my good woman,” replied the older stranger kindly. “An honest, hearty welcome works miracles on any meal, and can turn the plainest food into nectar and ambrosia.”
“You’ll have a welcome,” cried Baucis, “and a little honey that we happen to have left, and a bunch of purple grapes besides.”
“Why, Mother Baucis, it’s a feast!” exclaimed Quicksilver, laughing. “An absolute feast! And you’ll see how bravely I play my part in it! I don’t think I have ever felt hungrier in my life.”
“Goodness!” Baucis whispered to her husband. “With an appetite like that in the young man, I fear we won’t have anywhere near enough supper!”
They all went into the cottage.

And now, my little listeners, shall I tell you something that will make you open your eyes very wide? It is really one of the oddest parts of the whole story. Quicksilver’s staff, you remember, had stood itself up against the cottage wall. Well, when its master went in through the door and left this wonderful staff behind, what should it do but spread its little wings at once and go hopping and fluttering up the doorsteps! Tap, tap, went the staff across the kitchen floor, and it did not stop until it stood itself on end, with the greatest seriousness and good manners, beside Quicksilver’s chair. But old Philemon and his wife were so busy looking after their guests that neither of them noticed what the staff had been up to.

As Baucis had warned, the supper for the two hungry travelers was a meager one. In the middle of the table sat the leftover end of a brown loaf, with a piece of cheese on one side and a dish of honeycomb on the other. Each guest had a decent bunch of grapes. At one corner of the table stood an earthen pitcher of middling size, nearly full of milk. But once Baucis had filled two bowls and set them in front of the strangers, only a little milk was left at the bottom. It is a sad thing, alas, when a generous heart is hemmed in and squeezed by poverty. Poor Baucis wished she could go hungry for a whole week afterward, if only that would buy these hungry folk a bigger supper.
And since the meal was so very small, she couldn’t help wishing that her guests had smaller appetites. Why, the moment they sat down, both travelers had emptied their bowls of milk in a single gulp.
“A little more milk, if you please, kind Mother Baucis,” said Quicksilver. “It has been a hot day, and I’m terribly thirsty.”

“Oh, my dear people,” Baucis answered, flustered, “I am so sorry and so ashamed! The truth is, there’s hardly a drop left in the pitcher. Oh, husband! husband! Why didn’t we just go without our supper?”

“Well, now,” cried Quicksilver, jumping up from the table and taking the pitcher by its handle, “I think things aren’t nearly as bad as you make them out. There is certainly more milk in this pitcher.”

With these words, and to Baucis’s great astonishment, he filled not only his own bowl but his companion’s too, from a pitcher everyone had thought was nearly empty. The good woman could hardly believe her eyes. She had poured out almost all the milk herself, and as she set the pitcher on the table she had glanced inside and seen the bottom.
“But I’m old,” Baucis thought to herself, “and I forget things. I suppose I must have made a mistake. In any case, the pitcher can’t help being empty now, after filling those bowls twice over.”
“What excellent milk!” said Quicksilver, when he had drained the second bowl. “Forgive me, my kind hostess, but I really must ask you for a little more.”

Now Baucis had seen as clearly as she had ever seen anything that Quicksilver had turned the pitcher upside down, and so had poured out every last drop when he filled the second bowl. There simply couldn’t be any left. Still, to show him exactly how matters stood, she lifted the pitcher and made the motion of pouring milk into his bowl, without the faintest idea that anything would come out. Imagine her surprise when such a plentiful stream came bubbling out that the bowl filled to the brim and ran over onto the table! The two snakes twisted around Quicksilver’s staff (though neither Baucis nor Philemon noticed this) stretched out their heads and began to lap up the spilled milk.

And what a delicious smell that milk had! It seemed as though Philemon’s only cow must have grazed that day on the richest grass anywhere in the world. How I wish, my dear little ones, that every one of you could have a bowl of such milk at suppertime!
“Now cut me a slice of that brown loaf, Mother Baucis,” said Quicksilver, “and give me a little of that honey!”

So Baucis cut him a slice. When she and her husband ate that loaf, it had been too dry and crusty to be much of a pleasure, but now it was as soft and moist as if it had come out of the oven only a few hours before. She tasted a crumb that had dropped on the table and found it better than any bread had ever been. She could hardly believe it was a loaf she had kneaded and baked herself. And yet, what other loaf could it be?

But oh, the honey! I may as well not try to describe how wonderful it smelled and looked. Its color was that of the purest, clearest gold, and it smelled like a thousand flowers, though not the kind that ever grew in an earthly garden, but the kind the bees must have flown high above the clouds to find. The strange thing is that, after settling on a flower bed of such sweet scent and undying bloom, they were willing to fly back down to their hive in Philemon’s garden. No one ever tasted, saw, or smelled such honey. Its perfume drifted through the kitchen and made it so lovely that if you had shut your eyes, you would at once have forgotten the low ceiling and the smoky walls, and imagined yourself in an arbor hung with heavenly honeysuckle.

Good Mother Baucis was a simple old woman, but even she couldn’t help thinking that something quite out of the ordinary was going on. So after she had served her guests bread and honey and laid a bunch of grapes beside each plate, she sat down next to Philemon and whispered to him what she had seen.
“Did you ever hear of such a thing?” she asked.

“No, never,” Philemon answered with a smile. “And I rather think, my dear old wife, that you’ve been walking around in a kind of dream. If I had poured the milk, I would have understood it right away. There happened to be a little more in the pitcher than you thought. That’s all.”
“Ah, husband,” said Baucis, “think what you like, but these are no ordinary people.”
“Well, well,” Philemon replied, still smiling, “maybe they are. They certainly look as if they’ve seen better days, and I’m heartily glad to see them having such a comfortable supper.”

Each guest had by now put his bunch of grapes on his plate. Baucis rubbed her eyes to see better, and she was sure the clusters had grown bigger and richer, and that every single grape looked ready to burst with ripe juice. She couldn’t understand how such grapes could have grown on the old stunted vine that climbed the cottage wall.
“These are splendid grapes!” said Quicksilver, swallowing one after another without seeming to make his bunch any smaller. “Tell me, my good host, where did you pick them?”
“From my own vine,” Philemon answered. “You can see one of its branches twisting across the window over there. But my wife and I never thought the grapes were anything special.”
“I’ve never tasted better,” said the guest. “Another cup of that delicious milk, please, and then I will have dined better than a prince.”

This time old Philemon got up himself and took the pitcher, for he was curious to find out whether there was any truth in the marvels Baucis had whispered to him. He knew his good wife never lied and was seldom wrong about what she believed she had seen, but this was such a strange case that he wanted to look into it with his own eyes. So he picked up the pitcher and slyly peeked inside, and he was quite sure it held not a single drop. Then all at once he saw a little white fountain bubbling up from the bottom, and it quickly filled the pitcher to the brim with foaming, wonderfully fragrant milk. It was lucky that Philemon, in his astonishment, didn’t drop the miraculous pitcher.
“Who are you, you wonder-working strangers?” he cried, even more bewildered than his wife had been.

“We are your guests, my good Philemon, and your friends,” replied the elder traveler, in a gentle, deep voice that was at once sweet and awe-inspiring. “Give me a cup of the milk too. And may your pitcher never be empty, for kind Baucis and yourself, any more than for the needy wanderer!”

When supper was over, the strangers asked to be shown where they could rest. The old couple would gladly have talked with them a while longer, and told them how amazed they were, and how delighted that their poor, meager supper had turned out so much better and more plentiful than they had hoped. But the elder traveler had filled them with such awe that they didn’t dare ask him any questions. And when Philemon took Quicksilver aside and asked how on earth a fountain of milk had got into an old earthen pitcher, the younger traveler simply pointed to his staff.

“There’s the whole secret,” said Quicksilver, “and if you can work it out, I’d be grateful if you’d tell me. I don’t know what to make of my staff. It is always playing tricks like this, sometimes getting me a supper and just as often stealing one away. If I believed in such nonsense, I’d say the stick was bewitched!”

He said nothing more, but looked into their faces so slyly that they rather suspected he was laughing at them. The magic staff went hopping at his heels as Quicksilver left the room. Left alone, the good old couple talked for a little while about the evening’s events, and then lay down on the floor and fell fast asleep. They had given their bedroom to the guests and had no other bed, only these planks, which I wish had been as soft as their own hearts.

The old man and his wife were up early in the morning, and the strangers rose with the sun and got ready to leave. Philemon warmly urged them to stay a little longer, until Baucis could milk the cow, bake a cake on the hearth, and maybe find a few fresh eggs for breakfast. But the guests thought it best to cover a good part of their journey before the heat of the day set in. So they insisted on leaving at once, but asked Philemon and Baucis to walk a short way with them and show them the road they should take.

So all four of them left the cottage, chatting like old friends. It was truly remarkable how quickly the old couple felt at home with the elder traveler, and how their good, simple spirits blended into his, the way two drops of water would melt into the boundless ocean. As for Quicksilver, with his sharp, quick, laughing wits, he seemed to spot every little thought that so much as peeped into their minds before they knew it themselves. They did sometimes wish he weren’t quite so quick, and that he would throw away his staff, which looked so mysteriously mischievous with the snakes forever writhing around it. But then Quicksilver was so good-humored that they would have been overjoyed to keep him in their cottage, staff, snakes, and all, every day and all day long.

“Ah me! Alas!” Philemon exclaimed, when they had gone a little way from the door. “If only our neighbors knew what a blessing it is to show kindness to strangers, they would tie up all their dogs and never let their children throw another stone.”
“It’s a sin and a shame, the way they behave, that it is!” cried good old Baucis, fiercely. “And I mean to go this very day and tell some of them what wicked people they are!”
“I’m afraid,” said Quicksilver, with a sly smile, “that you won’t find any of them at home.”

Just then the elder traveler’s brow took on such a grave, stern, and awesome grandeur, yet calm all the same, that neither Baucis nor Philemon dared speak a word. They looked up into his face with reverence, as if they were gazing at the sky.

“When people do not feel toward even the humblest stranger as if he were a brother,” said the traveler, in a voice so deep it sounded like an organ, “they are unworthy to live on this earth, which was made to be the home of one great human brotherhood!”

“And by the way, my dear old friends,” cried Quicksilver, with the liveliest look of fun and mischief in his eyes, “where is this village you keep talking about? Which side of us is it on? I don’t seem to see it anywhere around here.”

Philemon and his wife turned toward the valley where, at sunset only the day before, they had seen the meadows, the houses, the gardens, the clumps of trees, the wide, green-edged street with children playing in it, and every sign of busy, happy, prosperous life. But how astonished they were! There was no village to be seen! Even the fertile valley in whose hollow it lay no longer existed. In its place they saw the broad blue surface of a lake, filling the great basin of the valley from rim to rim and mirroring the surrounding hills as calmly as if it had been there since the world began. For a moment the lake lay perfectly smooth. Then a little breeze sprang up and set the water dancing, glittering, and sparkling in the early sunbeams, and splashing with a pleasant rippling murmur against the near shore.

The lake looked so strangely familiar that the old couple were deeply puzzled, and felt as if they must only have dreamed that a village had ever stood there. But the next moment they remembered the vanished houses, and the faces and characters of the people who had lived in them, far too clearly for a dream. The village had been there yesterday, and now it was gone!
“Alas!” cried the kind-hearted old people. “What has become of our poor neighbors?”

“They no longer exist as men and women,” said the elder traveler, in his grand, deep voice, while a roll of thunder seemed to echo it from far away. “There was neither use nor beauty in a life like theirs, for they never softened or sweetened the hard lot of mortal life with kindly feeling between one person and another. They kept no image of a better life in their hearts. And so the lake that was there long ago has spread out again, to reflect the sky!”

“And as for those foolish people,” said Quicksilver, with his mischievous smile, “they have all been turned into fishes. It took very little change, since they were already a scaly bunch of rascals and the coldest-blooded creatures alive. So, kind Mother Baucis, whenever you or your husband feel like a dish of broiled trout, he can drop in a line and pull out half a dozen of your old neighbors!”
“Oh no,” cried Baucis, shuddering, “I wouldn’t put one of them on the gridiron for anything in the world!”
“No,” added Philemon, pulling a face, “we could never bring ourselves to eat them!”

“As for you, good Philemon,” the elder traveler went on, “and you, kind Baucis, poor as you are, you put so much heartfelt welcome into the way you treated a homeless stranger that the milk became an endless spring of nectar, and the brown loaf and the honey were ambrosia. So the gods have feasted at your table on the same food that fills their banquets on Olympus. You have done well, my dear old friends. Therefore ask whatever favor lies nearest your hearts, and it is granted.”
Philemon and Baucis looked at each other, and then, though I don’t know which of the two it was who spoke, that one said aloud the wish of both their hearts.
“Let us live out our lives together, and leave the world in the very same moment when we die! We have always loved each other so!”
“So be it!” the stranger replied, with majestic kindness. “Now look toward your cottage!”

They did as he said. But how astonished they were to see a tall white marble building, with a wide-open doorway, standing on the very spot where their humble little cottage had been only a moment before!

“There is your home,” said the stranger, smiling kindly at them both. “Be as generous with your hospitality in that palace over there as you were in the poor hovel where you welcomed us last evening.”
The old couple dropped to their knees to thank him. But when they looked up, he was gone, and so was Quicksilver.

So Philemon and Baucis moved into the marble palace. They spent their days, to their great satisfaction, making every passerby feel merry and comfortable. I should not forget to say that the milk-pitcher kept its marvelous gift of never being empty whenever someone needed it full. Any honest, good-humored, open-hearted guest who drank from it always found it the sweetest, most refreshing drink that ever went down his throat. But if some sour, disagreeable grump took a sip, he was sure to screw his face into a hard knot and declare it a pitcher of spoiled milk!

The old couple lived in their palace for a very long time, growing older and older, until they were very old indeed. Then came a summer morning when Philemon and Baucis did not appear as they did every other morning, with one welcoming smile shining on both their kind faces, to invite the overnight guests to breakfast. The guests searched the huge palace from top to bottom, and found nothing. But after much puzzling, they noticed two venerable trees standing in front of the doorway. Nobody could remember seeing them the day before. Yet there they stood, their roots sunk deep in the soil, and their wide spread of leaves shading the whole front of the building. One was an oak, and the other a linden. Their branches were twined together and wrapped around each other, which was strange and beautiful to see, so that each tree seemed to live in the other’s heart far more than in its own.

The guests were wondering how two trees that must have needed at least a hundred years to grow could have become so tall and ancient in a single night, when a breeze rose and set the tangled branches swaying. Then a deep, broad murmur filled the air, as though the two mysterious trees were speaking.
“I am old Philemon!” murmured the oak.
“I am old Baucis!” murmured the linden.

But as the breeze grew stronger, both trees spoke at the same moment: “Philemon! Baucis! Baucis! Philemon!” It sounded as if each were both, and both were one, talking together from the depths of their shared heart. It was plain enough that the good old couple had become young again, and were now to spend a quiet, happy hundred years or so, Philemon as an oak and Baucis as a linden. And oh, what welcoming shade they threw all around! Whenever a traveler stopped beneath it, he heard a pleasant whisper in the leaves above his head, and wondered why the sound was so much like these words:
“Welcome, welcome, dear traveler, welcome!”

And some kind person, who knew what would have pleased old Baucis and old Philemon most, built a round seat circling both their trunks. For a long time afterward, tired, hungry, and thirsty people rested there and drank all the milk they wanted from the miraculous pitcher.
And for all our sakes, I wish we had that pitcher here right now!

“How much did the pitcher hold?” asked Sweet Fern. “It held less than a quart,” the student answered. “But you could keep pouring milk out of it until you had filled a huge barrel, if you liked. The truth is that it would flow forever and never run dry, even in the middle of summer, which is more than anyone can say for that little stream over there, babbling down the hillside.”
“And what happened to the pitcher?” asked the little boy.

“I’m sorry to say it was broken about twenty-five thousand years ago,” Cousin Eustace replied. “The people mended it as well as they could. It held milk well enough after that, but nobody ever saw it fill itself again. So you see, it was no better than any other cracked clay pitcher.”
“What a shame!” all the children cried together.

The respectable dog Ben had come along with the group, and so had a half-grown Newfoundland puppy named Bruin, who was as black as a bear. Ben was elderly and very careful in his habits, so Cousin Eustace politely asked him to stay behind with the four little children and keep them out of trouble. Black Bruin was little more than a child himself, so the student thought it best to take him along, in case his rough play with the other children tripped them up and sent them tumbling down the hill. He told Cowslip, Sweet Fern, Dandelion, and Squash-Blossom to sit quite still where he left them. Then he, Primrose, and the older children started up the slope and were soon out of sight among the trees.

chapters.title: The Chimæra
paragraphs: Eustace Bright and his companions climbed up the steep, wooded hillside. The trees had not yet come into full leaf, but their buds had opened enough to cast a light shade, while the sunshine filled them with green glow. Moss-covered rocks lay half hidden among the old brown fallen leaves. Rotten tree trunks lay stretched out where they had fallen long ago, and broken branches, shaken down by winter gales, were scattered everywhere. Still, though all these things looked old, the woods felt full of brand-new life, because wherever you looked, something fresh and green was shooting up, getting ready for summer.

At last the young people reached the upper edge of the woods and found themselves almost at the top of the hill. It was not a peak, nor a great round dome, but a fairly wide plateau, with a house and a barn standing some distance away. That house was the home of a single family, and often the clouds that dropped rain and sent snowstorms drifting down into the valley hung lower than this bleak, lonely dwelling.

On the highest point of the hill there was a heap of stones, with a long pole stuck in the middle and a little flag fluttering at its tip. Eustace led the children over to it and told them to look around and see how much of our beautiful world they could take in at one glance. Their eyes grew wide as they looked.

Monument Mountain, to the south, still stood in the middle of the view, but it seemed to have sunk down, so that now it was just one ordinary member of a big family of hills. Beyond it, the Taconic range looked taller and bulkier than before. Our pretty lake could be seen with all its little bays and inlets, and not only that, but two or three new lakes were opening their blue eyes to the sun. Several white villages, each with its steeple, were scattered across the distance. There were so many farmhouses, with their acres of woodland, pasture, hayfields, and plowed land, that the children could hardly find room in their minds for so many different sights. And there was Tanglewood, which they had always thought of as the most important point in the world. It now took up so little space that they looked far past it and to either side, searching with all their eyes for a good while before they found where it stood.

White, fluffy clouds floated in the sky and cast dark patches of shadow here and there across the land. But soon the sunshine would be where the shadow had been, and the shadow would be somewhere else.

Far to the west lay a range of blue mountains, which Eustace Bright told the children were the Catskills. Somewhere among those hazy hills, he said, was a spot where some old Dutchmen were playing an endless game of nine-pins, and where a lazy fellow named Rip Van Winkle had fallen asleep and slept for twenty years straight. The children eagerly begged Eustace to tell them all about this wonderful business. But the student answered that the story had already been told once, and better than anyone could ever tell it again. Nobody, he said, had any right to change a word of it until it had grown as old as “The Gorgon’s Head,” “The Three Golden Apples,” and the rest of those miraculous legends.
“At least,” said Periwinkle, “while we rest here and look around, you can tell us another one of your own stories.”

“Yes, Cousin Eustace,” Primrose cried, “you should tell us a story right here. Choose something grand, and let’s see whether your imagination can climb that high. The mountain air might make a poet of you for once. And however strange or marvelous the tale, up here among the clouds we’ll believe anything.”
Eustace asked, “Could you believe that a horse with wings once lived?”
“Yes,” said saucy Primrose, “but I’m afraid you’ll never manage to catch him.”

“As for that, Primrose,” the student shot back, “I might very well catch Pegasus and climb on his back too, just as a dozen other fellows I know of might. In any case, here is a story about him, and of all places in the world, it surely ought to be told on a mountaintop.”
So Eustace sat down on the pile of stones while the children gathered around its base. He fixed his eyes on a white cloud sailing past and began.
The Chimaera

Once, in the old, old days (for all the strange things I am telling you about happened long before anyone can remember), a fountain gushed out of a hillside in the marvelous land of Greece. For all I know, after so many thousands of years, it is still gushing from the very same spot. In any case, there was the pleasant fountain, bubbling freshly up and sparkling down the hillside in the golden sunset, when a handsome young man named Bellerophon came up to its edge. In his hand he held a bridle, set with brilliant jewels and fitted with a golden bit. He saw an old man, a man of middle age, and a little boy near the fountain, and also a young woman dipping water into a pitcher. He stopped and asked if he might refresh himself with a drink.

“This is wonderfully delicious water,” he told the young woman, after he had drunk from her pitcher, rinsed it, and filled it again. “Would you be kind enough to tell me whether the fountain has a name?”

“Yes, it’s called the Fountain of Pirene,” the young woman answered. Then she added, “My grandmother told me that this clear fountain was once a beautiful woman. When her son was killed by the arrows of the huntress Diana, she melted away completely into tears. So the water you find so cool and sweet is the sorrow of that poor mother’s heart!”

“I never would have guessed,” said the young stranger, “that such a clear spring, with its gush and gurgle and its cheerful dance out of the shade into the sunlight, had even one teardrop in it! So this is Pirene? Thank you, pretty maiden, for telling me its name. I have come from a faraway country to find this very spot.”
A middle-aged country fellow, who had driven his cow to drink at the spring, stared hard at young Bellerophon and at the handsome bridle in his hand.

“The streams must be running low in your part of the world, friend,” he remarked, “if you came all this way just to find the Fountain of Pirene. But tell me, have you lost a horse? I see you’re carrying a bridle, and a very pretty one it is, with that double row of bright stones on it. If the horse was as fine as the bridle, I pity you for losing him.”

“I haven’t lost any horse,” said Bellerophon with a smile. “But I am looking for a very famous one, which wise people have told me can be found around here, if anywhere. Do you know whether the winged horse Pegasus still haunts the Fountain of Pirene, as he did in your forefathers’ days?”
But the country fellow just laughed.

Some of you, my little friends, have probably heard that this Pegasus was a snow-white horse with beautiful silvery wings, who spent most of his time on the top of Mount Helicon. He was as wild, as swift, and as light in his flight through the air as any eagle that ever soared into the clouds. There was nothing else like him in the world. He had no mate. No master had ever ridden him or put a bridle on him, and for many long years he lived a lonely and happy life.

Oh, what a fine thing it is to be a winged horse! Pegasus slept at night on a high mountaintop and spent most of the day in the air, so he hardly seemed a creature of the earth. Whenever he was seen far above people’s heads, with the sunshine on his silvery wings, you would have thought he belonged to the sky, and that he had flown a little too low and strayed into our mists and vapors, and was trying to find his way back. It was lovely to watch him plunge into the fluffy heart of a bright cloud, vanish in it for a moment or two, and then burst out the other side. Or in a gloomy rainstorm, when a gray floor of clouds covered the whole sky, the winged horse would sometimes dive right down through it, and the glad light of the upper sky would gleam after him. A moment later, it is true, both Pegasus and the cheerful light would be gone together. But anyone lucky enough to see this wonderful sight felt cheerful for the rest of the day, and for as long afterward as the storm lasted.

In summertime, in the loveliest weather, Pegasus often landed on solid ground, folded his silvery wings, and galloped over hill and valley for fun, as swift as the wind. He had been seen more often near the Fountain of Pirene than anywhere else, drinking the delicious water or rolling on the soft grass at its edge. Sometimes he would even nibble a few of the sweetest clover blossoms, though Pegasus was very fussy about his food.

So people’s great-grandfathers had made a habit of going to the Fountain of Pirene, as long as they were young and still believed in winged horses, hoping to catch a glimpse of the beautiful Pegasus. But in recent years he had hardly been seen at all. In fact, many of the country folk who lived within half an hour’s walk of the fountain had never laid eyes on Pegasus and did not believe such a creature existed. The country fellow Bellerophon was speaking to happened to be one of those doubters.
And that was why he laughed.

“Pegasus, indeed!” he cried, sticking his nose in the air as high as such a flat nose would go. “Pegasus, indeed! A flying horse! Have you lost your wits, friend? What good would wings be to a horse? Do you suppose he could pull a plow any better with them? Sure, you might save a little on horseshoes. But how would you like to watch your horse sail out the stable window? Or whisk you up above the clouds when all you wanted was a ride to the mill? No, no! I don’t believe in any Pegasus. Nobody ever made such a ridiculous horse-bird!”
“I have some reason to think differently,” Bellerophon said calmly.

Then he turned to an old, gray-haired man who was leaning on a stick and listening closely, with his head thrust forward and one hand cupped to his ear, since he had been rather deaf for the past twenty years.
“And what do you say, venerable sir?” he asked. “You must have seen the winged steed often enough in your younger days, I would think!”

“Ah, young stranger, my memory is very poor!” said the old man. “As a boy, if I remember right, I believed there was such a horse, and so did everyone else. These days, though, I hardly know what to think, and I rarely think about the winged horse at all. If I ever saw the creature, it was a very, very long time ago, and to be honest, I doubt that I ever did. I do remember that once, when I was quite young, I saw some hoofprints around the edge of the fountain. Pegasus might have made them. So might any other horse.”

“And you, my fair girl, have you never seen him?” Bellerophon asked the maiden, who stood with her pitcher on her head while this conversation went on. “If anyone could see Pegasus, it would be you, with such bright eyes.”

“Once I thought I did,” the girl answered, smiling and blushing. “It was either Pegasus or a big white bird, very far up in the sky. And another time, when I was coming to the fountain with my pitcher, I heard a neigh. Oh, it was such a lively, musical neigh! My heart jumped for joy at the sound. But it frightened me too, and I ran home without filling my pitcher.”
“What a shame!” said Bellerophon.
Then he turned to the child I mentioned at the start of the story, who was staring up at him with his rosy mouth hanging open, the way children like to stare at strangers.
“Well, little fellow,” Bellerophon said, giving one of his curls a playful tug, “I suppose you have seen the winged horse many times.”
“I have,” the child replied at once. “I saw him yesterday, and lots of times before that.”
“You’re a fine little man!” said Bellerophon, drawing the child close against him. “Come now, tell me all about it.”

“Well,” said the child, “I come here a lot to sail my little boats in the fountain and pick pretty pebbles out of the basin. Sometimes, when I look down into the water, I see the winged horse reflected in the picture of the sky. I wish he would come down and take me on his back and fly me up to the moon! But if I even move to look at him, he flies far away, out of sight.”

Bellerophon put his trust in the child, who had seen Pegasus’s image in the water, and in the maiden, who had heard his lovely neigh. He trusted them rather than the middle-aged lout who believed only in cart horses, or the old man who had forgotten the beautiful things of his youth.

So he lingered by the Fountain of Pirene for many days afterward. He kept constant watch, looking up at the sky or down into the water, always hoping to see either the horse’s reflection or the wonderful real thing. He kept the bridle, with its bright jewels and golden bit, ready in his hand. The country people who lived nearby and drove their cattle to the fountain to drink often laughed at poor Bellerophon, and sometimes scolded him quite sharply. They told him that a strong young man like himself should have better things to do than waste his time on such a silly pursuit. They offered to sell him a horse if he wanted one, and when Bellerophon turned them down, they tried to haggle with him over his fine bridle.

Even the village boys thought him so foolish that they made a great game of mocking him, and they were rude enough not to care that Bellerophon could see and hear them. One little rascal, for instance, would play Pegasus and cut the funniest capers, pretending to fly, while a schoolmate chased after him holding a twist of bulrushes meant to stand for Bellerophon’s fancy bridle. But the gentle child who had seen Pegasus in the water comforted the young stranger more than all the naughty boys could torment him. The dear little fellow often sat down beside him during his playtime, and without saying a word, looked down into the fountain and up at the sky with such innocent faith that Bellerophon could not help feeling encouraged.
Now you may want to know why Bellerophon had set out to catch the winged horse. We won’t find a better time to explain than now, while he waits for Pegasus to appear.

If I told you all of Bellerophon’s earlier adventures, they could easily turn into a very long story. It is enough to say that in a certain country of Asia, a terrible monster called a Chimaera had appeared, and it was causing more harm than anyone could describe between now and sunset. According to the best reports I have been able to get, this Chimaera was nearly, if not quite, the ugliest and most poisonous creature, the strangest and most baffling, the hardest to fight and the most difficult to escape, that ever crawled out of the inside of the earth. It had a tail like a boa constrictor, and a body like I-don’t-care-what, and it had three separate heads: one a lion’s, the second a goat’s, and the third a hideously huge snake’s. A hot blast of flame came roaring out of each of its three mouths! Since it was an earthly monster, I doubt it had any wings, but wings or no wings, it ran like a goat and a lion and slithered like a serpent, so that it managed to go about as fast as all three together.

Oh, the harm, and harm, and harm that this wicked creature did! With its flaming breath it could set a forest on fire, or burn up a field of grain, or even a whole village, fences and houses and all. It laid waste to the entire countryside, and it would eat people and animals alive and then cook them in the blazing oven of its belly. Heaven help us, little children, I hope neither you nor I ever happen to meet a Chimaera!

While this hateful beast (if we can call it a beast at all) was doing all these horrible things, Bellerophon happened to come to that part of the world to visit the king. The king’s name was Iobates, and the country he ruled was Lycia. Bellerophon was one of the bravest young men in the world, and wanted nothing so much as to do some valiant and generous deed that would make everyone admire and love him. In those days, the only way for a young man to make a name for himself was to fight battles, whether against his country’s enemies, or wicked giants, or troublesome dragons, or wild beasts when he could find nothing more dangerous to face. King Iobates saw the courage of his young guest and suggested that he go and fight the Chimaera, which everyone else was afraid of and which, unless it was killed soon, would likely turn Lycia into a desert. Bellerophon did not hesitate for a moment. He promised the king that he would either kill the dreaded Chimaera or die trying.

But first, since the monster was so tremendously fast, he realized that he would never win by fighting on foot. The wisest thing to do was to find the very best and swiftest horse anywhere. And what other horse in the whole world was even half as swift as the marvelous Pegasus, who had wings as well as legs and was even more nimble in the air than on the ground? Of course, a great many people denied that any such winged horse existed, and said the stories about him were all poetry and nonsense. But however wonderful it seemed, Bellerophon believed that Pegasus was a real horse, and hoped he might be lucky enough to find him. Once he was properly mounted on his back, he would be able to fight the Chimaera on much better terms.

That was why he had traveled from Lycia to Greece, carrying the beautifully decorated bridle in his hand. It was an enchanted bridle. If he could only slip the golden bit into Pegasus’s mouth, the winged horse would give in, accept Bellerophon as his master, and fly wherever he chose to turn the rein.

But it was a weary and anxious time, as Bellerophon waited and waited for Pegasus, hoping he would come to drink at the Fountain of Pirene. He worried that King Iobates might think he had run away from the Chimaera. It pained him, too, to think of all the harm the monster was doing while he sat idle, staring into the bright waters of Pirene as they bubbled up out of the sparkling sand, instead of fighting it. And since Pegasus had come there so rarely in recent years, and hardly landed there more than once in a lifetime, Bellerophon feared he might grow old, with no strength left in his arms and no courage in his heart, before the winged horse appeared. Oh, how slowly time passes while an adventurous young man longs to play his part in life and gather the harvest of his fame! What a hard lesson it is to wait! Our life is short, and how much of it is spent learning only this!

It was lucky for Bellerophon that the gentle child had grown so fond of him and never tired of keeping him company. Every morning the child gave him a fresh hope to tuck into his heart in place of yesterday’s withered one.
“Dear Bellerophon,” he would say, looking hopefully up into his face, “I think we’ll see Pegasus today!”

In the end, without the little boy’s unshaken faith, Bellerophon would have given up all hope. He would have gone back to Lycia and done his best to kill the Chimaera without the winged horse’s help. In that case, poor Bellerophon would at the very least have been badly scorched by the creature’s breath, and most likely killed and eaten. Nobody should ever try to fight an earth-born Chimaera unless he can first get onto the back of a steed of the air.
One morning the child spoke to Bellerophon with even greater hope than usual.
“Dear, dear Bellerophon,” he said, “I don’t know why, but I feel as if we will surely see Pegasus today!”

He would not move a step from Bellerophon’s side all that day. They shared a crust of bread and drank some of the fountain’s water. In the afternoon, they sat there, Bellerophon with his arm around the child, who in turn had slipped one little hand into Bellerophon’s. Bellerophon was lost in thought, staring blankly at the trunks of the trees shading the fountain and at the grapevines climbing among their branches. But the gentle child was gazing down into the water. He was sad, for Bellerophon’s sake, that another day’s hope would be disappointed like so many before it, and two or three silent tears dropped from his eyes and mingled with the many tears Pirene was said to have shed when she wept for her slain children.
But when Bellerophon was thinking of something else entirely, he felt the squeeze of the child’s small hand and heard a soft, almost breathless whisper.
“Look there, dear Bellerophon! There’s a picture in the water!”

Looking down into the dimpled mirror of the fountain, the young man saw what he took for the reflection of a bird flying at a great height in the air, with sunlight gleaming on its snow-white or silver wings.
“It must be a magnificent bird!” he said. “It looks so big, though it must really be flying above the clouds!”

“It makes me shiver!” the child whispered. “I’m afraid to look up at the sky! It’s so beautiful, but I only dare look at its picture in the water. Dear Bellerophon, can’t you see that it isn’t a bird? It’s the winged horse Pegasus!”

Bellerophon’s heart began to pound! He stared hard at the sky but could not make out the winged creature, bird or horse, because it had just plunged into the fluffy depths of a summer cloud. But in only a moment it came out again, drifting lightly down from the cloud, though still very far above the earth. Bellerophon scooped the child into his arms and shrank back with him, so that they were both hidden in the thick bushes growing all around the fountain. He was not afraid of any harm. He only feared that if Pegasus caught sight of them, he would fly far away and land on some unreachable mountaintop. For it really was the winged horse. After all their long waiting, he was coming to quench his thirst with the water of Pirene.

Closer and closer came the wonder of the air, flying in great circles, like a dove about to land.
