Pegasus came down in those wide, sweeping circles, which grew narrower and narrower as he slowly neared the ground. The closer he came, the more beautiful he looked, and the more marvelous the sweep of his silvery wings. At last, so lightly that he hardly bent the grass around the fountain or left a hoofprint in the sand at its edge, he landed, lowered his wild head, and began to drink. He drew in the water with long, contented sighs and calm pauses to enjoy it, and then took another drink, and another, and another. For nowhere in the world, or up among the clouds, did Pegasus love any water as much as this water of Pirene. When his thirst was quenched, he nibbled a few of the honey-sweet clover blossoms, tasting them delicately but not caring to make a hearty meal, since the grass just under the clouds on the high slopes of Mount Helicon suited his taste better than this ordinary grass.

Pegasus drank until he was satisfied, then daintily condescended to nibble a little food. After that he began to caper back and forth and dance about, out of pure idleness and play. No creature was ever made more playful than this very Pegasus. He frisked around in a way that delights me even to think about, fluttering his great wings as lightly as any linnet and running little races, half on the ground and half in the air, so that I can’t say whether it was a flight or a gallop. When a creature can fly perfectly well, he sometimes chooses to run, just for the fun of it. So it was with Pegasus, though it cost him some effort to keep his hoofs so close to the ground. Meanwhile Bellerophon, still holding the child’s hand, peeped out from the bushes. He thought he had never seen anything so beautiful, and never a horse with eyes as wild and spirited as those of Pegasus. It seemed a sin even to think of bridling him and riding on his back.

Once or twice Pegasus stopped and sniffed the air. He pricked up his ears, tossed his head and turned it every which way, as if he half suspected some trick. But he saw nothing and heard nothing, and soon he went back to his antics.

At last, not because he was tired but only because he felt lazy and pampered, Pegasus folded his wings and lay down on the soft green grass. But he was too full of life of the air to stay still for more than a moment, and soon he rolled onto his back with his four slender legs kicking in the air. It was lovely to watch him, this solitary creature who had never had a mate made for him and who needed no companion. He lived many hundreds of years, and was as happy as the centuries were long. The more he did the things ordinary horses do, the less earthly and the more wonderful he seemed. Bellerophon and the child almost held their breath, partly out of delighted awe, but even more because they feared that the slightest movement or whisper would send him shooting off like an arrow into the farthest blue of the sky.

At last, when he had rolled over and over enough, Pegasus turned himself around and lazily, just like any other horse, stretched out his front legs to get up. Bellerophon had guessed he would, and he sprang suddenly out of the thicket and leaped onto his back.
Yes, there he sat, on the back of the winged horse!

But what a leap Pegasus made when he felt the weight of a mortal man on his back for the first time! What a leap indeed! Before he could draw a breath, Bellerophon found himself five hundred feet up and still shooting higher, while the winged horse snorted and shook with terror and rage. Up he went, up, up, up, until he plunged into the cold, misty heart of a cloud, one that Bellerophon had been gazing at a little while earlier and imagining to be a very pleasant place. Then Pegasus shot back out of the middle of the cloud and plunged down like a thunderbolt, as if he meant to smash himself and his rider headlong against a rock. After that he performed something like a thousand of the wildest leaps and twists ever attempted by a bird or a horse.

I can’t tell you half of what he did. He skimmed straight ahead, and sideways, and backward. He reared up with his front legs resting on a ribbon of mist and his hind legs on nothing at all. He kicked out behind and dropped his head between his front legs, with his wings pointing straight up. About two miles above the earth he turned a somersault, so that Bellerophon’s heels were where his head should have been, and he seemed to be looking down into the sky instead of up. Pegasus twisted his head around and looked Bellerophon in the face with fire flashing from his eyes, and he made a terrible attempt to bite him. He beat his wings so wildly that one of the silver feathers was shaken loose. It floated down to earth, where the child picked it up, and he kept it as long as he lived in memory of Pegasus and Bellerophon.

But Bellerophon, who as you can guess was as good a horseman as ever galloped, had been watching for his chance, and at last he slipped the golden bit of the enchanted bridle between the winged steed’s jaws. The moment he did, Pegasus became as obedient as if he had eaten from Bellerophon’s hand all his life. To tell you honestly how I feel, it was almost sad to see so wild a creature suddenly turn so tame. Pegasus seemed to feel the same way. He looked around at Bellerophon with tears in his beautiful eyes, where only a moment before there had been fire. But when Bellerophon patted his head and spoke a few firm but kind and soothing words, a different look came into the eyes of Pegasus, for in his heart he was glad, after so many lonely centuries, to have found a companion and a master.
That is always how it goes with winged horses and with all such wild, solitary creatures. If you can catch them and master them, it is the surest way to win their love.

While Pegasus had been doing his best to shake Bellerophon off, he had flown a very long way, and by the time the bit was in his mouth they were within sight of a tall mountain. Bellerophon had seen it before and knew it was Helicon, where the winged horse made his home on the summit. Pegasus flew there now, first looking gently into his rider’s face as if to ask permission, and when he landed he waited patiently until Bellerophon chose to get off. The young man jumped down from his steed’s back, but still held him tightly by the bridle. Then he met the horse’s eyes. He was so touched by the gentleness of his look, and by the thought of the free life Pegasus had lived until now, that he could not bear to keep him prisoner if the horse truly wanted his freedom.
Following this generous impulse, he slipped the enchanted bridle off the head of Pegasus and took the bit out of his mouth.
“Pegasus, go away!” he said. “Either go, or stay and love me.”

In an instant the winged horse shot almost out of sight, soaring straight up from the top of Mount Helicon. It was long after sunset, so it was already twilight on the mountaintop and dusky evening over all the countryside around. But Pegasus flew so high that he caught up with the vanished day and was bathed in the sun’s last radiance. Climbing higher and higher, he looked like a bright speck, and finally he could not be seen at all in the hollow emptiness of the sky. Bellerophon was afraid he would never see him again. But while he was lamenting his own foolishness, the bright speck appeared again and came nearer and nearer, until it dropped below the sunlight, and there was Pegasus, come back! After this test there was no more fear that the winged horse would escape. He and Bellerophon were friends, and each trusted the other lovingly.

That night they lay down and slept side by side, with Bellerophon’s arm around the neck of Pegasus, not to hold him back but out of kindness. They woke at daybreak and wished each other good morning, each in his own language.

For several days Bellerophon and the wonderful steed spent their time like this, growing better acquainted and fonder of each other all the while. They made long journeys through the air, and sometimes climbed so high that the earth looked hardly bigger than—the moon. They visited faraway countries and amazed the people there, who thought the handsome young man on the winged horse must have come down from the sky. A thousand miles a day was an easy distance for swift Pegasus. Bellerophon was delighted with this way of life and would have liked nothing better than to go on living it, high up in the clear air, where the weather was always sunny however gloomy and rainy it might be down below. But he could not forget the horrible Chimaera that he had promised King Iobates to kill. So when at last he had grown quite used to feats of horsemanship in the air, could steer Pegasus with the slightest movement of his hand, and had taught him to obey his voice, he decided to attempt the dangerous adventure.

So at daybreak, as soon as he opened his eyes, he gently pinched the winged horse’s ear to wake him. Pegasus sprang up from the ground at once, pranced about a quarter of a mile up in the air, and made a grand sweep around the mountaintop to show that he was wide awake and ready for any kind of outing. All through this little flight he let out a loud, lively, musical neigh, and he finally came down beside Bellerophon as lightly as you ever saw a sparrow hop onto a twig.

“Wonderful, dear Pegasus! Wonderful, my sky-skimmer!” Bellerophon cried, patting the horse’s neck fondly. “Now, my swift and beautiful friend, it’s time to break our fast. Today we take on the terrible Chimaera.”

After they had eaten their morning meal and drunk some sparkling water from a spring called Hippocrene, Pegasus held out his head of his own accord so that his master could put on the bridle. Then he showed how eager he was to be off with a great many playful leaps and airy capers, while Bellerophon strapped on his sword, hung his shield around his neck and got ready for battle. When everything was ready, the rider mounted and, as was his habit on a long trip, climbed five miles straight up so that he could see better where he was heading. Then he turned the head of Pegasus toward the east and set out for Lycia. On the way they overtook an eagle and came so close to him, before he could get out of their way, that Bellerophon could easily have caught him by the leg. Flying onward at this speed, they saw the tall mountains of Lycia, with their deep, shaggy valleys, while it was still early in the morning. If Bellerophon had been told the truth, the hideous Chimaera had made its home in one of those gloomy valleys.

Now that they were so near the end of their journey, the winged horse slowly came down with his rider, and they used some clouds drifting over the mountaintops to hide themselves. Lying on top of a cloud and peeping over its edge, Bellerophon had a fairly clear view of the mountainous part of Lycia and could look into all its shadowy valleys at once. At first nothing seemed unusual. It was a wild, savage, rocky region of high, steep hills. On the flatter ground there were the ruins of burned houses, and here and there the bodies of dead cattle lay scattered over the pastures where they had been grazing.
Bellerophon thought, “This must be the Chimaera’s mischief. But where is the monster hiding?”

As I have said, at first glance there was nothing unusual to be seen in any of the valleys and glens among the steep mountain heights. Nothing at all, unless you count three columns of black smoke that rose from what looked like the mouth of a cave and crawled sullenly into the sky. Before they reached the mountaintop, these three black plumes of smoke merged into one. The cave was almost directly below the winged horse and his rider, about a thousand feet down. The smoke crept heavily upward with an ugly, choking smell of sulphur that made Pegasus snort and Bellerophon sneeze. The marvelous steed, who was used to breathing only the purest air, found it so unpleasant that he beat his wings and shot half a mile away from this foul vapor.

But when Bellerophon looked back, he saw something that made him first pull the bridle and then turn Pegasus around. He gave a signal that the winged horse understood, and they sank slowly through the air until the horse’s hoofs were barely a man’s height above the rocky floor of the valley. Ahead of them, about as far away as you could throw a stone, was the mouth of the cave with the three smoke-wreaths seeping out of it. And what else did Bellerophon see there?

Inside the cave there seemed to be a heap of strange and terrible creatures curled up together. Their bodies lay so close that Bellerophon could not tell them apart, but judging by their heads, one of them was a huge snake, the second a fierce lion and the third an ugly goat. The lion and the goat were asleep, but the snake was wide awake and kept glaring around with a great pair of fiery eyes. And, most amazing of all, the three columns of smoke were plainly coming from the nostrils of these three heads! The sight was so strange that, although Bellerophon had expected it all along, it did not at once occur to him that this was the terrible three-headed Chimaera. He had found the Chimaera’s cave. The snake, the lion and the goat, as he had taken them to be, were not three separate creatures but one monster!

The wicked, hateful thing! Even with two thirds of it asleep, it still held in its abominable claws the remains of an unfortunate lamb—or possibly (though I hate to think so) a dear little boy—that its three mouths had been gnawing before two of them fell asleep!

All at once Bellerophon started as if waking from a dream and knew that this was the Chimaera. Pegasus seemed to know it at the same instant and let out a neigh that sounded like a trumpet calling to battle. At the sound, the three heads reared up and belched great bursts of flame. Before Bellerophon had time to think what to do next, the monster hurled itself out of the cave and sprang straight at him, with its huge claws stretched out and its snaky tail lashing venomously behind. If Pegasus had not been as quick as a bird, the Chimaera’s headlong rush would have knocked down both him and his rider, and the battle would have ended before it had properly begun. But the winged horse was not to be caught so easily. In the blink of an eye he was high in the air, halfway to the clouds and snorting with anger. He shuddered too, not from fear, but from sheer disgust at the loathsomeness of this poisonous three-headed thing.

The Chimaera, for its part, raised itself up until it stood on the very tip of its tail, with its talons pawing fiercely at the air and its three heads spitting fire at Pegasus and his rider. My stars, how it roared and hissed and bellowed! Meanwhile Bellerophon was fastening his shield onto his arm and drawing his sword.

“Now, my beloved Pegasus,” he whispered in the winged horse’s ear, “you must help me kill this unbearable monster, or else you will have to fly back to your lonely mountain peak without your friend Bellerophon. For either the Chimaera dies, or its three mouths will gnaw this head of mine, which has slept on your neck!”

Pegasus whinnied and, turning his head around, rubbed his nose tenderly against his rider’s cheek. It was his way of telling him that, winged and immortal as he was, he would die, if it were possible for an immortal to die, rather than leave Bellerophon behind.
“Thank you, Pegasus,” answered Bellerophon. “Now, let’s make a dash at the monster!”

With these words he shook the bridle, and Pegasus plunged down at a slant, swift as an arrow in flight, straight toward the Chimaera’s three heads, which were all this time stretching as high into the air as they could reach. As he came within arm’s length, Bellerophon swung his sword at the monster, but his steed carried him onward before he could see whether the blow had landed. Pegasus flew on a little way, then wheeled around at about the same distance from the Chimaera as before. Now Bellerophon saw that he had very nearly cut off the goat’s head. It dangled by a strip of skin and seemed quite dead.
But, to make up for it, the snake’s head and the lion’s head had taken all the fierceness of the dead one into themselves. They spat flame, hissed and roared with far more fury than before.
“Don’t worry, brave Pegasus!” cried Bellerophon. “With one more stroke like that, we will shut up either its hissing or its roaring.”

And again he shook the bridle. Darting in at a slant as before, the winged horse made another arrow-swift flight toward the Chimaera, and as he shot past, Bellerophon aimed another downward stroke at one of the two remaining heads. But this time neither he nor Pegasus came off as well as the first time. With one claw the Chimaera had given the young man a deep scratch in the shoulder, and with the other it had slightly damaged the left wing of the flying horse. For his part, Bellerophon had given the lion’s head a deadly wound, so that it now hung down with its fire nearly gone, gasping out puffs of thick black smoke. The snake’s head, however, which was the only one left now, was twice as fierce and poisonous as ever. It belched out streams of fire five hundred yards long, and its hisses were so loud, so harsh and so piercing that King Iobates heard them fifty miles away and trembled until the throne shook beneath him.
“Alas!” thought the poor king. “The Chimaera is surely coming to devour me!”

Meanwhile Pegasus had stopped once more in the air and neighed angrily, with sparks of clear crystal flame flying from his eyes. How different it was from the sullen glare of the Chimaera’s fire! The winged horse’s spirit was thoroughly roused, and so was Bellerophon’s.

“Are you bleeding, my immortal horse?” cried the young man, who cared less for his own wound than for the pain of this glorious creature, who should never have had to feel pain. “The hateful Chimaera will pay for this with its last head!”

Then he shook the bridle, shouted aloud, and steered Pegasus not at a slant as before but straight at the monster’s hideous face. The attack was so quick that it seemed only a dazzle and a flash before Bellerophon was grappling with his enemy.

By now, having lost its second head, the Chimaera had worked itself into a red-hot fury of pain and rage. It thrashed about, half on the ground and half in the air, so wildly that no one could say which one it was resting on. It opened its snake jaws so horribly wide that Pegasus might almost—I was about to say—have flown straight down its throat, wings spread, rider and all! As they came near, it let out a tremendous blast of fiery breath that wrapped Bellerophon and his steed in a cloud of flame. It singed the wings of Pegasus, scorched off the whole of one side of the young man’s golden curls, and made them both a great deal hotter than was comfortable from head to foot.
But that was nothing compared with what came next.

When the winged horse’s swift rush had brought him within a hundred yards, the Chimaera gave a spring and flung its huge, clumsy, poisonous and utterly loathsome body right onto poor Pegasus. It clung around him with all its strength and tied its snaky tail into a knot! Up flew the steed, higher and higher and higher, above the mountain peaks, above the clouds, and almost out of sight of the solid earth. Still the earth-born monster held on, and it was carried upward along with the creature of light and air. Bellerophon, turning around, found himself face to face with the Chimaera’s ugly, grim visage, and the only way he could avoid being scorched to death or bitten in two was to hold up his shield. Over the top edge of the shield he looked sternly into the monster’s savage eyes.

But the Chimaera was so mad and wild with pain that it did not guard itself as well as it otherwise might have. Perhaps, after all, the best way to fight a Chimaera is to get as close to it as you can. In its efforts to dig its horrible iron claws into its enemy, the creature left its own chest wide open. Seeing this, Bellerophon drove his sword up to the hilt into its cruel heart. At once the snaky tail came untied. The monster let go of Pegasus and fell from that tremendous height. The fire inside its chest, instead of going out, burned fiercer than ever and soon began to consume the dead body. So it tumbled out of the sky all in flames, and since night was falling before it reached the ground, people took it for a shooting star or a comet. But at early sunrise some farm workers on their way to the day’s labor were astonished to see that several acres of ground were strewn with black ashes. In the middle of a field lay a heap of whitened bones, much higher than a haystack. Nothing else was ever seen of the dreadful Chimaera!
Once the victory was won, Bellerophon bent down and kissed Pegasus, his eyes brimming with tears.
“Now take me back, dear friend!” he said. “Back to the Fountain of Pirene!”

Pegasus skimmed through the air faster than ever before and reached the fountain in very little time. There he found the old man leaning on his staff, the country fellow watering his cow, and the pretty girl filling her pitcher.
“Now I remember,” said the old man. “I did see this winged horse once, long ago, when I was a youngster. He was ten times better looking then.”
“I’ve got a cart horse at home that’s worth three of him!” said the country fellow. “If this pony were mine, I’d start by clipping his wings!”
But the poor girl said nothing, for she always had the bad luck to be frightened at the wrong moment. So she ran away, dropped her pitcher, and broke it.
“Where is that gentle child,” asked Bellerophon, “the one who kept me company here, who never lost his faith and never tired of gazing into the fountain?”
“Here I am, dear Bellerophon!” said the child softly.

For the little boy had spent day after day at the edge of Pirene, waiting for his friend to return. But when he saw Bellerophon coming down through the clouds on the winged horse, he had shrunk back into the bushes. He was a delicate, tender-hearted child, and he was afraid that the old man and the country fellow would see the tears pouring from his eyes.
“You have won the victory,” he said joyfully, running up to the knee of Bellerophon, who was still sitting on Pegasus’s back. “I knew you would.”

“I did, dear child!” replied Bellerophon, stepping down from the winged horse. “But without your faith to help me, I would never have waited for Pegasus, never have risen above the clouds, and never have beaten the terrible Chimaera. It was you, my beloved little friend, who did all of it. And now let us set Pegasus free.”
With that he lifted the enchanted bridle off the head of the wonderful horse.
“Be free forevermore, my Pegasus!” he cried, with a touch of sadness in his voice. “Be as free as you are swift!”
But Pegasus laid his head on Bellerophon’s shoulder and could not be persuaded to fly away.
“Well then,” said Bellerophon, stroking the airy horse, “you shall stay with me as long as you like. And we will go together right now and tell King Iobates that the Chimaera is destroyed.”

Then Bellerophon hugged the gentle child, promised to come to him again, and left. But in later years that child soared higher on the winged horse than Bellerophon ever did, and did nobler deeds than his friend’s victory over the Chimaera. For, gentle and tender-hearted as he was, he grew up to be a mighty poet!

Eustace Bright told the legend of Bellerophon with as much fervor and liveliness as if he had really been out for a gallop on the winged horse. When he finished, he was pleased to see from the glowing faces of his listeners how deeply they had been interested. All their eyes were dancing, except Primrose’s. In her eyes there were actual tears, because she sensed something in the legend that the others were not yet old enough to feel. Child’s story though it was, the student had managed to breathe into it the ardor, the generous hope and the adventurous imagination of youth.
“I forgive you now, Primrose,” he said, “for all your mockery of me and my stories. One tear makes up for a great deal of laughter.”

“Well, Mr Bright,” answered Primrose, drying her eyes and flashing another of her teasing smiles, “getting your head above the clouds has certainly done your ideas some good. My advice is never to tell another story unless, as today, you tell it from a mountaintop.”
“Or from Pegasus’s back,” replied Eustace with a laugh. “Admit it, didn’t I do rather well at catching that marvelous pony?”

“It was just like one of your wild pranks!” cried Primrose, clapping her hands. “I can see you now on his back, two miles up, with your head hanging down! It’s a good thing you don’t really have the chance to test your riding on any wilder horse than our sober Davy, or Old Hundred.”

“For my part, I wish I had Pegasus here this very moment,” said the student. “I would hop on right away and gallop around the countryside, within a circle of a few miles, paying literary visits to my fellow authors. Dr Dewey would be within my reach, at the foot of Taconic. Over in Stockbridge is Mr James, visible to the whole world on his mountain of history and romance. Longfellow, I believe, is not yet at the Ox-bow, or the winged horse would neigh at the sight of him. But here in Lenox I would find our most truthful novelist, who has made the scenery and life of Berkshire entirely her own. On this side of Pittsfield sits Herman Melville, shaping the gigantic idea of his ‘White Whale,’ while the gigantic shape of Graylock looms at him through his study window. Another bound of my flying steed would bring me to the door of Holmes. I name him last because Pegasus would certainly throw me off a minute later and claim the poet as his rider.”

“Don’t we have an author for our next-door neighbor?” asked Primrose. “That silent man who lives in the old red house near Tanglewood Avenue, whom we sometimes meet in the woods or by the lake with two children at his side. I think I’ve heard that he wrote a poem, or a romance, or an arithmetic book, or a school history, or some other kind of book.”

“Hush, Primrose, hush!” exclaimed Eustace in a thrilling whisper, putting his finger to his lip. “Not a word about that man, even on a hilltop! If our chatter were to reach his ears and happen not to please him, all he has to do is toss a few sheets of paper into the stove, and you, Primrose, and I, and Periwinkle, Sweet Fern, Squash-Blossom, Blue Eye, Huckleberry, Clover, Cowslip, Plantain, Milkweed, Dandelion and Buttercup—yes, and wise Mr Pringle with his unfavorable criticisms of my legends, and poor Mrs Pringle too—would all turn to smoke and go whisking up the chimney! For all I know, our neighbor in the red house is a harmless enough person as far as the rest of the world goes, but something tells me that he has a terrible power over us, and that it reaches all the way to wiping us out completely.”
“And would Tanglewood turn to smoke along with us?” asked Periwinkle, quite horrified at the threatened destruction. “And what would become of Ben and Bruin?”

“Tanglewood would stay exactly as it is now,” replied the student, “only with a completely different family living in it. Ben and Bruin would still be alive, too, and they would be perfectly happy gnawing bones from the dinner table, never once thinking of the good times we have all had together!”
“What nonsense you talk!” exclaimed Primrose.

Chatting idly like this, the party had already started down the hill and was now in the shadow of the woods. Primrose gathered some mountain laurel. Its leaves, though they were last year’s growth, were still as green and springy as if frost and thaw had not taken turns testing them. From these laurel twigs she wove a wreath, and she took off the student’s cap to put it on his head.
“I doubt anyone else will ever crown you for your stories,” said saucy Primrose, “so you may as well have a wreath from me.”

“Don’t be too sure,” answered Eustace, who really looked like a young poet with the laurel in his glossy curls, “that I won’t win other wreaths with these wonderful and admirable stories. I mean to spend all my free time for the rest of the vacation, and all through the summer term at college, writing them out for the press. Mr J. T. Fields (whom I got to know when he was in Berkshire last summer, and who is a poet as well as a publisher) will see their unusual merit at a glance. He will have them illustrated, I hope, by Billings, and will present them to the world under the very best auspices, through the distinguished house of Ticknor & Co. In about five months from now, I have no doubt, I’ll be counted among the lights of this age!”
“Poor boy!” said Primrose, half to herself. “What a disappointment is waiting for him!”

A little farther down, Bruin began to bark, and the deeper bow-wow of respectable old Ben answered him. Soon they saw the good old dog keeping careful watch over Dandelion, Sweet Fern, Cowslip and Squash-Blossom. These little ones, fully rested from their tiredness, had started gathering checkerberries, and now came scrambling up to meet their playmates. All together again, the whole party went down through Luther Butler’s orchard and made their way home to Tanglewood.

chapters.title: The Wayside (Introductory)
paragraphs: A short time ago I had a flying visit from my young friend Eustace Bright, whom I had not seen since I left the breezy mountains of Berkshire. It was the winter vacation at his college, and Eustace was giving himself a little rest, in the hope, he told me, of repairing the damage that hard study had done to his health. Judging by the excellent condition he was in, I was glad to conclude that the remedy had already worked very well. He had come up from Boston on the noon train, partly out of the friendly regard with which he is kind enough to honor me, and partly, as I soon found out, on a matter of literary business.

I was delighted to welcome Mr Bright for the first time under a roof I could truly call my own, humble as it was. And like landowners everywhere, I made a point of marching the poor fellow up and down my half dozen acres. Secretly I was glad that the untidiness of the winter season, and especially the six inches of snow on the ground, kept him from seeing how raggedly the soil and shrubbery have been left to run wild. Still, it was foolish to imagine that a breezy visitor from Monument Mountain, Bald-Summit, and old Graylock, with their shaggy primeval forests, could find anything to admire on my poor little hillside, with its scattering of frail, insect-eaten locust trees. Eustace frankly called the view from my hilltop tame, and no doubt it was, compared with the rough, broken, rugged, headlong country of Berkshire, especially the northern part of the county that his years at college had taught him to know. But I find a special, quiet charm in these broad meadows and gentle rises. They are better than mountains, because they do not stamp themselves on the mind and then grow tiresome, the same strong impression repeated day after day. A few summer weeks among mountains, and a lifetime among green meadows and calm slopes whose outlines are always new because they keep fading from memory—that would be my sober choice.

I suspect Eustace privately decided the whole place was a bore, until I led him to the little ruined rustic summer-house my predecessor built, halfway down the hillside. It is only a skeleton of slender, rotting tree trunks, with no walls and no roof—just a lacework of branches and twigs that the next winter blast will probably scatter in pieces along the terrace. It looks as fleeting as a dream, and it is. Yet somehow its rustic network of boughs has caught a hint of spiritual beauty, and it has become a true emblem of the delicate, airy mind that planned it. I made Eustace Bright sit on a snowbank that had piled itself over the mossy seat, and when he looked out through the arched window opposite, he admitted that the scene suddenly became picturesque.

“Plain as it looks,” he said, “this little building seems to be the work of magic. It sets the mind going, and in its own way it is as good as a cathedral. Oh, it would be the perfect place to sit on a summer afternoon and tell the children some more of those wild stories from the classic myths!”

“It would indeed,” I answered. “The summer-house itself, so airy and so broken, is like one of those old tales that is only half remembered, and these living branches of the Baldwin apple tree, pushing so rudely in, are like your outrageous additions. But by the way, have you added any more legends to the series since the Wonder Book came out?”

“Plenty,” said Eustace. “Primrose, Periwinkle, and all the others make my life miserable unless I tell them a story every day or two. Part of why I ran away from home was to get away from the pestering of those little pests! But I have written out six of the new stories, and I’ve brought them along for you to read through.”
“Are they as good as the first ones?” I asked.
“Better chosen and better handled,” Eustace Bright replied. “You’ll say so yourself when you read them.”

“Maybe not,” I said. “I know from my own experience that an author always thinks his latest work is his best, until it cools off from the heat of writing. After that it settles quietly into its proper place. But let’s go to my study and look at these new stories. You would hardly do yourself justice by introducing me to them while we sit on this snowbank!”

So we walked down the hill to my small old cottage and shut ourselves into the southeastern room, where the sunshine comes in warm and bright through the better half of a winter day. Eustace handed me his bundle of manuscript, and I skimmed through it fairly quickly, trying to judge its strengths and weaknesses by the feel of the pages in my fingers, as any seasoned storyteller should know how to do.

You will remember that Mr Bright graciously made use of my literary experience by appointing me editor of the Wonder Book. Since he had no cause to complain of how the public received that learned work, he was now willing to keep me in the same position for this new volume, which he called “TANGLEWOOD TALES.” Eustace hinted that he had no real need of me as an introducer, since his own name had already won a fair amount of favor in the literary world. But he was kind enough to say that working with me had been very pleasant, and that he had no wish, as most people do, to kick away the ladder that may have helped him reach his present height. In short, my young friend was willing for the fresh green of his growing reputation to spread over my scraggly, half-bare branches, much as I have sometimes thought of training a vine, with its broad leaves and purple fruit, over the worm-eaten posts and rafters of the rustic summer-house. I was not blind to the advantages of his offer, and I gladly told him I accepted.

From the titles of the stories alone, I could see at once that the subjects were every bit as rich as those of the earlier volume. I also had no doubt that Mr Bright’s boldness, as far as boldness could help, had let him make full use of whatever possibilities they offered. Yet for all my experience of his free way of handling them, I confess I did not quite see how he could have overcome every difficulty in making them fit for children. These old legends are crammed with everything most hateful to our Christian moral sense. Some are hideous and others are sad and miserable, and from them the Greek tragedians took their themes and shaped them into the sternest forms of grief the world has ever seen. Was this the stuff that children’s playthings should be made of? How could such stories be cleansed? How could the blessed sunshine be let into them?

But Eustace told me that these myths were the most remarkable things in the world. Whenever he began to tell one, he said, he was always amazed at how readily it adapted itself to the childlike innocence of his listeners. The objectionable features seem to be a parasitic growth with no real connection to the original fable. They drop away and are forgotten the moment he puts his imagination in tune with the innocent little circle, whose wide-open eyes are fixed so eagerly on him. In this way the stories change themselves, with no forced effort from the teller but in keeping with the seed inside them, and take on again the shapes they might be supposed to have had in the pure childhood of the world. According to Eustace Bright, when the first poet or storyteller told these marvelous legends, it was still the Golden Age. Evil had not yet come into being, and sorrow, misfortune, and crime were only shadows that the mind imagined for itself as a shelter from too much sunny reality, or at most prophetic dreams that the dreamer did not believe when he woke. Children today are the only representatives of the men and women of that happy era, and so we must raise our intellect and imagination to the level of childhood in order to re-create the original myths.

I let the young author talk as much and as extravagantly as he liked, and I was glad to see him starting out in life with so much confidence in himself and his work. A few years will do whatever is needed to show him the truth on both counts. Meanwhile it is only fair to say that he really does seem to have overcome the moral objections to these fables, though at the cost of such liberties with their structure that they must plead their own excuse without any help from me. Indeed, apart from the fact that it was necessary, and that the inner life of the legends cannot be reached except by making them entirely one’s own property, there is no defense to be made.

Eustace told me that he had told his stories to the children in all sorts of places—in the woods, on the shore of the lake, in the dell of Shadow Brook, in the playroom, by the Tanglewood fireside, and in a magnificent palace of snow, with ice windows, that he helped his little friends build. His listeners were even more delighted with the contents of this volume than with the samples already given to the world. The classically learned Mr Pringle had also heard two or three of the tales, and criticized them even more bitterly than he had THE THREE GOLDEN APPLES. So between the praise and the criticism, Eustace Bright thinks there is good hope of at least as much success with the public as the Wonder Book had.

I asked all sorts of questions about the children, not doubting that some good little folks who have written to ask me for another volume of myths would be eager to hear how they are. I am happy to say they are all in excellent health and spirits, except perhaps Clover. Primrose is now almost a young lady and, Eustace tells me, just as saucy as ever. She pretends to think herself far too old to be interested in such idle stories as these, but even so, whenever a story is going to be told, Primrose never fails to be among the listeners, and to make fun of it when it is over. Periwinkle has grown a great deal, and in another month or two she is expected to shut up her baby-house and throw away her doll. Sweet Fern has learned to read and write and has started wearing a jacket and trousers—all of which improvements I am sorry about. Squash-Blossom, Blue Eye, Plantain, and Buttercup have had scarlet fever but came through it easily. Huckleberry, Milkweed, and Dandelion caught whooping cough but bore it bravely and stayed outdoors whenever the sun shone. Cowslip, in the autumn, had either the measles or some rash that looked a lot like it, but was hardly sick for a day. Poor Clover has been much troubled by her second teeth, which have made her look thin and made her rather cranky, and it does not help much when she smiles, since that shows a gap just inside her lips almost as wide as a barn door. But all this will pass, and people predict that she will grow into a very pretty girl.

As for Mr Bright himself, he is now in his senior year at Williams College and expects to graduate with a fair degree of honor at the next Commencement. In his oration for the bachelor’s degree, he lets me know, he will speak about the classical myths seen as baby stories, and he has a great mind to argue that it would be sensible to use up all of ancient history for the same purpose. I do not know what he plans to do with himself after he leaves college, but I trust that by dabbling so early in the dangerous and tempting business of authorship, he will not be drawn into becoming an author by profession. If he is, I shall be very sorry for the small part I have played in encouraging these first beginnings.

How I wish I could expect to see Primrose, Periwinkle, Dandelion, Sweet Fern, Clover, Plantain, Huckleberry, Milkweed, Cowslip, Buttercup, Blue Eye, and Squash-Blossom again before long. But I cannot say when I will next be at Tanglewood, and Eustace Bright is unlikely to invite me to edit a third Wonder Book. So the public of little folks should not look to me for any more news of those dear children. God bless them, and everyone else, whether grown up or not!
THE WAYSIDE, CONCORD, MASS.

chapters.title: The Minotaur
paragraphs: Long, long ago, in the old city of Troezene, at the foot of a tall mountain, there lived a little boy named Theseus. His grandfather, King Pittheus, ruled that country and was considered a very wise man. So Theseus, who was growing up in the royal palace and was a bright boy by nature, could hardly help learning a great deal from the old king. His mother’s name was AEthra. As for his father, the boy had never seen him. But for as long as he could remember, AEthra used to take little Theseus into a wood and sit down with him on a moss-covered rock that was sunk deep into the ground. There she often talked with her son about his father. She told him that his name was AEgeus, that he was a great king who ruled over Attica, and that he lived at Athens, a city as famous as any in the world. Theseus loved to hear about King AEgeus, and he often asked his good mother AEthra why his father did not come and live with them at Troezene.

“Ah, my dear son,” AEthra answered with a sigh, “a king has his people to look after. The men and women he rules are like children to him, and he can seldom spare the time to love his own children the way other parents do. Your father will never be able to leave his kingdom just to see his little boy.”
“But, dear mother,” the boy asked, “why can’t I go to this famous city of Athens and tell King AEgeus that I am his son?”
“That may happen before long,” said AEthra. “Be patient, and we shall see. You are not big or strong enough yet to set out on an errand like that.”
“And how soon will I be strong enough?” Theseus kept asking.
“You are only a tiny boy so far,” his mother replied. “See if you can lift this rock we are sitting on.”

The little fellow thought very highly of his own strength. So he took hold of the rough lumps of the rock and pulled and strained with all his might, until he was quite out of breath, but he could not make the heavy stone budge. It seemed to be rooted in the ground. No wonder he could not move it, for it would have taken all the strength of a very strong man to lift it out of its bed of earth.

His mother stood watching, with a sad sort of smile on her lips and in her eyes, as she saw the eager but feeble efforts of her little boy. She could not help feeling sorrowful that he was already so impatient to begin his adventures in the world.

“You see how it is, my dear Theseus,” she said. “You will need to be much stronger than you are now before I can trust you to go to Athens and tell King AEgeus that you are his son. But when you can lift this rock and show me what is hidden beneath it, I promise to give you my permission to leave.”

Again and again after that, Theseus asked his mother whether it was time yet for him to go to Athens. Each time she pointed to the rock and told him he would not be strong enough to move it for years to come. Still the rosy-cheeked, curly-haired boy kept tugging and straining at the huge block of stone, child that he was, trying to do what a giant could barely have managed with both of his great hands. Meanwhile the rock seemed to sink deeper and deeper into the ground. The moss grew thicker and thicker over it, until it looked almost like a soft green seat with only a few gray knobs of granite poking through. The trees above dropped their brown leaves on it every autumn, and ferns and wildflowers grew around its base, some of them creeping right over its surface. By every appearance, the rock was as firmly fixed as any other part of the earth.
But hard as the job looked, Theseus was growing into such a vigorous young man that, in his own opinion, the day would soon come when he could hope to get the better of this heavy lump of stone.
“Mother, I really believe it has moved!” he cried after one of his tries. “The earth around it is definitely a little cracked!”
“No, no, child!” his mother answered quickly. “You can’t possibly have moved it, a boy as young as you still are!”

She would not be convinced, even when Theseus showed her the spot where he thought the stem of a flower had been partly pulled up by the rock’s movement. But AEthra sighed and looked troubled, because she was surely beginning to realize that her son was no longer a child, and that before long she would have to send him out among the dangers and hardships of the world.

Not more than a year later, they were sitting on the mossy stone together again. AEthra had told him once more the story he had heard so often: how gladly his father would welcome Theseus to his grand palace, how he would introduce him to his courtiers and his people, and announce that here was the heir to his lands. The eyes of Theseus shone with eagerness, and he could hardly sit still while his mother spoke.

“Dear mother AEthra,” he said, “I have never felt half as strong as I do now! I am not a child anymore, or a boy, or even a young fellow! I feel like a man! It is time to make one serious try at moving the stone!”
“Oh, my dearest Theseus,” his mother answered, “not yet! Not yet!”
“Yes, mother,” he said firmly, “the time has come.”

Then Theseus set himself to the task in earnest and strained every muscle, with a man’s strength and determination. He put his whole brave heart into the effort. He wrestled with the big, sluggish stone as if it were a living enemy. He heaved and he lifted, determined now to succeed or die on the spot and let the rock be his monument forever! AEthra stood watching him with her hands clasped, partly with a mother’s pride and partly with a mother’s sorrow. The great rock stirred! Yes, it rose slowly out of the packed moss and earth, tearing up the shrubs and flowers with it, and turned over onto its side. Theseus had won!
While he caught his breath, he looked happily at his mother, and she smiled back at him through her tears.

“Yes, Theseus,” she said, “the time has come, and you must not stay at my side any longer! Look at what King AEgeus, your royal father, left for you under the stone, when he lifted it in his mighty arms and set it down on the spot you have just cleared.”

Theseus looked and saw that the rock had been laid over another slab of stone with a hollow in it, so that the two together looked something like a roughly made chest, with the upper stone as its lid. Inside the hollow lay a sword with a golden hilt, and a pair of sandals.

“That sword was your father’s,” said AEthra, “and so were those sandals. Before he left to rule Athens, he told me to keep treating you as a child until you showed you were a man by lifting this heavy stone. You have done that, so now you may wear his sandals and walk where your father walked, and strap on his sword to take on giants and dragons the way King AEgeus did when he was young.”
“I will set out for Athens this very day!” cried Theseus.

But his mother persuaded him to stay a day or two longer while she got together the things he would need for the journey. When his grandfather, the wise King Pittheus, heard that Theseus meant to present himself at his father’s palace, he urged him to board a ship and go by sea, since that way he could arrive within fifteen miles of Athens without any tiredness or danger.

“The roads by land are very bad,” said the respected old king, “and they are full of robbers and monsters. A mere boy like Theseus can’t be trusted to make such a dangerous journey all alone. No, no, let him go by sea!”

But when Theseus heard about robbers and monsters, his ears perked up, and he became all the more eager to take the road where they were to be found. So on the third day he said a respectful goodbye to his grandfather and thanked him for all his kindness. Then he hugged his mother and set off, with plenty of her tears glistening on his cheeks, and a few, if the truth be told, that had come from his own eyes. But he let the sun and wind dry them and walked on boldly, playing with the golden hilt of his sword and taking very manly strides in his father’s sandals.

I can’t stop to tell you more than a few of the adventures Theseus met on the road to Athens. It is enough to say that he rid that part of the country of the robbers King Pittheus had been so worried about. One of these villains was named Procrustes, and he was a terrible fellow, with a nasty way of making sport of the poor travelers who fell into his hands. In his cave he kept a bed, and with a great show of hospitality he invited his guests to lie down on it. But if they were shorter than the bed, this wicked man stretched them out by sheer force, and if they were too long, he chopped off their heads or feet, and laughed at what he had done as if it were a fine joke. So no matter how tired a man was, he never wanted to lie in the bed of Procrustes. Another of these robbers, named Scinis, was surely a great scoundrel too. He used to throw his victims off a high cliff into the sea, and to give him exactly what he deserved, Theseus threw him off the very same spot. But believe it or not, the sea refused to dirty itself by taking such a bad man into its depths, and the earth, once rid of him, would not take him back. So between the cliff and the sea, Scinis stuck fast in midair, and the air had to carry the weight of his wickedness.

After these famous deeds, Theseus heard about a huge sow that ran wild and terrified all the farmers for miles around. He did not think himself too good to do any useful thing that came his way, so he killed the monstrous creature and gave the carcass to the poor for bacon. The great sow had been a dreadful beast while she was rampaging through the woods and fields, but she made a pleasant enough sight cut up into joints and steaming on I don’t know how many dinner tables.

By the time he reached the end of his journey, then, Theseus had done many brave deeds with his father’s golden-hilted sword and had won a name as one of the bravest young men of the day. His fame traveled faster than he did and got to Athens before him. As he entered the city, he heard the people talking on the street corners. They said that Hercules was brave, and so was Jason, and so were Castor and Pollux, but that Theseus, the son of their own king, would turn out as great a hero as the best of them. Hearing this, Theseus walked with longer strides. He felt sure of a splendid welcome at his father’s court, since Fame was coming along ahead of him, blowing her trumpet and crying to King AEgeus, “Look, here is your son!”

Innocent young man that he was, he never suspected that here in Athens, where his father ruled, a greater danger waited for him than any he had met on the road. But it was true. You must understand that the father of Theseus, though not very old in years, was nearly worn out by the cares of government and had grown old before his time. His nephews, who did not expect him to live very long, planned to take all the power of the kingdom into their own hands. But when they heard that Theseus had come to Athens, and learned what a fine young man he was, they saw that he was not the sort of person who would let them steal his father’s crown and scepter, which by right of inheritance should be his. So these wicked-hearted nephews of King AEgeus, who were Theseus’s own cousins, immediately became his enemies. An even more dangerous enemy was Medea, the evil enchantress. She was now the king’s wife, and she wanted to give the kingdom to her own son Medus, instead of letting it go to the son of AEthra, whom she hated.

As it happened, the king’s nephews met Theseus just as he arrived at the entrance of the royal palace, and they found out who he was. For all their evil plans against him, they pretended to be their cousin’s best friends and said how delighted they were to meet him. They suggested that he go in to see the king as a stranger, to find out whether AEgeus would notice in the young man’s face any likeness to himself or to AEthra, and so recognize him as his son. Theseus agreed, because he imagined his father would know him in a moment by the love in his heart. But while he waited at the door, the nephews ran to King AEgeus and told him that a young man had arrived in Athens who, as they knew for certain, meant to kill him and seize his crown.
“And he is waiting right now to be admitted to your Majesty’s presence,” they added.
“Aha!” cried the old king when he heard this. “Why, he must be a truly wicked young fellow! Tell me, what do you advise me to do with him?”

To this question the wicked Medea added her own answer. As I have already told you, she was a famous enchantress. According to some stories, she used to boil old people in a large cauldron, pretending to make them young again. But King AEgeus, I suppose, did not like that uncomfortable way of growing young, or perhaps he was happy to be old, because he would never let himself be popped into the cauldron. If I had time to spare from more important matters, I would gladly tell you about Medea’s fiery chariot, pulled by winged dragons, in which the enchantress often went for a ride among the clouds. In fact, that chariot was how she first came to Athens, where she had done nothing but mischief since she arrived. But these and many other wonders must go untold. It is enough to say that Medea, among a thousand other bad things, knew how to prepare a poison that killed instantly anyone who so much as touched it with his lips.
So when the king asked what he should do with Theseus, this wicked woman had an answer ready on the tip of her tongue.

“Leave that to me, if it please your Majesty,” she said. “Just let this evil-minded young man into your presence, treat him politely, and invite him to drink a goblet of wine. Your Majesty knows that I sometimes amuse myself by making very powerful medicines. Here is one of them in this little vial. What it is made of is one of my state secrets. Just let me put a single drop into the goblet and let the young man taste it, and I promise you he will give up the bad plans he comes here with.”

As she said this, Medea smiled, but behind her smiling face she meant nothing less than to poison poor innocent Theseus right in front of his father. And King AEgeus, like most kings, thought no punishment too mild for a person accused of plotting against his life. So he raised little or no objection to Medea’s scheme, and as soon as the poisoned wine was ready, he ordered the young stranger to be brought in. The goblet was set on a table beside the king’s throne, and a fly that only meant to sip a little from the rim immediately tumbled in, dead. Seeing this, Medea glanced at the nephews and smiled again.

When Theseus was shown into the royal chamber, the only thing he seemed to see was the white-bearded old king. There he sat on his magnificent throne with a dazzling crown on his head and a scepter in his hand. He looked stately and majestic, though his years and weaknesses weighed heavily on him, as if each year were a lump of lead and each weakness a heavy stone, all bundled together and piled onto his weary shoulders. Tears of joy and sorrow filled the young man’s eyes, because he thought how sad it was to see his dear father so frail, and how sweet it would be to support him with his own youthful strength and cheer him up with the eagerness of a loving heart. When a son takes his father into his warm heart, it makes the old man young again in a better way than the heat of Medea’s magic cauldron. And this was what Theseus resolved to do. He could hardly wait to see whether King AEgeus would recognize him, so eager was he to throw himself into his arms.

He walked up to the foot of the throne and tried to make the little speech he had been working out as he climbed the stairs. But he was nearly choked by the many tender feelings that welled up from his heart into his throat, all struggling to come out at once. So unless he could have placed his full, overflowing heart in the king’s hand, poor Theseus did not know what to do or say. The cunning Medea saw what was going on in the young man’s mind. At that moment she was more wicked than she had ever been, for (and it makes me tremble to tell you) she did her worst to turn all this inexpressible love that stirred Theseus into his own ruin and destruction.

“Can your Majesty see how rattled he is?” she murmured into the king’s ear. “His guilt is so plain to him that he shakes and can’t say a word. The wretch has lived long enough! Hurry! Give him the wine!”

King AEgeus had been studying the young stranger intently as he came toward the throne. Something about him—his pale forehead, the fine shape of his mouth, his gentle and beautiful eyes, the king could not say which—gave him a vague feeling that he had seen this youth before. It was as if he had once bounced him on his knee as a baby, and then watched him grow into a strong man while he himself grew old. But Medea guessed what the king was feeling, and she would not let him give in to these natural stirrings. Yet they were the voice of his deepest heart, telling him as clearly as any voice could that here was his own dear son, AEthra’s son, come to claim him as a father. The enchantress whispered in the king’s ear once more, and by her witchcraft forced him to see everything in a false light.
So he made up his mind to let Theseus drink the poisoned wine.

“Young man,” he said, “welcome! I am proud to offer hospitality to so heroic a youth. Please do me the kindness of drinking what is in this goblet. As you see, it is filled to the brim with delicious wine, which I give only to those who deserve it. No one deserves to drink it more than you!”

With these words, King AEgeus lifted the golden goblet from the table and was about to hand it to Theseus. But his hand shook so badly that a good deal of the wine splashed out. Part of the reason was his frailty. Part was that it seemed so sad to take this young man’s life, however wicked he might be. And part, no doubt, was that his heart was wiser than his head and shuddered at what he was about to do. Afraid that all the precious poison would be wasted, and wanting to stiffen the king’s purpose, one of his nephews now whispered to him—

“Does your Majesty have any doubt of this stranger’s guilt? There is the very sword he meant to kill you with. Look how sharp and bright and terrible it is! Hurry! Make him taste the wine, or he may still do the deed.”

At these words AEgeus pushed every other thought and feeling out of his heart, except the single idea of how justly this young man deserved to die. He sat up straight on his throne, held out the goblet of wine in a steady hand, and fixed Theseus with a frown of royal sternness. After all, his spirit was too noble to murder even a treacherous enemy with a false smile on his face.
“Drink!” he said, in the grim voice he used for sentencing a criminal to be beheaded. “You have earned wine like this from me!”

Theseus reached out his hand for the wine. But before he could touch it, King AEgeus trembled again. His eyes had fallen on the gold-hilted sword hanging at the young man’s side. He pulled the goblet back.
“That sword!” he cried. “Where did you get it?”

“It was my father’s sword,” Theseus answered, his voice shaking. “These were his sandals. My dear mother, whose name is AEthra, told me his story when I was still a little child. But it was only a month ago that I grew strong enough to lift the heavy stone, take the sword and sandals from underneath it, and come to Athens to look for my father.”
“My son! My son!” cried King AEgeus. He threw away the deadly goblet and stumbled down from the throne to collapse into the arms of Theseus. “Yes, these are AEthra’s eyes. It is my son.”

I have completely forgotten what became of the king’s nephews. But when the wicked Medea saw how things had turned out, she hurried from the room to her private chamber and wasted no time setting her enchantments to work. Within moments she heard a great noise of hissing snakes outside her window. And there, look! was her fiery chariot, with four huge winged serpents wriggling and twisting in the air. They were lashing their tails higher than the roof of the palace, all ready for a flight through the sky. Medea waited only long enough to take her son along and to steal the crown jewels, the king’s finest robes, and any other valuables she could get her hands on. Then she climbed into the chariot, whipped up the snakes, and rose high above the city.

The king heard the serpents hissing and scrambled to the window as fast as he could. He bellowed at the hateful enchantress never to come back. All the people of Athens had run outside to watch this amazing sight, and they let out a shout of joy at the thought of being rid of her. Medea was nearly bursting with rage. She hissed exactly like one of her own snakes, only ten times more poisonous and spiteful. Glaring out of the blaze of the chariot, she shook her hands over the crowd below, as if she were flinging a million curses among them. As she did so, though, she accidentally dropped about five hundred diamonds of the finest quality, a thousand big pearls, and two thousand emeralds, rubies, sapphires, opals, and topazes, all of which she had helped herself to from the king’s strongbox. They came pelting down like a shower of many-colored hailstones on the heads of grown-ups and children, who promptly gathered them up and carried them back to the palace. But King AEgeus told them they were welcome to keep the lot, and twice as much more if he had it, because he was so delighted to have found his son and lost the wicked Medea. And in fact, if you had seen how hateful her last look was as the flaming chariot soared away, you would not be surprised that king and people alike thought her departure a good riddance.

Prince Theseus was now treated with great favor by his royal father. The old king never got tired of having him sit beside him on the throne (which was quite wide enough for two), or of hearing him talk about his dear mother, his childhood, and all his boyish attempts to lift the enormous stone. But Theseus was much too brave and active a young man to spend all his time telling about things that had already happened. He longed to do other, more heroic deeds, which would be better worth telling about in prose and verse. He had not been in Athens long before he captured and chained a terrible mad bull and put him on public display, to the great wonder and admiration of good King AEgeus and his people. But soon he took on a task that made all his earlier adventures look like child’s play. It came about like this:—

One morning when Prince Theseus woke up, he thought he must have had a very sad dream and that it was still running through his mind, even though his eyes were open. The air seemed to be full of a mournful wailing. When he listened more closely, he could hear sobs and groans and screams of grief, mixed with deep, quiet sighs. They came from the king’s palace, from the streets, from the temples, and from every home in the city. All these sorrowful sounds, rising from thousands of separate hearts, had joined into one great cry of misery, and it was this that had startled Theseus out of his sleep. He dressed as quickly as he could (not forgetting his sandals and gold-hilted sword), hurried to the king, and asked what it all meant.

“Alas, my son,” said King AEgeus with a long sigh, “this is a most sorrowful business. This is the saddest day of the whole year. It is the day when we draw lots to decide which of the young men and maidens of Athens will be sent to be devoured by the horrible Minotaur!”

“The Minotaur!” exclaimed Prince Theseus. Like the brave young prince he was, he put his hand on the hilt of his sword. “What sort of monster is that? Is there no way to kill him, even at the risk of one’s life?”

But King AEgeus shook his venerable head. To show Theseus that the case was hopeless, he explained the whole affair. On the island of Crete, it seemed, there lived a dreadful monster called a Minotaur. He was shaped partly like a man and partly like a bull, and he was such a hideous creature that it is really unpleasant to think about him. If he had to exist at all, it should have been on some desert island, or in the darkness of some deep cave, where nobody would ever be tormented by the sight of him. But King Minos, who ruled Crete, had spent a vast amount of money building a home for the Minotaur and took great care of his health and comfort, just out of spite. A few years earlier Athens and Crete had gone to war, and the Athenians were beaten and had to beg for peace. They could get peace only on one condition: every year they must send seven young men and seven maidens to be devoured by the pet monster of the cruel King Minos. For three years this terrible misery had been endured. And the sobs, groans, and shrieks that now filled the city came from the people’s grief, because the fatal day had come around again, when the fourteen victims were to be chosen by lot. The old people were afraid their sons or daughters would be taken, and the young men and girls dreaded that they themselves might be fated to feed the hungry belly of that detestable man-beast.
But when Theseus heard the story, he drew himself up until he seemed taller than ever before. His face showed anger, scorn, boldness, tenderness, and pity all in one look.
“This year let the people of Athens draw lots for only six young men instead of seven,” he said. “I will be the seventh myself, and let the Minotaur devour me if he can!”
“Oh, my dear son,” cried King AEgeus, “why would you throw yourself into this horrible fate? You are a royal prince, and you have every right to consider yourself above the fortunes of common men.”

“I am a prince, your son, and the rightful heir to your kingdom. That is exactly why I willingly take your subjects’ misfortune on myself,” Theseus replied. “And you, Father, are king of this people and answer to Heaven for their welfare. You must give up what you love best before you let even the poorest citizen’s son or daughter come to harm.”

The old king wept and begged Theseus not to leave him alone in his old age, especially since he had only just begun to know the joy of having a good and valiant son. But Theseus felt he was in the right, and so he would not give up his decision. He assured his father, though, that he had no intention of being eaten like a sheep without a fight, and that if the Minotaur devoured him, it would not be without a battle for his dinner. At last, since there was nothing else he could do, King AEgeus agreed to let him go. A ship was made ready and fitted with black sails. Theseus, six other young men, and seven gentle and lovely maidens came down to the harbor to board. A sorrowing crowd went with them to the shore. The poor old king was there too, leaning on his son’s arm, looking as if his one heart held all the grief of Athens.
Just as Prince Theseus was about to go aboard, his father remembered one last thing to say.

“My beloved son,” he said, gripping the prince’s hand, “you can see that the sails of this ship are black. They should be, since it sails on a voyage of sorrow and despair. Now, I am so weighed down by age and weakness that I do not know whether I can live until the ship returns. But as long as I do live, I will drag myself every day to the top of that cliff over there to watch for a sail on the sea. And, dearest Theseus, if by some happy chance you escape the jaws of the Minotaur, then tear down those gloomy sails and hoist others as bright as the sunshine. When I see them on the horizon, I and all the people will know that you are coming home victorious, and we will welcome you with a joyful uproar such as Athens has never heard before.”

Theseus promised that he would. Then he went aboard, and the sailors set the black sails to the wind. It blew only faintly from the shore, since it was made up mostly of the sighs everyone kept pouring out on this sad occasion. But after a while, once they were well out to sea, a strong breeze came up from the northwest and drove them over the white-capped waves as cheerfully as if they were on the most delightful errand imaginable. It was sad business enough, but I rather doubt that fourteen young people, with no old folks to keep them in line, could stay miserable for the whole voyage. I suspect there were a few dances on the rolling deck, some hearty bursts of laughter, and other such unsuitable merriment among the victims before the tall blue mountains of Crete began to show among the faraway clouds. That sight, of course, made them all very serious again.

Theseus stood among the sailors, gazing eagerly toward the land. As yet it looked hardly more solid than the clouds in which the mountains were rising. Once or twice he thought he saw a glare from some bright object a long way off, throwing a gleam across the waves.
“Did you see that flash of light?” he asked the ship’s master.
“No, prince, but I have seen it before,” the master answered. “I suppose it came from Talus.”

The breeze was freshening just then, and the master was busy trimming his sails and had no time to answer more questions. But as the ship flew faster and faster toward Crete, Theseus was amazed to see a gigantic human figure that appeared to be striding along the edge of the island with a steady, measured step. It stepped from cliff to cliff, and sometimes from one headland to the next, while the sea foamed and thundered on the shore below and flung spray over the giant’s feet. Even more remarkable, whenever the sun shone on this huge figure, it flickered and glimmered. Its enormous face had a metallic shine and threw great flashes of brilliance through the air. And the folds of its clothing did not wave in the wind but hung heavily around its limbs, as if they were woven from some kind of metal.

The closer the ship came, the more Theseus wondered what this immense giant could be, and whether it was really alive. It walked and made other lifelike movements, but there was a kind of jerk in its stride. That, along with its brassy look, made the young prince suspect that it was no true giant but only a marvelous piece of machinery. The figure looked all the more terrible because it carried an enormous brass club on its shoulder.
“What is this wonder?” Theseus asked the ship’s master, who now had time to answer him.
“It is Talus, the Man of Brass,” said the master.
“And is he a living giant, or a brass statue?” asked Theseus.

“That, truly,” replied the master, “is the very question that has always puzzled me. Some people say this Talus was hammered out for King Minos by Vulcan himself, the most skillful metalworker there ever was. But who ever heard of a brass statue with enough sense to walk around an island three times a day, the way this giant walks around Crete, challenging every ship that comes near the shore? And on the other hand, what living creature, unless its sinews were made of brass, wouldn’t get tired of marching eighteen hundred miles in twenty-four hours, as Talus does, without once sitting down to rest? He is a puzzle, whichever way you look at him.”

The ship kept bounding onward, and soon Theseus could hear the brassy clang of the giant’s footsteps as he stomped over the sea-battered rocks. Some of them could be seen cracking and crumbling into the foaming waves under his weight. As the ship neared the mouth of the harbor, the giant planted a foot firmly on each headland and straddled the entrance. He raised his club so high that its handle disappeared into a cloud, and there he stood in that fearsome pose, with the sun gleaming all over his metal skin. It seemed certain that in the next moment he would bring his great club down, slam bang, and smash the ship into a thousand pieces, never caring how many innocent people he killed. After all, giants rarely show any mercy, you know, and a piece of brass clockwork shows even less. But just when Theseus and his companions thought the blow was about to fall, the brazen lips opened and the figure spoke.
“Where do you come from, strangers?”
And when the ringing voice stopped, there was an echo just like the one you may have heard inside a great church bell, for a moment or two after the hammer strikes it.
“From Athens!” the master shouted back.
“And why have you come?” the Man of Brass thundered.

And he swung his club overhead, more menacingly than ever, as if he meant to strike them with a thunderbolt right through the middle of the ship, because Athens had been at war with Crete not so long before.
“We are bringing the seven young men and the seven young women,” the master answered, “to be eaten by the Minotaur!”
“Pass!” cried the brazen giant.

That one loud word rolled across the whole sky, and again a booming echo sounded inside the figure’s chest. The ship slid in between the headlands of the harbor, and the giant went back to his march. In a few moments this marvelous sentinel was far away, flashing in the distant sunshine and circling the island of Crete with enormous strides, as it was his never-ending task to do.

The moment they entered the harbor, a party of King Minos’s guards came down to the water’s edge and took charge of the fourteen young men and women. With these armed warriors around them, Prince Theseus and his companions were marched to the king’s palace and shown into his presence. Now, Minos was a stern and pitiless king. If the figure that guarded Crete was made of brass, then the king who ruled it might be thought to have an even harder metal in his chest, and might have been called a man of iron. He knitted his shaggy brows at the poor Athenian captives. Any other person, seeing how fresh and tender and innocent they looked, would have felt as if he were sitting on thorns until he had made every one of them happy by telling them they were free to go, like the summer wind. But this merciless Minos cared only to check whether they were plump enough to satisfy the Minotaur’s appetite. For my part, I wish he had been the only victim himself; the monster would have found him pretty tough going.

One after another, King Minos called these pale, frightened young men and sobbing young women up to his footstool. He gave each of them a poke in the ribs with his scepter (to see whether they were in good condition or not) and sent them away with a nod to his guards. But when his eyes fell on Theseus, the king looked at him more closely, because his face was calm and brave.
“Young man,” he asked in his stern voice, “aren’t you horrified at the certainty of being eaten by this terrible Minotaur?”

“I have offered my life for a good cause,” answered Theseus, “and so I give it freely and gladly. But you, King Minos, are you not horrified yourself, you who have done this dreadful wrong year after year, giving seven innocent young men and as many young women to be eaten by a monster? Do you not tremble, wicked king, to look into your own heart? Sitting there on your golden throne in your royal robes, I tell you to your face, King Minos, you are a far more hideous monster than the Minotaur himself!”

“Ha! Is that what you think of me?” cried the king, laughing his cruel laugh. “Tomorrow at breakfast time you will have the chance to judge which is the greater monster, the Minotaur or the king! Take them away, guards, and let this outspoken young man be the Minotaur’s first mouthful!”

Standing near the king’s throne (though I haven’t had time to tell you so until now) was his daughter Ariadne. She was a beautiful, tenderhearted girl, and she looked at these poor doomed prisoners with very different feelings from those of the iron-hearted King Minos. She actually wept at the thought of how much human happiness would be thrown away for nothing, by giving so many young people, in the first bloom and rose blossom of their lives, to be gobbled up by a creature who would no doubt have preferred a fat ox, or even a large pig, to the plumpest of them. And when she saw how brave and spirited Prince Theseus looked, carrying himself so calmly in his terrible danger, she felt a hundred times more pity than before. As the guards were leading him away, she threw herself at the king’s feet and begged him to set all the prisoners free, and this one young man above all.

“Quiet, foolish girl!” answered King Minos. “What do you have to do with a matter like this? It is a question of state policy, and far beyond your feeble understanding. Go and water your flowers, and think no more about these wretched Athenians. The Minotaur will eat them for breakfast as surely as I will eat a partridge for my supper.”

As he said this, the king looked cruel enough to eat Theseus and all the other prisoners himself, if there had been no Minotaur to save him the trouble. Since he would not listen to another word in their favor, the prisoners were led away and shut up in a dungeon, where the jailer advised them to get to sleep as soon as they could, because the Minotaur was in the habit of asking for his breakfast early. The seven young women and six of the young men soon sobbed themselves to sleep! But Theseus was not like them. He knew that he was wiser and braver and stronger than his companions, and that he therefore carried the responsibility for all their lives. He had to think whether there was any way to save them, even in this last extremity. So he stayed awake and paced back and forth across the gloomy dungeon where they were locked up.
Shortly before midnight the door was quietly unbarred, and the gentle Ariadne showed herself in the doorway, holding a torch in her hand.
“Are you awake, Prince Theseus?” she whispered.
“Yes,” answered Theseus. “With so little time left to live, I don’t care to waste any of it sleeping.”
“Then follow me,” said Ariadne, “and walk softly.”
Theseus never found out what had happened to the jailer and the guards. However that may have been, Ariadne opened every door and led him out of the gloomy prison into the pleasant moonlight.
“Theseus,” said the girl, “you can get aboard your ship now and sail back to Athens.”
“No,” the young man answered. “I will never leave Crete until I have killed the Minotaur, saved my poor companions and freed Athens from this cruel tribute.”

“I knew that was what you would decide,” said Ariadne. “Then come with me, brave Theseus. Here is your own sword, which the guards took from you. You will need it, and I pray Heaven that you will use it well.”

Then she led Theseus by the hand until they came to a dark, shadowy grove, where the moonlight spilled over the treetops but hardly let a single glimmering beam fall on their path.
