They went a long way through this darkness and reached a high marble wall, so overgrown with creeping plants that it looked shaggy with leaves. The wall seemed to have no door and no windows. It rose up tall, massive and mysterious, and it could not be climbed over or, as far as Theseus could see, passed through. Even so, Ariadne simply pressed one of her soft little fingers against a certain block of marble. Although it looked as solid as the rest of the wall, it gave way at her touch and opened a gap just wide enough for them to enter. They crept through, and the marble stone swung back into place.

“We are now,” said Ariadne, “in the famous labyrinth that Daedalus built before he made himself a pair of wings and flew away from our island like a bird. Daedalus was a very clever craftsman, but of all his ingenious inventions, this labyrinth is the most marvelous. If we took just a few steps away from the entrance, we could wander around for the rest of our lives and never find it again. Yet at the very center of this labyrinth is the Minotaur, and you, Theseus, must go there to find him.”
“But how will I ever find him,” asked Theseus, “if the labyrinth confuses me as much as you say it will?”

Just as he spoke, they heard a rough and very unpleasant roar. It was a lot like the bellowing of a fierce bull, yet it also had something of a human voice in it. Theseus even imagined he could make out crude speech, as if the creature were trying to shape its hoarse breath into words. It was some distance away, though, and he could not really tell whether it sounded more like a bull’s roar or a man’s harsh voice.

“That is the Minotaur’s noise,” Ariadne whispered, gripping Theseus’s hand tightly and pressing her other hand to her heart, which was trembling. “You must follow that sound through the twists of the labyrinth, and before long you will find him. Wait! Take the end of this silken string. I will hold the other end, and if you win the victory, it will lead you back to this spot. Farewell, brave Theseus.”

So the young man took the end of the silken string in his left hand and, in the other, his gold-hilted sword, already drawn from its sheath, and boldly walked into the mysterious labyrinth. How this labyrinth was built, I cannot tell you. But so cleverly twisted a maze was never seen in the world, before or since. Nothing else could be so tangled, unless it were the brain of a man like Daedalus, who designed it, or the heart of any ordinary person, which, to be sure, is ten times as great a mystery as the labyrinth of Crete. Theseus had not gone five steps before he lost sight of Ariadne, and after five more his head began to spin. But he kept going, creeping through a low arch, then climbing a flight of steps, then turning down one crooked passage and another, with a door opening in front of him in one place and another slamming shut behind him in the next, until it truly seemed that the walls were spinning and whirling him around with them. And all the while, through these hollow corridors, sometimes nearer and sometimes farther away, came the cry of the Minotaur. The sound was so fierce, so cruel and so ugly, so much like a bull’s roar and yet so much like a human voice, and still unlike either, that the brave heart of Theseus grew sterner and angrier with every step. He felt it was an insult to the moon and the sky, and to our dear, simple Mother Earth, that such a monster should dare to exist.

As he went on, clouds gathered over the moon, and the labyrinth grew so dim that Theseus could no longer see the confusing maze he was passing through. He would have felt completely lost, and utterly hopeless of ever walking in a straight line again, if he had not felt, every little while, a gentle tug on the silken cord. Then he knew that tenderhearted Ariadne was still holding the other end, that she was afraid for him and hoping for him, and that she was giving him as much of her sympathy as if she stood right beside him. Oh, I can assure you, a great deal of human sympathy ran along that slender thread of silk. Still he followed the dreadful roar of the Minotaur, which grew louder and louder, until it was so loud that Theseus fully expected to come upon him at every new zigzag and twist of the path. And at last, in an open space at the very center of the labyrinth, he did catch sight of the hideous creature.

And sure enough, what an ugly monster he was! Only his horned head belonged to a bull, and yet somehow he looked like a bull all over, waddling absurdly on his hind legs. Or, if you happened to look at him another way, he seemed entirely a man, and all the more monstrous for it. And there he was, the wretched thing, with no company, no companion, no mate of any kind, living only to do harm and unable to know what affection means. Theseus hated him and shuddered at him, and yet he could not help feeling a certain pity, which grew stronger the uglier and more detestable the creature was. For he kept striding back and forth in a lonely frenzy of rage, roaring hoarsely, and mixed oddly into the roar were half-formed words. After listening for a while, Theseus understood that the Minotaur was telling himself how miserable he was, and how hungry, and how he hated everybody, and how he longed to eat the whole human race alive.

Ah, the bull-headed villain! And, my good little people, perhaps one of these days you will see, as I do now, that every human being who lets anything evil into his nature, or lets it stay there, is a kind of Minotaur: an enemy of his fellow creatures, cut off from all good company, as this poor monster was.

Was Theseus afraid? Not at all, my dear listeners. What! A hero like Theseus afraid! Not even if the Minotaur had had twenty bull heads instead of one. Bold as he was, though, I rather think it strengthened his brave heart, just at this moment, to feel a trembling tug on the silken cord that he still held in his left hand. It was as if Ariadne were giving him all her strength and courage. Much as he already had, and little as she had to give, it made his own seem twice as great. And to tell the honest truth, he needed every bit of it, because the Minotaur now turned around suddenly, caught sight of Theseus, and at once lowered his horribly sharp horns, exactly as an angry bull does when he means to charge an enemy. At the same moment he let out a tremendous roar, with something like the words of human speech in it, but all broken up and shaken to pieces by passing through the throat of a miserably enraged brute.

Theseus could only guess what the creature meant to say, and that more from his gestures than from his words, because the Minotaur’s horns were sharper than his wits and a good deal more useful to him than his tongue. But this was probably the sense of what he said:—
“Ah, you miserable human! I’ll run my horns through you, toss you fifty feet into the air, and gobble you up the moment you land.”
“Come on, then, and try it!” was all Theseus bothered to answer. He was far too noble to trade insults with his enemy.

With no more words on either side, the most terrible fight began that ever took place under the sun or moon, between Theseus and the Minotaur. I honestly can’t say how it would have ended if the monster, in his very first headlong charge, hadn’t missed Theseus by a hair and snapped one of his horns clean off against the stone wall. The mishap made him bellow so horribly that part of the labyrinth collapsed, and everyone in Crete took the noise for an unusually violent thunderstorm. Stinging with pain, he galloped around the open space in such a ridiculous way that Theseus laughed about it years afterward, though not at the time. Then the two enemies squared off bravely and fought, sword against horn, for a long while. At last the Minotaur rushed at Theseus, grazed his left side with the horn, and knocked him down. Thinking he had stabbed him through the heart, he cut a great caper in the air, opened his bull’s mouth from ear to ear, and got ready to bite off his head. But by then Theseus had jumped back up, and he caught the monster off guard. He swung his sword with all his strength and struck him squarely on the neck, and the bull’s head went skipping six yards away from its human body, which dropped flat on the ground.

So the battle was over. At once the moon shone out as brightly as if every trouble in the world, and all the wickedness and ugliness that plague human life, were gone forever. Theseus leaned on his sword to catch his breath, and he felt another tug on the silken cord, for he had gripped it tightly in his left hand all through the dreadful struggle. Eager to tell Ariadne he had won, he followed the thread, and before long he was back at the entrance of the labyrinth.
“You have killed the monster,” cried Ariadne, clasping her hands.
“And I owe it to you, dear Ariadne,” Theseus answered. “I come back the winner.”
“Then,” said Ariadne, “we must quickly wake your friends and get them and yourself aboard the ship before dawn. If morning finds you here, my father will take revenge for the Minotaur.”

To make a long story short, the poor captives were woken up. Hardly knowing whether they were dreaming for joy, they were told what Theseus had done and that they must sail for Athens before daybreak. They hurried down to the ship and all climbed aboard, except Prince Theseus, who stayed behind on the shore, holding Ariadne’s hand in his.

“Dear girl,” he said, “you will surely come with us. You are far too gentle and sweet a child for a father as hard-hearted as King Minos. He cares no more about you than a granite rock cares about the little flower growing in one of its cracks. But my father, King AEgeus, and my dear mother, AEthra, and all the fathers and mothers in Athens, and all the sons and daughters too, will love you and honor you as the one who saved them. So come with us, because King Minos will be furious when he learns what you have done.”

Now, some small-minded people who claim to tell the story of Theseus and Ariadne have the nerve to say that this royal and honorable girl really did run away in the dark of night with the young stranger whose life she had saved. They say, too, that Prince Theseus (who would have died sooner than wrong the humblest creature in the world) ungratefully abandoned Ariadne on a lonely island where the ship stopped on its way to Athens. But if the noble Theseus had heard these lies, he would have dealt with the people who spread them just as he dealt with the Minotaur! Here is what Ariadne really answered when the brave Prince of Athens begged her to go with him:—

“No, Theseus,” the girl said, squeezing his hand and then stepping back a pace or two, “I can’t go with you. My father is old, and he has no one but me to love him. However hard you think his heart is, it would break to lose me. At first King Minos will be angry, but he will soon forgive his only child, and in time, I know, he will be glad that no more young men and women have to come from Athens to be eaten by the Minotaur. I saved you, Theseus, as much for my father’s sake as for your own. Farewell! May heaven bless you!”

All this was so true, so like a maiden, and said with such sweet dignity, that Theseus would have been ashamed to press her further. Nothing was left for him to do but say a warm goodbye to Ariadne, climb aboard the ship, and sail away.

Within moments white foam was churning at the bow, as Prince Theseus and his companions sailed out of the harbor with a whistling wind behind them. Talus, the giant made of brass, was marching on his endless watch and happened to be coming toward that part of the coast. They could see him from a long way off, by the moonlight gleaming on his polished body. But since the figure moved like clockwork and could neither hurry nor slow his huge strides, he reached the port just when they were beyond the range of his club. Still, as he always did, he straddled from headland to headland and swung a blow at the ship. He overreached himself and fell flat into the sea, which splashed high over his gigantic body, the way it does when an iceberg turns a somersault. There he lies still, and anyone who wants to get rich on brass had better go there with a diving bell and fish up Talus.

On the voyage home, the fourteen young men and women were in excellent spirits, as you can easily imagine. They spent most of their time dancing, except when a wind from the side tilted the deck too steeply. In good time they came in sight of the coast of Attica, their native land. But here, I am sorry to tell you, a sad misfortune happened.

You will remember (what Theseus unfortunately forgot) that his father, King AEgeus, had told him to hoist sunshine-colored sails instead of black ones if he beat the Minotaur and came home victorious. But in the joy of their success, amid the games, dancing and other fun with which these young people passed the time, they never once wondered whether their sails were black, white or rainbow-colored. In fact, they left it entirely to the sailors whether the ship had any sails at all. So the vessel came back like a raven, with the same dark wings that had carried her away. Meanwhile poor King AEgeus, frail as he was, had climbed day after day to the top of a cliff that overhung the sea, and sat there watching for Prince Theseus to come home. The moment he saw the fatal blackness of the sails, he decided that his dear son, whom he loved so much and was so proud of, had been eaten by the Minotaur. He could not bear the thought of living any longer. First he flung his crown and scepter into the sea (useless trinkets that they were to him now!), and then King AEgeus simply leaned forward and tumbled headfirst off the cliff, and the poor man drowned in the waves foaming at its foot!

This was sorrowful news for Prince Theseus. When he stepped ashore, he found himself king of the whole country, whether he liked it or not, and a turn of fortune like that was enough to leave any young man feeling very low. Still, he sent for his dear mother to come to Athens, and by taking her advice on matters of state he became an excellent king, greatly loved by his people.

chapters.title: The Pygmies
paragraphs: A long time ago, when the world was full of wonders, there lived an earth-born Giant named Antaeus, together with a million or more curious little earth-born people called Pygmies. The Giant and the Pygmies were children of the same mother (that is, of our good old Grandmother Earth), so they were all brothers and lived together in a very friendly and affectionate way, far, far away in the middle of hot Africa. The Pygmies were so small, and so many sandy deserts and tall mountains lay between them and the rest of humankind, that nobody got a glimpse of them more than once in a hundred years. As for the Giant, he was so very tall that he was easy enough to see, but it was safest to stay out of his sight.

Among the Pygmies, I suppose, anyone who grew to six or eight inches was thought a tremendously tall man. Their little cities must have been very pretty to look at, with streets two or three feet wide, paved with the tiniest pebbles and lined with houses about as big as a squirrel’s cage. The king’s palace reached the astonishing size of Periwinkle’s dollhouse and stood in the middle of a roomy square that our hearth rug could hardly have covered. Their main temple, or cathedral, was as tall as that dresser over there, and they considered it a wonderfully grand and magnificent building. None of these buildings was made of stone or wood. The Pygmy workmen plastered them together neatly, rather like birds’ nests, out of straw, feathers, eggshells and other small scraps, using stiff clay for mortar. Once the hot sun had dried them, they were as snug and comfortable as any Pygmy could wish.

The countryside around was neatly divided into fields, and the biggest of them was about the size of one of Sweet Fern’s flower beds. Here the Pygmies planted wheat and other grains. When the grain grew tall and ripe, it towered over these tiny people the way pines, oaks, walnuts and chestnuts tower over you and me when we walk through our own woods. At harvest time they had to go out with their little axes and chop the grain down, just as a woodcutter clears a patch of forest. When a stalk of wheat with its heavy top happened to come crashing down on some unlucky Pygmy, it was likely to be a very sad business. Even if it didn’t flatten him completely, I’m sure it must have given the poor little fellow a headache. And goodness me! If the fathers and mothers were that small, what must the children and babies have been like? A whole family of them could have been tucked into bed in a shoe, or crept into an old glove and played hide-and-seek in the thumb and fingers. You could have hidden a one-year-old baby under a thimble.

Now, as I told you, these funny Pygmies had a Giant for a neighbor and brother, who was as big as they were little, or bigger. He was so tall that he used a pine tree eight feet thick at the base as his walking stick. I can assure you it took a Pygmy with sharp eyes to make out his head without a telescope, and in misty weather they sometimes couldn’t see his top half at all, only his long legs, which seemed to be striding around on their own. But at noon, when the air was clear and the sun shone brightly on him, the Giant Antaeus made a very grand sight. He would stand there, a perfect mountain of a man, with his great face smiling down at his little brothers and his one enormous eye (as big as a cartwheel, right in the middle of his forehead) giving a friendly wink to the whole nation at once.

The Pygmies loved to chat with Antaeus. Fifty times a day one or another of them would tip back his head, cup his hands around his mouth and shout, “Hello, brother Antaeus! How are you, my good fellow?” When the tiny, faraway squeak of their voices reached his ear, the Giant would answer, “Pretty well, brother Pygmy, thank you,” in a thundering roar that would have shaken down the walls of their strongest temple, if it hadn’t come from so far overhead.

It was lucky that Antaeus was a friend to the Pygmy people, because his little finger had more strength in it than ten million bodies like theirs. If he had been as bad-tempered toward them as he was toward everybody else, he could have flattened their biggest city with one kick and barely noticed. With the hurricane of his breath he could have torn the roofs off a hundred houses and sent thousands of people spinning through the air. He could have set his huge foot down on a crowd, and when he lifted it again, it would certainly have been a pitiful sight. But since he was a son of Mother Earth, as they were too, the Giant treated them with brotherly kindness and loved them as much as anyone could love creatures so very small. And for their part, the Pygmies loved Antaeus with all the affection their tiny hearts could hold. He was always ready to do them any favor he could. For example, when they wanted a breeze to turn their windmills, the Giant would set all the sails spinning just by breathing naturally. When the sun was too hot, he often sat down and let his shadow fall across the kingdom from one border to the other. And as for everything else, he was wise enough to leave it alone and let the Pygmies run their own affairs—which, after all, is about the best thing great people can do for little ones.

In short, as I said before, Antaeus loved the Pygmies, and the Pygmies loved Antaeus. The Giant’s life was as long as his body was large, while a Pygmy’s lifetime was only a span, so this friendship had gone on through countless generations and ages. It was written about in the Pygmy histories and talked about in their ancient traditions. The oldest, whitest-bearded Pygmy had never heard of a time, even back in his great-great-grandfather’s days, when the Giant had not been their enormous friend. Once, it is true (as an obelisk three feet high, put up at the site of the disaster, recorded), Antaeus sat down on about five thousand Pygmies who had gathered for a military review. But this was one of those unlucky accidents that nobody is to blame for. So the little folks never took it to heart, and only asked the Giant to be careful ever afterward to check the acre of ground where he meant to sit.

It is a pleasant picture to imagine Antaeus standing among the Pygmies, tall as the spire of the greatest cathedral ever built, while they scurried around his feet like ants, and to think that, for all the difference in their sizes, there was real affection and fellow feeling between them and him. To my mind, the Giant needed the little people far more than they needed him. If they had not been his neighbors and well-wishers, and, we might say, his playmates, Antaeus would not have had a single friend in the world. There was no other being like him; none had ever been made. No creature of his own size had ever talked with him face to face in a voice of thunder. When he stood with his head among the clouds, he was completely alone, as he had been for hundreds of years and would be forever. Even if he had met another Giant, Antaeus would have thought the world too small for two such enormous persons, and instead of making friends he would have fought him until one of them was dead. But with the Pygmies he was the most playful, funny, merry-hearted and good-tempered old Giant who ever washed his face in a wet cloud.
His little friends, like all small people, thought very highly of themselves, and they liked to act quite condescending toward the Giant.

“Poor creature!” they would say to one another. “His life is very dull, all alone as he is, and we shouldn’t begrudge giving up a little of our precious time to cheer him up. He isn’t nearly as clever as we are, of course, and that is exactly why he needs us to look after his comfort and happiness. Let’s be kind to the old fellow. After all, if Mother Earth hadn’t been so good to us, we might have turned out to be Giants too.”

On every holiday the Pygmies had wonderful sport with Antaeus. Often he stretched out at full length on the ground, where he looked like the long ridge of a hill, and a short-legged Pygmy would surely have needed a good hour’s walk to get from his head to his feet. He would lay his huge hand flat on the grass and dare the tallest of them to climb onto it and stride from finger to finger. They were so fearless that they thought nothing of creeping in among the folds of his clothes. When his head lay sideways on the ground, they would march right up and peer into the great cave of his mouth, and they took it all as a joke, as it was meant to be, when Antaeus suddenly snapped his jaws as if to swallow fifty of them at once. You would have laughed to see the children darting in and out of his hair or swinging from his beard. I could not tell you the half of the funny tricks they played on their enormous companion, but I don’t know that anything was odder than the sight of a gang of boys racing across his forehead to see who could first make it all the way around his one great eye. Another favorite stunt was to march along the bridge of his nose and jump down onto his upper lip.

To tell the truth, they could be as much of a nuisance to the Giant as a swarm of ants or mosquitoes, especially since they loved mischief and liked to poke his skin with their little swords and lances to find out how thick and tough it was. Antaeus took it all quite kindly, though now and then, when he happened to be sleepy, he would grumble a cross word or two, like the muttering of a storm, and ask them to stop their nonsense. Much more often, however, he watched their fun and games until his huge, heavy, clumsy wits were thoroughly stirred up, and then he would let out such a tremendous burst of enormous laughter that the whole nation of Pygmies had to cover their ears, or it would surely have deafened them.
“Ho! ho! ho!” the Giant boomed, shaking his mountainous sides. “How funny it is to be small! If I weren’t Antaeus, I’d happily be a pygmy, just for the fun of it.”

The Pygmies had only one trouble in the world. They were always at war with the cranes, and had been for as long as the long-lived Giant could remember. From time to time there had been terrible battles, and sometimes the little men won and sometimes the cranes did. According to some historians, the Pygmies rode into battle on the backs of goats and rams, but animals like those would have been far too big for Pygmies to ride. So I rather suppose they rode on squirrels, or rabbits, or rats, or perhaps on hedgehogs, whose prickly quills would have been very frightening to the enemy. However that may be, and whatever creatures the Pygmies rode, I have no doubt they looked formidable, armed with sword and spear, bow and arrow, blowing their tiny trumpets and shouting their little war cry. They never failed to urge one another to fight bravely and to remember that the whole world had its eyes on them, though in plain truth the only spectator was the Giant Antaeus, with his one great, stupid eye in the middle of his forehead.

When the two armies met, the cranes would rush forward, flapping their wings and stretching out their necks, and sometimes they would snatch up a few Pygmies crosswise in their beaks. When that happened, it was a truly awful sight to see those little men of might kicking and sprawling in the air and finally vanishing down the crane’s long, crooked throat, swallowed alive. A hero, you know, must be ready for any sort of fate, and no doubt the glory of it comforted him even inside the crane’s gizzard. If Antaeus saw that the battle was going badly for his little allies, he usually stopped laughing and ran to help them with mile-long strides, waving his club overhead and shouting at the cranes, who quacked and croaked and retreated as fast as they could. Then the Pygmy army would march home in triumph, crediting the victory entirely to their own courage and to the military skill and strategy of whoever happened to be captain general, and for a tiresome while afterward you would hear of nothing but grand processions, public banquets, brilliant illuminations, and waxwork shows with portraits of the distinguished officers as small as life.

In this warfare, if a Pygmy happened to pull out a crane’s tail feather, it was a very great feather in his cap. Once or twice, believe it or not, a little man was made chief ruler of the nation for no other merit than bringing home such a feather.

That is enough, though, to show you what a gallant little people they were, and how contentedly they and their forefathers, back through who knows how many generations, had lived beside the vast Giant Antaeus. Later in this story I will tell you of a much more astonishing battle than any the Pygmies ever fought with the cranes.

One day the mighty Antaeus was lounging at full length among his little friends. His pine-tree walking stick lay on the ground right beside him. His head was in one part of the kingdom and his feet stretched across the border into another, and he was making himself as comfortable as he could while the Pygmies scrambled over him, peered into his cavernous mouth and played in his hair. Now and then the Giant dozed off for a minute or two and snored like a rushing whirlwind. During one of these little naps, a Pygmy happened to climb up onto his shoulder and look around at the horizon, as if from the top of a hill. He saw something far away that made him rub the bright specks of his eyes and look harder than before. At first he took it for a mountain and wondered how it had sprung up out of the earth so suddenly. But soon he saw the mountain move. As it came nearer and nearer, what should it turn out to be but a human figure! It was not as big as Antaeus, it is true, but still very enormous compared with Pygmies, and a great deal bigger than the men we see nowadays.
When the Pygmy was quite sure his eyes had not fooled him, he ran as fast as his legs would carry him to the Giant’s ear, bent over its opening, and shouted into it at the top of his voice—
“Hello, brother Antaeus! Get up this minute and take your pine-tree walking stick in your hand. Here comes another Giant to wrestle with you.”
“Pooh, pooh!” grumbled Antaeus, only half awake. “None of your nonsense, my little fellow! Can’t you see I’m sleepy? There isn’t a Giant on earth I would bother to get up for.”

But the Pygmy looked again and now saw that the stranger was coming straight toward Antaeus, who was lying on the ground. With every step he looked less like a blue mountain and more like an immensely large man. Soon he was so near that there could be no mistake. There he was, with the sun blazing on his golden helmet and flashing off his polished breastplate. He had a sword at his side and a lion’s skin over his back, and on his right shoulder he carried a club that looked bulkier and heavier than the pine-tree walking stick of Antaeus.
By this time the whole nation of Pygmies had seen the new marvel, and a million of them gave a shout all together, which made quite an audible squeak.
“Wake up, Antaeus! Stir yourself, you lazy old Giant! Another Giant is coming, every bit as strong as you, and he wants a fight!”
“Nonsense, nonsense!” growled the sleepy Giant. “I’m going to finish my nap.”

Still the stranger came nearer, and now the Pygmies could clearly see that although he was not as tall as the Giant, his shoulders were even broader. And what a pair of shoulders they must have been! As I told you long ago, they once held up the sky. The Pygmies, who were ten times livelier than their great blockhead of a brother, could not stand the Giant’s slowness and were determined to get him on his feet. So they kept shouting at him, and even went so far as to poke him with their swords.
“Up, up, up!” they cried. “Out of bed with you, lazybones! That strange Giant has a bigger club than yours and broader shoulders, and we think he’s the stronger one.”

Antaeus could not bear to hear anyone say that a mere mortal was half as mighty as himself. This last remark of the Pygmies stung him deeper than their swords, and he sat up in rather a sulky mood, gave a yawn several yards wide, rubbed his eye, and at last turned his stupid head in the direction his little friends were eagerly pointing.

The moment he laid eyes on the stranger, he leaped to his feet, snatched up his walking stick, and strode a mile or two to meet him, swinging the sturdy pine tree so hard that it whistled through the air.
“Who goes there?” the Giant thundered. “What business have you in my realm?”

There was one strange thing about Antaeus that I have not told you yet, because I was afraid that if I told you so many wonders all at once, you might not believe more than half of them. You must know, then, that whenever this mighty Giant touched the ground, with his hand or his foot or any other part of his body, he grew stronger than he had been before. The Earth, you remember, was his mother, and she was very fond of him, since he was almost the biggest of her children, so she used this way to keep him always at full strength. Some people say he grew ten times stronger at every touch, and others say only twice as strong. But just think of it! Whenever Antaeus took a walk, even a ten-mile one, with a hundred yards to a stride, you can try to work out how much mightier he was when he sat down again than when he first set out. And whenever he flung himself on the ground to rest, even if he got up again the very next instant, he was as strong as ten giants just like his former self. It was lucky for the world that Antaeus was lazy by nature and liked ease better than exercise, because if he had frisked about like the Pygmies and touched the earth as often as they did, he would have been strong enough long ago to pull the sky down about people’s ears. But these great clumsy fellows are like mountains, not only in size but in how little they care to move.

Any other man, except the very one Antaeus had just met, would have been frightened half to death by the Giant’s fierce look and terrible voice. But the stranger did not seem the least bit troubled. He lifted his club casually and balanced it in his hand, looking Antaeus over from head to foot, not as if he were amazed at his size, but as if he had seen plenty of Giants before and this was by no means the biggest. In fact, if the Giant had been no bigger than the Pygmies (who stood with their ears pricked up, watching and listening to everything going on), the stranger could not have been less afraid of him.
“Who are you, I say?” roared Antaeus again. “What is your name? What brings you here? Speak up, you scoundrel, or my walking stick will find out how thick your skull is.”

“You are a most ill-mannered Giant,” the stranger replied in a calm voice, “and I expect I will have to give you a lesson in courtesy before we part. My name is Hercules. I came this way because it is the handiest road to the garden of the Hesperides, where I am going to fetch three golden apples for King Eurystheus.”

“Wretch, you will go no farther!” bellowed Antaeus, looking grimmer than before, for he had heard of the mighty Hercules and hated him because he was said to be so strong. “And you will not go back the way you came, either!”
“And how do you plan to stop me,” Hercules asked, “from going where I like?”

“With a good thump from this pine tree!” shouted Antaeus, scowling until he was the ugliest monster in all Africa. “I am fifty times stronger than you are, and now that my foot is stamping the ground, I am five hundred times stronger! I’d be ashamed to kill a puny little dwarf as you seem to be. No, you will be my slave, and the slave of my brothers the Pygmies here as well. Throw down your club and your other weapons. As for that lion’s skin, I plan to have gloves made from it.”
“Then come and take it off my shoulders,” Hercules answered, and he raised his club.

Grinning with rage, the Giant strode toward the stranger like a walking tower, growing ten times stronger with every step. He swung his pine tree at Hercules in a monstrous blow, but Hercules caught it on his club. Hercules was more skillful than Antaeus, and he paid him back with such a whack on the head that the great lumbering man-mountain crashed flat onto the ground. The poor little Pygmies had never imagined that anyone in the world was half as strong as their brother Antaeus, and they were badly shaken by this. But the Giant was hardly down before he bounced up again with ten times the might, and with a face so furious it was horrible to look at. He aimed another blow at Hercules, but he was blind with anger and missed, and only struck his poor, innocent Mother Earth, who groaned and trembled under the hit. His pine tree sank so deep into the ground and stuck so fast that before Antaeus could pull it free, Hercules brought his club down across the Giant’s shoulders with a mighty thwack. The Giant let out a roar as if every unbearable noise in the world had come screeching and rumbling out of his enormous lungs in a single cry. It rolled away over mountains and valleys, and for all I know it was heard on the far side of the African deserts.

As for the Pygmies, the shock and the shaking of the air knocked their capital city into ruins. There was uproar enough without them, but they all set up a shriek anyway, from three million little throats, no doubt imagining that they made the Giant’s bellow at least ten times louder. Meanwhile Antaeus had scrambled back to his feet and pulled his pine tree out of the earth. Blazing with fury, and more outrageously strong than ever, he charged at Hercules and brought down another blow.
“This time, you rascal,” he shouted, “you won’t get away from me!”

But once again Hercules turned the stroke aside with his club, and the Giant’s pine tree burst into a thousand splinters. Most of them flew into the Pygmies and did them more harm than I like to think about. Before Antaeus could get out of the way, Hercules struck again and knocked him down once more, sending him head over heels. All it did was add to his strength, which was already huge and unbearable. As for his rage, there is no telling what a roaring furnace it had become. His one eye was nothing but a circle of red flame. Since he had no weapon left but his fists, he doubled them up, each one bigger than a barrel, and smashed them together. He danced up and down in a frenzy, waving his huge arms as if he meant not only to kill Hercules but to smash the whole world to pieces.
“Come on!” roared the thundering Giant. “Just let me hit you once on the ear, and you’ll never have a headache again!”

Now Hercules, who was strong enough, as you already know, to hold up the sky, began to realize that he would never win if he kept knocking Antaeus down. If he hit the Giant such hard blows, then sooner or later, with the help of his Mother Earth, Antaeus would grow stronger than even the mighty Hercules. So he threw down the club he had used in so many dreadful battles, and stood ready to meet his opponent with bare arms.
“Step forward,” he cried. “Now that I’ve broken your pine tree, let’s see which of us is the better man in a wrestling match.”

“Aha! Then I’ll soon settle this,” shouted the Giant. If there was one thing he was prouder of than anything else, it was his skill at wrestling. “You villain, I’ll fling you where you’ll never get up again!”

On came Antaeus, hopping and capering in the scorching heat of his rage, and gaining fresh strength for his fury every time he hopped. But Hercules, you must understand, was wiser than this blockhead of a Giant. He had thought of a way to fight him, huge earth-born monster though he was, and to beat him in spite of everything his Mother Earth could do. He waited for his chance, and as the maddened Giant rushed at him, Hercules caught him around the middle with both hands, lifted him high into the air, and held him up over his head.

Just imagine it, my dear little friends! What a sight it must have been to see this monstrous fellow sprawling in the air face down, kicking out his long legs and wriggling his whole vast body, like a baby whose father is holding him up at arm’s length toward the ceiling.

But the most wonderful thing was this. As soon as Antaeus was properly off the ground, he began to lose the strength he had gained by touching it. Hercules soon noticed that his troublesome enemy was growing weaker. He struggled and kicked less violently, and the thunder of his big voice sank to a grumble. The truth was that unless the Giant touched Mother Earth at least once every five minutes, he would lose not only his overgrown strength but the very breath of life. Hercules had guessed this secret, and it may be good for all of us to remember it, in case we ever have to fight a battle against someone like Antaeus. These earth-born creatures are hard to beat only on their own ground, but they are easily handled if we can find a way to lift them up into a higher and purer air. So it turned out with the poor Giant, whom I am truly sorry for, even though he treated strangers who came to visit him so rudely.

When his strength and breath were completely gone, Hercules gave his huge body a toss and flung it about a mile away. It landed heavily and lay as still as a sand hill. It was too late now for Mother Earth to help him. I would not be surprised if his massive bones are lying on the same spot to this very day, and people mistake them for the bones of an unusually large elephant.

But, alas! What a wailing the poor little Pygmies set up when they saw their enormous brother treated in this terrible way! If Hercules heard their shrieks, he paid no attention. Perhaps he took them for the shrill, mournful twittering of small birds frightened out of their nests by the uproar of his battle with Antaeus. In fact, he had been so busy thinking about the Giant that he had never once looked at the Pygmies, and he did not even know there was such a funny little nation in the world. Now he had traveled a long way and was rather worn out from the fight. So he spread his lion’s skin on the ground, lay down on it, and fell fast asleep.

As soon as the Pygmies saw Hercules getting ready for a nap, they nodded their little heads at one another and winked their little eyes. When his deep, steady breathing told them he was asleep, they gathered in an immense crowd, covering a patch of ground about twenty-seven feet square. One of their most eloquent speakers climbed up on a toadstool and addressed the crowd from that high spot. He was also a brave enough warrior, though he was hardly as good with any weapon as he was with his tongue. His words went more or less like this, or at any rate something like this was probably the gist of his speech:

“Tall Pygmies and mighty little men! All of us have seen what a public disaster has come upon us, and what an insult has been offered to the majesty of our nation. Over there lies Antaeus, our great friend and brother, killed on our own land by a scoundrel who caught him at a disadvantage. He fought him, if you can call it fighting, in a way that no man, Giant, or Pygmy ever dreamed of fighting until this hour. And to add a grievous insult to the wrong already done to us, the scoundrel has now fallen asleep as calmly as if he had nothing to fear from our anger! Fellow countrymen, we must consider how we will look in the eyes of the world, and what the fair verdict of history will be, if we let these piled-up outrages go unavenged.

“Antaeus was our brother, born of the same beloved mother to whom we owe the muscle and sinew, and the courageous hearts, that made him proud to be related to us. He was our faithful ally, and he fell fighting as much for our national rights and privileges as for his own. We and our forefathers have lived in friendship with him and kept up an affectionate friendship, man to man, through generations beyond memory. You remember how often our whole people have rested in his great shadow, and how our little ones have played hide-and-seek in the tangles of his hair, and how his mighty footsteps have gone to and fro among us so familiarly and never trodden on any of our toes. And now there lies this dear brother, this sweet and kindly friend, this brave and faithful ally, this virtuous Giant, this blameless and excellent Antaeus, dead! Dead! Silent! Powerless! A mere mountain of clay! Forgive my tears! No, I see your own! If we drowned the world with them, could the world blame us?

“But to go on: Shall we, my countrymen, let this wicked stranger leave unharmed and boast of his treacherous victory among far-off peoples of the earth? Shall we not rather force him to leave his bones here on our soil, beside the bones of our slain brother? Then one skeleton will stand as the everlasting monument of our sorrow, and the other will last just as long, showing the whole human race a terrible example of Pygmy vengeance. That is the question. I put it to you with full confidence that your answer will be worthy of our national character, and will add to, rather than lessen, the glory our ancestors handed down to us, and which we ourselves have proudly defended in our war with the cranes.”

At this point a burst of irrepressible enthusiasm interrupted the speaker, as every single Pygmy cried out that the national honor must be kept at all costs. He bowed, signaled for silence, and finished his address in the following splendid manner:

“All that remains, then, is for us to decide whether to wage this war as a whole nation, one united people against a common enemy, or whether some champion, famous from earlier fights, should be chosen to challenge the killer of our brother Antaeus to single combat. If it is the latter, I am well aware that there may be taller men among you, but I hereby offer myself for that enviable duty. And believe me, dear countrymen, whether I live or die, the honor of this great country and the fame our heroic ancestors left us will suffer no loss in my hands. Never, as long as I can wield this sword, whose scabbard I now fling away, never, never, never, even if the crimson hand that killed the great Antaeus should lay me flat, as it did him, on the soil I give my life to defend.”

With these words, the valiant Pygmy drew his weapon, which was terrible to look at, being as long as the blade of a penknife, and sent the scabbard whirling over the heads of the crowd. His speech was met with a roar of applause, as its patriotism and self-sacrifice certainly deserved. The shouts and clapping would have gone on much longer, if a deep breath, commonly called a snore, from the sleeping Hercules had not drowned them out completely.

In the end it was decided that the whole nation of Pygmies should set to work to destroy Hercules. This was not because they doubted that a single champion could put him to the sword, but because he was a public enemy and everyone wanted a share in the glory of defeating him. There was a debate about whether national honor required sending a herald with a trumpet to stand over the ear of Hercules, blow a blast right into it, and challenge him to battle by formal proclamation. But two or three old and wise Pygmies, experienced in affairs of state, gave their opinion that war already existed, and that they had every right to take the enemy by surprise. Besides, if he were woken and allowed to get onto his feet, Hercules might do them some harm before they could beat him down again. For, as these wise counselors pointed out, the stranger’s club was really very big, and it had rattled like a thunderbolt against the skull of Antaeus. So the Pygmies decided to drop all foolish fussing over formalities and attack their opponent at once.

So all the fighting men of the nation took up their weapons and marched boldly up to Hercules, who was still fast asleep, with no idea of the harm the Pygmies meant to do him. A body of twenty thousand archers marched in front, with their little bows ready and arrows on the string. The same number were ordered to climb onto Hercules. Some carried spades to dig out his eyes, and others carried bundles of hay and all sorts of rubbish to stuff into his mouth and nostrils, so that he would die for lack of breath. These last, however, could not do their job at all, because the enemy’s breath rushed out of his nose in a roaring hurricane and whirlwind, which blew the Pygmies away as fast as they came near. So they had to think of some other way of carrying on the war.

After holding a council, the captains ordered their troops to gather sticks, straw, dry weeds, and any other stuff that would burn, and to pile it up high around the head of Hercules. Many thousands of Pygmies worked at this task, so they soon brought together several bushels of firewood and built the pile so tall that, standing on top, they were level with the sleeper’s face. The archers, meanwhile, were stationed within bowshot, with orders to shoot at Hercules the instant he moved. When everything was ready, a torch was put to the pile, which burst into flames at once and soon grew hot enough to roast the enemy, if only he had chosen to lie still. A Pygmy, you know, though so very small, could set the world on fire just as easily as a Giant could. So this was certainly the very best way of dealing with their enemy, provided they could have kept him quiet while the fire was going on.
But as soon as Hercules began to feel the scorching, up he jumped, with his hair in a red blaze.
“What on earth is going on?” he cried, still groggy from sleep, and he stared around as though he expected another Giant to be standing there.

Just then the twenty thousand archers let go of their bowstrings with a twang. The arrows came whizzing right into the face of Hercules like so many winged mosquitoes. But I doubt that even half a dozen of them broke the skin, which was remarkably tough, as you know the skin of a hero has good reason to be.

“Scoundrel!” all the Pygmies shouted together. “You have murdered the Giant Antaeus, our great brother and our nation’s ally. We declare bloody war against you, and we will put you to death right here!”

Hercules was surprised by the shrill piping of so many little voices. He put out the fire in his hair and looked all around, but he could see nothing. At last, though, he looked closely at the ground and spotted the countless crowd of Pygmies at his feet. He stooped down, picked up the nearest one between his thumb and finger, set him on the palm of his left hand, and held him at a good distance to look him over. It happened to be the very same Pygmy who had spoken from the top of the toadstool and had offered himself as the champion to meet Hercules in single combat.
“Well, what on earth are you, my little fellow?” exclaimed Hercules.

“I’m your enemy,” the brave Pygmy answered, in the loudest squeak he could manage. “You have killed the mighty Antaeus, our brother on our mother’s side and, for ages, the loyal ally of our famous nation. We have sworn to put you to death, and for my part, I challenge you to fight me right now, on even ground.”

Hercules found the Pygmy’s big words and warlike poses so funny that he burst out in a roar of laughter. He very nearly dropped the poor little scrap of a creature off his palm, he shook so hard with delight.

“Upon my word,” he cried, “I thought I had seen marvels enough before today—hydras with nine heads, stags with golden horns, men with six legs, three-headed dogs, giants with furnaces in their bellies, and goodness knows what else. But here on my own palm stands a marvel that beats them all! Your body, my little friend, is about as big as an ordinary man’s finger. Tell me, how big is your soul?”
“As big as yours!” said the Pygmy.
The little man’s fearless courage touched Hercules, and he could not help feeling the kind of kinship that one hero feels for another.

“My good little people,” he said, bowing low to the great nation, “I wouldn’t hurt brave fellows like you on purpose for anything in the world! Your hearts seem so enormous that, on my honor, I wonder how your small bodies hold them. I ask for peace, and as my part of the bargain I will take five steps and be out of your kingdom by the sixth. Good-bye. I’ll watch where I put my feet, so I don’t squash fifty of you without knowing it. Ha, ha, ha! Ho, ho, ho! For once, Hercules admits that he has been beaten.”

Some writers claim that Hercules scooped the whole race of Pygmies into his lion’s skin and carried them home to Greece, so that King Eurystheus’s children would have something to play with. That is a mistake. He left every one of them in their own land, where, for all I know, their descendants are still living today. They are building their little houses, plowing their little fields, spanking their little children, fighting their little war against the cranes, running their little businesses, whatever those may be, and reading their little histories of ancient times. Perhaps those histories record that, many centuries ago, the brave Pygmies avenged the death of the giant Antaeus by frightening the mighty Hercules away.

chapters.title: The Dragon’s Teeth
paragraphs: Cadmus, Phoenix, and Cilix, the three sons of King Agenor, were playing near the seashore in their father’s kingdom of Phoenicia, together with their little sister Europa, who was a very beautiful child. They had wandered some way from the palace where their parents lived, and had come to a green meadow. On one side of it lay the sea, sparkling and dimpling in the sunshine and murmuring softly against the beach. The three boys were happily picking flowers and twisting them into garlands to decorate little Europa. She sat on the grass, nearly buried in buds and blossoms, with her rosy face peeping merrily out of them. Cadmus said it was the prettiest flower of all.

Just then a splendid butterfly came fluttering across the meadow. Cadmus, Phoenix, and Cilix ran after it, shouting that it was a flower with wings. Europa was a little tired from playing all day, so she did not chase the butterfly with her brothers. She stayed where they had left her and closed her eyes. For a while she listened to the soothing sound of the sea, which seemed to say “Hush!” and tell her to go to sleep. But if the pretty child slept at all, it cannot have been for more than a moment. Soon she heard something trampling on the grass not far away, and peeping out from her pile of flowers, she saw a snow-white bull.

Where could this bull have come from? Europa and her brothers had been playing in the meadow for a long time, and they had seen no cattle and no other living creature, either there or on the nearby hills.
“Brother Cadmus!” cried Europa, jumping up from among the roses and lilies. “Phoenix! Cilix! Where are you? Help! Help! Come and chase this bull away!”

But her brothers were too far away to hear her, especially since fright had weakened her voice and kept her from calling loudly. So she stood there with her pretty mouth wide open, as pale as the white lilies twisted into her garlands.

Still, what scared Europa so badly was how suddenly she had noticed the bull, not anything frightening about him. When she looked at him more carefully, she began to see that he was a beautiful animal, and she even imagined a particularly kind look on his face. His breath—and you know that the breath of cattle is always sweet—smelled as if he had eaten nothing but rosebuds, or at least the most delicate clover blossoms. No bull ever had such bright, tender eyes or such smooth ivory horns as this one. He ran little races and bounded playfully around the child, until she forgot how big and strong he was. From his gentle, playful ways she soon thought of him as a creature as harmless as a pet lamb.

So, frightened as she had been at first, before long you could have seen Europa stroking the bull’s forehead with her small white hand and taking the garlands off her own head to hang them on his neck and ivory horns. Then she pulled up some blades of grass, and he ate them from her hand. He was not hungry, but he wanted to be friends with the child, and he liked eating what she had touched. Goodness me! Was there ever such a gentle, sweet, pretty, friendly creature as this bull, or such a nice playmate for a little girl?

When the animal saw that Europa was no longer afraid of him—and it is truly amazing how clever this bull was—he was overjoyed and could hardly hold himself in. He frisked about the meadow, here and there, with light leaps, as easily as a bird hops from twig to twig. In fact, he moved as lightly as if he were flying, and his hoofs hardly seemed to leave a print in the grassy ground. With his spotless coat he looked like a snowdrift blown along by the wind. Once he galloped so far off that Europa feared she might never see him again, so she raised her childish voice and called him back.
“Come back, pretty creature!” she cried. “Here’s a nice clover blossom.”

And then it was lovely to see how grateful the friendly bull was. He was so full of joy and thanks that he leaped higher than ever. He came running up and bowed his head before Europa, as if he knew she was a king’s daughter, or else understood the important truth that a little girl is everybody’s queen. He did not only bend his neck, either. He actually knelt down at her feet, and he nodded so cleverly and made such inviting gestures that Europa understood what he meant as well as if he had said it in words.
“Come, dear child,” was what he wanted to say, “let me give you a ride on my back.”

At first, Europa shrank back from the very idea. But then she reasoned, in her wise little head, that there could be no harm in taking just one gallop on the back of this gentle, friendly animal, who would surely set her down the moment she asked. And how surprised her brothers would be to see her riding across the green meadow! What fun they could have, taking turns for a gallop, or even climbing on the gentle creature all four together and racing around the field, laughing so loudly that they would be heard all the way to King Agenor’s palace!
“I think I’ll do it,” the child said to herself.

And why not? She glanced around and spotted Cadmus, Phoenix, and Cilix, still chasing the butterfly, almost at the far end of the meadow. Climbing onto the white bull’s back would be the quickest way to catch up with them. So she stepped a little closer to him, and he, friendly creature that he was, showed such joy at this sign of her trust that she could not bring herself to hesitate any longer. With one jump (for this little princess was as nimble as a squirrel), Europa was sitting on the beautiful bull, holding an ivory horn in each hand so she would not fall off.
“Gently, pretty bull, gently!” she said, a bit scared by what she had done. “Don’t gallop too fast.”

Once he had the child on his back, the animal leaped into the air and came down as softly as a feather, so that Europa could not tell when his hoofs touched the ground. Then he raced toward the part of the flowery plain where her three brothers were, and where they had just caught their splendid butterfly. Europa squealed with delight. Phoenix, Cilix, and Cadmus stood staring at their sister riding a white bull, not sure whether to be frightened or to wish the same good luck for themselves. The gentle, harmless creature (and who could possibly doubt that he was?) pranced among the children as playfully as a kitten. All the while Europa looked down at her brothers, nodding and laughing, though with a certain dignity in her rosy little face. As the bull wheeled around to gallop across the meadow again, she waved and said, “Good-bye,” playfully pretending that she was setting off on a faraway journey and might not see her brothers again for who knew how long.
“Good-bye,” Cadmus, Phoenix, and Cilix shouted together, all in one breath.

But along with her enjoyment of the game, a little fear still lingered in the child’s heart. Her last look at the three boys was a troubled one, and it made them feel as if their dear sister were truly leaving them forever. And what do you think the snowy bull did next? Why, he set off as fast as the wind, straight down to the shore, raced across the sand, took a light leap, and plunged right into the foaming waves. White spray rose over him and little Europa in a shower and fell splattering onto the water.

Then what a scream of terror the poor child let out! The three brothers screamed bravely too, and ran to the shore as fast as their legs could carry them, with Cadmus in the lead. But it was too late. By the time they reached the edge of the sand, the treacherous animal was already far out in the wide blue sea, with only his snowy head and tail above the water and poor little Europa between them. She was stretching one hand toward her dear brothers while she gripped the bull’s ivory horn with the other. Cadmus, Phoenix, and Cilix stood there watching this sad sight through their tears, until they could no longer tell the bull’s snowy head from the white-capped waves that seemed to boil up out of the depths around him. The white bull was never seen again, and neither was the beautiful child.

As you can imagine, this was a sad story for the three boys to bring home to their parents. King Agenor, their father, ruled the whole country, but he loved his little daughter Europa more than his kingdom, more than all his other children, and more than anything else in the world. So when Cadmus and his two brothers came home crying and told him that a white bull had carried off their sister and swum away with her across the sea, the king was beside himself with grief and rage. Though it was already twilight and quickly getting dark, he ordered them to set out at once to search for her.

“You will never see my face again,” he cried, “unless you bring me back my little Europa, to cheer me with her smiles and her sweet ways. Go, and don’t come into my presence again until you come leading her by the hand.”

As King Agenor said this, his eyes flashed fire (for he was a very hot-tempered king), and he looked so terribly angry that the poor boys did not even dare to ask for supper. They slunk out of the palace and stopped for a moment on the steps to decide where to go first. While they stood there, all dismayed, their mother, Queen Telephassa, who had not been present when they told the king, came hurrying after them and said that she, too, would go looking for her daughter.
“Oh no, Mother!” cried the boys. “The night is dark, and there’s no telling what troubles and dangers we may meet.”
Poor Queen Telephassa answered through bitter tears, “Dear children, that is exactly why I must go with you. If I lost you as well as my little Europa, what would I do?”
“And let me come too!” said their playmate Thasus, who ran up to join them.

Thasus was the son of a seafaring man who lived nearby. He had grown up with the young princes, was their close friend, and loved Europa very much, so they agreed that he could come along. The whole party set out together. Cadmus, Phoenix, Cilix, and Thasus clustered around Queen Telephassa, holding on to her skirts and begging her to lean on their shoulders whenever she felt tired. This is how they went down the palace steps and began a journey that turned out to be much longer than they ever imagined. The last they saw of King Agenor, he came to the door with a servant holding a torch beside him, and called after them into the gathering darkness:
“Don’t forget! You may not set foot on these steps again unless you bring the child!”
Queen Telephassa sobbed, “Never!” and the three brothers and Thasus echoed her: “Never! Never! Never! Never!”

And they kept their word. Year after year King Agenor sat alone in his beautiful palace, listening in vain for their footsteps coming back. He hoped to hear the queen’s familiar voice, the cheerful talk of his sons and their playmate Thasus coming in at the door together, and the sweet, childish voice of little Europa in the middle of them. But so much time went by that, in the end, if they had really come, the king would not have known this was Telephassa’s voice, or that these were the younger voices that used to fill the palace with happy echoes when the children played there. For now we must leave King Agenor sitting on his throne and go along with Queen Telephassa and her four young companions.

On and on they went, a long way, over mountains and rivers and across seas. Everywhere, in every place, they kept asking whether anyone could tell them what had happened to Europa. The country people they questioned would stop their work in the fields for a moment and stare in great surprise. It seemed strange to them to see a woman dressed like a queen, roaming the countryside with four boys around her on an errand like this. (In her hurry, Telephassa had forgotten to take off her crown and royal robes.) But nobody could give them any news of Europa. Nobody had seen a little girl dressed like a princess, riding a snow-white bull that galloped as fast as the wind.

I can’t say how long Queen Telephassa wandered like this, along highways and side paths and through trackless wilderness, with her three sons Cadmus, Phoenix and Cilix, and their playmate Thasus. But this much is certain: before they found anywhere to rest, their fine clothes were completely worn out. They all looked travel-stained, and they would have had the dust of many countries on their shoes if the streams they waded through hadn’t washed it all away. After they had been gone a year, Telephassa threw away her crown, because it rubbed her forehead sore.
“Many a headache this crown has given me,” said the poor queen, “and it does nothing for my aching heart.”

As their princely robes tore and fell to tatters, they swapped them for the plain clothes that ordinary people wore. Before long they looked wild and homeless, so much so that you would have taken them for a family of gypsies sooner than for a queen, three princes and a young nobleman who once had a palace for a home and a crowd of servants to do their bidding. The four boys grew into tall young men with sunburnt faces. Each of them strapped on a sword to defend himself against the dangers of the road. When the farmers whose houses they asked for shelter needed help in the harvest field, they gladly gave it, and Queen Telephassa (who had never done any work in her palace except braid silk threads with golden ones) followed behind them to tie up the sheaves. If anyone offered to pay them, they shook their heads and asked only for news of Europa.

“There are bulls enough in my pasture,” the old farmer would answer, “but I never heard of one like the one you describe. A snow-white bull with a little princess on his back! Ha, ha! Forgive me, good folks, but nobody has ever seen a sight like that around here.”

At last, when the first down was appearing on his upper lip, Phoenix grew tired of drifting from place to place for nothing. So one day, as they were passing through a pleasant, lonely stretch of country, he sat down on a heap of moss.

“I can’t go any farther,” said Phoenix. “It’s a plain, foolish waste of life to spend it the way we do, always wandering up and down and never coming home at nightfall. Our sister is lost and will never be found. Perhaps she drowned in the sea, or perhaps the white bull carried her to some distant shore. Either way it was so many years ago that if we met again, there would be no love or familiarity left between us. Our father has forbidden us to go back to his palace, so I will build myself a hut of branches and live here.”
“Well, my son Phoenix,” said Telephassa sadly, “you are a grown man now, and you must do what you think best. But I will keep searching for my poor child.”
“And the three of us will go with you!” cried Cadmus and Cilix, and their loyal friend Thasus.

But before setting out, they all helped Phoenix build a home. When it was finished, it was a lovely country bower, roofed by an arch of living branches. Inside were two pleasant rooms. One had a soft heap of moss for a bed, and the other held a seat or two, oddly shaped from the crooked roots of trees. It looked so comfortable and homelike that Telephassa and her three companions couldn’t help sighing at the thought that they must go on roaming the world, instead of spending the rest of their lives in a cheerful home like the one they had just built for Phoenix. But when they said goodbye to him, Phoenix wept, and he probably regretted that he would no longer be traveling with them.

Still, he had picked an excellent place to live. Before long other people who happened to have no homes came by, and seeing what a pleasant spot it was, they built huts near Phoenix’s dwelling. So within a few years a city had grown up there. In the middle of it stood a stately marble palace, where Phoenix lived, dressed in a purple robe and wearing a golden crown. The people of the new city had learned that he had royal blood, and they had chosen him as their king. The very first law King Phoenix issued was this: if a maiden should arrive in the kingdom riding a snow-white bull and calling herself Europa, his subjects must treat her with the greatest kindness and respect and bring her to the palace at once. From this you can see that Phoenix’s conscience never quite stopped troubling him for giving up the search for his dear sister and settling down in comfort while his mother and her companions went on.

But again and again, at the end of a tiring day’s journey, Telephassa, Cadmus, Cilix and Thasus remembered the pleasant spot where they had left Phoenix. It was a sad thought for these wanderers that tomorrow they would have to set out again, and that after many more nights they might be no closer to the end of their weary pilgrimage than they were now. These thoughts made them all gloomy at times, but they seemed to torment Cilix more than the others. At last, one morning as they were picking up their staffs to set out, he spoke to them like this:

“My dear mother, and you, good brother Cadmus, and my friend Thasus, I think we are like people in a dream. There is nothing solid in the life we are leading. It has been such a dreary length of time since the white bull carried off my sister Europa that I have completely forgotten how she looked and what her voice sounded like, and I almost doubt that such a little girl ever lived. And whether she lived or not, I’m convinced that she is not alive now, so it is pure folly to waste our own lives and happiness looking for her. If we did find her, she would be a grown woman and would see us all as strangers. So, to tell you the truth, I have decided to make my home here, and I beg you, mother, brother and friend, to follow my example.”

“Not I, for one,” said Telephassa. The poor queen spoke firmly, though she was so worn out from the road that she could hardly set her foot on the ground. “Not I, for one! Deep in my heart, little Europa is still the rosy child who ran off to pick flowers so many years ago. She hasn’t grown into a woman, and she hasn’t forgotten me. At noon, at night, while we travel, while we sit down to rest, I always hear her childish voice calling, ‘Mother! Mother!’ Let anyone stop here who wants to. For me there is no rest.”
“Nor for me,” said Cadmus, “as long as my dear mother wants to go on.”
And the loyal Thasus was determined to keep them company as well. They stayed with Cilix for a few days, though, and helped him build a country bower like the one they had built before for Phoenix.

When they said goodbye, Cilix burst into tears and told his mother that staying behind alone seemed just as sad a dream as going on. If she truly believed they would ever find Europa, he said, he was willing to keep searching with them even now. But Telephassa told him to stay there and be happy, if his own heart would let him. So the pilgrims took their leave and left. They were barely out of sight when some other wandering people came along, saw Cilix’s dwelling, and were delighted with the look of the place. There was plenty of unused land nearby, so these strangers built huts for themselves. Soon a crowd of new settlers joined them, and they quickly formed a city. In the middle of it stood a magnificent palace of colored marble, and on its balcony every noon appeared Cilix, in a long purple robe and a jeweled crown. When the people found out he was a king’s son, they had decided he was the best man of all to be their king.

One of the first things King Cilix did as ruler was to send out an expedition: a serious ambassador and an escort of bold, hardy young men, with orders to visit the main kingdoms of the earth and ask whether a young maiden had passed through them, galloping fast on a white bull. So it seems clear to me that Cilix secretly blamed himself for giving up the search for Europa while he was still able to put one foot in front of the other.

As for Telephassa, Cadmus and the good Thasus, it grieves me to think of them, still going on with that weary pilgrimage. The two young men did their best for the poor queen. They helped her over the rough places, often carried her across streams in their loyal arms, and tried to find her shelter at nightfall even when they themselves had to sleep on the ground. It was sad, so sad, to hear them asking every passer-by whether he had seen Europa, so long after the white bull had carried her away. The gray years came between, and the child’s figure grew dim in their memory, but none of these three true-hearted people ever dreamed of giving up the search.
One morning, however, poor Thasus found that he had sprained his ankle and could not go another step.

“In a few days, of course,” he said sadly, “I could manage to hobble along with a stick. But that would only slow you down, and it might keep you from finding dear little Europa after all your pains and trouble. So go on without me, my beloved companions, and I will follow as best I can.”

“You have been a true friend, dear Thasus,” said Queen Telephassa, kissing his forehead. “You are neither my son nor the brother of our lost Europa, yet you have shown yourself more faithful to me and to her than Phoenix and Cilix, whom we left behind. Without your loving help and my son Cadmus’s, my legs could not have carried me half this far. Now rest, and be at peace. For I begin to wonder whether we will ever find my beloved daughter in this world, and this is the first time I have admitted it to myself.”

As she said this, the poor queen wept, because it was a bitter trial for a mother’s heart to admit that her hopes were fading. From that day on, Cadmus noticed that she no longer traveled with the lively spirit that had carried her until then. She leaned more heavily on his arm.

Before they left, Cadmus helped Thasus build a bower. Telephassa was too frail to help much, so she advised them on how to fit it out and furnish it, to make it as comfortable as a hut of branches could be. Thasus did not spend all his days in this green bower, though. As had happened with Phoenix and Cilix, other homeless people came to the spot, liked it, and built themselves homes nearby. So in a few years there was another thriving city, with a red sandstone palace in the middle of it. There Thasus sat on a throne and gave justice to the people, with a purple robe over his shoulders, a scepter in his hand and a crown on his head. The people had made him king, not because of any royal blood (he had none), but because Thasus was an honest, true-hearted and courageous man, and so fit to rule.

But when the affairs of his kingdom were all settled, King Thasus put aside his purple robe, crown and scepter and told his worthiest subject to give justice to the people in his place. Then he took up the pilgrim’s staff that had supported him so long, and set out again, still hoping to find some hoofprint of the snow-white bull, some trace of the vanished child. After a long absence he came back and sat down wearily on his throne. To his last hour, though, King Thasus showed how faithfully he remembered Europa. He ordered that a fire should always be burning in his palace, a bath steaming hot, food ready to serve, and a bed with snow-white sheets, in case the maiden should arrive and need refreshment at once. And though Europa never came, good Thasus won the blessings of many a poor traveler who made use of the food and lodging meant for the little playmate of the king’s boyhood.

From then on Telephassa and Cadmus made their tiring way with only each other for company. The queen put much of her weight on her son’s arm and managed just a few miles a day. Yet weak and worn out as she was, nothing could talk her out of the search. Even bearded men found their eyes filling with tears at the sorrowful voice in which she asked each stranger for word of her lost child.
“Have you seen a little girl—no, no, I mean a young woman, full grown—pass this way, riding a snow-white bull that gallops as fast as the wind?”

“We have seen no such wonderful sight,” the people would answer. Very often they took Cadmus aside and whispered to him, “Is this dignified, sad-looking woman your mother? Surely she is not in her right mind. You ought to take her home, make her comfortable, and do your best to get this dream out of her head.”
“No dream,” said Cadmus. “Everything else is a dream. That is the one thing that isn’t.”

But one day Telephassa seemed weaker than usual. She leaned almost her whole weight on Cadmus’s arm and walked more slowly than ever before. At last they came to a lonely spot, and there she told her son that she had to lie down and take a good, long rest.
“A good, long rest!” she repeated, looking tenderly into Cadmus’s face—“a good, long rest, my dearest one!”
“As long as you like, dear mother,” answered Cadmus.
Telephassa told him to sit on the grass next to her, and she took his hand in hers.

“My son,” she said, resting her dim eyes lovingly on him, “this rest I’m speaking of will be very long indeed! You must not wait until it is over. Dear Cadmus, you don’t understand me. You must dig a grave here and lay your mother’s weary body in it. My pilgrimage is over.”

Cadmus burst into tears and for a long time refused to believe that his dear mother was about to be taken from him. But Telephassa reasoned with him and kissed him, and at last made him see that it was better for her spirit to pass out of the toil, weariness, grief and disappointment that had weighed on her on earth ever since the child was lost. So he held back his sorrow and listened to her last words.

“Dearest Cadmus,” she said, “you have been the truest son a mother ever had, faithful to the very end. Who else would have put up with my weakness as you have! It is thanks to your care, my tenderest child, that my grave was not dug long years ago, in some valley or on some hillside far, far behind us. That is enough. You must not wander any longer on this hopeless search. But when you have laid your mother in the earth, go to Delphi, my son, and ask the oracle what you should do next.”
“Oh, Mother, Mother,” cried Cadmus, “if only you could have seen my sister before this hour!”
“It matters little now,” Telephassa answered, with a smile on her face. “I am going to a better world, and sooner or later I will find my daughter there.”

I will not make you sad, my little listeners, by telling how Telephassa died and was buried. I will only say that her dying smile grew brighter instead of fading from her lifeless face, so that Cadmus was sure that with her very first step into the better world she had caught Europa in her arms. He planted some flowers on his mother’s grave and left them to grow there and beautify the place after he had gone far away.

When this last sad duty was done, he set out alone on the road to the famous oracle of Delphi, as Telephassa had told him to. Along the way he still asked most of the people he met whether they had seen Europa; to tell the truth, Cadmus had grown so used to asking that the question came to his lips as easily as a remark about the weather. The answers he got were all different. One person told him one thing and another told him something else. Among them was a sailor who claimed that, many years before and in a distant country, he had heard a rumor of a white bull that came swimming across the sea with a child on its back, dressed in flowers that the salt water had withered. He did not know what had become of the child or the bull. Cadmus suspected, from a queer twinkle in the sailor’s eye, that the man was playing a joke on him and had never really heard anything of the sort.

Poor Cadmus found it more tiring to travel alone than it had been to carry all his dear mother’s weight while she kept him company. His heart, you must understand, was so heavy that sometimes it seemed impossible to carry it any farther. But his legs were strong and active, and used to exercise. He walked briskly along, thinking of King Agenor and Queen Telephassa, of his brothers and the friendly Thasus, all of whom he had left behind at one point or another on his pilgrimage and never expected to see again. Lost in these memories, he came in sight of a tall mountain, which the people there told him was called Parnassus. The famous town of Delphi, where Cadmus was headed, lay on its slope.

Delphi was believed to be the very middle of the whole world. The oracle was in a hollow place in the mountainside, and when Cadmus arrived he found a rough arbor of branches built over it.
