It reminded him of the ones he had helped to build for Phoenix and Cilix, and later for Thasus. In later times, when crowds of people traveled great distances to put questions to the oracle, a large marble temple was built on the spot. But in the days of Cadmus, as I have told you, there was only this country arbor, thick with green leaves, and a tangle of bushes growing wild over the mysterious hole in the hillside.

Cadmus pushed a way through the tangled branches and into the arbor, but at first he could not make out the half-hidden opening. Soon, though, he felt a cold stream of air rushing out of it, so strongly that it stirred the curls on his cheek. He pulled away the bushes that crowded around the hole, leaned forward, and spoke in a clear but respectful voice, as if addressing someone unseen inside the mountain.
“Sacred oracle of Delphi,” he said, “where should I go next to look for my dear sister Europa?”

At first there was a deep silence. Then came a rushing sound, like a long sigh, from somewhere deep inside the earth. You should know that this hollow was thought of as a kind of fountain of truth, which sometimes burst out in words that could be heard, though most of the time those words were such a riddle that they might as well have stayed at the bottom of the hole. But Cadmus was luckier than many who went to Delphi looking for the truth. After a while the rushing noise began to sound like speech. It repeated the following sentence over and over, and yet it was so much like the empty whistle of a gust of wind that Cadmus honestly could not tell whether it meant anything at all:—
“Seek her no more! Seek her no more! Seek her no more!”
“What, then, should I do?” asked Cadmus.

Ever since he was a child, you see, finding his sister had been the great purpose of his life. From the very hour he left off chasing the butterfly in the meadow near his father’s palace, he had done his best to follow Europa over land and sea. And now, if he had to give up the search, he seemed to have nothing left to do in the world.
Then the sighing gust of wind swelled again into something like a rough voice.
“Follow the cow!” it said again. “Follow the cow! Follow the cow!”

When these words had been repeated until Cadmus was tired of hearing them (especially since he could not imagine which cow it was, or why he should follow her), the windy hole let out another sentence.
“Where the stray cow lies down, there is your home.”

These words were spoken only once, and they faded into a whisper before Cadmus was sure he had understood them. He asked more questions but got no answer. The wind only went on sighing out of the hollow and blowing the dry leaves rustling along the ground ahead of it.
“Did any words really come out of that hole?” Cadmus wondered. “Or have I been dreaming all this time?”

He turned away from the oracle feeling no wiser than when he had arrived. He cared little what became of him, so he took the first path he came to and plodded along slowly; with nothing in view and no reason to go one way rather than another, it would certainly have been foolish to hurry. Whenever he met anyone, the old question was on the tip of his tongue:—
“Have you seen a beautiful girl, dressed like a king’s daughter and riding a snow-white bull that gallops as fast as the wind?”
But remembering what the oracle had said, he spoke only half of the words and mumbled the rest, and he looked so confused that people must have thought this handsome young man had lost his wits.

I do not know how far Cadmus had gone, and he could not have told you himself, when he saw a brindled cow not far ahead of him. She was lying by the roadside, quietly chewing her cud, and she paid no attention to the young man until he came quite close. Then she got lazily to her feet, gave her head a gentle toss, and began to walk along at an easy pace, stopping now and then just long enough to nip off a mouthful of grass. Cadmus dawdled behind her, whistling idly to himself and hardly noticing the cow, until it occurred to him to wonder whether this could possibly be the animal that, according to the oracle, was to be his guide. But he smiled at himself for imagining such a thing. He could not seriously believe this was the cow, because she walked along so calmly, behaving just like any other cow. Clearly she neither knew nor cared a wisp of hay about Cadmus; she was only thinking about finding her dinner along the roadside, where the grass was green and fresh. Perhaps she was on her way home to be milked.
“Cow, cow, cow!” Cadmus shouted. “Hey there, Brindle! Hold up, good cow!”

He wanted to catch up with the cow so that he could look her over and see whether she seemed to know him, or whether anything set her apart from a thousand other cows, whose only business is to fill the milk pail and sometimes kick it over. But the brindled cow kept plodding on, switching her tail to drive off the flies and taking as little notice of Cadmus as she possibly could. If he walked slowly, so did the cow, and she used the chance to graze. If he sped up, the cow went just that much faster. Once, when Cadmus tried to catch her by running, she kicked up her heels, stuck her tail straight up in the air, and took off at a gallop, looking as odd as cows usually do when they race.

When Cadmus saw that he could not possibly catch her, he went back to walking at an easy pace. The cow, too, strolled on without looking back. Wherever the grass was greenest, she nibbled a mouthful or two. Wherever a brook sparkled across the path, she drank, sighed contentedly, drank again, and ambled on at the pace that suited both herself and Cadmus.
“I really think,” Cadmus thought, “that this may be the cow I was told about. If she is, I suppose she will lie down somewhere around here.”

Whether she was the cow of the oracle or some other cow, it did not seem likely that she would travel much farther. So whenever they came to an especially pleasant spot, on a breezy hillside or in a sheltered valley or flowery meadow, beside a calm lake or along the bank of a clear stream, Cadmus looked around eagerly to see whether it would make a good home. But whether he liked the place or not, the brindled cow never made any move to lie down. On she went at the quiet pace of a cow heading home to the barnyard, and every moment Cadmus expected to see a milkmaid coming with a pail, or a herdsman running to head off the stray and turn her back toward the pasture. But no milkmaid came, and no herdsman drove her back, and Cadmus followed the wandering Brindle until he was ready to drop from weariness.
“Oh, brindled cow,” he cried in despair, “are you never going to stop?”

By now he was so set on following her that he never thought of falling behind, however long the road or however tired he might be. In fact, there seemed to be something about the animal that bewitched people. Several people who happened to see the brindled cow with Cadmus trailing behind began to trudge after her, exactly as he did. Cadmus was glad to have someone to talk to, and he spoke very freely to these good people. He told them all his adventures: how he had left King Agenor in his palace, Phoenix in one place, Cilix in another, Thasus in a third, and his dear mother, Queen Telephassa, under a flowery patch of turf, so that now he was all alone, without friends or home. He also mentioned that the oracle had told him to be guided by a cow, and he asked the strangers whether they thought this brindled animal could be the one.

“Well, that is a most remarkable thing,” said one of his new companions. “I know cattle pretty well, and I never knew a cow to go so far without stopping when she was left to herself. If my legs hold out, I’ll follow that beast until she lies down.”
“So will I!” said a second.
“So will I!” cried a third. “If she goes a hundred miles farther, I’m determined to see how it ends.”

The truth, you should know, was that the cow was enchanted, and without being aware of it, everyone who walked as much as half a dozen steps behind her fell a little under her spell. They simply could not help following her, though the whole time they imagined they were doing it of their own free will. The cow was not at all fussy about choosing her path, so sometimes they had to scramble over rocks or wade through mud and mire, and they were all in a dreadfully muddy state, tired to death, and very hungry besides. What a wearisome business it was!

Still, they kept trudging bravely on, talking as they went. The strangers grew very fond of Cadmus and resolved never to leave him, but to help him build a city wherever the cow might lie down. In the middle of it would stand a grand palace where Cadmus could live and be their king, with a throne, a crown and scepter, a purple robe, and everything else a king ought to have; for he had royal blood in him, and a royal heart, and a head that knew how to rule.
While they were chatting about these plans and passing the tedious miles by drawing up the design of the new city, one of the group happened to glance at the cow.
“Hurrah! Hurrah!” he cried, clapping his hands. “Brindle is going to lie down.”

They all looked, and sure enough, the cow had stopped and was gazing calmly about, the way cows do just before lying down. Then, slowly, slowly, she settled onto the soft grass, bending her front legs first and then crouching down on her back ones. When Cadmus and his companions reached her, there lay the brindled cow at her ease, chewing her cud and looking them peacefully in the face, as if this was exactly the spot she had been looking for and it was all perfectly ordinary.
“So this,” said Cadmus, looking around him, “this is to be my home.”

It was a rich and lovely plain, with great trees casting dappled shade over it and hills sheltering it from rough weather. Not far off they could see a river shining in the sun. A feeling of home crept into poor Cadmus’s heart. He was very glad to know that here he could wake in the morning without having to pull on his dusty sandals and travel farther and farther. The days and years would pass over him and find him still in this pleasant spot. If he could have had his brothers with him, and his friend Thasus, and could have seen his dear mother under a roof of his own, he might have been happy here, after all his disappointments. Some day, too, his sister Europa might have come quietly to the door of his house and smiled around at the familiar faces. But since there was no hope of getting back the friends of his boyhood or ever seeing his dear sister again, Cadmus decided to make himself happy with these new companions, who had grown so fond of him while following the cow.

“Yes, my friends,” he told them, “this is to be our home. Here we will build our houses. The brindled cow that has led us here will give us milk. We will farm the land around us and live a harmless and happy life.”

His companions gladly agreed to this plan. First, since they were very hungry and thirsty, they began looking for a way to get a decent meal. Not far away they spotted a clump of trees that looked as if it might hide a spring. They went off to fetch water from it and left Cadmus lying on the ground next to the brindled cow. Now that he had found a place to rest, all the weariness of his long journey, from the day he left King Agenor’s palace, seemed to come down on him at once. But his new friends had not been gone long when he was startled by cries, shouts and screams, and the noise of a terrible struggle. Over it all came an awful hissing that went through his ears like a rough saw.

He ran toward the clump of trees. There he saw the head and fiery eyes of an enormous serpent, a dragon with the widest jaws any dragon ever had and a great many rows of horribly sharp teeth. Before Cadmus could get there, this merciless creature had already killed his poor companions and was busy swallowing them, taking each man in a single mouthful.

It turns out that the spring was enchanted, and the dragon had been put there to guard it so that no human being could ever drink from it. The people who lived nearby kept carefully away from the place, so it had been a long time since the monster had eaten, not less than a hundred years or so. Naturally his appetite had grown enormous, and the poor men he had just gobbled up were not half enough for him. When he caught sight of Cadmus, he let out another horrible hiss and threw his huge jaws wide open, until his mouth looked like a great red cave. At the far end of it you could see the legs of his latest victim, whom he had barely had time to swallow.

But Cadmus was so furious about the death of his friends that he did not care how big the dragon’s jaws were, or how many hundreds of sharp teeth he had. He drew his sword, ran at the monster and threw himself straight into its gaping mouth. This daring way of attacking took the dragon by surprise. Cadmus had jumped so far down its throat that the rows of terrible teeth could not close on him or hurt him in the least. So the fight was tremendous, and the dragon’s lashing tail smashed the clump of trees into splinters. But all the while Cadmus kept slashing and stabbing at its insides, and before long the scaly wretch thought of slinking away. He had not gone his own length, though, when brave Cadmus gave him a sword thrust that ended the battle. Cadmus crept out through the gateway of the creature’s jaws and saw it still wriggling its huge body, though it no longer had enough life left to hurt a small child.

But don’t imagine that Cadmus felt no sorrow when he thought of the sad fate of those poor, friendly people who had followed the cow with him. It seemed he was doomed to lose everyone he loved, or to watch them die one way or another. And here he was, after all his labors and troubles, in a lonely place, with not one human being to help him build a hut.
“What shall I do?” he cried aloud. “It would have been better if the dragon had eaten me, as it ate my poor companions.”
“Cadmus,” said a voice—but whether it came from above him or below him, or spoke inside his own heart, the young man could not tell—“Cadmus, pull out the dragon’s teeth and plant them in the ground.”

This was a strange thing to be told to do, and I imagine it was not easy to dig all those deeply rooted fangs out of the dead dragon’s jaws. But Cadmus worked and tugged, and after pounding the monstrous head nearly to pieces with a big stone, he finally gathered as many teeth as would fill a bushel or two. Next he had to plant them. That was tiresome work too, especially since Cadmus was already worn out from killing the dragon and smashing its head, and had nothing to dig with, as far as I know, except his sword blade. In the end, though, he turned over a large enough patch of ground and sowed it with this new kind of seed, although half of the dragon’s teeth were still left to be planted some other day.

Cadmus, completely out of breath, stood leaning on his sword and wondering what would happen next. He had waited only a few moments when he began to see something that was as great a marvel as anything I have ever told you about.

The sun was shining low across the field and showed the damp, dark soil looking like any other newly planted ground. All at once Cadmus thought he saw something glitter brightly, first in one spot, then in another, and then in a hundred and a thousand spots at once. Soon he saw that they were the steel heads of spears, shooting up everywhere like stalks of grain and growing taller and taller. Next came a great number of bright sword blades, pushing up the same way. A moment later the whole surface of the ground was broken by a crowd of polished brass helmets, coming up like a crop of giant beans. They grew so fast that Cadmus soon made out the fierce face of a man under every one. In short, before he had time to think what a wonderful thing this was, he saw a rich harvest of what looked like human beings, armed with helmets, breastplates, shields, swords and spears. Before they were even fully out of the ground they were waving their weapons and clashing them against each other, as if they thought, young as they were, that they had already gone too long in life without a battle. Every tooth of the dragon had produced one of these sons of deadly mischief.

A good many trumpeters sprouted up as well. With their very first breath they raised their brass trumpets to their lips and blew a tremendous, ear-splitting blast. The whole place, so quiet and lonely a moment before, rang with the crash and clang of weapons, the blare of war music and the shouts of angry men. They all looked so furious that Cadmus fully expected them to put the whole world to the sword. What a lucky thing it would be for a great conqueror if he could get a bushel of dragon’s teeth to sow!
The same voice he had heard before spoke again. “Cadmus, toss a stone in among the armed men.”

So Cadmus picked up a large stone and flung it into the middle of the earth army. It struck the breastplate of a huge, fierce-looking warrior. The moment he felt the blow, he seemed to take it for granted that somebody had hit him. He raised his weapon and struck his nearest neighbor so hard that it split the man’s helmet in two and stretched him on the ground. In an instant the men closest to the fallen warrior began hacking at each other with their swords and stabbing with their spears. The confusion spread wider and wider. Every man struck down his brother and was himself struck down before he had time to enjoy his victory. All the while the trumpeters blew their blasts shriller and shriller, and each soldier shouted a battle cry and often fell with it still on his lips. It was the strangest sight of pointless rage and mischief for no good purpose that anyone had ever seen. Still, it was neither more foolish nor more wicked than a thousand battles that have been fought since, in which men have killed their brothers for just as little reason as these children of the dragon’s teeth. We should also remember that the dragon people were made for nothing else, while other human beings are born to love and help one another.

Well, this memorable battle raged on until the ground was littered with helmeted heads that had been cut off. Of all the thousands who began the fight, only five were left standing. These five now rushed from different parts of the field and met in the middle, where they clashed their swords and struck at each other’s hearts as fiercely as ever.
“Cadmus,” the voice said once more, “order those five warriors to sheathe their swords. They are the ones who will help you raise the city.”
Without a moment’s hesitation, Cadmus stepped forward with the look of a king and a leader. He held out his drawn sword among them and spoke to the warriors in a stern, commanding voice.
“Put away your weapons!” he said.

At once, feeling that they had to obey him, the five remaining sons of the dragon’s teeth saluted him with their swords like soldiers, slid them back into their sheaths, and stood before Cadmus in a row. They looked at him the way soldiers look at their captain while they wait for the order to move.

These five men had probably sprung from the biggest of the dragon’s teeth, and they were the boldest and strongest of the whole army. They were almost giants, and they needed to be, or they could never have lived through so terrible a fight. They still looked very fierce, and whenever Cadmus happened to glance away, they glared at one another with fire flashing from their eyes. It was strange, too, to see how the earth they had so lately grown out of stuck here and there to their bright breastplates and even smudged their faces, just as you may have seen it cling to beets and carrots pulled out of the ground. Cadmus hardly knew whether to think of them as men or as some odd kind of vegetable. On the whole, though, he decided there was human nature in them, because they were so fond of trumpets and weapons and so ready to spill blood.

The five stared hard at his face, waiting to hear what he would command next. Plainly they wanted nothing better than to trail after him from one battlefield to the next across the whole wide world. Cadmus, though, had more wisdom than these creatures born of the earth, with the dragon’s savagery inside them, and he had a better idea of what to do with their strength and hardiness.
“Come!” he said. “You are sturdy fellows. Make yourselves useful! Cut stone with those great swords of yours and help me build a city.”

The five soldiers grumbled a little and muttered that their business was to knock cities down, not to put them up. But Cadmus gave them a stern look and spoke with such authority that they knew him for their master and never again thought of disobeying him. They set to work in earnest and labored so hard that in a very short time a city began to appear. At first, it is true, the workmen were quarrelsome. Like wild beasts, they would surely have hurt one another if Cadmus had not kept watch over them. Whenever he saw the fierce old serpent that lurked in their hearts gleaming out of their wild eyes, he put it down. But in time they got used to honest work, and they had sense enough to feel that there was more real enjoyment in living peacefully and doing good to your neighbor than in hacking at him with a two-edged sword. It may not be too much to hope that the rest of mankind will someday grow as wise and peaceable as these five earth-smudged warriors who sprang from the dragon’s teeth.

Now the city was built, and there was a home in it for each of the workmen. But the palace of Cadmus had not yet been put up, because they had left it for last. They meant to include all the latest improvements in building and to make it very comfortable as well as grand and beautiful. When they had finished the rest of their work, they all went to bed early so they could get up at dawn and at least lay the foundation of the palace before nightfall. But when Cadmus got up and made his way toward the spot where the palace was to stand, followed by his five sturdy workmen marching in a row, what do you think he saw?

What should it be but the most magnificent palace the world had ever seen! It was built of marble and other beautiful kinds of stone, and it rose high into the air, with a splendid dome, a porch across the front, carved pillars, and everything else that suited the home of a mighty king. It had sprung up out of the ground in almost as short a time as the armed host had taken to spring from the dragon’s teeth. And what made it stranger still was that no seed of this grand building had ever been planted.
The five workmen caught sight of the dome shining golden in the early sunshine, and they let out a mighty cheer.
“Hooray for King Cadmus!” they shouted. “Long may he live in his lovely palace!”

And the new king, with his five faithful followers at his heels, marching in a row with their pickaxes on their shoulders (for they still behaved like soldiers, as was their nature), climbed the palace steps. They stopped at the entrance and gazed down a long avenue of tall pillars that stood side by side from one end of a great hall to the other. At the far end of the hall, walking slowly toward him, Cadmus saw a woman of wonderful beauty. She wore a royal robe, a crown of diamonds over her golden ringlets, and the richest necklace any queen ever wore. His heart thrilled with joy. He imagined it was his long-lost sister Europa, grown to womanhood, who had come to make him happy and to repay him with her sweet sisterly love for all those weary wanderings in search of her since he left King Agenor’s palace—for the tears he had shed when he parted from Phoenix, Cilix and Thasus—for the heartbreak that had made the whole world seem gloomy to him beside his dear mother’s grave.

But as Cadmus went forward to meet the beautiful stranger, he saw that her face was unknown to him. Even so, in the short time it took to walk along the hall, he had already felt a kinship between himself and her.

Then Cadmus heard the voice that had spoken to him in the field of armed men. “No, Cadmus. This is not your dear sister Europa, whom you searched for so faithfully across the whole wide world. She is Harmonia, a daughter of the sky, and she is given to you to take the place of a sister, brothers, a friend and a mother. In her alone you will find all of them.”

So King Cadmus lived in the palace with his new friend Harmonia. He found a great deal of comfort in his magnificent home, though no doubt he would have found as much, or more, in the humblest cottage by the roadside. Before many years had passed, a crowd of rosy little children (how they got there has always been a mystery to me) were playing in the great hall and on the marble steps of the palace. They ran happily to meet King Cadmus whenever the business of the kingdom left him free to play with them. They called him father, and Queen Harmonia mother. The five old soldiers of the dragon’s teeth grew very fond of these little rascals and never got tired of showing them how to carry sticks on their shoulders, wave wooden swords, and march in military order, blowing a penny trumpet or beating a dreadful rub-a-dub on a little drum.

But King Cadmus did not want his children to inherit too much of the dragon’s tooth, so he made time between his royal duties to teach them their A B C. He had invented the alphabet for their benefit, and I’m afraid many little people today are not nearly as thankful to him for it as they should be.

chapters.title: Circe’s Palace
paragraphs: Some of you have surely heard of the wise King Ulysses: how he went to the siege of Troy, and how, after that famous city was captured and burned, he spent ten long years trying to get back to his own small kingdom of Ithaca. At one point on this weary voyage, he came to an island that looked green and pleasant, but he did not know its name. A little while before, he had been caught in a terrible hurricane—or rather, a great many hurricanes at once—which had driven his fleet into a strange part of the sea where neither he nor any of his sailors had ever been. All of this was the fault of his shipmates’ foolish curiosity. While Ulysses lay asleep, they had untied some very bulky leather bags, thinking a valuable treasure was hidden inside. But in each of those sturdy bags King AEolus, the ruler of the winds, had tied up a storm, and he had given the bags to Ulysses to keep so that he would be sure of a favorable passage home to Ithaca. When the strings were loosened, the whistling gales rushed out like air from a blown-up bladder, whipping the sea into foam and scattering the ships in every direction.

Right after escaping this danger, he ran into an even greater one. Racing before the hurricane, he arrived at a place that he later learned was called Laestrygonia. There monstrous giants ate many of his companions and sank every one of his ships but the one he was sailing in, hurling huge chunks of rock at them from the cliffs along the shore. After troubles like these, you can hardly wonder that King Ulysses was glad to tie up his storm-battered ship in a quiet cove of the green island I began by telling you about. But he had met with so many dangers from giants, one-eyed Cyclopes, and monsters of land and sea that he could not help fearing mischief, even in this pleasant and seemingly empty spot. So for two days the poor, weather-beaten travelers stayed quiet. They either remained on board or only crept along beneath the cliffs that edged the shore, and to keep themselves alive they dug shellfish out of the sand and hunted for any little stream of fresh water running down to the sea.

Before the two days were over, they had grown very tired of this way of living. The followers of King Ulysses—and you will find it important to remember this—were terrible gluttons, and they were sure to grumble if they missed their regular meals, plus their irregular ones. Now their supplies were completely gone, and even the shellfish were getting scarce. They had to choose between starving to death and venturing into the middle of the island, where some huge three-headed dragon or other horrible monster might have its den. Misshapen creatures like that were very common in those days, and nobody ever expected to make a voyage or a journey without running some risk of being eaten by one.

But King Ulysses was bold as well as careful, and on the third morning he decided to find out what kind of place the island was and whether there was any way to get food for his companions’ hungry mouths. So he took a spear in his hand, climbed to the top of a cliff, and looked all around. Far off toward the middle of the island he saw the stately towers of what looked like a palace, built of snow-white marble and rising from a grove of tall trees. The thick branches of the trees stretched across the front of the building and hid more than half of it. Still, from the part he could see, Ulysses judged it to be roomy and very beautiful, probably the home of some great nobleman or prince. A thread of blue smoke curled up from a chimney, and to Ulysses that was almost the most pleasant part of the view. All that smoke was good reason to think there was a roaring fire in the kitchen, and that at dinnertime a generous feast would be served to the people of the palace and to any guests who happened to drop in.

With such a cheerful prospect in front of him, Ulysses thought the best thing he could do was to go straight to the palace gate and tell its master that a crew of poor shipwrecked sailors was waiting not far away. They had eaten nothing for a day or two except a few clams and oysters, he would say, and would be grateful for a little food. And surely the prince or nobleman would have to be a very stingy old miser if he did not, once his own dinner was finished, invite them to the leftovers from his table.

King Ulysses was pleased with this idea and had taken a few steps toward the palace when he heard a great twittering and chirping from the branch of a nearby tree. A moment later a bird came flying at him and hovered in the air, so close that its wings almost brushed his face. It was a very pretty little bird, with purple wings and body, yellow legs, a ring of golden feathers around its neck, and on its head a golden tuft that looked like a tiny king’s crown. Ulysses tried to catch the bird, but it fluttered easily out of his reach, still chirping in a pitiful tone, as if it could have told a sad story if only it had been given human speech. And when he tried to shoo it away, the bird flew no farther than the branch of the next tree, then came fluttering around his head again with its mournful chirp as soon as he showed any sign of going on.
“Do you have something to tell me, little bird?” asked Ulysses.

He was ready to listen closely to whatever the bird might say. At the siege of Troy and elsewhere he had seen such strange things happen that he would not have thought it very unusual if this little feathered creature had talked as plainly as he did.

“Peep!” said the bird. “Peep, peep, pe—weep!” That was all it would say, only “Peep, peep, pe—weep!” in a sad singsong, over and over and over again. Whenever Ulysses moved forward, the bird seemed greatly alarmed and did its best to drive him back, beating its purple wings anxiously. Its strange behavior led him to decide at last that the bird knew of some danger waiting for him, and it must certainly be a terrible one, since it moved even a little bird to feel pity for a human being. So he made up his mind, for now, to go back to the ship and tell his companions what he had seen.

This seemed to satisfy the bird. As soon as Ulysses turned back, it ran up the trunk of a tree and began picking insects out of the bark with its long, sharp bill. It was a kind of woodpecker, you see, and had to earn its living the same way as other birds of that kind. But every so often, as it pecked at the bark, the purple bird remembered some secret sorrow and sang its sad little note again: “Peep, peep, pe—weep!”

On his way down to the shore, Ulysses had the good luck to kill a large stag by driving his spear into its back. He was remarkably strong, so he hoisted it onto his shoulders, carried it back, and dropped it in front of his hungry companions. I have already hinted what gluttons some of King Ulysses’ comrades were. From what is told about them, I would guess that their favorite food was pork, and that they had lived on it so long that a good part of their bodies had turned to pig’s flesh, and their tempers were a lot like a hog’s. Still, a dish of venison was a welcome meal even to them, especially after living so long on oysters and clams. So when they saw the dead stag, they felt its ribs like experts and wasted no time building a fire of driftwood to cook it. They spent the rest of the day feasting, and if these enormous eaters left the table at sunset, it was only because they could not scrape another bite off the poor animal’s bones.

The next morning their appetites were as sharp as ever. They looked at Ulysses as if they expected him to climb the cliff again and come back with another fat deer on his shoulders. Instead of setting out, though, he called the whole crew together and told them there was no use hoping he could kill a stag every day for their dinner, so they had better think of some other way to satisfy their hunger.

“Now,” he said, “when I was up on the cliff yesterday, I found out that people live on this island. A good way inland there stands a marble palace that looks very spacious, and a lot of smoke was curling out of one of its chimneys.”

“Aha!” some of his companions muttered, licking their lips. “Where there’s smoke like that, there’s a kitchen fire. A fine dinner was turning on the spit, and I’ll bet there’s another just as good cooking now.”

“But,” the wise Ulysses went on, “my good friends, you must remember our misadventure in the cave of one-eyed Polyphemus the Cyclops! Instead of his usual diet of milk, didn’t he eat two of our comrades for his supper, then a couple more for breakfast, and two again for supper? I can almost see him now, the hideous monster, looking us over with that great red eye in the middle of his forehead to pick out the fattest. And then, only a few days ago, didn’t we fall into the hands of the king of the Laestrygons and the other horrible giants who were his subjects? They devoured many more of us than are left now. To tell you the truth, if we go to that palace, there is no doubt that we will turn up at the dinner table. But whether we sit there as guests or are served up as the meal is something we should think about very seriously.”
“Either way,” murmured some of the hungriest men in the crew, “it would be better than starving. Especially if we could be sure of being well fattened first and daintily cooked afterward.”

“That’s a matter of taste,” said King Ulysses. “For my part, neither the most careful fattening nor the daintiest cooking would make me happy about ending up on a platter. So here is my proposal: we divide ourselves into two equal groups and draw lots to see which of them goes to the palace to beg for food and help. If we can get them, all is well. If not, and the people there turn out to be as unwelcoming as Polyphemus or the Laestrygons, then only half of us will die, and the rest can sail away and escape.”

Nobody objected to this plan, so Ulysses counted the whole company and found that there were forty-six men, himself included. He then counted off twenty-two of them and put Eurylochus at their head. Eurylochus was one of his chief officers and second only to himself in good sense. Ulysses took command of the other twenty-two men himself. Then he took off his helmet and put two shells into it. On one was written “Go,” and on the other “Stay.” Another man held the helmet while Ulysses and Eurylochus each drew out a shell, and the word “Go” was written on the one Eurylochus drew. So it was settled that Ulysses and his twenty-two men would wait by the sea until the other party had found out what sort of treatment to expect at the mysterious palace. There was no help for it, so Eurylochus set out at once at the head of his twenty-two followers, who went off in a very gloomy mood and left their friends behind in hardly better spirits.

As soon as they had climbed the cliff, they saw the tall marble towers of the palace, white as snow, rising out of the lovely green shade of the trees around it. A puff of smoke came from a chimney at the back of the building. The vapor rose high in the air, caught a breeze, and drifted out toward the sea, right over the heads of the hungry sailors. When people’s appetites are keen, they have a very quick nose for anything savory on the wind.
“That smoke is from the kitchen!” cried one of them, tilting his nose up as far as he could and sniffing hungrily. “I’m a half-starved wretch, but I’d swear I smell roast meat on it.”
“Pig, roast pig!” said another. “Ah, that juicy little porker! My mouth waters for him.”
“Let’s hurry,” cried the others, “or we’ll be too late for the good food!”

But they had barely taken half a dozen steps from the cliff edge when a bird came fluttering toward them. It was the same pretty little bird as before, with purple wings and body, yellow legs, a golden ring at its neck, and a tuft like a tiny crown on its head, the one that had puzzled Ulysses so much. It circled Eurylochus, its wings almost touching his face.
“Peep, peep, pe—weep!” chirped the bird.
The sound was so plaintive and so full of meaning that it seemed as if the little creature would break its heart over some mighty secret it had to tell, with only this one poor note to tell it with.
“My pretty bird,” said Eurylochus—for he was a cautious man and let no sign of danger escape him—“my pretty bird, who sent you here? And what message do you bring?”
“Peep, peep, pe—weep!” the bird answered, very sorrowfully.

Then it flew to the edge of the cliff and looked back at them, as if it very much wanted them to return where they came from. Eurylochus and a few of the others were inclined to turn back. They could not help suspecting that the purple bird knew of some harm that would come to them at the palace, and that knowing it filled its airy spirit with human sympathy and sorrow. But the rest of the sailors, sniffing the smoke from the palace kitchen, laughed at the idea of going back to the ship. One of them, more brutal than the others and the most notorious glutton in the whole crew, said something so cruel and wicked that I wonder the very thought did not turn him into a wild beast in shape, as he already was in nature.

“This annoying, impudent little bird,” he said, “would make a delicate morsel to start dinner with. Just one plump bite, melting away between the teeth. If he comes within my reach, I’ll catch him and hand him to the palace cook to roast on a skewer.”
The words were barely out of his mouth when the purple bird flew away, crying “Peep, peep, pe—weep” more mournfully than ever.
“That bird,” Eurylochus remarked, “knows something about what awaits us at the palace that we don’t.”
“Then let’s get going,” shouted his comrades, “and we’ll soon learn it for ourselves.”

So the party went on through the green, pleasant woods. Every so often they caught another glimpse of the marble palace, and the closer they came, the lovelier it looked. Soon they turned onto a broad, tidy path that wound along ahead of them, with streaks of sunshine lying across it and little flecks of light trembling among the deep shadows of the tall trees. Along both edges grew masses of sweet-smelling flowers, unlike any the sailors had ever seen. They were so rich and beautiful that if they grew wild here, this island must be the flower garden of the whole earth. And if they had been brought from some other land, they could only have come from the Happy Islands that lie toward the golden sunset.

“What a lot of effort has been foolishly wasted on these flowers,” remarked one of the men. I am telling you what he said so that you will remember what gluttons they were. “If I owned this palace, I’d tell my gardener to grow nothing but tasty herbs, to stuff a roast with or to season a stew.”
“Well said!” cried the others. “And I bet there’s a kitchen garden behind the palace, too.”

Somewhere along the way they came to a crystal spring and stopped to drink from it, for want of anything they liked better. When they looked into the water, they saw their own faces faintly mirrored there, but so wildly twisted by the bubbling and rippling that every man seemed to be laughing at himself and at all his friends. The reflections looked so ridiculous that the men really did burst out laughing, and once they had started they could hardly stop. After they had drunk, they were even merrier than before.
“There’s a taste of the wine cask in it,” said one, smacking his lips.
“Hurry up!” cried his companions. “We’ll find the wine cask itself at the palace, and that will beat a hundred crystal fountains.”
Then they walked faster and danced for joy at the thought of the delicious banquet they hoped to be invited to. Eurylochus, though, told them he felt as if he were walking in a dream.

“If I’m truly awake,” he went on, “then I think we are about to meet a stranger adventure than any that happened to us in the cave of Polyphemus, or among the giant man-eating Laestrygons, or in the windy palace of King AEolus on his island with its walls of brass. A dreamy feeling like this always comes over me just before something wonderful happens. If you take my advice, you will turn back.”

“No, no,” his comrades answered, sniffing the air, which by now smelled strongly of the palace kitchen. “We wouldn’t turn back even if we knew that the king of the Laestrygons, big as a mountain, would be sitting at the head of the table, and huge one-eyed Polyphemus the Cyclops at the foot.”

At last the palace came fully into view. It turned out to be very large and tall, with a great many airy pinnacles along its roof. It was midday and the sun shone brightly on the marble front, yet the snowy whiteness and the fanciful design made the palace look unreal, like frost patterns on a windowpane, or like the castles you see in the clouds by moonlight. But just then a puff of wind blew the smoke of the kitchen chimney down over them, and each man smelled the dish he loved best. After one sniff of it they decided that everything else was moonshine, and that nothing was real except this palace and the banquet that was clearly ready to be served inside.

So they hurried toward the entrance, but they were not even halfway across the wide lawn when a pack of lions, tigers, and wolves came bounding toward them. The terrified sailors jumped back, expecting nothing better than to be torn to pieces and eaten. But to their surprise and joy, the wild beasts only frisked around them, wagging their tails, holding up their heads to be stroked and patted, and acting just like well-mannered house dogs greeting their master or their master’s friends. The biggest lion licked the feet of Eurylochus. And every other lion, wolf, and tiger picked out one of his twenty-two followers and fawned over him as if it loved him better than a beef bone.

Even so, Eurylochus thought he saw something fierce and savage in their eyes. He would not have been surprised, at any moment, to feel the big lion’s terrible claws, or to see each tiger make its deadly spring, or each wolf leap at the throat of the man who had petted it. Their gentleness seemed unreal, a mere whim, while their wild nature was as real as their teeth and claws.

Still, the men crossed the lawn safely, with the wild beasts frolicking around them and doing no harm at all. Though as they climbed the palace steps, you might perhaps have heard a low growl, especially from the wolves, as if they thought it a shame to let the strangers pass without even a taste of what they were made of.

Eurylochus and his men now walked under a lofty doorway and looked through the open door into the palace. The first thing they saw was a spacious hall with a fountain in the middle, shooting up toward the ceiling out of a marble basin and splashing back down into it without a pause. As the water leaped upward, it kept taking on new shapes, not sharply, but clearly enough for a quick imagination to make them out. Now it was a man in a long robe, whose fleecy whiteness was made of the fountain’s spray. Now it was a lion, or a tiger, or a wolf, or a donkey, or, as often as anything else, a hog, wallowing in the marble basin as if it were his sty. It was either magic or some very clever machinery that made the water take all these forms. But before the strangers had time to look closely at this wonderful sight, a sweet and pleasant sound drew their attention away. A woman’s voice was singing beautifully in another room of the palace, and mixed with her voice was the noise of a loom. She was probably sitting at it, weaving a rich cloth, and twining the high and low notes of her voice into a rich fabric of harmony.

After a while the song ended, and then, all at once, several women’s voices could be heard, talking lightly and cheerfully, with an occasional merry burst of laughter, the kind you always hear when three or four young women sit working together.
“What a lovely song!” one of the travelers cried.

“Too sweet, in fact,” answered Eurylochus, shaking his head. “Yet it was not as sweet as the song of the Sirens, those birdlike maidens who wanted to lure us onto the rocks, so that our ship would be wrecked and our bones left to whiten along the shore.”

“But just listen to the pleasant voices of those girls, and the hum of the loom as the shuttle goes back and forth,” said another of the men. “What a cozy, homelike sound! Ah, before that weary siege of Troy, I used to hear a humming loom and women’s voices under my own roof. Will I never hear them again? Or taste the nice little dishes my dear wife knew how to make?”

“Pah! We’ll do better here,” said another. “But how innocently those women are chattering, never guessing that we can hear them! And listen to that richest voice of all, so pleasant and familiar, yet with the authority of a mistress among them. Let’s show ourselves right away. What harm can the lady of the palace and her maids do to sailors and warriors like us?”
“Don’t forget,” Eurylochus said, “that a young girl lured three of our friends into the palace of the Laestrygon king, and he gobbled up one of them before you could blink.”

But no warning or argument had any effect on his companions. They walked up to a pair of folding doors at the far end of the hall, threw them wide open, and went into the next room. Eurylochus, meanwhile, had stepped behind a pillar. In the short moment while the folding doors were open before they closed again, he caught a glimpse of a very beautiful woman rising from the loom and coming to meet the poor weather-beaten wanderers, with a welcoming smile and her hand held out in greeting. Four other young women joined hands and danced merrily forward, bowing to the strangers. They were only a little less beautiful than the lady who seemed to be their mistress. Yet Eurylochus fancied that one of them had sea-green hair, that the tight bodice of another looked like the bark of a tree, and that the other two also had something odd about them, though in the little time he had to look, he could not quite make out what it was.

The folding doors swung shut again, leaving him standing behind the pillar, alone in the outer hall. Eurylochus waited there until he was thoroughly tired, listening closely to every sound, but he heard nothing that could help him guess what had become of his friends. He did hear footsteps going back and forth in other parts of the palace. Then came a clatter of silver dishes, or golden ones, which made him picture a rich feast in some splendid banqueting hall. But after a while he heard a tremendous grunting and squealing, followed by a sudden scampering, like small hard hoofs on a marble floor, while the mistress and her four handmaidens all screamed together in angry, mocking voices. Eurylochus could not imagine what had happened, unless a herd of pigs had broken into the palace, drawn by the smell of the feast. Then he happened to glance at the fountain, and saw that it no longer changed its shape as it had before, and no longer looked like a man in a long robe, or a lion, a tiger, a wolf, or a donkey. It looked like nothing but a hog, wallowing in the marble basin and filling it from rim to rim.

Now we must leave careful Eurylochus waiting in the outer hall and follow his friends into the hidden heart of the palace. The moment the beautiful woman saw them, she got up from her loom, as I told you, and walked toward them with a smile and an outstretched hand. She took the hand of the one standing first and bade him, and all his companions, welcome.

“You have been expected for a long time, my good friends,” she said. “My maidens and I know you well, although you don’t seem to recognize us. Look at this tapestry, and judge for yourselves whether your faces must not have been familiar to us.”

So the travelers looked at the cloth the beautiful woman had been weaving on her loom, and to their great astonishment they saw their own figures perfectly pictured in threads of different colors. It was a lifelike picture of their recent adventures. It showed them in the cave of Polyphemus, putting out his one great moonlike eye. In another part of the tapestry they were untying the leather bags stuffed with contrary winds, and farther along they saw themselves running away from the gigantic king of the Laestrygons, who had caught one of them by the leg. And last of all, there they were, sitting on the empty shore of this very island, hungry and downcast, gazing sadly at the bare bones of the stag they had eaten the day before. That was as far as the work had gotten. But when the beautiful woman sat down at her loom again, she would probably make a picture of what had happened to the strangers since, and of what was about to happen to them.

“You see,” she said, “that I know all about your troubles, and you can’t doubt that I want to make you happy for as long as you stay with me. To that end, my honored guests, I have ordered a banquet to be prepared. Fish, fowl, and meat, roasted and in rich stews, seasoned, I hope, to suit all your tastes, are ready to be served. If your appetites tell you it is dinnertime, then come with me to the dining hall.”

The hungry sailors were overjoyed at this kind invitation. One of them took it on himself to speak for the rest, and assured their gracious hostess that any hour of the day was dinnertime for them, whenever they could get meat for the pot and a fire to boil it on. So the beautiful woman led the way, and the four maidens followed behind, hurrying the guests along. One of them had sea-green hair, another a bodice of oak bark, a third sprinkled showers of water drops from her fingertips, and the fourth had some other oddity that I have forgotten. In this way they all came into a magnificent hall. It was built in a perfect oval and lit by a crystal dome overhead. Around the walls stood twenty-two thrones, hung with canopies of crimson and gold and fitted with the softest cushions, which were tasseled and fringed with gold cord. Each of the strangers was invited to sit down. And there they were, twenty-two storm-beaten sailors in worn and ragged clothes, sitting on twenty-two canopied thrones so rich and gorgeous that the proudest monarch had nothing grander in his stateliest hall.
At that point you could have watched the guests nodding, winking, and leaning across from throne to throne, whispering hoarsely about how pleased they were.
“Our kind hostess has turned us all into kings,” said one. “Ha! Do you smell that feast? I’d wager it’s good enough for twenty-two kings at once.”

“I hope,” said another, “that it will mostly be good solid joints, sirloins, spareribs, and hindquarters, without too many fancy trifles. If I thought the good lady wouldn’t take offense, I’d ask for a fat slice of fried bacon to start with.”

Ah, the gluttons and gorgers! You see how it was with them. Seated on the highest seats of honor, on royal thrones, they could think of nothing but their greedy appetite, the part of their nature that they shared with wolves and swine. So they were far more like those vilest of animals than like kings, if indeed kings were what they ought to be.

Now the beautiful woman clapped her hands, and in came a line of twenty-two servants carrying dishes of the richest food, fresh and hot from the kitchen fire. The steam rose from them so thickly that it hung like a cloud under the crystal dome of the hall. Just as many attendants brought in large flasks of wine of every kind. Some of it sparkled as it was poured and went bubbling down the throat, while other kinds were a deep purple so clear that you could see the carved figures at the bottom of the goblet. As the servants waited on the twenty-two guests, the lady of the house and her four maidens moved from one throne to the next. They urged the sailors to eat all they wanted and to drink plenty of wine, and so to make up at this one feast for all the days when they had gone without dinner. But whenever the sailors weren’t looking (which was fairly often, since they were mostly staring into their bowls and plates), the beautiful woman and her maidens turned away and laughed. Even the servants could be seen grinning and sneering as they knelt to offer the dishes, while the guests helped themselves to the treats.
Once in a while, too, the strangers seemed to bite into something they didn’t like.
“There’s a strange sort of spice in this dish,” said one. “I can’t say it quite suits my taste. Down it goes anyway.”

“Wash it down with a good swig of wine,” said his friend on the next throne. “That’s what makes this kind of cooking taste right. I have to admit the wine tastes odd too. But the more of it I drink, the better I like it.”

Whatever small fault they found with the dishes, they sat at that table a tremendously long time, and it would really have shamed you to see how they guzzled the drink and wolfed down the food. They sat on golden thrones, it is true, but they behaved like pigs in a pigpen. If they had had their wits about them, they might have guessed that this was just what their beautiful hostess and her maidens thought of them. My face turns red when I try to reckon how many mountains of meat and pudding, and how many gallons of wine, these twenty-two gluttons and guzzlers put away. They forgot their homes, their wives and children, Ulysses, and everything else except this banquet, which they wanted to go on enjoying forever. But in the end they began to slow down, simply because they could not hold any more.
“That last bit of fat is more than I can manage,” said one.
“And I have no room for another bite,” said the man beside him, with a sigh. “What a shame! I’m just as hungry as ever.”

In short, they all stopped eating and leaned back on their thrones, looking so dull and helpless that it was ridiculous to see. When their hostess saw this, she laughed out loud. So did her four maidens, and so did the twenty-two servants who had carried in the dishes, and the twenty-two others who had poured the wine. The louder they all laughed, the duller and more helpless the twenty-two gluttons looked. Then the beautiful woman stood in the middle of the hall and stretched out a slim rod. It had been in her hand the whole time, though they had not noticed it until now. She pointed it at one guest after another until every man had felt it aimed at him. Lovely as her face was, and smiling as she was, it looked as wicked and mischievous as the ugliest snake ever seen. And thickheaded as the travelers had made themselves, they began to suspect that they had fallen into the power of an evil enchantress.

“You wretches,” she cried, “you have abused a lady’s hospitality. In this princely hall you have behaved like animals in a hogpen. You are already swine in everything except your shape, which is human, and which you disgrace. I would be ashamed to keep it myself for another moment if I had to share it with you. But it will take only a little magic to make your outsides match your hoggish natures. Take your proper shapes, you gluttons, and off to the sty with you!”

With these last words she waved her wand and stamped her foot commandingly. Each of the guests was horrified to see that, in place of his companions in human form, twenty-one hogs were sitting on the same number of golden thrones. Each man (for so he still thought of himself) tried to cry out in surprise, but he could only grunt. In a word, he was exactly the same kind of beast as his companions. It looked so absurd to see hogs on cushioned thrones that they hurried to get down on all fours and wallow like other swine. They tried to groan and beg for mercy, but all that came out were the most dreadful grunts and squeals ever heard from a hog’s throat. They would have wrung their hands in despair, but when they tried, they only grew more desperate at the sight of themselves squatting on their haunches and pawing the air with their front trotters. Dear me! What floppy ears they had! What little red eyes, half buried in fat! And what long snouts, instead of Grecian noses!

But brutes as they certainly were, they still had enough human feeling left to be shocked at their own ugliness. They meant to groan again, but out came a grunt and squeal even worse than before. It was so harsh and piercing that you would have thought a butcher was sticking his knife into every one of their throats, or at the very least that someone was yanking each hog by his funny little curly tail.
“Away to your sty!” cried the enchantress, and she gave them a few sharp smacks with her wand. Then she turned to the servants. “Chase these swine out, and scatter some acorns for them to eat.”

The door of the hall was flung open, and the herd of hogs ran in every direction except the right one, as stubborn as hogs always are. At last they were driven into the back yard of the palace. It was a sight to bring tears to your eyes (and I hope none of you is cruel enough to laugh at it) to watch the poor creatures go snuffling along, picking up a cabbage leaf here and a turnip top there, and digging their noses into the dirt for whatever they could find. Once in their sty, they behaved even more like pigs than the ones born that way. They bit and snorted at one another, stuck their feet in the trough, and gobbled their food in a ridiculous rush. When there was nothing left to eat, they piled themselves into a heap on some dirty straw and fell fast asleep. If any human reason remained in them, it was just enough to make them wonder when they would be slaughtered and what kind of bacon they would make.

Meanwhile, as I told you before, Eurylochus had waited and waited and waited in the entrance hall of the palace, unable to make out what had happened to his friends. At last the uproar of squealing swine rang through the palace, and he saw the image of a hog in the marble basin. Then he decided it was best to hurry back to the ship and tell the wise Ulysses about these marvelous events. So he ran down the steps as fast as he could and did not stop to catch his breath until he reached the shore.
“How is it that you’re alone?” King Ulysses asked the moment he saw him. “Where are the twenty-two men who went with you?”
At these questions Eurylochus burst into tears.
“Alas!” he cried. “I am afraid we will never see a single one of them again.”

Then he told Ulysses everything that had happened, as far as he understood it. He added that he suspected the beautiful woman was a vile enchantress, and that the marble palace, magnificent as it looked, was really nothing but a dismal cave. As for his companions, he couldn’t imagine what had become of them, unless they had been thrown to the swine to be eaten alive. This news terrified all the sailors. But Ulysses wasted no time. He buckled on his sword, slung his bow and quiver over his shoulders, and took his spear in his right hand. When his followers saw their wise leader getting ready, they asked where he was going and begged him earnestly not to leave them.

“You are our king,” they cried, “and what is more, the wisest man alive. Only your wisdom and courage can bring us safely out of this danger. If you leave us and walk into the enchanted palace, the same thing will happen to you as to our poor friends, and none of us will ever see our beloved Ithaca again.”

“Because I am your king,” answered Ulysses, “and wiser than any of you, it is all the more my duty to find out what has happened to our comrades and whether anything can still be done to rescue them. Wait for me here until tomorrow. If I haven’t returned by then, you must hoist sail and try to find your way to our homeland. As for me, I am responsible for the fate of these poor sailors, who have stood beside me in battle and have been soaked to the skin with me so many times by the same stormy waves. I will either bring them back with me or die trying.”

If his followers had dared, they would have held him back by force. But King Ulysses frowned sternly at them, shook his spear, and told them to try and stop him at their own risk. Seeing how determined he was, they let him go. They sat down on the sand, as miserable a group of people as you could find, to wait and pray for his return.

Just as before, when Ulysses had gone a few steps from the edge of the cliff, the purple bird came fluttering toward him, crying, “Peep, peep, pe—weep!” and doing everything it could to persuade him to go no farther.

“What do you mean, little bird?” cried Ulysses. “You are dressed like a king in purple and gold, and you wear a golden crown on your head. Is it because I am a king too that you want so badly to speak to me? If you can talk in human language, tell me what you want me to do.”
“Peep!” answered the purple bird, very mournfully. “Peep, peep, pe—we—ep!”

There was certainly some heavy sorrow in the little bird’s heart, and it was a sad situation that he could not even have the comfort of telling what it was. But Ulysses had no time to waste trying to solve the mystery. So he walked faster, and had gone a good way along the pleasant forest path when he met a young man. He looked lively and clever and was dressed in rather unusual clothes. He wore a short cloak and a kind of cap that seemed to have a pair of wings on it, and he stepped so lightly that you would have guessed there might be wings on his feet too. To help him walk even better (for he was always off on one journey or another), he carried a winged staff, with two snakes wriggling and twisting around it. In short, I have told you enough to guess that it was Quicksilver. Ulysses, who had known him for a long time and had learned a great deal of his wisdom from him, recognized him at once.

“Where are you going in such a hurry, wise Ulysses?” asked Quicksilver. “Don’t you know that this island is enchanted? The wicked enchantress, whose name is Circe and who is the sister of King AEetes, lives in the marble palace you can see over there among the trees. By her magic arts she changes every human being into the brute, beast, or bird that he most resembles.”
“That little bird that met me at the edge of the cliff,” exclaimed Ulysses. “Was he once a human being?”

“Yes,” answered Quicksilver. “He was once a king named Picus, and a pretty good king too, only a bit too proud of his purple robe, his crown, and the golden chain around his neck. So he was forced to take the shape of a gaudy, feathered bird. The lions, wolves, and tigers that will come running to meet you in front of the palace were once fierce, cruel men. They resembled in character the wild beasts whose forms they now wear, and rightly so.”
“And my poor companions,” said Ulysses. “Have they been changed in the same way by this wicked Circe’s arts?”

“You know very well what gluttons they were,” replied Quicksilver. Rogue that he was, he couldn’t help laughing at his own joke. “So you won’t be surprised to hear that they have all turned into swine! If Circe had never done anything worse, I really wouldn’t think she was very much to blame.”
“But is there nothing I can do to help them?” asked Ulysses.

“It will take all your wisdom,” said Quicksilver, “and a little of mine as well, to keep your own royal and clever self from being turned into a fox. But do as I tell you, and things may end better than they began.”

While he was speaking, Quicksilver seemed to be looking for something. He went along bent over the ground, and soon laid his hand on a little plant with a snow-white flower, which he picked and sniffed. Ulysses had been looking at that very spot only a moment before, and it seemed to him that the plant burst into full bloom the instant Quicksilver touched it.

“Take this flower, King Ulysses,” he said. “Guard it as you would your eyesight, for I assure you it is extremely rare and precious, and you could search the whole earth without finding another like it. Keep it in your hand once you enter the palace, and smell it often while you talk with the enchantress. Above all, when she offers you food, or a drink of wine from her goblet, be sure to fill your nose with the flower’s fragrance. Follow these directions, and her magic will not be able to turn you into a fox.”

Quicksilver then gave him some more advice on how to behave. He told him to be bold and careful, and assured him again that, powerful as Circe was, he had a good chance of coming safely out of her enchanted palace. Ulysses listened closely, thanked his good friend, and went on his way. But he had gone only a few steps when he remembered some other questions he wanted to ask. He turned around and saw no one where Quicksilver had been standing, for that winged cap and those winged shoes, with the help of the winged staff, had carried him quickly out of sight.

When Ulysses reached the lawn in front of the palace, the lions and other fierce animals came bounding up to meet him. They would have fawned on him and licked his feet. But the wise king struck at them with his long spear and sternly ordered them out of his way. He knew they had once been bloodthirsty men, and that if they could do the harm that was in their hearts, they would tear him limb from limb instead of fawning on him. The wild beasts yelped and glared at him, and kept their distance while he climbed the palace steps.

When Ulysses walked into the hall, he saw the magic fountain standing in the middle of it. The water gushing upward had taken the shape of a man again, in a long, white, fleecy robe, and he seemed to be waving a welcome. The king could also hear the shuttle clacking in the loom, the sweet music of the beautiful woman’s singing, and then the pleasant voices of the woman and her four maidens chatting, with bursts of cheerful laughter mixed in. But Ulysses did not spend long listening to the laughter or the song. He leaned his spear against one of the pillars, loosened his sword in its sheath, strode boldly forward, and flung the folding doors wide open. The moment the beautiful woman saw his stately figure in the doorway, she rose from the loom and hurried to meet him with both hands held out, her face lit up by a glad smile that shone over it like sunshine.
“Welcome, brave stranger!” she cried. “We have been expecting you.”

The nymph with the sea-green hair curtsied right down to the ground and welcomed him too. So did her sister in the bodice of oak bark, and the one who sprinkled dewdrops from her fingertips, and the fourth, who had some peculiarity I can’t remember. Then Circe, which was the name of the beautiful enchantress, spoke to him again. She had fooled so many people that she never doubted she could fool Ulysses as well, since she had no idea how wise he was.

“Your companions,” she said, “are already guests in my palace, and they have been treated with all the hospitality that their good manners so richly deserve. If you like, you may first have some refreshment and then join them in the handsome room where they are now. Look, my maidens and I have been weaving their pictures into this tapestry.”

She pointed to the beautifully woven cloth on the loom. Circe and the four nymphs must have worked very busily since the sailors arrived, because many more yards of tapestry had been finished than I described earlier. In this new part Ulysses saw his twenty-two friends sitting on cushioned thrones under canopies, greedily gobbling delicacies and gulping down great cups of wine. The picture went no further than that. Oh no, indeed! The enchantress was far too cunning to let Ulysses see the harm her magic had done to those gluttons since then.
“As for you, brave sir,” said Circe, “from the dignity of your face I take you for nothing less than a king. Please follow me, and you will be treated as your rank deserves.”

So Ulysses followed her into the oval hall where his twenty-two comrades had eaten the feast that ended so disastrously for them. All this time, though, he had been holding the snow-white flower and smelling it steadily while Circe spoke, and as he stepped over the threshold of the hall, he took care to breathe in several long, deep whiffs of its fragrance. The twenty-two thrones that had stood along the wall before were gone, and in the middle of the room there was now only a single throne. It was surely the most magnificent seat any king or emperor ever rested on. It was made entirely of carved gold set with precious stones, with a cushion that looked like a soft heap of living roses and a canopy of sunlight, which Circe knew how to weave into curtains. The enchantress took Ulysses by the hand and seated him on this dazzling throne. Then she clapped her hands and called for the chief butler.

“Bring me,” she said, “the goblet reserved for kings to drink from. And fill it with the same delicious wine that my royal brother, King AEetes, praised so highly when he last visited me with my lovely daughter Medea. What a good and sweet child she is! If she were here now, she would be delighted to see me offering this wine to my honored guest.”
But while the butler was off fetching the wine, Ulysses held the snow-white flower up to his nose.
“Is it a healthy wine?” he asked.
At this the four maidens giggled, and the enchantress turned and glared at them sternly.
“It is the healthiest juice ever pressed from a grape,” she said. “Other drinks tend to disguise a man, but this one brings out his true self and shows him as he ought to be.”

The chief butler liked nothing better than seeing people turned into pigs, or making beasts of themselves in any way, so he hurried to bring the royal goblet. It was filled with a liquid as bright as gold, which kept sparkling upward and tossing a sunny spray over the rim. But however lovely the wine looked, it was laced with the strongest spells Circe knew how to brew. For every drop of pure grape juice there were two drops of pure mischief, and the danger was that the mischief made it taste even better. The mere smell of the bubbles fizzing at the brim was enough to turn a man’s beard into pig bristles, or make lion’s claws grow out of his fingers, or give him a fox’s tail behind.
Smiling, Circe held out the goblet to him. “Drink, my noble guest,” she said. “You will find in this cup a comfort for all your troubles.”

King Ulysses took the goblet in his right hand, while he held the snow-white flower to his nostrils with his left and breathed in so deeply that his lungs filled with its pure, simple fragrance. Then he drained all the wine and looked the enchantress calmly in the face.

“Wretch,” cried Circe, giving him a sharp rap with her wand, “how dare you keep your human shape a moment longer? Take the form of the beast you most resemble! If you are a hog, go join your fellow swine in the sty. If you are a lion, a wolf, or a tiger, go howl with the wild beasts on the lawn. If you are a fox, go use your cunning to steal chickens. You have drunk my wine, and you can be a man no longer.”

But such was the power of the snow-white flower that Ulysses did not tumble from his throne in the shape of a pig or any other beast. He looked even more manly and kingly than before. He flung the magic goblet away so that it went clattering across the marble floor to the far end of the hall. Then he drew his sword, seized the enchantress by her beautiful curls, and made as if to cut off her head with a single blow.

“Wicked Circe,” he cried in a terrible voice, “this sword will put an end to your enchantments. You will die, vile wretch, and never again do harm in the world by tempting people into the vices that turn them into beasts.”

The voice and face of Ulysses were so dreadful, and his sword flashed so brightly and looked so terribly sharp, that Circe was nearly killed by fright alone, before any blow fell. The chief butler scrambled out of the hall, snatching up the golden goblet as he went, while the enchantress and the four maidens dropped to their knees, wringing their hands and screaming for mercy.

“Spare me!” cried Circe. “Spare me, royal and wise Ulysses! Now I know you are the man Quicksilver warned me about, the most prudent of mortals, whom no enchantment can overcome. Only you could have defeated Circe. Spare me, wisest of men! I will show you true hospitality, and I will even become your slave and give you this magnificent palace to be your home from now on.”

Meanwhile the four nymphs were making a pitiful fuss. The ocean nymph with the sea-green hair in particular wept buckets of salt water, and the fountain nymph, besides scattering dewdrops from her fingertips, nearly melted away in tears. But Ulysses would not calm down until Circe had sworn a solemn oath to change his companions back, along with as many others as he named, from their present shapes of beasts or birds into their old shapes as men.
“On those terms,” he said, “I will spare your life. Otherwise you die on the spot.”

With a drawn sword hanging over her head, the enchantress was ready to agree to do as much good as she had done harm until then, however little she liked the work. So she led Ulysses out the back door of the palace and showed him the pigs in their sty. There were about fifty of these filthy creatures in the herd, and although most of them were hogs by birth and upbringing, there was surprisingly little difference to be seen between them and their new brothers, who had so recently been men. Strictly speaking, the new ones went rather too far, and seemed determined to wallow in the muddiest corner of the sty and to beat the real pigs at their own natural business. When men turn into brutes, the little scrap of human wit they keep only makes them ten times more brutish.

Still, the comrades of Ulysses had not quite forgotten that they once stood upright. When he came near the sty, twenty-two enormous pigs broke away from the herd and raced toward him, squealing in such a horrible chorus that he clapped both hands over his ears. Yet they did not seem to know what they wanted, or whether they were only hungry or miserable for some other reason. It was strange to watch them, in the middle of their distress, shoving their noses into the mud to look for something to eat. The nymph in the oak-bark bodice, who was the hamadryad of an oak, threw a handful of acorns among them, and the twenty-two hogs scrambled and fought for the prize as if they hadn’t tasted so much as a mug of sour milk for a year.

“These must certainly be my comrades,” said Ulysses. “I recognize their characters. They’re hardly worth the trouble of turning back into men. Still, we will do it, so that their bad example doesn’t corrupt the other hogs. So let them have their own shapes back, Dame Circe, if your skill is up to it. I suspect it will take stronger magic than it took to make pigs of them.”

So Circe waved her wand again and spoke a few magic words, and at the sound the twenty-two hogs pricked up their drooping ears. It was a wonder to see their snouts get shorter and shorter, and their mouths (which they seemed sorry to lose, because they could no longer gobble so quickly) grow smaller and smaller, and one after another start to stand on their hind legs and scratch their noses with their front trotters. At first the onlookers hardly knew whether to call them hogs or men, but before long they decided they looked more like men. At last the twenty-two comrades of Ulysses stood there, looking much as they had when they left the ship.

You mustn’t imagine, though, that the piggishness had left them entirely. Once it takes hold of a person’s character, it is very hard to get rid of. The hamadryad proved this. She was very fond of mischief, and she threw another handful of acorns in front of the twenty-two newly restored men. Down they went on the ground at once and gobbled the acorns up in a most shameful way. Then they remembered themselves, scrambled to their feet, and looked even sillier than usual.
“Thank you, noble Ulysses!” they cried. “You have turned us from brute beasts back into men.”
“Don’t trouble yourselves to thank me,” said the wise king. “I’m afraid I have done very little for you.”
To tell the truth, there was a suspicious sort of grunt in their voices, and for a long time afterward they talked gruffly and were likely to break into a squeal.
“Whether you end up back in the sty,” Ulysses added, “will depend on how you behave from now on.”
Just then a bird’s call sounded from the branch of a nearby tree.
“Peep, peep, pe—wee—ep!”

It was the purple bird, who had been perched over their heads all this time, watching everything that happened. He hoped Ulysses would remember how hard he had tried to keep him and his followers out of harm’s way. Ulysses ordered Circe to make a king of this good little bird at once, just as she had found him. The words were hardly out of his mouth, and the bird had no time to say another “Pe—weep,” before King Picus leaped down from the branch, as majestic a ruler as any in the world. He wore a long purple robe and splendid yellow stockings, with a finely made collar around his neck and a golden crown on his head. He and King Ulysses exchanged the courtesies proper to their high rank. But from that time on, King Picus was no longer proud of his crown and his royal finery, or even of being a king. He thought of himself as merely the chief servant of his people, and felt that it must be his lifelong task to make them better and happier.

As for the lions, tigers, and wolves, Circe would have changed them back at his slightest word, but Ulysses thought it wiser to leave them as they were. That way they would give warning of their cruel natures, instead of going about disguised as men and pretending to human feelings while their hearts were as bloodthirsty as wild beasts’. So he let them howl as much as they pleased and never troubled himself about them. When everything was settled to his liking, he sent for the rest of his comrades, whom he had left on the seashore. When they arrived, with the prudent Eurylochus at their head, they all made themselves comfortable in Circe’s enchanted palace, until they were fully rested and refreshed from the hardships of their voyage.

chapters.title: The Pomegranate Seeds
