paragraphs: Mother Ceres was extremely fond of her daughter Proserpina and seldom let her go out into the fields alone. But just at the time my story begins, the good lady was very busy. She looked after the wheat, the Indian corn, the rye and barley, and in short the crops of every kind all over the earth, and since the season had been unusually late so far, she had to make the harvest ripen faster than usual. So she put on her turban, which was made of poppies (a flower she was always known for wearing), climbed into her chariot drawn by a pair of winged dragons, and was just ready to set off.
“Mother dear,” said Proserpina, “it will be so lonely here with you away. Could I go down to the shore and invite some sea nymphs up out of the waves to play with me?”

“Yes, child,” answered Mother Ceres. “The sea nymphs are good creatures, and they will never lead you into any harm. But be careful not to stray away from them, and don’t go wandering through the fields by yourself. Young girls without their mothers to look after them very easily get into mischief.”

The child promised to be as sensible as a grown woman. By the time the winged dragons had whirled the car out of sight, she was already down on the shore, calling the sea-nymphs to come and play. They knew Proserpina’s voice and soon showed their shining faces and sea-green hair above the water, where their home lay far below. They had brought a great many beautiful shells with them. Sitting down on the damp sand, where the surf broke over them, they set to work making a necklace and hung it around Proserpina’s neck. To thank them, the child begged them to come a little way into the fields with her, so that they could pick plenty of flowers and she could make a wreath for each of her kind playmates.

“Oh no, dear Proserpina,” cried the sea-nymphs. “We don’t dare go with you onto dry land. We tend to grow faint unless we can breathe in the salt breeze of the ocean with every breath. And haven’t you noticed how careful we are to let the surf wash over us every minute or so, to keep ourselves nicely damp? Without that, we would soon look like bunches of seaweed pulled up and dried in the sun.”

“What a pity,” said Proserpina. “But wait for me here, and I will run and fill my apron with flowers and be back before the surf has broken ten times over you. I want to make you wreaths as lovely as this necklace of many-colored shells.”

“Then we will wait,” answered the sea-nymphs. “But while you’re gone, we may as well lie down on a bed of soft sponge under the water. The air is a little too dry for our comfort today. We will pop our heads up every few minutes to see whether you are coming.”

The young Proserpina ran quickly to a spot where she had seen a great many flowers only the day before. Now, though, they were a little past their best, and since she wanted to give her friends the freshest and loveliest blossoms, she wandered farther into the fields. There she found some that made her scream with delight. She had never seen such wonderful flowers: violets so large and sweet-smelling, roses with such a rich and delicate blush, magnificent hyacinths and fragrant pinks, and many others, some of which seemed to have new shapes and colors. Two or three times she could not help thinking that a clump of splendid flowers had suddenly sprouted from the ground right before her eyes, as if to lure her a few steps farther. Soon Proserpina’s apron was full and spilling over with lovely blossoms. She was just about to turn back to the sea-nymphs and sit with them on the damp sand, all of them twining wreaths together. But a little farther on, what should she see? A large shrub, completely covered in the most magnificent flowers in the world.
“Oh, the darlings!” cried Proserpina. Then she thought to herself, “I was looking at that very spot a moment ago. How strange that I didn’t see the flowers!”

The closer she came to the shrub, the more attractive it looked. When she was right beside it, though, even though its beauty was richer than words can say, she hardly knew whether she liked it or not. It bore over a hundred flowers in the most brilliant colors, each one different from the others, yet all alike in some way that showed them to be sister blossoms. But the leaves of the shrub and the petals of the flowers had a deep, glossy shine that made Proserpina wonder whether they might be poisonous. To tell you the truth, foolish as it sounds, she was half inclined to turn around and run away.

“How silly of me!” she thought, plucking up her courage. “This is truly the loveliest shrub that ever grew out of the earth. I will pull it up by the roots, take it home, and plant it in my mother’s garden.”

Holding up her apron full of flowers with her left hand, Proserpina grabbed the big shrub with the other and pulled and pulled, but she could barely loosen the soil around its roots. What a deeply rooted plant it was! She pulled again with all her might and saw the ground begin to stir and crack for some distance around the stem. She gave one more pull, then let go, because she thought she heard a rumbling right under her feet. Did the roots go down into some enchanted cavern? Then, laughing at herself for such a childish idea, she tried once more. Up came the shrub, and Proserpina staggered backward, holding the stem triumphantly in her hand and staring at the deep hole its roots had left in the ground.

To her great astonishment, the hole kept spreading wider and wider and growing deeper and deeper, until it seemed to have no bottom at all. All the while a rumbling noise rose out of it, louder and louder and nearer and nearer, like the tramp of horses’ hoofs and the rattle of wheels. She was too frightened to run. She stood straining her eyes into the strange pit, and soon she saw a team of four black horses, snorting smoke from their nostrils, tearing their way out of the earth with a splendid golden chariot whirling behind them. They leaped out of the bottomless hole, chariot and all, and there they were beside Proserpina, tossing their black manes, swishing their black tails, and prancing with all four hoofs off the ground at once. In the chariot sat a man, richly dressed, with a crown on his head that blazed with diamonds. He had a noble look and was rather handsome, but he seemed sullen and discontented. He kept rubbing his eyes and shading them with his hand, as if he did not spend enough time in the sunshine to be fond of its light.
The moment this figure noticed the terrified Proserpina, he waved for her to step closer.
“There’s nothing to be afraid of,” he said, wearing the friendliest smile he could put on. “Come along! Wouldn’t you enjoy a short ride with me in my beautiful chariot?”

But Proserpina was so alarmed that she wanted nothing except to get out of his reach. And no wonder. The stranger did not look especially good-natured, in spite of his smile, and his voice was deep and stern, sounding as much like an earthquake rumbling underground as anything else. As children in trouble always do, Proserpina thought first of calling for her mother.
“Mother, Mother Ceres!” she cried, trembling all over. “Come quickly and save me!”

But her voice was too faint for her mother to hear. In fact, Ceres was most likely a thousand miles away just then, making the corn grow in some far-off country. And even if she had been within hearing, it would not have helped her poor daughter, because the moment Proserpina began to cry out, the stranger jumped down, caught the child in his arms, climbed back into the chariot, shook the reins, and shouted to the four black horses to go. They broke into such a swift gallop that it seemed more like flying through the air than running on the ground. In a moment Proserpina lost sight of the pleasant valley of Enna, where she had always lived. A moment later even the top of Mount AEtna had grown so blue in the distance that she could hardly tell it from the smoke pouring out of its crater. But the poor child kept screaming, scattering her apron full of flowers along the way, and leaving a long cry trailing behind the chariot. Many mothers who heard it ran quickly to see whether some harm had come to their children. But Mother Ceres was a long way off and could not hear the cry.
As they rode on, the stranger did his best to comfort her.

“Why are you so frightened, my pretty child?” he said, trying to soften his rough voice. “I promise I won’t hurt you. Why, you have been picking flowers! Wait until we reach my palace, and I will give you a garden full of prettier flowers than those, all made of pearls, diamonds, and rubies. Can you guess who I am? My name is Pluto, and I am the king of diamonds and every other precious stone. Every speck of the gold and silver under the earth belongs to me, not to mention the copper and iron, and the coal mines that supply me with plenty of fuel. Do you see this splendid crown on my head? You can have it as a toy. Oh, we will be very good friends, and you will find me more pleasant than you expect, once we are out of this tiresome sunshine.”
“Let me go home!” cried Proserpina. “Let me go home!”

“My home beats your mother’s,” King Pluto replied. “It’s a golden palace with windows of crystal, and since hardly any sunshine ever reaches it, diamond lamps light the rooms. You have never laid eyes on anything half as grand as my throne. If you want, you can sit on it and be my little queen, and I’ll take the footstool.”
“Golden palaces and thrones mean nothing to me,” Proserpina sobbed. “Oh, Mother, Mother! Please take me back to her!”
But the one who called himself King Pluto just yelled at his horses to hurry.

“Please don’t be foolish, Proserpina,” he said, in a rather sullen tone. “I offer you my palace, my crown, and all the riches under the earth, and you treat me as if I were wronging you. The one thing my palace needs is a merry little girl to run up and down the stairs and brighten the rooms with her smile. And that is what you must do for King Pluto.”
“Never!” Proserpina replied, making herself look as wretched as she could. “Not until you put me down at my mother’s door will I smile again.”

But she might as well have talked to the wind whistling past them, because Pluto urged his horses on and went faster than ever. Proserpina kept crying out, and she screamed so long and so loudly that her poor little voice was almost screamed away. When it was down to a whisper, she happened to glance over a great, broad field of waving grain, and whom do you think she saw? None other than Mother Ceres, making the corn grow and too busy to notice the golden chariot rattling past. The child gathered all her strength and gave one more scream, but she was out of sight before Ceres had time to turn her head.

King Pluto had taken a road that now began to grow very gloomy. Rocks and cliffs rose on both sides, and between them the rumble of the chariot wheels echoed like rolling thunder. The trees and bushes growing in the cracks of the rocks had dismal leaves, and before long, although it was barely noon, the air darkened into a gray twilight. The black horses had run so fast that they were already beyond the reach of the sunshine. But the darker it grew, the more satisfied Pluto’s face became. After all, he was not an ugly man, especially when he stopped twisting his features into a smile that did not belong there. Proserpina peeped at his face through the gathering dusk and hoped he might not be as wicked as she had first thought.

“Ah, this twilight is truly refreshing,” said King Pluto, “after being tormented by the ugly, rude glare of the sun. How much more pleasant lamplight or torchlight is, especially when it shines back from diamonds! It will be a magnificent sight when we get to my palace.”
“How much farther is it?” asked Proserpina. “And once I’ve seen it, will you take me home?”

“We’ll discuss that later,” Pluto replied. “Now we are coming to the edge of my kingdom. See that tall gateway up ahead? Once we are through those gates, we’re home. And there is my loyal mastiff, lying at the threshold. Cerberus! Cerberus! Here, good dog!”

With these words Pluto pulled on the reins and stopped the chariot right between the tall, massive pillars of the gateway. The mastiff he had spoken of got up from the threshold and stood on his hind legs to rest his front paws on the chariot wheel. But, my stars, what a strange dog it was! He was a huge, shaggy, ugly monster with three separate heads, each one fiercer than the other two. Yet fierce as they were, King Pluto patted them all. He seemed as fond of his three-headed dog as if it were a sweet little spaniel with silky ears and curly hair. Cerberus, for his part, was plainly delighted to see his master and showed his affection the way other dogs do, by wagging his tail vigorously. Proserpina’s eyes were drawn to the tail by its brisk motion, and she saw that it was nothing less than a living dragon, with fiery eyes and fangs that looked very poisonous. And while the three-headed Cerberus fawned so lovingly on King Pluto, the dragon tail wagged against its will, looking as cross and ill-tempered as you can imagine, all on its own account.
“Is that dog going to bite me?” Proserpina asked, huddling nearer to Pluto. “He’s so ugly!”

“Oh, don’t worry,” her companion said. “He only hurts people who try to get into my kingdom uninvited, or who try to slip away when I want them kept here. Down, Cerberus! Now, my pretty Proserpina, let’s drive on.”

On went the chariot, and King Pluto seemed very pleased to be back in his own kingdom. He pointed out to Proserpina the rich veins of gold showing among the rocks, and showed her several places where a single stroke of a pickaxe would knock loose a bushel of diamonds. All along the road, in fact, gems sparkled that would have been priceless above ground but were counted as common down here, hardly worth a beggar’s bending down for.

Not far from the gateway they came to a bridge that seemed to be made of iron. Pluto stopped the chariot and told Proserpina to look at the stream gliding so lazily beneath it. Never in her life had she seen such a sluggish, black, muddy-looking stream. Its waters reflected nothing on the banks, and it moved as slowly as if it had forgotten which way to flow and would rather stand still than flow in either direction.
“That is the river Lethe,” King Pluto announced. “Don’t you think it’s a lovely stream?”
“I think it is a very gloomy one,” said Proserpina.

“It suits my taste, though,” answered Pluto, who tended to turn sullen when anyone disagreed with him. “In any case, its water has one excellent quality. A single drink of it makes people forget every care and sorrow that has ever troubled them. Just sip a little, my dear Proserpina, and you will stop grieving for your mother at once, and nothing in your memory will keep you from being perfectly happy in my palace. I will send for some in a golden goblet the moment we arrive.”

“Oh, no, no, no!” cried Proserpina, starting to weep again. “I would a thousand times rather be miserable and remember my mother than be happy and forget her. My dear, dear mother! I will never, never forget her.”
“We’ll see about that,” said King Pluto. “You have no idea what a fine time we’re going to have in my palace. And here we are at the entrance. These pillars are solid gold, I promise you.”

He stepped down from the chariot, picked Proserpina up in his arms, and carried her up a tall flight of steps into the great hall of the palace. Large precious stones of many colors lit it brilliantly. They seemed to burn like lamps, and their glow filled the vast room a hundred times over. And yet a kind of gloom hung in the middle of all that enchanted light. There was not one thing in the hall that was truly pleasant to look at, except little Proserpina herself, a lovely child still holding one flower from the earthly fields that she had not let fall. In my opinion, even King Pluto had never been happy in his palace. I think that was the real reason he had stolen Proserpina away: he wanted something to love, so he could stop fooling his heart with all this tiresome splendor. And although he pretended to dislike the sunshine of the upper world, the child’s presence, dimmed as it was by her tears, felt as if a faint, watery sunbeam had somehow found its way into the enchanted hall.
Pluto then called for his servants. He told them to waste no time preparing a magnificent feast, and, above all, not to forget to put a golden cup of the water of Lethe beside Proserpina’s plate.
“I won’t drink that, or anything else,” said Proserpina. “And I won’t taste one bite of food, even if you keep me in your palace forever.”

“I would be sorry to see that,” King Pluto answered, patting her cheek. He truly wanted to be kind; he just did not know how. “I can see you are a spoiled child, my little Proserpina. But once you see the good things my cook will make for you, your appetite will soon come back.”

Then he sent for the head cook and gave strict orders that every kind of treat that young people usually love should be set before Proserpina. He had a secret reason for this. You must understand that there is a fixed law: when people are carried off to the land of magic, if they taste any food there, they can never return to their friends. Now, if King Pluto had been clever enough to offer Proserpina some fruit, or bread and milk (the simple food she had always been used to), she would very likely have been tempted to eat it before long. But he left the whole matter to his cook. Like all cooks, this one thought nothing was worth eating unless it was rich pastry, heavily seasoned meat, or spiced sweet cakes. Proserpina’s mother had never given her such things, and the smell of them took away her appetite instead of sharpening it.

But now my story has to climb out of King Pluto’s kingdom and find out what Mother Ceres has been doing since she lost her daughter. We caught a glimpse of her, you remember, half hidden among the waving grain, while the four black horses raced along with the chariot that was carrying her beloved Proserpina away against her will. You also remember the loud scream Proserpina gave just as the chariot disappeared from view.

Of all the child’s cries, only this last shriek reached Mother Ceres’s ears. She had mistaken the rumble of the chariot wheels for a clap of thunder. She thought a rain shower was coming, and that it would help her make the corn grow. But when she heard Proserpina’s shriek, she jumped and looked all around, not knowing where it came from, yet almost sure it was her daughter’s voice. Still, it seemed so impossible that the girl could have wandered across so many lands and seas (which Ceres herself could not have crossed without her winged dragons) that the good Ceres tried to believe the cry must have come from some other parent’s child, and not from her own darling Proserpina. Even so, it filled her with many tender fears, the kind that stir in every mother’s heart when she has to leave her dear children without putting them in the care of some maiden aunt or other trustworthy guardian. So she quickly left the field where she had been working so hard. And because her work was only half done, the next day the grain looked as if it needed both sun and rain, as if the ears were blighted and something was wrong with the roots.

Her pair of dragons must have had very quick wings, because in less than an hour Mother Ceres landed at the door of her home and found it empty. She knew the child loved to play by the sea, so she hurried there as fast as she could. There she saw the poor sea-nymphs, their wet faces peeping over a wave. All this time the good creatures had been waiting on the sponge bank, and about every half-minute they had popped their four heads up out of the water to see whether their playmate was coming back yet. When they saw Mother Ceres, they sat down on the crest of a surf wave and let it toss them onto the shore at her feet.
“Where’s Proserpina?” Ceres cried. “Where is my child? Answer me, you wicked sea-nymphs! Did you coax her down beneath the waves?”

“Oh, no, good Mother Ceres,” said the innocent sea-nymphs, tossing back their green curls and looking her in the eye. “We would never dream of such a thing. It is true that Proserpina was playing with us. But she left us a long time ago. She only meant to run a little way onto dry land and pick some flowers for a wreath. That was early in the day, and we haven’t seen her since.”

Ceres hardly waited to hear what the nymphs had to say before she rushed off to ask questions all around the neighborhood. But nobody could tell her anything that would help the poor mother guess what had happened to Proserpina. A fisherman, it is true, had noticed her little footprints in the sand as he walked home along the beach with a basket of fish. A country man had seen the child bending down to pick flowers. Several people had heard either the rattle of chariot wheels or the rumble of distant thunder. And one old woman, who was gathering vervain and catnip, had heard a scream, but took it for some childish nonsense and did not bother to look up. The foolish people! It took them such a tiresome time to tell the nothing they knew that it was dark night before Mother Ceres realized she would have to look for her daughter somewhere else. So she lit a torch and set out, determined never to return until Proserpina was found.

In her hurry and distress, she forgot all about her chariot and the winged dragons. Or perhaps she thought she could search more thoroughly on foot. In any case, that is how she began her sorrowful journey, holding her torch out in front of her and looking carefully at everything along the path. And as it happened, she had not gone far before she found one of the magnificent flowers from the shrub that Proserpina had pulled up.

“Ha!” thought Mother Ceres, studying it by torchlight. “There is something wicked about this flower! The earth did not grow it with any help from me, or on its own. This is the work of enchantment, so it is poisonous. And perhaps it has poisoned my poor child.”
But she tucked the poisonous flower into her dress anyway, since she did not know whether she would ever find any other keepsake of Proserpina.

All night long, Ceres knocked at the door of every cottage and farmhouse and woke the tired workers to ask whether they had seen her child. They stood in the doorway, yawning and half asleep, and answered her with pity, and begged her to come in and rest. At the gate of every palace she also knocked so loudly that the servants hurried to throw the gate open, thinking it must be some great king or queen who would demand a feast for supper and a grand room to sleep in. And when they saw only a sad, worried woman with a torch in her hand and a wreath of withered poppies on her head, they spoke rudely to her, and sometimes threatened to set the dogs on her. But nobody had seen Proserpina, and nobody could give Mother Ceres the slightest hint of where to look. So the night went by, and still she kept up her search. She did not sit down to rest, or stop to eat, or even remember to put out the torch, although first the rosy dawn and then the cheerful light of the morning sun made its red flame look thin and pale. But I wonder what that torch was made of. By day it burned dimly, yet at night it was as bright as ever, and neither rain nor wind put it out in all the weary days and nights that Ceres spent looking for Proserpina.

She did not ask only human beings for news of her daughter. In the woods and beside the streams she met creatures of a different nature. In those old times they lived in the pleasant, lonely places, and they were very friendly with anyone who understood their language and customs, as Mother Ceres did. Sometimes, for instance, she would tap her finger against the knotted trunk of a mighty oak, and at once its rough bark would split open and a beautiful maiden would step out. She was the hamadryad of the oak, who lived inside it, shared its long life, and rejoiced when its green leaves played in the breeze. But not one of these leafy maidens had seen Proserpina. Then, going a little farther, Ceres might come to a fountain gushing from a pebbly hollow in the ground, and she would dabble her hand in the water. Look! Up through the sandy, pebbly bottom, along with the gush of the fountain, a young woman with dripping hair would rise and stand gazing at Mother Ceres, half out of the water, swaying up and down with its restless motion. But when the mother asked whether her poor lost child had stopped to drink at the fountain, the naiad, her eyes full of tears (for these water-nymphs had tears to spare for anyone’s grief), would answer “No!” in a murmuring voice, just like the murmur of the stream.

She often met fauns, too. They looked like sunburned country folk, except that they had hairy ears, little horns on their foreheads, and the hind legs of goats, on which they skipped merrily around the woods and fields. They were a playful sort of creature, but when Ceres asked about her daughter and they had no good news to give, they grew as sad as their cheerful natures would allow. Sometimes, though, she came suddenly upon a rough gang of satyrs, who had faces like monkeys and horses’ tails behind them, and who were usually dancing wildly and shouting with loud laughter. When she stopped to question them, they only laughed louder, and made new fun out of the lonely woman’s distress. How unkind of those ugly satyrs! And once, as she crossed a lonely sheep pasture, she saw a figure named Pan sitting at the foot of a tall rock, playing music on a shepherd’s flute. He had horns, too, and hairy ears, and goat’s feet. But since he knew Mother Ceres, he answered her question as politely as he knew how, and invited her to taste some milk and honey from a wooden bowl. Still, Pan could no more tell her what had become of Proserpina than any of the other wild folk could.

And so Mother Ceres wandered for nine long days and nights, finding no trace of Proserpina except for an occasional withered flower. She picked these up and tucked them into her dress, because she imagined they might have fallen from her poor child’s hand. All day she traveled on under the hot sun, and when night came again, the flame of her torch would glow red and gleam along the path, and she kept on searching by its light, never stopping to sit down and rest.

On the tenth day she happened to spot the mouth of a cave. Though it was bright noon everywhere else, inside there would have been only a dusky twilight, but as it happened, a torch was burning there. It flickered and struggled against the darkness, but with all its mournful glimmer it could not light even half of the gloomy cave. Ceres had resolved to leave no spot unsearched, so she peeped in at the entrance and lit it up a little more by holding her own torch in front of her. As she did, she caught sight of what looked like a woman sitting on the brown leaves of last autumn, a great heap of which the wind had swept into the cave. This woman (if she was a woman) was nowhere near as beautiful as many of her sex, for her head, they tell me, was shaped very much like a dog’s, and for decoration she wore a wreath of snakes around it. But Mother Ceres knew the moment she saw her that this was an odd sort of person, who took all her pleasure in being miserable, and would never say a word to anyone unless they were as sad and wretched as she loved to be.
“I am wretched enough now,” thought poor Ceres, “to talk with this gloomy Hecate, even if she were ten times sadder than she has ever been.”
So she stepped into the cave and sat down on the dead leaves beside the dog-headed woman. Since losing her daughter, she had found no other companion in all the world.
“Oh, Hecate,” she said, “you won’t know what real sorrow is until you lose a daughter of your own. For pity’s sake, tell me: did my poor child Proserpina pass by the entrance to your cave?”

“No,” answered Hecate in a cracked voice, sighing after every word or two. “No, Mother Ceres, I have seen nothing of your daughter. But my ears, you should know, are made in such a way that every cry of distress and fright anywhere in the world is pretty sure to find its way to them. And nine days ago, as I sat in my cave making myself very miserable, I heard the voice of a young girl, shrieking as if in terrible distress. Something dreadful has happened to the child, you can be sure of that. As far as I could tell, a dragon, or some other cruel monster, was carrying her off.”
“You are killing me by saying so,” cried Ceres, nearly fainting. “Where did the sound come from, and which way did it seem to go?”

“It went by very fast,” said Hecate, “and at the same time there was a heavy rumbling of wheels toward the east. I can tell you nothing more, except that, in my honest opinion, you will never see your daughter again. The best advice I can give you is to move into this cave, where the two of us will be the most wretched women in the world.”

“Not yet, dark Hecate,” Ceres answered. “First come with your torch and help me look for my lost child. And when there is no hope left of finding her (if that black day is meant to come), then, if you will let me throw myself down, whether on these withered leaves or on the bare rock, I will show you what misery really is. But until I know she has vanished from the face of the earth, I won’t allow myself even a moment to grieve.”

Gloomy Hecate did not much like the idea of going out into the sunny world. But then she thought about it. Ceres’s sorrow would hang around the two of them like a dim twilight, however brightly the sun shone, so she could enjoy her bad mood just as well as if she had stayed in her cave. So in the end she agreed to go, and they set out together, each carrying a torch, even though it was broad daylight and the sun was shining clear. The torchlight seemed to make its own gloom, so that the people they passed on the road could not see them very distinctly. And indeed, if anyone caught so much as a glimpse of Hecate, with the wreath of snakes around her forehead, they usually decided it was wise to run away without waiting for a second look.
As the two traveled along in this miserable way, an idea struck Ceres.
“There is someone,” she exclaimed, “who must have seen my poor child and can surely tell me what became of her. Why didn’t I think of him before? It is Phoebus.”

“What?” said Hecate. “That young man who is always sitting in the sunshine? Oh, please don’t think of going near him. He is a gay, light-headed, frivolous fellow, and he will only smile in your face. Besides, there is such a glare of sun around him that he will blind my poor eyes, which I have nearly wept away already.”
“You promised to be my companion,” Ceres replied. “Come, let’s hurry, or the sunshine will be gone, and Phoebus with it.”

So they went off in search of Phoebus, both of them sighing deeply, and Hecate, to tell the truth, wailing a good deal louder than Ceres. All her pleasure, you see, lay in being miserable, so she made the most of it. After a fairly long journey, they came at last to the sunniest spot in the whole world. There they saw a beautiful young man with long, curling locks that seemed to be made of golden sunbeams. His clothes were like light summer clouds, and his face was so dazzlingly bright that Hecate held her hands in front of her eyes and muttered that he ought to wear a black veil. Phoebus (for he was the very person they were looking for) had a lyre in his hands and was making its strings tremble with sweet music, while he sang a most delightful song that he had just composed. Among his many other talents, this young man was famous for his excellent poetry.

As Ceres and her gloomy companion came near him, Phoebus smiled at them so cheerfully that the wreath of snakes on Hecate’s head gave a spiteful hiss, and Hecate wished with all her heart that she were back in her cave. Ceres, however, was too deep in her grief to notice or care whether Phoebus smiled or frowned.
“Phoebus!” she called out. “I’m in terrible trouble, and I’ve come to you for help. Do you know what has happened to my beloved child Proserpina?”

“Proserpina! Did you say Proserpina?” answered Phoebus, trying to remember. So many pleasant thoughts flowed through his mind all the time that he tended to forget things that had happened only yesterday. “Ah, yes, I remember her now. A very lovely child indeed. I am happy to tell you, my dear lady, that I saw little Proserpina only a few days ago. You can set your mind completely at rest about her. She is safe, and in excellent hands.”
“Oh, where is my dear child?” cried Ceres, clasping her hands and flinging herself at his feet.

“Why,” said Phoebus—and as he spoke, he kept brushing his lyre so that a thread of music ran in and out among his words—“while the little girl was picking flowers (and she has really exquisite taste in flowers), King Pluto suddenly snatched her up and carried her off to his kingdom. I have never been to that part of the universe, but I’m told the royal palace is built in a very grand style, out of the most splendid and costly materials. Gold, diamonds, pearls, and every kind of precious stone will be your daughter’s everyday playthings. I advise you, my dear lady, not to worry at all. Proserpina’s love of beauty will be well satisfied, and even without any sunshine, she will lead a very enviable life.”

“Hush! Don’t say such a thing!” Ceres answered indignantly. “What is there to satisfy her heart? What are all the splendors you talk about, without love? I must have her back. Will you come with me, Phoebus, to demand my daughter from this wicked Pluto?”

“Please excuse me,” replied Phoebus, with a graceful bow. “I certainly wish you success, and I’m sorry that my own business is so pressing that I can’t have the pleasure of going with you. Besides, I am not on the best of terms with King Pluto. To tell you the truth, his three-headed mastiff would never let me through the gateway, because I would have to carry a sheaf of sunbeams with me, and those, you know, are forbidden in Pluto’s kingdom.”
“Ah, Phoebus,” said Ceres, with bitter meaning in her voice, “you have a harp where your heart should be. Farewell.”
“Won’t you stay a moment,” asked Phoebus, “and let me turn the sweet and touching story of Proserpina into a poem on the spot?”

But Ceres shook her head and hurried away with Hecate. Phoebus (who, as I told you, was a fine poet) immediately began to compose an ode about the poor mother’s grief. If we judge his feelings by this beautiful work, he must have had a very tender heart. But when a poet gets into the habit of using his heartstrings as strings for his lyre, he can pluck at them as much as he likes without much pain to himself. So although Phoebus sang a very sad song, he stayed as merry the whole time as the sunbeams he lived among.

Poor Mother Ceres now knew what had become of her daughter, but she was not one bit happier than before. Her case, on the contrary, looked more hopeless than ever. As long as Proserpina was above ground, there might have been a chance of winning her back. But now that the poor child was shut inside the iron gates of the king of the mines, with the three-headed Cerberus lying at the threshold, there seemed no possible way for her to escape. Gloomy Hecate, who loved to take the darkest view of everything, told Ceres that she had better come back to the cavern with her and spend the rest of her life being miserable. Ceres answered that Hecate was welcome to go back there herself, but that she would wander the earth looking for the entrance to King Pluto’s kingdom. And Hecate took her at her word and hurried back to her beloved cave, frightening a great many little children with a glimpse of her dog’s face as she went.

Poor Mother Ceres! It is sad to think of her plodding wearily on her way all alone, holding up that never-dying torch, whose flame seemed a symbol of the grief and hope burning together in her heart. She suffered so much that, although she had looked quite young when her troubles began, she came to look elderly in a very short time. She did not care how she was dressed, and it never occurred to her to throw away the wreath of withered poppies that she had put on the very morning Proserpina disappeared. She roamed about so wildly, with her hair so untidy, that people took her for some poor distracted creature and never dreamed that this was Mother Ceres, who watched over every seed the farmer planted. These days, though, she gave no thought to seed-time or harvest, but left the farmers to look after their own affairs and the crops to wither or flourish as they happened to. Nothing now seemed to interest Ceres, except when she saw children playing or picking flowers along the roadside. Then she would stand and gaze at them with tears in her eyes. The children seemed to feel for her sorrow, too, and would gather in a little group around her knees and look up wistfully into her face. Ceres would kiss them all in turn, lead them home, and advise their mothers never to let them out of their sight.

“Because if you do,” she would say, “the same thing may happen to you as happened to me. Iron-hearted King Pluto may take a liking to your darlings, snatch them up in his chariot, and carry them away.”

One day, on her journey in search of the entrance to Pluto’s kingdom, she came to the palace of King Celeus, who ruled at Eleusis. She climbed a high flight of steps and went in through the doorway, and she found the whole royal household in great alarm about the queen’s baby. The infant, it seems, was sickly (troubled by its teeth, I suppose), and would not eat anything, and moaned with pain all the time. The queen—her name was Metanira—wanted to find a nurse, and when she saw a motherly-looking woman coming up the palace steps, she thought to herself that here was exactly the person she needed. So Queen Metanira ran to the door with the poor wailing baby in her arms and begged Ceres to take charge of him, or at least to tell her what would do him good.
“Will you trust the child entirely to me?” asked Ceres.
“Yes, and gladly,” answered the queen, “if you will give him all your time. I can see that you have been a mother.”

“You are right,” said Ceres. “I once had a child of my own. Well then, I will be the nurse of this poor, sickly boy. But I warn you, be careful not to interfere with any treatment I decide is right for him. If you do, the poor infant will suffer for his mother’s foolishness.”
Then she kissed the child, and it seemed to do him good, for he smiled and snuggled close against her chest.

So Mother Ceres set her torch down in a corner (where it went on burning all the time) and made her home in the palace of King Celeus as nurse to little Prince Demophoon. She treated him as if he were her own child, and she did not let the king or queen say whether he should be bathed in warm or cold water, or what he should eat, or how often he should go out in the fresh air, or when he should be put to bed. You would hardly believe me if I told you how quickly the baby prince shook off his ailments, and grew plump and rosy and strong, and got two rows of ivory teeth in less time than any other little fellow, before or since. Instead of the palest, most wretched, and puniest little imp in the world (as his own mother admitted he was when Ceres first took charge of him), he was now a sturdy baby, crowing and laughing and kicking up his heels and rolling from one end of the room to the other. All the good women of the neighborhood crowded into the palace and held up their hands in utter amazement at the beauty and health of this darling little prince. Their wonder was all the greater because he was never seen to eat any food at all, not even a cup of milk.
“Tell me, nurse,” the queen kept saying, “how do you make the child thrive so?”
“I was a mother once,” Ceres would always answer, “and having nursed my own child, I know what other children need.”

But Queen Metanira, naturally enough, was very curious to know exactly what the nurse did to her child. So one night she hid herself in the room where Ceres and the little prince slept. There was a fire in the chimney, which had by now burned down to big coals and embers glowing on the hearth, with a flame flickering up now and then and throwing a warm, ruddy light on the walls. Ceres sat in front of the hearth with the child on her lap, and the firelight made her shadow dance on the ceiling above. She undressed the little prince and bathed him all over with some fragrant liquid from a vase. The next thing she did was to rake back the red embers and make a hollow among them, right where the backlog had been. Finally, while the baby was crowing and clapping his fat little hands and laughing in his nurse’s face (just as you may have seen your own little brother or sister do before going into a warm bath), Ceres suddenly laid him down, naked as he was, in the hollow among the red-hot embers. Then she raked the ashes over him and quietly turned away.

Imagine, if you can, how Queen Metanira shrieked, thinking nothing less than that her dear child would be burned to a cinder. She burst out of her hiding place, ran to the hearth, raked the fire open, and snatched poor little Prince Demophoon out of his bed of live coals, with one of them gripped in each of his fists. He immediately started crying bitterly, as babies usually do when they are roughly woken from a sound sleep. To the queen’s astonishment and joy, she could not find any sign that the child had been hurt by the hot fire he had lain in. She now turned to Mother Ceres and asked her to explain the mystery.

“Foolish woman,” Ceres answered, “didn’t you promise to trust this poor infant entirely to me? You have no idea what harm you have done him. If you had left him in my care, he would have grown up like a child of heavenly birth, with superhuman strength and intelligence, and he would have lived forever. Do you imagine that earthly children can become immortal without being toughened for it in the fiercest heat of fire? But you have ruined your own son. He will be a strong man and a hero in his day, but because of your folly, he will grow old and finally die like the sons of other women. His mother’s weak tenderness has cost the poor boy his immortality. Farewell.”

With these words she kissed little Prince Demophoon, sighing at the thought of what he had lost, and went on her way. She paid no attention to Queen Metanira, who begged her to stay and bury the child in the hot embers as often as she liked. Poor baby! He never slept so warmly again.

While Mother Ceres lived in the king’s palace, she had been so busy caring for the little prince that her grief over Proserpina eased a bit. But now that she had nothing else to occupy her, she was as miserable as ever. At last, in her despair, she made a terrible decision. Not one stalk of grain, not one blade of grass, not a potato or a turnip, nor any other plant that people or animals could eat, would be allowed to grow until her daughter was given back. She even forbade the flowers to bloom, in case their beauty cheered someone’s heart.

Now, not so much as a spear of asparagus ever dared to poke out of the ground without Ceres’s special permission, so you can imagine what a dreadful disaster struck the earth. The farmers plowed and planted as usual, but the rich black furrows lay as barren as a sandy desert. The pastures were as brown in lovely June as they ever were in bleak November. The rich man’s wide fields and the cottager’s little garden plot were blighted alike. Every little girl’s flower bed held nothing but dry stalks. The old people shook their white heads and said the earth had grown old like them and could no longer wear the warm smile of summer on its face. It was truly pitiful to see the starving cattle and sheep trailing after Ceres, lowing and bleating, as though instinct told them she could help. Everyone who knew of her power begged her to take pity on the human race and, at the very least, to let the grass grow. But Mother Ceres, kind-hearted as she normally was, would not give way.
“Never,” she said. “If the earth is ever to be green again, the green must first spring up along the path my daughter walks on her way back to me.”

At last, since nothing else seemed to work, our old friend Quicksilver was sent racing off to King Pluto, in the hope of persuading him to undo the harm he had caused and put everything right by giving Proserpina up. Quicksilver hurried to the great gate, leaped clean over the three-headed mastiff, and in an astonishingly short time was standing at the palace door. The servants knew him by his face and clothes, since his short cloak, his winged cap and shoes, and his snaky staff had often been seen there in earlier days. He asked to be taken to the king at once, but Pluto heard his voice from the top of the stairs, and since he loved to be entertained by Quicksilver’s merry talk, he called down for him to come up. While the two of them talk over their business, we must find out what Proserpina has been doing since we last saw her.

As you may remember, the child had declared that she would not taste a bite of food as long as she was forced to stay in King Pluto’s palace. How she kept her resolve and still stayed fairly plump and rosy is more than I can explain. But I am told that some young ladies have the knack of living on air, and Proserpina seems to have had it too. In any case, it had now been six months since she left the surface of the earth, and as far as the attendants could say, not a crumb had passed her lips. This was all the more to her credit because King Pluto had arranged for her to be tempted day after day with every kind of sweet, with richly preserved fruits, and with delicacies of every sort, the things young people like best. But her good mother had often warned her how harmful such things were, and for that reason alone, even if she had had no other, she would have firmly refused to touch them.

Being cheerful and lively by nature, the little girl was not as unhappy all this while as you might think. The enormous palace had a thousand rooms and was full of beautiful and marvelous things. It is true that a constant gloom half hid itself among the countless pillars, gliding ahead of the child as she wandered among them and creeping along behind her in the echo of her footsteps. All the glitter of the jewels, which blazed with a light of their own, was not worth one gleam of real sunshine, and the most brilliant of the many-colored gems that Proserpina had for toys could not match the plain beauty of the flowers she used to pick. Still, wherever the girl went through those gilded halls and chambers, it seemed that she carried nature and sunshine with her, scattering dewy blossoms to her right and left. After Proserpina arrived, the palace was no longer the stately, artificial, gloomily magnificent place it had been before. Everyone who lived there felt the change, and King Pluto felt it more than any of them.

“My dear little Proserpina,” he would say, “I wish you could like me a little more. People like me, with gloomy, cloudy natures, often have hearts as warm underneath as those of cheerier folk. If you would only stay with me because you wanted to, I would be happier than if I owned a hundred palaces like this one.”

“Ah,” said Proserpina, “you should have tried to make me like you before you carried me off. The best thing you can do now is let me go. Then I might remember you sometimes and think that you were as kind as you knew how to be. And perhaps one day I might even come back and visit you.”

“No, no,” answered Pluto with his gloomy smile, “I won’t trust you on that. You are far too fond of living in broad daylight and picking flowers. What a silly, childish taste that is! Look at these gems I had dug up for you, richer than any in my crown. Aren’t they prettier than a violet?”
“Not half as pretty,” said Proserpina, snatching the gems out of Pluto’s hand and hurling them to the far end of the hall. “Oh, my sweet violets, will I never see you again?”

Then she burst into tears. But young people’s tears have very little salt or sting in them, and they don’t inflame the eyes as much as grown-ups’ tears do. So it is no wonder that a few moments later Proserpina was frolicking through the hall almost as merrily as she and the four sea nymphs had once played along the edge of the foaming surf. King Pluto gazed after her and wished that he were a child too. And when little Proserpina turned around and saw this great king standing in his splendid hall, looking so grand and so sad and so lonely, she was struck by a kind of pity. She ran back to him and, for the first time in her life, put her small, soft hand in his.
“I love you a little,” she whispered, looking up into his face.

“Do you really, my dear child?” cried Pluto, bending his dark face down to kiss her. But Proserpina shrank away from the kiss, because although his features were noble, they were very dusky and grim. “Well, I haven’t earned it, after keeping you prisoner for so many months and starving you as well. Aren’t you terribly hungry? Isn’t there something I can get you to eat?”
In asking this, the king of the mines had a very sly purpose. As you will remember, if Proserpina tasted even a morsel of food in his lands, she could never afterward leave them.

“No, thank you,” said Proserpina. “Your head cook is forever baking and stewing and roasting and rolling out pastry, trying one dish after another that he thinks I might like. He might as well save himself the trouble, poor fat little man. I have no appetite for anything in the world, unless it were a slice of bread my mother baked herself, or a bit of fruit from her garden.”

When Pluto heard this, he began to see that he had gone about tempting Proserpina the wrong way. The cook’s fancy dishes and artificial treats were nowhere near as delicious, in the good child’s opinion, as the plain food Mother Ceres had raised her on. Wondering why he had never thought of it before, the king sent one of his trusted attendants with a large basket to fetch the finest, juiciest pears, peaches, and plums that could be found anywhere in the world above. Unfortunately, this was just when Ceres had forbidden any fruit or vegetable to grow. After searching all over the earth, King Pluto’s servant found only a single pomegranate, and it was so dried up that it was hardly worth eating. Still, since there was nothing better to be had, he carried this dry, shriveled old pomegranate back to the palace, set it on a magnificent golden tray, and took it up to Proserpina. And, oddly enough, just as the servant was bringing the pomegranate in at the back door of the palace, our friend Quicksilver was going up the front steps on his errand to take Proserpina away from King Pluto.
The moment Proserpina spotted the pomegranate sitting on the golden tray, she told the servant to carry it off again.
“I won’t touch it, I promise you,” she said. “Even if I were starving, I would never think of eating a miserable, dried-up pomegranate like that.”
“It is the only one in the world,” said the servant.

He put down the golden tray with the shriveled pomegranate on it and left the room. Once he was gone, Proserpina couldn’t help stepping up to the table and looking eagerly at this poor sample of dried fruit. To tell the truth, the sight of something that suited her taste made her feel all six months of appetite rush over her at once. It was certainly a wretched-looking pomegranate, with no more juice in it than an oyster shell. But there was no choice of such things in King Pluto’s palace. This was the first fruit she had seen there, and probably the last she would ever see, and if she didn’t eat it right away, it would only get drier and become completely unfit to eat.
“I can at least smell it,” thought Proserpina.

So she picked up the pomegranate and held it to her nose. Then somehow, since the nose is so close to the mouth, the fruit found its way into that little red cave. Dear me, what a lasting pity! Before Proserpina knew what she was doing, her teeth had bitten into it, all on their own. Just as this fatal deed was done, the door of the room opened, and in came King Pluto, followed by Quicksilver, who had been urging him to let his little prisoner go. At the first sound of them coming in, Proserpina took the pomegranate out of her mouth. But Quicksilver, whose eyes were very keen and whose wits were the sharpest anyone ever had, noticed that the child looked a little flustered. Seeing the empty tray, he guessed that she had been sneaking a nibble of something. Honest Pluto, however, never suspected the secret.

“My little Proserpina,” said the king, sitting down and fondly drawing her between his knees, “here is Quicksilver, who tells me that many troubles have fallen on innocent people because I kept you in my lands. To tell the truth, I had already thought to myself that it was wrong to take you away from your good mother. But you must understand, my dear child, that this vast palace tends to be gloomy, though the jewels certainly shine brightly, and that I am not of the cheeriest temper. So it was natural enough for me to look for the company of someone merrier than myself. I hoped you would take my crown as a toy, and me—ah, you’re laughing, naughty Proserpina—me, grim as I am, as a playmate. It was a foolish hope.”
“Not so very foolish,” whispered Proserpina. “You have really amused me a great deal, sometimes.”

“Thank you,” said King Pluto, rather dryly. “But I can see plainly that you think my palace a dark prison and me its iron-hearted jailer. And I would have an iron heart indeed if I kept you here any longer, my poor child, when it has been six months since you ate anything. I give you your freedom. Go with Quicksilver. Hurry home to your dear mother.”

Now, you might not have guessed it, but Proserpina found she could not say goodbye to poor King Pluto without some regret, and a good deal of guilt for not telling him about the pomegranate. She even shed a tear or two at the thought of how lonely and cheerless the great palace would seem to him, with all its ugly glare of artificial light, once she had gone—she, his one little ray of natural sunshine, whom he had stolen, to be sure, but only because he valued her so much. I don’t know how many kind things she might have said to the heartbroken king of the mines if Quicksilver had not hurried her away.
“Come along quickly,” he whispered in her ear, “or His Majesty may change his royal mind. And above all, be careful to say nothing about what was brought to you on the golden tray.”

Before long they had passed through the great gateway, leaving the three-headed Cerberus behind them barking and yelping and growling with triple noise, and they came out onto the surface of the earth. It was delightful to see, as Proserpina hurried along, how the path turned green behind her and on both sides. Wherever she set her blessed foot, a dewy flower sprang up at once. Violets gushed up along the roadside. Grass and grain began to sprout with ten times their usual vigor and richness, to make up for the dreary months wasted in barrenness. The starved cattle set to grazing right away after their long fast, ate enormously all day, and got up at midnight to eat more. And I can assure you that it was a busy time of year for the farmers, who found summer rushing upon them all at once. I must not forget to say that all the birds in the whole world hopped about in the newly blossoming trees and sang together in a tremendous outburst of joy.

Mother Ceres had come back to her empty home and was sitting sadly on the doorstep with her torch burning in her hand. She had been watching the flame absently for a while when, all at once, it flickered and went out.
“What can this mean?” she wondered. “This torch is enchanted. It ought to burn until my child returns.”

Lifting her eyes, she was amazed to see a sudden greenness flashing across the brown, barren fields, like the golden glow you may have seen spreading far and wide over a landscape when the sun has just risen.
“Does the earth disobey me?” cried Mother Ceres angrily. “Does it dare to be green, when I have ordered it to stay barren until my daughter is back in my arms?”
“Then hold out your arms, dear mother,” said a voice she knew well, “and gather your little daughter into them.”

Proserpina came running and threw herself into her mother’s arms. There is no describing how happy they both were. They had cried a great many tears while they were apart, and now they cried a great many more, because there was no better way for their joy to show itself.
When their hearts had settled a little, Mother Ceres looked at Proserpina with worry.
“My child,” she said, “did you eat anything while you were in King Pluto’s palace?”

“Dearest mother,” Proserpina answered, “I’ll tell you the whole truth. Until this very morning, not a bite of food had crossed my lips. But today they brought me a pomegranate (a very dry one, all shriveled up, with almost nothing left of it but seeds and skin). I hadn’t seen any fruit for so long, and I was faint with hunger, so I was tempted to take just one bite. The moment I tasted it, King Pluto and Quicksilver walked into the room. I hadn’t swallowed anything. But—dear mother, I hope it was no harm—six of the pomegranate seeds, I’m afraid, were still in my mouth.”

“Oh, my unlucky child, and oh, poor me!” cried Ceres. “For each of those six seeds, you must spend one month of every year in King Pluto’s palace. I get you back only by half. Six months with me, and six with that good-for-nothing King of Darkness!”

“Please don’t talk so harshly about poor King Pluto,” said Proserpina, kissing her mother. “He has some very good qualities. And I truly think I can stand six months in his palace, as long as he lets me spend the other six with you. He was certainly wrong to carry me off. But as he says, his life was a gloomy one, living all alone in that great dark place. Having a little girl to run up and down the stairs has made a wonderful change in his spirits. It’s some comfort to have made him so happy. So, all things considered, dearest mother, let’s be thankful that he doesn’t get to keep me the whole year round.”

chapters.title: The Golden Fleece
paragraphs: When Jason, the son of the dethroned King of Iolchos, was a little boy, he was sent away from his parents and put in the care of the oddest schoolmaster you ever heard of. This learned person was one of the creatures called Centaurs, who walked on four legs. He lived in a cave, and he had the body and legs of a white horse, with the head and shoulders of a man. His name was Chiron. Odd-looking as he was, he was an excellent teacher, and he had several students who later did him proud by becoming famous. The great Hercules was one, and so were Achilles and Philoctetes, and also AEsculapius, who became renowned as a doctor. Chiron taught his pupils to play the harp, to cure illnesses, and to use the sword and shield, along with other subjects that boys of those days were taught instead of writing and arithmetic.

I have sometimes suspected that Master Chiron was really not so different from other people. I think he was a kind, merry old fellow who liked to pretend he was a horse, scrambling around the schoolroom on all fours and letting the little boys ride on his back. Then, when his students had grown up and grown old, and were bouncing their grandchildren on their knees, they told them about the games of their school days. The youngsters got the idea that their grandfathers had learned their letters from a Centaur, half man and half horse. Small children, you know, don’t always understand what they are told, and they often get such silly notions into their heads.

Whatever the truth, people have always said (and will go on saying as long as the world lasts) that Chiron, who had a schoolmaster’s head, also had a horse’s body and legs. Just picture the solemn old gentleman clattering and stamping into the schoolroom on his four hooves, maybe stepping on some little fellow’s toes, swishing his tail instead of a rod, and every now and then trotting outside for a mouthful of grass! I wonder what the blacksmith charged him for a set of iron shoes.

So Jason lived in the cave with the four-footed Chiron from the time he was a baby only a few months old until he was fully grown. I suppose he became a very good harp player, skilled with weapons, fairly well acquainted with herbs and other doctor’s supplies, and above all a fine horseman. When it came to teaching young people to ride, good Chiron must have had no equal among schoolmasters. At last, now a tall, strong young man, Jason decided to go out and seek his fortune in the world. He did it without asking Chiron’s advice or telling him anything about it. That was very unwise, of course, and I hope none of you, my little listeners, will ever follow Jason’s example. But you should understand that he had learned he was a royal prince. He had learned that his father, King AEson, had been robbed of the kingdom of Iolchos by a man named Pelias, who would have killed Jason too if he had not been hidden in the Centaur’s cave. Now that he had a man’s strength, Jason was determined to set all this right: to punish the wicked Pelias for wronging his dear father, to throw him down from the throne, and to sit there himself instead.

With this plan in mind, he took a spear in each hand, threw a leopard’s skin over his shoulders to keep off the rain, and set out on his travels, his long yellow curls blowing in the wind. What he was proudest of was a pair of sandals that had belonged to his father. They were richly embroidered and tied onto his feet with golden strings. His whole outfit was unlike anything people usually saw, and as he went along, women and children ran to their doors and windows. They wondered where this handsome young man was heading in his leopard’s skin and golden-tied sandals, and what heroic deeds he planned to do with a spear in his right hand and another in his left.

I don’t know how far Jason had gone when he came to a wild river rushing straight across his path. White flecks of foam floated among its black whirlpools as it hurried noisily along, roaring angrily. In the dry seasons of the year it was not a very wide river, but now it was swollen by heavy rains and by melting snow from the slopes of Mount Olympus. It thundered so loudly and looked so wild and dangerous that Jason, brave as he was, thought it wise to stop at the edge. The riverbed seemed to be littered with sharp, jagged rocks, and some of them stuck up above the water. After a while an uprooted tree with broken branches came drifting down the current and got tangled among the rocks. Now and then a drowned sheep floated past, and once the body of a cow.

In short, the flooded river had already done a great deal of damage. It was clearly too deep for Jason to wade across and too rough for him to swim. He could see no bridge, and as for a boat, if there had been one, the rocks would have smashed it to pieces in an instant.

“Look at the poor boy,” said a cracked voice right beside him. “He can’t have had much of an education, if he doesn’t know how to cross a little stream like this. Or is he afraid of getting his fine golden-stringed sandals wet? What a pity his four-footed schoolmaster isn’t here to carry him safely over on his back!”

Jason turned around, very surprised, because he hadn’t known anyone was near. Beside him stood an old woman with a ragged cloak over her head, leaning on a staff carved at the top in the shape of a cuckoo. She looked very old, wrinkled and frail. Yet her eyes, which were as brown as an ox’s, were so large and beautiful that when they met Jason’s eyes, he could see nothing else. The old woman was holding a pomegranate, even though the fruit was well out of season.
“Where are you headed, Jason?” she asked.

She knew his name, you will notice. Indeed, those great brown eyes looked as if they knew everything, past and future. While Jason was staring at her, a peacock strutted forward and took its place at the old woman’s side.
“I’m going to Iolchos,” the young man answered, “to tell the wicked King Pelias to come down from my father’s throne and let me rule in his place.”

“Well, then,” said the old woman, in the same cracked voice, “if that’s all you have to do, there’s no need to hurry so much. Be a good lad and take me on your back and carry me across the river. My peacock and I have business on the other side too, just as you do.”

“Good mother,” Jason replied, “your business can hardly be as important as pulling a king off his throne. Besides, as you can see for yourself, the river is very rough. If I stumbled, it would sweep us both away even more easily than it carried off that uprooted tree over there. I would gladly help you if I could, but I doubt I’m strong enough to carry you across.”

“Then,” she said scornfully, “you aren’t strong enough to pull King Pelias off his throne either. And Jason, unless you’ll help an old woman in her need, you have no business being a king. What are kings for, if not to help the weak and the suffering? But do as you like. Either take me on your back, or I’ll do my best to struggle across the stream on my poor old legs.”

As she said this, the old woman prodded the river with her staff, as if looking for the safest spot in the rocky bed to take her first step. By now, though, Jason was ashamed of his unwillingness to help. He felt he could never forgive himself if this poor frail creature came to harm trying to fight the rushing current. Good Chiron, half horse or not, had taught him that the finest use of strength is to help the weak. He had also taught him to treat every young woman like a sister and every old one like a mother. Remembering these rules, the strong, handsome young man knelt down and asked the good lady to climb onto his back.
“This crossing doesn’t look very safe to me,” he said. “But since your business is so urgent, I’ll try to carry you over. If the river sweeps you away, it will take me with you.”
“No doubt that will be a great comfort to us both,” said the old woman. “But don’t worry. We’ll get across safely.”

She threw her arms around Jason’s neck, and he lifted her off the ground, stepped boldly into the raging, foaming current, and began to stagger away from the shore. The peacock landed on the old woman’s shoulder. Jason’s two spears, one in each hand, kept him from stumbling and helped him feel his way among the hidden rocks. Still, at every moment he expected that he and his passenger would be swept downstream along with the driftwood of broken trees and the bodies of the sheep and the cow. The cold, snowy flood came pouring down from the steep side of Olympus, raging and thundering as if it held a real grudge against Jason, or at least was set on snatching his living burden from his shoulders. When he was halfway across, the uprooted tree (the one I told you about earlier) broke loose from the rocks and bore down on him, its splintered branches sticking out like the hundred arms of the giant Briareus. It rushed past without touching him. But the next moment his foot was caught in a crack between two rocks and stuck so fast that, in struggling to get free, he lost one of his golden-stringed sandals.
At this mishap Jason could not help crying out in annoyance.
“What’s wrong, Jason?” asked the old woman.
“Plenty,” said the young man. “I’ve lost a sandal among the rocks. And what kind of figure will I cut at King Pelias’s court, with a golden-stringed sandal on one foot and the other foot bare?”
“Don’t take it to heart,” his companion answered cheerfully. “You never had better luck than losing that sandal. It convinces me that you are the very person the Speaking Oak has been talking about.”

There was no time just then to ask what the Speaking Oak had said. But her lively tone cheered the young man. Besides, he had never in his life felt so strong and mighty as he did since taking this old woman on his back. Instead of growing tired, he got stronger as he went. Fighting his way up against the torrent, he finally reached the far shore, climbed the bank, and set the old woman and her peacock safely down on the grass. As soon as he had done so, though, he could not help looking rather glumly at his bare foot, with only a scrap of the golden string still clinging around his ankle.

“You’ll get a handsomer pair of sandals before long,” said the old woman, with a kind look from her beautiful brown eyes. “Just let King Pelias catch sight of that bare foot, and you’ll see him turn pale as ashes, I promise you. There’s your path. Go on, my good Jason, and my blessing goes with you. And when you sit on your throne, remember the old woman you helped across the river.”

With these words she hobbled away, giving him a smile over her shoulder as she went. Maybe the light of her beautiful brown eyes cast a glow around her, or maybe it was something else, but Jason imagined there was something noble and majestic about her after all. Though she seemed to walk with a rheumatic hobble, she moved with as much grace and dignity as any queen on earth. Her peacock, which had now fluttered down from her shoulder, strutted along behind her in tremendous style and spread out its magnificent tail on purpose for Jason to admire.

When the old woman and her peacock were out of sight, Jason continued his journey. After traveling quite a long way, he came to a town at the foot of a mountain, not far from the seashore. Outside the town was an enormous crowd, not only men and women but children too, all in their best clothes and obviously enjoying a holiday. The crowd was thickest toward the shore, and in that direction, above the people’s heads, Jason saw a wreath of smoke curling up into the blue sky. He asked one of the crowd what town this was, and why so many people had gathered.

“This is the kingdom of Iolchos,” the man answered, “and we are the subjects of King Pelias. Our king has called us together to watch him sacrifice a black bull to Neptune, who, they say, is his Majesty’s father. The king is over there, where you see the smoke rising from the altar.”

As the man spoke, he studied Jason with great curiosity. The young stranger’s clothes were nothing like what people wore in Iolchos, and it was a strange sight to see a youth with a leopard’s skin draped over his shoulders and a spear in each hand. Jason noticed that the man kept staring at his feet in particular. As you remember, one of them was bare, while the other wore his father’s sandal with its golden strings.
“Look at him! Just look at him!” the man said to the person standing next to him. “Do you see? He’s wearing only one sandal!”

At this, one person after another began to stare at Jason, and everyone seemed deeply struck by something about him, though their eyes went to his feet far more often than to any other part of him. He could also hear them whispering to each other.
“One sandal! One sandal!” they kept whispering. “The one-sandaled man! He has finally come! Where did he come from? What is he planning? And what will the king say to a man with only one sandal?”

Poor Jason was thoroughly embarrassed. He decided that the people of Iolchos had terrible manners, to make such a public fuss over a small accident in his dress. Meanwhile, either the crowd pushed him forward or Jason himself shoved a path through it, and before long he found himself right beside the smoking altar, where King Pelias was sacrificing the black bull. The buzzing and murmuring of the crowd, astonished at the sight of Jason with one bare foot, grew so loud that it interrupted the ceremony. The king was just about to cut the bull’s throat with his great knife, but he turned around angrily and fixed his eyes on Jason. By now the people had drawn back from the young man, so he stood in an open space by the smoking altar, face to face with the furious King Pelias.
“Who are you?” the king cried, scowling terribly. “How dare you make such a commotion while I am offering a black bull to my father Neptune?”
“It is not my fault,” Jason answered. “Your Majesty should blame the rudeness of your subjects. They have created all this uproar just because one of my feet happens to be bare.”
At these words the king glanced down, quickly and with a start, at Jason’s feet.
“Ha!” he muttered. “Here is the one-sandaled fellow, sure enough! What am I going to do with him?”

He gripped the great knife in his hand more tightly, as if he half wanted to kill Jason instead of the black bull. The people nearby only half heard what the king said, and they caught his words as he muttered them. First a murmur ran through them, and then a loud shout went up.
“The one-sandaled man has come! The prophecy will come true!”

You should know that many years earlier the Speaking Oak of Dodona had told King Pelias that a man with one sandal would throw him down from his throne. Because of this, he had given strict orders that nobody was ever to come into his presence unless both sandals were tied firmly on his feet. In his palace he kept an officer whose only job was to inspect people’s sandals and give them a new pair, paid for by the royal treasury, as soon as the old ones started to wear out. In all the years of his reign, the king had never been so frightened and shaken as he was by the sight of poor Jason’s bare foot. But he was a bold, hard-hearted man by nature, so he soon pulled himself together and began to think about how he could get rid of this dreadful one-sandaled stranger.

“My good young man,” said King Pelias, in the gentlest tone imaginable, to put Jason off his guard, “you are most welcome to my kingdom. Judging by your clothes, you must have traveled a long way, since nobody in this part of the world wears leopard skins. Tell me, what is your name? And where were you educated?”

“My name is Jason,” the young stranger answered. “Since I was a baby, I have lived in the cave of Chiron the Centaur. He was my teacher. He taught me music and horsemanship, and how to heal wounds, and also how to cause wounds with my weapons!”

“I have heard of Chiron the schoolmaster,” King Pelias replied, “and how there is a tremendous amount of learning and wisdom in his head, even though it happens to sit on a horse’s body. I am delighted to see one of his pupils at my court. But to find out how much you have gained from such an excellent teacher, will you let me ask you one question?”
“I don’t claim to be very wise,” said Jason. “But ask me whatever you like, and I will answer as well as I can.”
Now King Pelias meant to trap the young man cleverly, and to get him to say something that would lead to his own harm and destruction. So, with a sly and wicked smile, he spoke as follows:

“What would you do, brave Jason,” he asked, “if there were a man in the world who, as you had reason to believe, was fated to ruin and kill you? What would you do, I say, if that man stood in front of you and you had him in your power?”

Jason saw the malice and wickedness that King Pelias could not keep from gleaming in his eyes. He probably guessed that the king had found out what he had come for, and meant to turn his own words against him. Still, he refused to tell a lie. Being an upright and honorable prince, he decided to speak the plain truth. The king had chosen to ask the question, and Jason had promised an answer. So the only right thing was to say exactly what would be the wisest course if he had his worst enemy in his power.
So, after thinking for a moment, he answered in a firm, manly voice.
“I would send such a man,” he said, “to find the Golden Fleece!”

You must understand that this task was the hardest and most dangerous in the world. To begin with, it meant a long voyage across unknown seas. There was hardly any hope, or even any chance, that a young man who set out on this voyage would either win the Golden Fleece or live to come home and tell of the dangers he had faced. So the eyes of King Pelias sparkled with joy when he heard Jason’s answer.
“A fine answer, wise man with the one sandal!” he cried. “Then go, and at the risk of your life, bring me the Golden Fleece.”

“I will,” Jason replied calmly. “If I fail, you will never have to worry about me troubling you again. But if I come back to Iolchos with the prize, then, King Pelias, you must come down from your high throne and hand over your crown and scepter to me.”
“I certainly will,” said the king, with a sneer. “Until then, I will keep them safe for you.”

After leaving the king, the first thing Jason thought of doing was to go to Dodona and ask the Talking Oak what he should do. This wonderful tree stood in the middle of an ancient forest. Its stately trunk rose a hundred feet into the air and cast a wide, thick shadow over more than an acre of ground. Standing beneath it, Jason looked up among the knotted branches and green leaves, into the mysterious heart of the old tree, and spoke out loud, as if he were talking to someone hidden deep in the foliage.
“What should I do,” he asked, “to win the Golden Fleece?”

At first there was a deep silence, not only in the shade of the Talking Oak but all through the lonely forest. Then, after a moment or two, the leaves of the oak began to stir and rustle, as if a gentle breeze were wandering among them, though the other trees in the forest were perfectly still. The sound grew louder until it was like the roar of a strong wind. After a while Jason thought he could make out words, but only dimly, because every single leaf on the tree seemed to be a tongue, and thousands upon thousands of tongues were babbling at once. But the noise grew broader and deeper, until it was like a tornado sweeping through the oak and turning the thousands of tiny murmurs from the rustling leaf-tongues into one great utterance. And now, though it still sounded like a mighty wind roaring among the branches, it was also like a deep bass voice, speaking as clearly as a tree could be expected to speak, with these words:
“Go to Argus the shipbuilder, and tell him to build a galley with fifty oars.”

Then the voice faded back into the blurred murmur of rustling leaves and slowly died away. When it was completely gone, Jason began to wonder whether he had really heard the words, or whether his imagination had made them out of the ordinary sound of a breeze passing through the thick leaves of the tree.

But when he asked around among the people of Iolchos, he found that there really was a man in the city named Argus, who was a very skilled shipbuilder. This showed some intelligence in the oak, since otherwise how would it have known that such a person existed? At Jason’s request, Argus gladly agreed to build him a galley so big that it would take fifty strong men to row it, though no ship of such size and weight had ever been seen in the world before. So the head carpenter and all his workmen and apprentices set to work, and for a good while afterward there they were, busily cutting timbers and making a great racket with their hammers, until the new ship, which was called the Argo, seemed quite ready for sea. And since the Talking Oak had already given him such good advice, Jason thought it wouldn’t hurt to ask for a little more. So he visited it again, and standing beside its huge, rough trunk, he asked what he should do next.
