This time the leaves did not all quiver together through the whole tree as they had before. But after a while Jason noticed that the leaves of one large branch stretching over his head had begun to rustle, as if the wind were stirring that one bough while all the other boughs of the oak were still.
“Cut me off!” the branch said, as soon as it could make itself understood. “Cut me off! Cut me off! Then carve me into a figurehead for your galley.”

So Jason took the branch at its word and chopped it off the tree. A carver in the neighborhood agreed to make the figurehead. He was a fairly good workman and had already carved several figureheads, meant to be women and looking much like the ones we see today stuck out under a ship’s bowsprit, with great staring eyes that never blink at the splash of the spray. But, strangely, the carver found that his hand was being guided by some unseen power, with a skill beyond his own, and that his tools were shaping an image he had never imagined. When the work was done, it turned out to be the figure of a beautiful woman with a helmet on her head, and long curls falling from beneath it onto her shoulders. On her left arm was a shield, and in the center of it was a lifelike picture of the head of Medusa with its snaky hair. Her right arm was stretched out, as if pointing the way ahead. The face of this wonderful statue was not angry or forbidding, but it was so grave and majestic that you might call it stern. As for the mouth, it looked ready at any moment to open and speak words of the deepest wisdom.
Jason was delighted with the oaken figure. He gave the carver no peace until it was finished, and then had it set up in the ship’s prow, where a figurehead has stood ever since.
“And now,” he cried, as he stood gazing at the calm, majestic face of the statue, “I must go to the Talking Oak and ask what to do next.”
“You don’t need to, Jason,” said a voice that was much quieter but still reminded him of the great oak’s mighty tones. “Whenever you want good advice, you can ask me.”

Jason had been looking straight into the face of the figure when these words were spoken, and he could hardly believe his ears or his eyes. But the truth was that the wooden lips had moved, and it was plain that the voice had come from the statue’s mouth. Recovering a little from his surprise, Jason reminded himself that the figure had been carved from the wood of the Talking Oak. So it was no great wonder at all, but the most natural thing in the world, that it could speak. It would have been very odd if it couldn’t. But it was certainly a great piece of luck that he could carry such a wise block of wood along with him on his dangerous voyage.

“Tell me, wonderful figure,” Jason exclaimed, “since you have inherited the wisdom of the Speaking Oak of Dodona, whose daughter you are, tell me where I can find fifty bold young men, each to take an oar of my galley. They must have strong arms for rowing and brave hearts to face danger, or we will never win the Golden Fleece.”
“Go,” replied the oaken figure, “and call together all the heroes of Greece.”

And really, considering what a great deed was to be done, could any advice be wiser than what Jason received from the figure-head of his ship? He lost no time in sending messengers to all the cities, announcing to the whole people of Greece that Prince Jason, son of King AEson, was setting out to find the Fleece of Gold. He wanted the help of forty-nine of the bravest and strongest young men alive, to row his ship and share his dangers. Jason himself would be the fiftieth.

When this news spread, adventurous young men all over the country began to stir. Some of them had already fought giants and killed dragons. The younger ones, who hadn’t yet had such good luck, thought it a shame to have lived so long without riding a flying serpent, or sticking their spears into a Chimaera, or at least shoving their right arms down a monstrous lion’s throat. There was a good chance they would meet plenty of such adventures before they found the Golden Fleece. So as soon as they could polish up their helmets and shields and buckle on their trusty swords, they came crowding into Iolchos and climbed aboard the new galley. Shaking hands with Jason, they promised him that they didn’t care a pin for their lives, and would help row the ship to the farthest edge of the world, and as much farther as he thought best to go.

Many of these brave fellows had been trained by Chiron, the schoolteacher with four legs, so they were old schoolmates of Jason and knew him for a lad with plenty of spirit. The mighty Hercules, who would later hold up the sky on his shoulders, was among them. So were the twin brothers Castor and Pollux, whom nobody ever called cowardly, even though they had hatched out of an egg. There was Theseus, famous for killing the Minotaur. There was Lynceus, whose wonderfully sharp eyes could see straight through a millstone, or down into the depths of the earth to spot the treasures buried there. And there was Orpheus, the best harper in the world, who sang and played his lyre so sweetly that wild animals stood up on their hind legs and danced merrily to the music. Yes, and when he played some of his more moving tunes, the rocks heaved their mossy bulk up out of the ground, and a whole grove of forest trees pulled up their roots, nodded their tops to one another, and danced a country dance.

One of the rowers was a beautiful young woman named Atalanta, who had been raised in the mountains and nursed by a bear. This fair maiden was so light on her feet that she could step from the foamy crest of one wave to the next without wetting more than the soles of her sandals. She had grown up quite wild, talked a great deal about the rights of women, and liked hunting and fighting much better than sewing. But in my opinion, the most remarkable members of this famous company were two sons of the North Wind. They were airy youngsters with a rather blustering nature, and they had wings on their shoulders. If the wind died down, they could puff out their cheeks and blow up nearly as fresh a breeze as their father. I mustn’t forget the prophets and wizards either. There were several of them in the crew, and they could tell you what would happen tomorrow, or the next day, or a hundred years from now, but they usually had no idea what was going on at that very moment.

Jason made Tiphys the helmsman, since he studied the stars and knew the points of the compass. Lynceus, thanks to his sharp sight, was posted as lookout at the front of the ship. He could see a whole day’s sail ahead, but he tended to miss things right under his nose. Still, if the sea was only deep enough, Lynceus could tell you exactly what kind of rocks or sand lay on the bottom. He often called out to his companions that they were sailing over heaps of sunken treasure, though seeing it did not make him a penny richer. To tell the truth, hardly anyone believed him when he said so.

Well! When these fifty brave adventurers, who were called the Argonauts, had everything ready for the voyage, an unexpected problem threatened to end it before it began. You see, the ship was so long, so broad and so heavy that all fifty of them together could not shove her into the water. Hercules, I suppose, had not yet reached his full strength, or he could have floated her as easily as a little boy sets his toy boat on a puddle. But there stood the fifty heroes, pushing and straining and turning red in the face, and the Argo would not budge an inch. At last, worn out, they sat down on the shore, very gloomy. They thought the ship would have to be left there to rot and fall to pieces, and that they would either have to swim across the sea or give up the Golden Fleece.
All at once Jason remembered the ship’s magical figure-head.
“O daughter of the Talking Oak,” he cried, “how can we get our ship into the water?”
“Sit down,” answered the image (for it had known from the very beginning what to do, and had only been waiting to be asked),—“sit down, take hold of your oars, and let Orpheus play his harp.”

At once the fifty heroes climbed aboard, grabbed their oars, and held them straight up in the air, while Orpheus (who far preferred this job to rowing) ran his fingers across the harp. At the first ringing note they felt the ship stir. Orpheus strummed away briskly, and the galley slid right into the sea. She dipped her prow so deep that the figure-head drank a mouthful of wave with its wonderful lips, and then she rose again as light as a swan. The rowers worked their fifty oars. White foam boiled up in front of the prow, and the water gurgled and bubbled behind them. Orpheus kept playing such a lively tune that the ship seemed to dance over the waves in time to it. And so the Argo sailed triumphantly out of the harbor, with cheers and good wishes from everyone except the wicked old Pelias. He stood on a headland, scowling at her and wishing he could blow the storm of rage in his heart out of his lungs and sink the galley with everyone on board. When they were more than fifty miles out to sea, Lynceus happened to glance back with his sharp eyes. He reported that the bad-hearted king was still standing on the headland, scowling so darkly that he looked like a black thundercloud on the horizon.

To make the time pass more pleasantly on the voyage, the heroes talked about the Golden Fleece. It had first belonged, it seems, to a ram from Boeotia. When two children were in danger of their lives, the ram had carried them on his back and fled with them over land and sea, all the way to Colchis. One of the children, whose name was Helle, fell into the sea and drowned. But the other, a little boy named Phrixus, was brought safely ashore by the faithful ram, who was so worn out that he lay down at once and died. To honor this good deed and the ram’s true heart, the fleece of the poor dead ram was magically turned to gold, and it became one of the most beautiful things ever seen on earth. It was hung on a tree in a sacred grove, where it had stayed for I don’t know how many years, and mighty kings envied it, because none of them had anything so magnificent in their palaces.

If I told you all the adventures of the Argonauts, it would take me until nightfall and probably a good deal longer. There was no shortage of wonderful events, as you may guess from what you have already heard. On one island, King Cyzicus, the ruler there, welcomed them warmly, gave a feast for them, and treated them like brothers. But the Argonauts noticed that the good king looked sad and very troubled, so they asked him what was the matter. King Cyzicus then told them that he and his people were being badly mistreated and plagued by the inhabitants of a nearby mountain, who made war on them, killed many people, and laid waste to the country. While they were talking about it, Cyzicus pointed to the mountain and asked Jason and his companions what they saw there.

“I see some very tall shapes,” answered Jason, “but they are so far away that I can’t make out what they are. To tell you the truth, Your Majesty, they look so strange that I am inclined to think they are clouds that happen to have taken on something like human shapes.”

“I see them very clearly,” remarked Lynceus, whose eyes, you know, could see as far as a telescope. “They are a band of enormous giants, and every one of them has six arms and holds a club, a sword, or some other weapon in each hand.”
“You have excellent eyes,” said King Cyzicus. “Yes, they are six-armed giants, just as you say, and they are the enemies that I and my people have to fight.”

The next day, as the Argonauts were getting ready to sail, down came these terrible giants, taking a hundred yards in each stride and waving their six arms apiece, and they looked very fearsome so high up in the air. Each of these monsters could fight a whole war by himself. With one arm he could hurl huge stones, with another swing a club, and with a third wield a sword, while the fourth jabbed a long spear at the enemy and the fifth and sixth shot arrows at him. But luckily, though the giants were so huge and had so many arms, each had only one heart, and it was no bigger or braver than an ordinary man’s heart. Besides, even if they had been like the hundred-armed Briareus, the brave Argonauts would have given them all the fighting they could handle. Jason and his friends went boldly out to meet them, killed a great many, and sent the rest running. If the giants had had six legs apiece instead of six arms, they would have been better off for running away.

Another strange adventure happened when the voyagers reached Thrace. There they found a poor blind king named Phineus, abandoned by his subjects and living in misery, all alone. When Jason asked whether they could help him in any way, the king answered that he was terribly tormented by three huge winged creatures called Harpies, who had the faces of women and the wings, bodies, and claws of vultures. These ugly wretches made a habit of snatching away his dinner and never left him in peace. When they heard this, the Argonauts laid out a plentiful feast on the seashore. From what the blind king said about the Harpies’ greed, they knew the creatures would catch the scent of the food and quickly come to steal it. And so it turned out. The table was hardly set before the three hideous vulture women came flapping up, grabbed the food in their talons, and flew off as fast as they could. But the two sons of the North Wind drew their swords, spread their wings, and flew after the thieves. After a chase of hundreds of miles, they caught up with them among some islands. The two winged youths blustered fiercely at the Harpies (they had their father’s rough temper) and frightened them so badly with their drawn swords that the Harpies solemnly promised never to trouble King Phineus again.

Then the Argonauts sailed on and met with many other marvelous happenings, any one of which would make a story of its own. Once they landed on an island, and while they were resting on the grass, they suddenly found themselves under attack by what seemed to be a shower of steel-tipped arrows. Some stuck in the ground, some struck their shields, and several pierced their flesh. The fifty heroes jumped up and looked around for the hidden enemy, but they could not find one. There was no spot on the whole island where even a single archer could hide. Still the steel-tipped arrows came whizzing among them. At last they happened to look up and saw a huge flock of birds circling and wheeling overhead, shooting their feathers down at the Argonauts. These feathers were the steel-tipped arrows that had been tormenting them. There was no way to fight back, and the fifty heroic Argonauts might all have been killed or wounded by a flock of pesky birds, without ever laying eyes on the Golden Fleece, if Jason had not thought of asking the advice of the oaken image.
Off he dashed to the galley, running as hard as he could.

Gasping for breath, he cried, “O daughter of the Speaking Oak, we need your wisdom now more than ever! A flock of birds is shooting steel-pointed feathers at us, and we are in terrible danger. How do we drive them off?”
“Make a racket by banging on your shields,” said the image.

Jason took this excellent advice and hurried back to his companions, who were much more frightened than they had been when they fought the six-armed giants. He told them to beat their swords against their brass shields. At once the fifty heroes set to work, banging with all their might and making such a terrible clatter that the birds flew off as fast as they could. Even though they had shot half the feathers out of their wings, they were soon seen skimming among the clouds far away, looking like a flock of wild geese. Orpheus celebrated the victory by playing a triumphant anthem on his harp, and he sang so beautifully that Jason begged him to stop. The steel-feathered birds had been driven away by an ugly sound, Jason feared, and a sweet one might lure them back.

While the Argonauts stayed on this island, they saw a small boat coming toward the shore. In it were two young men who carried themselves like princes and were very handsome, as young princes generally were in those days. Now, who do you suppose these two travelers turned out to be? Why, believe it or not, they were the sons of that very Phrixus who, as a child, had been carried to Colchis on the back of the golden-fleeced ram. Since then Phrixus had married the king’s daughter, and the two young princes had been born and raised in Colchis. They had spent their playtimes on the edge of the grove, at the center of which the Golden Fleece hung on a tree. Now they were on their way to Greece, hoping to win back a kingdom that had been unjustly taken from their father.

When the princes learned where the Argonauts were headed, they offered to turn around and guide them to Colchis. At the same time, though, they spoke as if it were very doubtful that Jason would ever get the Golden Fleece. According to them, the tree it hung on was guarded by a terrible dragon, who never failed to swallow in a single mouthful anyone who dared come within his reach.

“There are other difficulties in the way,” the young princes went on. “But isn’t that enough? Ah, brave Jason, turn back before it is too late. It would break our hearts if you and your nine-and-forty brave companions were eaten up, in fifty mouthfuls, by this loathsome dragon.”

“My young friends,” Jason replied calmly, “I am not surprised that you think the dragon so terrible. You have grown up afraid of this monster since you were babies, so you still look at him with the dread that children feel for the bogeymen and goblins their nurses have told them about. But the way I see it, the dragon is only a pretty big snake. He is not half as likely to gobble me up in one mouthful as I am to cut off his ugly head and strip the skin from his body. At any rate, let whoever wants to turn back do so. I will never see Greece again unless I bring the Golden Fleece with me.”
“Not one of us is turning back!” shouted his nine-and-forty brave comrades. “Everyone aboard the galley, right now! And if the dragon wants to eat us for breakfast, he is welcome to us.”

And Orpheus, who liked to set everything to music, began to play his harp and sing so gloriously that every last one of them felt as if nothing in the world was so delightful as fighting dragons, and nothing so truly honorable as being eaten in one mouthful, if the worst should happen.

After this, with the two princes as guides, since they knew the way well, they soon sailed to Colchis. When the king of the country, whose name was AEetes, heard of their arrival, he immediately summoned Jason to court. The king was a stern, cruel-looking ruler. Though he put on as polite and welcoming an expression as he could, Jason liked his face no better than that of the wicked King Pelias, who had driven his father from the throne.

“Welcome, brave Jason,” said King AEetes. “Tell me, are you traveling for pleasure? Or are you hoping to discover unknown islands? Or what else has brought me the happiness of seeing you at my court?”

“Great sir,” Jason replied, bowing low—for Chiron had taught him how to behave properly, whether before kings or beggars—“I have come here with a purpose, and I ask your Majesty’s permission to carry it out. King Pelias now sits on my father’s throne, though he has no more right to it than to the one your excellent Majesty is sitting on. He has promised to step down and hand me his crown and scepter if I bring him the Golden Fleece. As your Majesty knows, the Fleece is hanging on a tree here in Colchis, and I humbly ask your kind leave to take it away.”

In spite of himself, the king’s face twisted into an angry scowl. Of everything in the world he valued the Golden Fleece most, and people even suspected that he had done something very wicked to get it. So it put him in the worst possible mood to hear that the gallant Prince Jason and forty-nine of the bravest young warriors of Greece had come to Colchis for the sole purpose of carrying off his greatest treasure.
“Do you know,” King AEetes asked, staring sternly at Jason, “what you must do before you can get the Golden Fleece?”
“I have heard,” the young man answered, “that a dragon lies under the tree where the prize hangs, and that anyone who goes near him risks being swallowed in a single mouthful.”

“True,” said the king, with a smile that did not look especially kind. “Very true, young man. But there are other tasks just as hard, or maybe a little harder, that you must finish before you earn the privilege of being eaten by the dragon. First, for example, you must tame my two bulls with brazen feet and brazen lungs, which Vulcan, the wonderful blacksmith, made for me. Each has a furnace in its belly, and they blow such hot fire from their mouths and nostrils that no one who has gone near them has escaped being burned instantly to a small black cinder. What do you think of that, my brave Jason?”
“I must face the danger,” Jason said calmly, “since it stands between me and my goal.”

“After you have tamed the fiery bulls,” King AEetes went on, determined to frighten Jason if he could, “you must harness them to a plow and plow the sacred ground in the grove of Mars. Then you must sow some of the very same dragon’s teeth from which Cadmus raised a crop of armed men. Those sons of the dragon’s teeth are a lawless gang of scoundrels, and unless you handle them properly, they will attack you with swords in their hands. You and your forty-nine Argonauts, my bold Jason, are hardly enough in number or strength to fight the army that will spring up.”
“My teacher Chiron told me the story of Cadmus long ago,” Jason replied. “Perhaps I can deal with the quarrelsome sons of the dragon’s teeth as well as Cadmus did.”

“I wish the dragon would take him,” King AEetes muttered to himself, “and that four-footed know-it-all of a schoolmaster along with him. What a reckless, conceited show-off! We’ll see what my fire-breathing bulls make of him. Well, Prince Jason,” he went on aloud, as pleasantly as he could manage, “make yourself comfortable for today, and tomorrow morning, since you insist, you may try your skill at the plow.”

While the king was talking with Jason, a beautiful young woman stood behind the throne. She kept her eyes fixed earnestly on the young stranger and listened closely to every word. When Jason left the king’s presence, she followed him out of the room.

“I’m the king’s daughter,” she told him. “My name is Medea. I understand many things that other princesses have never heard of, and I can do things they would be too frightened even to imagine. Put your trust in me, and I will show you how to master the fiery bulls, plant the dragon’s teeth, and carry off the Golden Fleece.”
“Truly, beautiful princess,” Jason answered, “if you will do this for me, I promise to be grateful to you as long as I live.”

As he gazed at Medea, he saw a remarkable intelligence in her face. Her eyes were full of mystery. Looking into them, you seemed to see a very long way, as into a deep well, yet you could never be sure whether you had seen to the bottom or whether something else lay hidden down there. If Jason had been capable of fear, he would have feared making an enemy of this young princess. Beautiful as she looked now, she might the very next moment turn as terrible as the dragon that guarded the Golden Fleece.
“Princess,” he cried, “you do seem wise, and powerful too. But how could you possibly help me with all this? Are you an enchantress?”

“Yes, Prince Jason,” Medea answered with a smile, “you have guessed the truth. I am an enchantress. Circe, my father’s sister, taught me. If I wanted, I could tell you who the old woman was, the one with the peacock, the pomegranate, and the cuckoo on her staff, whom you carried across the river. I could also tell you who speaks through the lips of the oaken figure at the front of your ship. You see, I know some of your secrets. It’s lucky for you that I like you, because otherwise you would hardly escape being snapped up by the dragon.”
“I wouldn’t worry much about the dragon,” Jason replied, “if only I knew how to handle the brazen-footed bulls with their fiery lungs.”

“If you are as brave as I think you are, and as brave as you will need to be,” said Medea, “your own bold heart will tell you that there is only one way to deal with a raging bull. I’ll leave you to find out what it is when the danger comes. As for the fiery breath of these animals, I have an enchanted ointment here that will keep you from being burned up, and will heal you if you do get a little scorched.”
Then she put a golden box in his hand and showed him how to use the sweet-smelling ointment inside it, and where to meet her at midnight.
“Just be brave,” she added, “and before daybreak the brazen bulls will be tamed.”

The young man assured her that his courage would not fail him. Then he went back to his companions, told them what had passed between himself and the princess, and warned them to be ready in case he needed their help.

At the agreed hour he met the beautiful Medea on the marble steps of the king’s palace. She handed him a basket holding the dragon’s teeth, exactly as Cadmus had pulled them from the monster’s jaws long ago. Then Medea led Jason down the palace steps, through the silent streets of the city, and into the royal pasture where the two brazen-footed bulls were kept. It was a starry night, with a bright glow along the eastern edge of the sky where the moon would soon appear. Once they were inside the pasture, the princess stopped and looked around.

“There they are,” she said, “resting and chewing their fiery cud in the farthest corner of the field. It will be excellent sport, I promise you, when they catch sight of you. My father and his whole court enjoy nothing so much as watching a stranger try to yoke them so he can get to the Golden Fleece. Whenever it happens, Colchis takes a holiday. I enjoy it enormously myself. You can’t imagine how fast their hot breath shrivels a young man into a black cinder.”
“Are you sure, beautiful Medea,” Jason asked, “completely sure, that the ointment in the gold box will cure those terrible burns?”

“If you doubt it, if you are even a little afraid,” said the princess, looking into his face by the dim starlight, “you would be better off never having been born than going one step closer to the bulls.”

But Jason had set his heart firmly on winning the Golden Fleece. I honestly doubt he would have turned back without it, even if he had been certain of becoming a red-hot cinder or a handful of white ashes the moment he took another step. So he let go of Medea’s hand and walked boldly in the direction she had pointed. Some distance ahead he saw four streams of fiery vapor that kept appearing and vanishing, lighting up the surrounding darkness for a moment each time. These, you must understand, came from the breath of the brazen bulls, which was drifting quietly out of their four nostrils as they lay chewing their cud.

At Jason’s first two or three steps, the four fiery streams seemed to gush out a little more strongly, because the two brazen bulls had heard his footsteps and were lifting their hot noses to sniff the air. He went a little farther, and from the way the red vapor now spouted out, he could tell that the creatures were on their feet. Now he could see glowing sparks and bright jets of flame. At the next step, each bull made the whole pasture echo with a terrible roar, and the burning breath they belched out lit up the entire field in a sudden flash. Bold Jason took one more stride, and all at once, quick as lightning, the fiery animals charged, roaring like thunder and throwing out sheets of white flame. The flames lit the scene so brightly that the young man could see everything more clearly than in daylight. Most clearly of all he saw the two horrible creatures galloping straight at him, their brazen hooves clattering and ringing on the ground, and their tails sticking stiffly up in the air, as angry bulls always carry them. Their breath scorched the grass ahead of them. It was so hot, in fact, that it set fire to a dry tree under which Jason was now standing, and the whole tree blazed up. But as for Jason himself, thanks to Medea’s enchanted ointment, the white flames curled around his body without hurting him any more than if he had been made of asbestos.

Greatly encouraged to find that he had not yet been turned into a cinder, the young man waited for the bulls to attack. Just as the brazen brutes thought they were sure to toss him into the air, he seized one by the horn and the other by its curled-up tail. He held them in a grip like an iron vise, one in his right hand and one in his left. He must have had wonderfully strong arms, to be sure. But the real secret was that the brazen bulls were enchanted creatures, and Jason had broken the spell of their fiery fierceness by handling them so boldly. Ever since then, brave men facing danger have favored what they call “taking the bull by the horns.” Grabbing him by the tail comes to much the same thing—that is, throwing aside fear and beating the danger by refusing to be afraid of it.

Now it was easy to yoke the bulls and harness them to the plow, which had lain rusting on the ground for many years, since for so long no one could be found who was able to plow that piece of land. I suppose Jason had been taught how to cut a furrow by the good old Chiron, who perhaps let himself be harnessed to the plow. At any rate, our hero broke up the grassy turf with complete success. By the time the moon had climbed a quarter of the way up the sky, the plowed field lay before him, a large stretch of black earth ready to be sown with the dragon’s teeth. So Jason scattered them far and wide, raked them into the soil with a brush harrow, and took his stand at the edge of the field, eager to see what would happen next.
“Will we have to wait long for harvest time?” he asked Medea, who was now standing beside him.
“Sooner or later, it is sure to come,” the princess answered. “A crop of armed men always springs up once the dragon’s teeth have been sown.”

The moon was now high in the sky and shone brightly over the plowed field, where there was still nothing to see. Any farmer looking at it would have said that Jason must wait weeks before green blades showed among the clods, and whole months before the yellow grain was ripe for the sickle. But after a while, all over the field, something began to glisten in the moonlight like sparkling drops of dew. These bright things shot up higher and turned out to be the steel tips of spears. Then a vast number of polished brass helmets flashed dazzlingly, and as they rose farther out of the soil, the dark, bearded faces of warriors appeared beneath them, struggling to free themselves from the earth that held them. The first look they gave the upper world was a glare of anger and defiance. Next their bright breastplates came into view. Every right hand held a sword or a spear and every left arm a shield. When this strange crop of warriors had grown only halfway out of the earth, they struggled so impatiently against being held that they practically tore themselves up by the roots. Wherever a dragon’s tooth had fallen, a man stood armed for battle. They clanged their swords against their shields and glared fiercely at one another. They had come into this beautiful world and this peaceful moonlight full of rage and stormy passions, ready to take the life of every human brother as thanks for the gift of their own existence.

Many other armies in the world have seemed to have the same fierce nature as the one that had just sprouted from the dragon’s teeth. But these warriors in the moonlit field had more excuse, because they never had women for their mothers. And how delighted any great captain bent on conquering the world, like Alexander or Napoleon, would have been to raise a crop of armed soldiers as easily as Jason did.

For a while the warriors stood waving their weapons, clashing their swords against their shields, and boiling over with a red-hot thirst for battle. Then they began to shout, “Show us the enemy! Lead us to the charge! Death or victory! Come on, brave comrades! Conquer or die!” and a hundred other cries, the kind men always bellow on a battlefield, which these dragon people seemed to have ready on the tips of their tongues. At last the front rank caught sight of Jason, who, seeing so many weapons flash in the moonlight, had thought it wise to draw his sword. In a moment all the sons of the dragon’s teeth seemed to take Jason for an enemy. Crying with one voice, “Guard the Golden Fleece!” they rushed at him with swords raised and spears thrust forward. Jason knew he could not hold out against this bloodthirsty battalion with his single arm. Since nothing better could be done, he decided to die as bravely as if he himself had sprung from a dragon’s tooth.
Medea, however, told him to snatch up a stone from the ground.
“Throw it into the middle of them, quickly!” she cried. “It is the only way to save yourself.”

The armed men were now so close that Jason could see the fire flashing in their furious eyes. That was when he threw the stone. It struck the helmet of a tall warrior who was charging at him with his sword raised high. From that helmet it bounced off the shield of the man beside him, and from there it flew straight into the angry face of a third, hitting him squarely between the eyes. Each of the three who had been struck assumed that his nearest neighbor had hit him. Instead of running any farther toward Jason, they started fighting among themselves. The confusion spread through the whole army, and in no time at all they were hacking, chopping, and stabbing at one another, cutting off arms, heads, and legs, and performing such unforgettable feats that Jason was filled with admiration. At the same time he could not help laughing to see these mighty men punishing one another for something he himself had done. In an astonishingly short time (hardly longer, in fact, than it had taken them to grow up), every one of the heroes of the dragon’s teeth but one lay dead on the field. The last survivor, the bravest and strongest of them all, had just enough strength left to wave his crimson sword over his head and shout in triumph, “Victory! Victory! Immortal fame!” Then he too fell down and lay still among his slain brothers.
And that was the end of the army that had sprung up from the dragon’s teeth. That fierce, feverish fight was the only pleasure they ever had in all their time on this beautiful earth.

“Let them sleep in the bed of honor,” said the Princess Medea, with a sly smile at Jason. “The world will always have plenty of fools just like them, fighting and dying for they don’t know what, and imagining that future ages will bother to hang laurel wreaths on their rusty, dented helmets. Prince Jason, could you help smiling at the conceit of that last fellow, just as he toppled over?”
“It made me very sad,” Jason answered gravely. “And to tell you the truth, princess, after what I have seen here, the Golden Fleece no longer seems worth winning.”

“You will think differently in the morning,” said Medea. “It’s true that the Golden Fleece may not be as valuable as you thought. But there is nothing better in the world, and a person has to have some goal, you know. Come! You have done a good night’s work, and tomorrow you can tell King AEetes that the first part of your task is finished.”
As Medea advised, Jason went to King AEetes’s palace early the next morning. He entered the throne room, stood at the foot of the throne, and bowed low.

“Your eyes look heavy, Prince Jason,” the king remarked. “You seem to have spent a sleepless night. I hope you have thought the matter over more sensibly, and decided not to get yourself burned to a cinder trying to tame my brazen-lunged bulls.”

“That is already done, if it please Your Majesty,” Jason replied. “The bulls have been tamed and yoked. The field has been plowed. The dragon’s teeth have been scattered over it and harrowed into the soil. The crop of armed warriors has sprung up, and they have killed one another to the last man. Now I ask Your Majesty’s permission to face the dragon, so that I may take the Golden Fleece down from the tree and leave with my forty-nine comrades.”

King AEetes scowled. He looked very angry and badly shaken, because he knew that, by his royal promise, he now had to let Jason try for the fleece if his courage and skill were up to it. But the young man had been so lucky with the brazen bulls and the dragon’s teeth that the king feared he would be just as successful at killing the dragon. So, although he would gladly have seen Jason swallowed in a single mouthful, he made up his mind (and it was a very wicked thing for a king to do) not to risk losing his beloved fleece any further.

“You never would have managed this, young man,” he said, “if my disobedient daughter Medea had not helped you with her enchantments. If you had played fair, you would be a black cinder or a handful of white ashes right now. I forbid you, on pain of death, to make any more attempts at the Golden Fleece. To speak plainly, you will never so much as set eyes on one of its glistening locks.”

Jason left the king’s presence full of sorrow and anger. The best plan he could think of was to gather his forty-nine brave Argonauts, march straight to the grove of Mars, kill the dragon, seize the Golden Fleece, climb aboard the Argo, and set every sail for Iolchos. The plan did depend, it is true, on the doubtful question of whether the dragon might swallow all fifty heroes, one mouthful each. But as Jason was hurrying down the palace steps, Princess Medea called after him and beckoned him back. Her black eyes rested on him with such sharp cleverness that he felt as if a serpent were peeping out of them. Though she had done him so much good only the night before, he was by no means sure that she would not do him just as much harm before sunset. You must understand that these enchantresses can never be relied on.
“What does King AEetes say, my royal and honest father?” asked Medea with a faint smile. “Will he give you the Golden Fleece without any more risk or trouble?”

“Quite the opposite,” Jason answered. “He is very angry with me for taming the brazen bulls and sowing the dragon’s teeth. He forbids me to make any more attempts, and he flatly refuses to hand over the Golden Fleece, whether I kill the dragon or not.”

“Yes, Jason,” said the princess, “and I can tell you more. Unless you sail from Colchis before sunrise tomorrow, the king means to burn your fifty-oared ship and put you and your forty-nine brave comrades to the sword. But take courage. You shall have the Golden Fleece, if my enchantments have the power to get it for you. Wait for me here an hour before midnight.”

At the appointed hour you could again have seen Prince Jason and Princess Medea, side by side, slipping through the streets of Colchis on their way to the sacred grove, where the Golden Fleece hung from a tree in the very center. As they crossed the pasture, the brazen bulls came toward Jason, lowing, nodding their heads, and pushing out their snouts, which, like other cattle, they loved to have rubbed and petted by a friendly hand. Their fierce nature was completely tamed, and along with their fierceness the two furnaces in their bellies had gone out too, so that they were probably far more comfortable grazing and chewing their cud than ever before. In fact, it had always been a great nuisance to these poor animals that whenever they tried to eat a mouthful of grass, the fire from their nostrils shriveled it up before they could bite it off. How they managed to stay alive is more than I can imagine. But now, instead of blowing out jets of flame and streams of sulphurous vapor, they breathed the sweetest cow breath.

After patting the bulls kindly, Jason let Medea lead him into the grove of Mars. There the great oak trees, which had been growing for centuries, cast such a thick shade that the moonbeams struggled in vain to get through. Only here and there did a glimmer fall on the leaf-covered ground, or a breeze push the branches aside and give Jason a glimpse of the sky, as if to keep him from forgetting, in all that deep darkness, that there was a sky overhead. At last, when they had gone farther and farther into the heart of the gloom, Medea squeezed Jason’s hand.
“Look over there,” she whispered. “Do you see it?”

Among the ancient oaks there was a radiance, not like moonlight, but more like the golden glow of the setting sun. It came from something that seemed to hang about as high as a man’s height above the ground, a little farther into the wood.
“What is it?” asked Jason.
“Have you come all this way to find it,” exclaimed Medea, “and you don’t recognize the reward of all your labors and dangers when it glitters right before your eyes? It is the Golden Fleece.”

Jason went a few steps farther and then stopped to gaze. Oh, how beautiful it looked, shining with a wonderful light of its own, that priceless prize that so many heroes had longed to see, but had died trying to win, either from the dangers of the voyage or from the fiery breath of the brazen-lunged bulls!
“How gloriously it shines!” cried Jason, overjoyed. “It must have been dipped in the richest gold of sunset. Let me hurry forward and clasp it to my heart.”
“Not so fast,” said Medea, pulling him back. “Have you forgotten who stands guard over it?”

To tell the truth, in the joy of seeing what he had wanted so long, Jason had quite forgotten the terrible dragon. Very soon, however, something happened to remind him of the dangers still ahead. An antelope, which probably took the yellow glow for sunrise, came bounding swiftly through the grove. It was racing straight toward the Golden Fleece when suddenly there was a frightful hiss, and the huge head and half the scaly body of the dragon shot out (for he was coiled around the trunk of the tree where the fleece hung). He seized the poor antelope and swallowed it in a single snap of his jaws.

Once that was done, the dragon seemed to feel that another living creature was nearby, one he might like to eat to round off his meal. He kept thrusting his ugly snout this way and that among the trees, stretching his neck out a terrible distance, now in one direction, now another, and now very near the oak where Jason and the princess were hiding. Upon my word, it was a hideous and most unpleasant sight, that head swaying and rippling through the air until it came within arm’s reach of Prince Jason. His enormous jaws gaped as wide as the gateway of the king’s palace.
“So, Jason,” Medea whispered (for she was spiteful, as all enchantresses are, and she wanted to see the bold young man shake), “how do you like your chances of winning the Golden Fleece now?”
Jason’s only answer was to pull out his sword and step forward.

“Wait, foolish boy,” said Medea, catching his arm. “Can’t you see that you are lost without me as your good angel? In this gold box I have a magic potion that will deal with the dragon far better than your sword.”

The dragon had probably heard their voices, because, quick as lightning, his black head and forked tongue came hissing through the trees again, darting a full forty feet at a stretch. As it came near, Medea flung the contents of the gold box right down the monster’s wide-open throat. At once, with a furious hiss and a tremendous wriggle—flinging his tail up to the top of the tallest tree and smashing all its branches as it crashed heavily down again—the dragon dropped full length on the ground and lay perfectly still.

“It is only a sleeping potion,” the enchantress told Prince Jason. “One can always find a use for these mischievous creatures sooner or later, so I didn’t want to kill him outright. Quick! Grab the prize and let’s be gone. You have won the Golden Fleece.”

Jason snatched the fleece from the tree and hurried through the grove, whose deep shadows were lit up as he passed by the golden glow of the precious thing he carried. A little way ahead he saw the old woman he had once helped across the stream, with her peacock beside her. She clapped her hands for joy and waved him on to hurry, then vanished among the dark trees. Spotting the two winged sons of the North Wind (who were playing in the moonlight a few hundred feet up), Jason asked them to tell the other Argonauts to board the ship as fast as they could. But Lynceus, with his sharp eyes, had already caught sight of Jason carrying the Golden Fleece, even though several stone walls, a hill, and the black shadows of the grove of Mars stood in between. On his advice, the heroes had already taken their seats on the benches of the ship, with their oars held upright, ready to drop into the water.
As Jason came closer, he heard the Talking Image calling to him, more urgently than usual, in its grave, sweet voice:
“Hurry, Prince Jason! For your life, hurry!”

With one leap he jumped aboard. At the sight of the glorious radiance of the Golden Fleece, the forty-nine heroes gave a mighty shout, and Orpheus struck his harp and sang a song of triumph. To its rhythm the ship flew over the water, homeward bound, as if it were sailing on wings!
